docs.text: Return the median of two sorted arrays without merging them. One array may be empty, but their combined length is positive.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Partition both arrays so the left side holds half the combined elements.
  2. What inequalities make every left element no larger than every right element?
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 024 · #981 · Next: 026 · #56

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Binary-search partition O(log(min(m,n)+1)) O(1) Merge until middle O(m+n) O(1)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Binary-search partition
docs.text: Binary search a cut in the shorter array; the required left-side size determines the other cut. Use infinite sentinels at empty sides. A valid partition satisfies left_a<=right_b and left_b<=right_a. Move the cut left if left_a is too large, otherwise right.

docs.title: Merge until middle
docs.text: Advance two sorted-array pointers until the middle position, retaining only the last two values. This educational baseline misses the mandated logarithmic-time bound.

docs.title: Binary-search partition
docs.text: Sortedness reduces cross-partition ordering to those two boundary comparisons. Moving the cut in the indicated direction fixes its violated inequality. At a valid partition, the greatest left value is the odd-length median; for an even length, average it with the smallest right value.

docs.title: Merge until middle
docs.text: Choosing the smaller next head emits the globally sorted order. The last emitted value and its predecessor at the middle position are exactly the median element or central pair.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [1,4] and [2,3,8], cuts after 1 and after 3 make left=[1,2,3], right=[4,8]. The median is max(1,3)=3.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Binary-search partition):

O(log(min(m,n)+1)) time and O(1) space; inputs are unchanged. Search the shorter array so the derived cut stays valid. Use (m+n+1)//2 for left size. This is a partition search, not a search for the median's numeric value.

Binary-search partition: O(log(min(m,n)+1)) time; O(1) space. Merge until middle: O(m+n) time; O(1) space. Advance two sorted-array pointers until the middle position, retaining only the last two values. This educational baseline misses the mandated logarithmic-time bound.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Binary-search partition
docs.text:
Time: O(log(min(m,n)+1))

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary-search partition
    Time: O(log(min(m,n)+1))
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def findMedianSortedArrays(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> float:
        if len(nums1) > len(nums2):
            nums1, nums2 = nums2, nums1
        m, n = len(nums1), len(nums2)
        left, right = 0, m
        while left <= right:
            i = (left + right) // 2
            j = (m + n + 1) // 2 - i
            a_left = nums1[i - 1] if i else float("-inf")
            a_right = nums1[i] if i < m else float("inf")
            b_left = nums2[j - 1] if j else float("-inf")
            b_right = nums2[j] if j < n else float("inf")
            if a_left <= b_right and b_left <= a_right:
                if (m + n) % 2:
                    return float(max(a_left, b_left))
                return (max(a_left, b_left) + min(a_right, b_right)) / 2
            if a_left > b_right:
                right = i - 1
            else:
                left = i + 1
        raise ValueError("Inputs must be sorted")

docs.title: 2. Merge until middle
docs.text:
Time: O(m+n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Merge until middle
    Time: O(m+n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def findMedianSortedArrays(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> float:
        i = j = 0
        previous = current = 0
        total = len(nums1) + len(nums2)
        for _ in range(total // 2 + 1):
            previous = current
            if j == len(nums2) or (i < len(nums1) and nums1[i] <= nums2[j]):
                current = nums1[i]
                i += 1
            else:
                current = nums2[j]
                j += 1
        return float(current) if total % 2 else (previous + current) / 2

docs.title: Hints

  2. Mirror symmetry avoids repeating expansions already known to match.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Expand odd and even centers O(n^2) O(n) including returned substring Manacher transformed-string radii O(n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Expand odd and even centers
docs.text: Expand every character and gap center while endpoints match, retaining the longest interval rather than copying each candidate.

docs.title: Manacher transformed-string radii
docs.text: Insert separators so odd and even palindromes share one representation. Initialize each radius from its mirrored center inside the rightmost known palindrome, then expand beyond the guaranteed part.

docs.title: Expand odd and even centers
docs.text: Every palindrome has exactly one center. Expanding that center discovers it, and the longest discovered interval is therefore globally optimal.

docs.title: Manacher transformed-string radii
docs.text: Mirror symmetry gives all radius comparisons already inside the known boundary. Every additional successful expansion advances the right boundary, bounding total work linearly. Transformed radius equals original substring length.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "caba", the longest palindrome is "aba"; for "babad", either "bab" or "aba" is accepted.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Expand odd and even centers: O(n^2) time; O(n) including returned substring space. Manacher transformed-string radii: O(n) time; O(n) space.

Input contains only letters and digits, so the chosen separators/sentinels cannot collide with it. Both preserve s; final slicing allocates the output. The center variant uses O(1) auxiliary space excluding that output.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Expand odd and even centers
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n) including returned substring

class Solution:
    """Approach: Expand odd and even centers
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n) including returned substring
    """

    def longestPalindrome(self, s: str) -> str:
        start, length = 0, 1
        for center in range(2 * len(s) - 1):
            left, right = center // 2, (center + 1) // 2
            while left >= 0 and right < len(s) and s[left] == s[right]:
                if right - left + 1 > length:
                    start, length = left, right - left + 1
                left -= 1
                right += 1
        return s[start : start + length]

docs.title: 2. Manacher transformed-string radii
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Manacher transformed-string radii
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def longestPalindrome(self, s: str) -> str:
        transformed = "^#" + "#".join(s) + "#$"
        radii = [0] * len(transformed)
        center = right = best_center = best_radius = 0
        for index in range(1, len(transformed) - 1):
            if index < right:
                radii[index] = min(right - index, radii[2 * center - index])
            while transformed[index + radii[index] + 1] == transformed[index - radii[index] - 1]:
                radii[index] += 1
            if index + radii[index] > right:
                center, right = index, index + radii[index]
            if radii[index] > best_radius:
                best_center, best_radius = index, radii[index]
        start = (best_center - best_radius) // 2
        return s[start : start + best_radius]

docs.title: 6 Zigzag Conversion
docs.text:
Medium · String processing extensions · Extension · Learning step 281 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Matrix simulation.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Write a string down and diagonally up across the requested number of rows, then read the rows from top to bottom. Return that reading order.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. The active row moves by one and reverses direction at either endpoint.
  2. For r > 1, the row pattern repeats every 2*r-2 input characters.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 280 · #1029 · Next: 282 · #12

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Row buffers O(n) O(n), including output buffers Cycle indices O(n) O(n) output storage; O(1) other state

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Row buffers
docs.text: Append each character to its current row. Reverse the step at row zero and at row r-1, then concatenate the buffers. Return s directly if only one row is requested or there are at least as many rows as characters.

docs.title: Cycle indices
docs.text: Visit one output row at a time. Its vertical entries are at row + cyclet. Interior rows also have a diagonal entry at cycle(t+1)-row. Append that entry only when it exists; endpoint rows have no separate diagonal entry.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Row buffers simulate every move, so each buffer contains exactly its row in input order. Cycle indices enumerate the same positions algebraically. Their two progressions are disjoint for interior rows, and every input position belongs to one row. Both therefore produce the requested row-major reading.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "ABCDEFG" with three rows, the buffers are "AE", "BDF", and "CG". The result is "AEBDFCG". The cycle length is four; row one takes indices 1, 3, and 5, which explains its alternating vertical and diagonal entries.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: For n characters, both approaches take O(n) time and O(n) output/buffer space. The row-buffer version also allocates r lists, but the early return ensures r < n when they are allocated. Cycle indices use O(1) working state besides their O(n) output list and joined string. Strings are not modified. Do not append the diagonal entry for the first or last row: it would duplicate an endpoint. Handle one row before computing the zero cycle length.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Row buffers
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n), including output buffers

class Solution:
    """Approach: Row buffers
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n), including output buffers
    """

    def convert(self, s: str, numRows: int) -> str:
        if numRows == 1 or numRows >= len(s):
            return s
        rows = [[] for _ in range(numRows)]
        row, step = 0, 1
        for char in s:
            rows[row].append(char)
            if row == 0:
                step = 1
            elif row == numRows - 1:
                step = -1
            row += step
        return "".join("".join(row) for row in rows)

docs.title: 2. Cycle indices
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n) output storage; O(1) other state

class Solution:
    """Approach: Cycle indices
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n) output storage; O(1) other state
    """

    def convert(self, s: str, numRows: int) -> str:
        if numRows == 1 or numRows >= len(s):
            return s
        cycle = 2 * numRows - 2
        result = []
        for row in range(numRows):
            for vertical in range(row, len(s), cycle):
                result.append(s[vertical])
                diagonal = vertical + cycle - 2 * row
                if 0 < row < numRows - 1 and diagonal < len(s):
                    result.append(s[diagonal])
        return "".join(result)

docs.title: 1. Character scanner with early clamp

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Character scanner with early clamp
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def myAtoi(self, s: str) -> int:
        index = 0
        while index < len(s) and s[index] == " ":
            index += 1
        sign = 1
        if index < len(s) and s[index] in "+-":
            sign = -1 if s[index] == "-" else 1
            index += 1
        limit = 2**31 if sign < 0 else 2**31 - 1
        number = 0
        while index < len(s) and "0" <= s[index] <= "9":
            digit = ord(s[index]) - ord("0")
            if number > (limit - digit) // 10:
                return sign * limit
            number = number * 10 + digit
            index += 1
        return sign * number

docs.title: 2. Anchored prefix regular expression
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Anchored prefix regular expression
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def myAtoi(self, s: str) -> int:
        import re

        match = re.match(r" *([+-]?)([0-9]+)", s)
        if match is None:
            return 0
        number = int(match.group(2))
        if match.group(1) == "-":
            number = -number
        return max(-(2**31), min(2**31 - 1, number))

docs.title: Task

docs.title: Hints

  2. A starred atom either contributes zero characters or consumes one while staying available.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Rolling pattern-prefix DP O((m+1)*(n+1)) O(n) Active pattern states with epsilon closure O((m+1)*(n+1)) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Rolling pattern-prefix DP
docs.text: Keep one Boolean row for each processed string prefix. Initialize the empty-string row with true at the empty pattern; starred pairs may extend an empty match by contributing zero repetitions. For each character, build a fresh row. An ordinary atom uses the preceding row's diagonal if it matches. A star uses the current row two columns back for zero repetitions, or the preceding row at the same column if its atom consumes this character.

docs.title: Active pattern states with epsilon closure
docs.text: Tokenize the pattern into atoms with a starred flag. Track active automaton positions; a starred token may be skipped through an epsilon transition or consume a matching character while staying in place.

docs.title: Rolling pattern-prefix DP
docs.text: An unstarred atom must consume exactly the final character, leaving the diagonal prefix pair. A starred atom either consumes nothing or consumes the final character after an earlier match of the same pattern prefix. These cases cover every repetition count and construct only legal matches. Induction over prefixes proves the final state represents a whole-string match.

docs.title: Active pattern states with epsilon closure
docs.text: Epsilon closure includes every zero-repetition choice. Character transitions include exactly the tokens able to consume that character, retaining starred tokens for further repetitions. Thus active states are precisely all partial pattern matches after each prefix.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "aab" and "ab", the empty prefix matches a with zero repetitions. The next two rows keep a* true by consuming each a. The b row succeeds through the diagonal preceding b, completing the match.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Rolling pattern-prefix DP approach:

O((string_length+1)(pattern_length+1)) time and O(pattern_length) space; inputs are unchanged. Each fresh row has a false empty-pattern state. "" repeats its preceding atom, not arbitrary text. Valid patterns guarantee every star has a preceding atom. Do not confuse this syntax with glob matching.

Rolling pattern-prefix DP: O((m+1)(n+1)) time; O(n) space. Active pattern states with epsilon closure: O((m+1)(n+1)) time; O(n) space. Automaton simulation retains a set rather than a Boolean DP row and demonstrates zero-width transitions. Neither is the unrestricted backtracking regex engine; input patterns follow the promised valid syntax.

docs.title: 1. Rolling pattern-prefix DP
docs.text:
Time: O((m+1)*(n+1))

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Rolling pattern-prefix DP
    Time: O((m+1)*(n+1))
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def isMatch(self, s: str, p: str) -> bool:
        previous = [False] * (len(p) + 1)
        previous[0] = True
        for end in range(2, len(p) + 1):
            if p[end - 1] == "*":
                previous[end] = previous[end - 2]
        for character in s:
            current = [False] * (len(p) + 1)
            for end, atom in enumerate(p, 1):
                if atom == "*":
                    repeated = p[end - 2]
                    matches = repeated == "." or repeated == character
                    current[end] = current[end - 2] or (previous[end] and matches)
                else:
                    current[end] = previous[end - 1] and (atom == "." or atom == character)
            previous = current
        return previous[-1]

docs.title: 2. Active pattern states with epsilon closure
docs.text:
Time: O((m+1)*(n+1))

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Active pattern states with epsilon closure
    Time: O((m+1)*(n+1))
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def isMatch(self, s: str, p: str) -> bool:
        atoms = []
        for character in p:
            if character == "*":
                atoms[-1] = (atoms[-1][0], True)
            else:
                atoms.append((character, False))

        def closure(states):
            result = set(states)
            for index in range(len(atoms)):
                if index in result and atoms[index][1]:
                    result.add(index + 1)
            return result

        active = closure({0})
        for character in s:
            following = set()
            for index in active:
                if index < len(atoms):
                    atom, starred = atoms[index]
                    if atom == "." or atom == character:
                        following.add(index if starred else index + 1)
            active = closure(following)
        return len(atoms) in active

Approach Time Space Inward height pointers O(n) O(1) Enumerate wall pairs O(n squared) O(1)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Inward height pointers
docs.text: All pairs take O(n squared) time. Evaluate the two outside lines, then move the shorter endpoint inward. Continue until the endpoints meet.

docs.title: Enumerate wall pairs
docs.text: Evaluate every pair of walls directly. This educational baseline may time out at full constraints and is useful as a small-input oracle.

docs.title: Inward height pointers
docs.text: Keeping the shorter line while decreasing width cannot improve the current area: the limiting height stays at most that short line. Thus no better pair needs that endpoint among the remaining candidates. Repeating this safe elimination preserves an optimal pair until its area is considered.

docs.title: Enumerate wall pairs
docs.text: Every possible container is one unordered pair of indices. Its width times the shorter height is its exact area, so the maximum over all pairs is the answer.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [2, 5, 4, 3], the outside pair gives 32=6. Move left to height 5: the pair with height 3 gives 23=6. The last pair gives 4, so the answer is 6.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Inward height pointers):

O(n) time and O(1) space. Inputs are unchanged. Width is right-left, not the number of included bars. Equal heights allow either endpoint to move. Do not confuse this with Trapping Rain Water, which sums water across all positions.

Inward height pointers: O(n) time; O(1) space. Enumerate wall pairs: O(n squared) time; O(1) space. Evaluate every pair of walls directly. This educational baseline may time out at full constraints and is useful as a small-input oracle.

docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Inward height pointers
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def maxArea(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
        left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
        best = 0
        while left < right:
            best = max(best, (right - left) * min(height[left], height[right]))
            if height[left] <= height[right]:
                left += 1
            else:
                right -= 1
        return best

class Solution:
    """Approach: Enumerate wall pairs
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def maxArea(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
        best = 0
        for left in range(len(height)):
            for right in range(left + 1, len(height)):
                best = max(best, (right - left) * min(height[left], height[right]))
        return best

docs.title: Hints

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Descending token subtraction O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain Decimal place tables O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Descending token subtraction
docs.text: Process token values from 1000 down to 1, including subtractive tokens in their numeric positions. Divide the remaining number by each token value; append that many copies and keep the remainder.

docs.title: Decimal place tables
docs.text: Split the integer into thousands, hundreds, tens, and units. Use four fixed lookup tables and concatenate their entries. Each table encodes the permitted repetitions and the fourth/ninth subtractive cases directly.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: For each decimal place, standard Roman notation fixes its canonical encoding. Descending tokens emit exactly those encodings: the fourth and ninth cases are consumed by the subtractive token before individual symbols can repeat. Place tables store the same complete cases explicitly. Higher decimal places always precede lower places, so concatenation preserves canonical order.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For 2449, thousands contribute MM, hundreds CD, tens XL, and units IX. The result is MMCDXLIX. Descending tokens consume 2000, 400, 40, then 9.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Both versions take O(1) time and O(1) space under the fixed 1..3999 domain. The tables and number of tokens are fixed, and even the output length is bounded. For a generalized unbounded numeral system these bounds would need reconsideration. The integer input is immutable. Do not use arbitrary subtraction pairs such as IL for 49; its canonical form is XLIX.

class Solution:
    """Approach: Descending token subtraction
    Time: O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain
    Space: O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain
    """

    def intToRoman(self, num: int) -> str:
        tokens = (
            (1000, "M"),
            (900, "CM"),
            (500, "D"),
            (400, "CD"),
            (100, "C"),
            (90, "XC"),
            (50, "L"),
            (40, "XL"),
            (10, "X"),
            (9, "IX"),
            (5, "V"),
            (4, "IV"),
            (1, "I"),
        )
        pieces = []
        for value, symbol in tokens:
            count, num = divmod(num, value)
            pieces.append(symbol * count)
        return "".join(pieces)

Time: O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain

Space: O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain

class Solution:
    """Approach: Decimal place tables
    Time: O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain
    Space: O(1) for the stated bounded integer domain
    """

    def intToRoman(self, num: int) -> str:
        thousands = ("", "M", "MM", "MMM")
        hundreds = ("", "C", "CC", "CCC", "CD", "D", "DC", "DCC", "DCCC", "CM")
        tens = ("", "X", "XX", "XXX", "XL", "L", "LX", "LXX", "LXXX", "XC")
        ones = ("", "I", "II", "III", "IV", "V", "VI", "VII", "VIII", "IX")
        return (
            thousands[num // 1000]
            + hundreds[num // 100 % 10]
            + tens[num // 10 % 10]
            + ones[num % 10]
        )

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Sort with two pointers O(n squared) O(n) plus output Per-anchor complement sets O(n squared) expected O(n) plus output

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Sort with two pointers
docs.text: Sort a copy. For each distinct first value, move two pointers over its suffix. After finding a zero sum, advance both pointers and skip repeated endpoint values. This improves cubic enumeration to quadratic scanning.

docs.title: Per-anchor complement sets
docs.text: Fix one anchor, then find complement pairs using a hash set of already-seen later values. Canonical sorted triplet tuples remove repeated answers without sorting the input.

docs.title: Sort with two pointers
docs.text: For a fixed first value, sorted two-pointer elimination cannot skip a valid pair. Every triplet has a smallest sorted position that is considered as the anchor. Skipping equal anchors and equal successful endpoints removes duplicate value triplets without removing a distinct answer.

docs.title: Per-anchor complement sets
docs.text: For each anchor, a later value completes a triplet exactly when its required complement was seen at a distinct earlier later index. Every index triple is considered at its largest later index.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [-2, 0, 1, 1, 2], anchor -2 finds endpoint pairs (0,2) and (1,1). The answer is [[-2,0,2], [-2,1,1]].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Sort with two pointers):

O(n squared) time, O(n) auxiliary sorting space, plus output storage. The original array is unchanged because sorted makes a copy. Start left after the anchor. Skipping every repeated value before evaluating pairs can lose valid repeated-value triplets such as [-2,1,1].

Sort with two pointers: O(n squared) time; O(n) plus output space. Per-anchor complement sets: O(n squared) expected time; O(n) plus output space. Fix one anchor, then find complement pairs using a hash set of already-seen later values. Canonical sorted triplet tuples remove repeated answers without sorting the input.

docs.title: 1. Sort with two pointers
docs.text:
Time: O(n squared)

Space: O(n) plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sort with two pointers
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(n) plus output
    """

    def threeSum(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        values = sorted(nums)
        result = []
        for i in range(len(values) - 2):
            if i and values[i] == values[i - 1]:
                continue
            left, right = i + 1, len(values) - 1
            while left < right:
                total = values[i] + values[left] + values[right]
                if total < 0:
                    left += 1
                elif total > 0:
                    right -= 1
                else:
                    result.append([values[i], values[left], values[right]])
                    left += 1
                    right -= 1
                    while left < right and values[left] == values[left - 1]:
                        left += 1
                    while left < right and values[right] == values[right + 1]:
                        right -= 1
        return result

docs.title: 2. Per-anchor complement sets
docs.text:
Time: O(n squared) expected

Space: O(n) plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Per-anchor complement sets
    Time: O(n squared) expected
    Space: O(n) plus output
    """

    def threeSum(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        answers = set()
        for i, anchor in enumerate(nums):
            seen = set()
            for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
                value = nums[j]
                complement = -anchor - value
                if complement in seen:
                    answers.add(tuple(sorted((anchor, value, complement))))
                seen.add(value)
        return [list(values) for values in sorted(answers)]

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Sort with two pointers
docs.text: Sort a copy, fix each first value, and scan the remaining suffix from both ends. Record any closer sum. Move left for a sum below target and right for a sum above target. An exact match is immediately optimal.

docs.title: Binary-search nearest third value
docs.text: Sort a copy, fix the first two indices, and inspect the lower-bound neighbor and predecessor for the third value. This is slower than two pointers but demonstrates nearest-value binary search.

docs.title: Sort with two pointers

Symmetrically, when it is above target, all larger left choices with the same right endpoint are no closer. The eliminated candidates cannot improve the recorded result.

docs.text: For a fixed pair, the absolute error is minimized by the third value closest to the remaining target. The lower-bound neighbor and predecessor cover both sides of that target.

O(n squared) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the sorted copy. Input is unchanged. Initialize the best sum from three actual values. Compare absolute distances, not raw sums, and return the sum rather than its distance from target.

Sort with two pointers: O(n squared) time; O(n) space. Binary-search nearest third value: O(n squared log n) time; O(n) space. Sort a copy, fix the first two indices, and inspect the lower-bound neighbor and predecessor for the third value. This is slower than two pointers but demonstrates nearest-value binary search.

Time: O(n squared)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sort with two pointers
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def threeSumClosest(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
        values = sorted(nums)
        best = sum(values[:3])
        for i in range(len(values) - 2):
            left, right = i + 1, len(values) - 1
            while left < right:
                total = values[i] + values[left] + values[right]
                if abs(total - target) < abs(best - target):
                    best = total
                if total == target:
                    return total
                if total < target:
                    left += 1
                else:
                    right -= 1
        return best

docs.title: 2. Binary-search nearest third value
docs.text:
Time: O(n squared log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary-search nearest third value
    Time: O(n squared log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def threeSumClosest(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
        values = sorted(nums)
        best = sum(values[:3])
        for i in range(len(values) - 2):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(values) - 1):
                left, right = j + 1, len(values)
                wanted = target - values[i] - values[j]
                while left < right:
                    middle = (left + right) // 2
                    if values[middle] < wanted:
                        left = middle + 1
                    else:
                        right = middle
                for index in (left - 1, left):
                    if j < index < len(values):
                        total = values[i] + values[j] + values[index]
                        if abs(total - target) < abs(best - target):
                            best = total
        return best

docs.title: Task

Approach Time Space Digit-by-digit backtracking O(d*4^d) loose bound O(d) auxiliary plus output Mixed-radix enumeration O(d*4^d) loose bound O(d) auxiliary plus output

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Digit-by-digit backtracking
docs.text: Choose one mapped letter at each digit, append it to a shared path, recurse, and undo. Join the path only at full length.

docs.title: Mixed-radix enumeration
docs.text: Treat each digit's letter count as a radix. Enumerate integers below their product and decode each into one letter index per position.

docs.title: Digit-by-digit backtracking
docs.text: Every output corresponds to one choice at every position. Trying every mapped letter at each depth enumerates those choice vectors exactly once.

docs.text: Mixed-radix representation gives a bijection between the counter range and all position-wise letter selections, including digits with four rather than three letters.

The input is unchanged. d is at most four, so recursion is shallow. Avoid returning [""] for empty input; that is an internal product seed, not the requested answer.

docs.title: 1. Digit-by-digit backtracking
docs.text:
Time: O(d*4^d) loose bound

Space: O(d) auxiliary plus output

LETTERS = {
    "2": "abc",
    "3": "def",
    "4": "ghi",
    "5": "jkl",
    "6": "mno",
    "7": "pqrs",
    "8": "tuv",
    "9": "wxyz",
}


class Solution:
    """Approach: Digit-by-digit backtracking
    Time: O(d*4^d) loose bound
    Space: O(d) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def letterCombinations(self, digits: str) -> list[str]:
        if not digits:
            return []
        result, path = [], []

        def visit(index):
            if index == len(digits):
                result.append("".join(path))
                return
            for char in LETTERS[digits[index]]:
                path.append(char)
                visit(index + 1)
                path.pop()

        visit(0)
        return result

docs.title: 2. Mixed-radix enumeration
docs.text:
Time: O(d*4^d) loose bound

Space: O(d) auxiliary plus output

LETTERS = {
    "2": "abc",
    "3": "def",
    "4": "ghi",
    "5": "jkl",
    "6": "mno",
    "7": "pqrs",
    "8": "tuv",
    "9": "wxyz",
}


class Solution:
    """Approach: Mixed-radix enumeration
    Time: O(d*4^d) loose bound
    Space: O(d) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def letterCombinations(self, digits: str) -> list[str]:
        if not digits:
            return []
        count = 1
        for digit in digits:
            count *= len(LETTERS[digit])
        result = []
        for number in range(count):
            chars = []
            for digit in reversed(digits):
                number, index = divmod(number, len(LETTERS[digit]))
                chars.append(LETTERS[digit][index])
            result.append("".join(reversed(chars)))
        return result

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Two anchors and two pointers O(n cubed) O(n) plus output Incremental disjoint pair sums O(n to the fourth) worst case O(n squared) plus output

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Two anchors and two pointers
docs.text: Skip repeated anchors in sorted order, then move the remaining pair inward and skip equal pair values after a match.

docs.title: Incremental disjoint pair sums
docs.text: Before examining a third index, add all earlier index pairs. Match these pairs with third/fourth choices, storing canonical quadruplets in a set. Many equal pair sums can make this educational baseline time out.

docs.title: Two anchors and two pointers
docs.text: For each fixed anchor pair, increasing the smaller pointer raises the sum and decreasing the larger pointer lowers it. Every feasible sorted quadruplet is reached; duplicate skips preserve one representative.

docs.title: Incremental disjoint pair sums
docs.text: Stored pairs end strictly before the current third index, which guarantees disjoint indices. Every increasing index quadruple is considered once at its third/fourth pair; canonical tuples remove repeated values.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Two anchors and two pointers: O(n cubed) time; O(n) plus output space.

Incremental disjoint pair sums: O(n to the fourth) worst case time; O(n squared) plus output space.

Inputs are unchanged. Count values through distinct indices; a set of values alone would lose repeated zeros. The default cubic approach avoids large equal-sum pair cross products.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Two anchors and two pointers
docs.text:
Time: O(n cubed)

Space: O(n) plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Two anchors and two pointers
    Time: O(n cubed)
    Space: O(n) plus output
    """

    def fourSum(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        values = sorted(nums)
        answer = []
        for i in range(len(values) - 3):
            if i and values[i] == values[i - 1]:
                continue
            for j in range(i + 1, len(values) - 2):
                if j > i + 1 and values[j] == values[j - 1]:
                    continue
                left, right = j + 1, len(values) - 1
                while left < right:
                    total = values[i] + values[j] + values[left] + values[right]
                    if total < target:
                        left += 1
                    elif total > target:
                        right -= 1
                    else:
                        answer.append([values[i], values[j], values[left], values[right]])
                        a, b = values[left], values[right]
                        while left < right and values[left] == a:
                            left += 1
                        while left < right and values[right] == b:
                            right -= 1
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Incremental disjoint pair sums
docs.text:
Time: O(n to the fourth) worst case

Space: O(n squared) plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Incremental disjoint pair sums
    Time: O(n to the fourth) worst case
    Space: O(n squared) plus output
    """

    def fourSum(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        pairs = {}
        answer = set()
        for third in range(2, len(nums) - 1):
            second = third - 1
            for first in range(second):
                pairs.setdefault(nums[first] + nums[second], []).append((nums[first], nums[second]))
            for fourth in range(third + 1, len(nums)):
                wanted = target - nums[third] - nums[fourth]
                for a, b in pairs.get(wanted, []):
                    answer.add(tuple(sorted((a, b, nums[third], nums[fourth]))))
        return [list(values) for values in sorted(answer)]

1. Keep a gap of n nodes between two pointers.
  2. A dummy node makes removing the original head an ordinary link update.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Fixed pointer gap O(n) O(1) Count then unlink O(n) O(1)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Fixed pointer gap
docs.text: Start fast and slow at a dummy predecessor. Advance fast n times, then move both until fast is the last node. Slow now precedes the node to remove; bypass it and return dummy.next.

docs.title: Count then unlink
docs.text: Count the list length, then walk length-n links from a dummy predecessor and bypass the following node. This uses two passes instead of maintaining a moving gap.

docs.title: Fixed pointer gap
docs.text: The distance between fast and slow stays n. When fast reaches the last node, slow is therefore exactly n positions before it, which is the predecessor of the nth-from-end node. Bypassing one link removes precisely that node.

docs.title: Count then unlink
docs.text: The nth node from the end has zero-based index length-n from the head. Walking that many predecessor links from the dummy locates exactly its incoming link.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [4,5,6] and n=3, fast reaches 6 before the paired walk starts. Slow remains at dummy, so bypass 4 and return [5,6].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

O(length) time and O(1) space. The original list's links are modified; remaining nodes are reused. Advancing n versus n+1 steps depends on the chosen stopping condition. Here the paired loop checks fast.next, not fast. A single-node list with n=1 returns None.

Alternative tradeoff: O(n) time; O(1) space.

docs.title: 1. Fixed pointer gap
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Fixed pointer gap
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: ListNode, n: int) -> ListNode | None:
        dummy = ListNode(next=head)
        slow = fast = dummy
        for _ in range(n):
            fast = fast.next
        while fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next
        slow.next = slow.next.next
        return dummy.next

docs.title: 2. Count then unlink
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Count then unlink
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: ListNode, n: int) -> ListNode | None:
        length = 0
        current = head
        while current:
            length += 1
            current = current.next
        dummy = ListNode(next=head)
        before = dummy
        for _ in range(length - n):
            before = before.next
        before.next = before.next.next
        return dummy.next

  2. A balanced string is an opening parenthesis, a balanced interior, a closing parenthesis, and a balanced suffix.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Balance-constrained backtracking O(n*C_n) O(n) auxiliary plus output Catalan concatenation DP O(n^2*C_n) loose bound O(n^2*C_n) loose bound

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Balance-constrained backtracking
docs.text: Track opened and closed counts. Add an opening while opened<n and a closing while closed<opened. Record strings of length 2n.

docs.title: Catalan concatenation DP
docs.text: For each size, combine every smaller interior and suffix as "("+inside+")"+after. Store all strings by pair count.

docs.title: Balance-constrained backtracking
docs.text: Every prefix maintains nonnegative balance and never exceeds n openings. Complete strings have equal counts, and every valid string follows one permitted sequence of choices.

docs.title: Catalan concatenation DP
docs.text: The closing parenthesis matching the first opening uniquely splits a nonempty valid string into its interior and suffix. Enumerating that split generates all and only balanced strings without duplicates.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For n=2, an empty interior with suffix "()" gives "()()"; interior "()" with empty suffix gives "(())".

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Balance-constrained backtracking: O(nC_n) time; O(n) auxiliary plus output space. Catalan concatenation DP: O(n^2C_n) loose bound time; O(n^2*C_n) loose bound space. C_n counts balanced strings. Strings and path joins incur copying included in the bounds. DP retains intermediate strings; DFS needs only one working path. Recursion is bounded by n<=8.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Balance-constrained backtracking
docs.text:
Time: O(n*C_n)

Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Balance-constrained backtracking
    Time: O(n*C_n)
    Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def generateParenthesis(self, n: int) -> list[str]:
        result, path = [], []

        def visit(opened, closed):
            if closed == n:
                result.append("".join(path))
                return
            if opened < n:
                path.append("(")
                visit(opened + 1, closed)
                path.pop()
            if closed < opened:
                path.append(")")
                visit(opened, closed + 1)
                path.pop()

        visit(0, 0)
        return result

docs.title: 2. Catalan concatenation DP
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2*C_n) loose bound

Space: O(n^2*C_n) loose bound

class Solution:
    """Approach: Catalan concatenation DP
    Time: O(n^2*C_n) loose bound
    Space: O(n^2*C_n) loose bound
    """

    def generateParenthesis(self, n: int) -> list[str]:
        values = [[""]]
        for size in range(1, n + 1):
            values.append(
                [
                    "(" + inside + ")" + after
                    for left in range(size)
                    for inside in values[left]
                    for after in values[size - left - 1]
                ]
            )
        return values[n]

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Merge k ascending linked lists into one ascending list. Some or all input lists may be empty.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. The smallest unmerged node must be at the head of one remaining list.
  2. A heap can maintain those k candidates without repeatedly scanning them.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Heap of list heads O(k + N log(k+1)) O(k) Pairwise merging O(k + N log(k+1)) O(k)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Heap of list heads
docs.text: Heapify one head per nonempty list. Pop the smallest node, append it to the result, and push its successor from the same list. Heap entries include the source list index to break equal-value ties without comparing node objects.

docs.title: Pairwise merging
docs.text: Copy the head array and merge adjacent pairs of sorted chains in rounds. Each round halves the number of chains. Rewire original nodes, while leaving the caller's list-of-heads array unchanged.

docs.title: Heap of list heads
docs.text: Each heap entry is its list's smallest remaining node. Their minimum is therefore the global smallest unmerged node. Replacing it with its successor restores the invariant, so repeated extraction builds a sorted list containing every node.

docs.title: Pairwise merging
docs.text: Two-way merging always chooses the smaller front node and preserves every node. By induction each round produces sorted unions of disjoint input groups; after logarithmically many rounds the single chain contains all nodes.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [1,4], [1,3], and [2], heap heads begin as 1,1,2. After extracting the two 1s, their successors 4 and 3 join 2. Output is [1,1,2,3,4].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

O(k + N log(k+1)) time and O(k) space for N total nodes. Reuses nodes and mutates their next links; this is not a persistent copy. Heap tuples containing only (value,node) fail on duplicate values because nodes are not orderable.

Alternative tradeoff: O(k + N log(k+1)) time; O(k) space.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Heap of list heads
docs.text:
Time: O(k + N log(k+1))

Space: O(k)

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Heap of list heads
    Time: O(k + N log(k+1))
    Space: O(k)
    """

    def mergeKLists(self, lists: list[ListNode | None]) -> ListNode | None:
        heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
        heapify(heap)
        dummy = tail = ListNode()
        while heap:
            _, i, node = heappop(heap)
            tail.next = node
            tail = node
            if node.next:
                heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
        return dummy.next

docs.title: 2. Pairwise merging
docs.text:
Time: O(k + N log(k+1))

Space: O(k)

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Pairwise merging
    Time: O(k + N log(k+1))
    Space: O(k)
    """

    def mergeKLists(self, lists: list[ListNode | None]) -> ListNode | None:
        current = list(lists)
        while len(current) > 1:
            merged = []
            for i in range(0, len(current), 2):
                left = current[i]
                right = current[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(current) else None
                dummy = tail = ListNode()
                while left and right:
                    if left.val <= right.val:
                        tail.next, left = left, left.next
                    else:
                        tail.next, right = right, right.next
                    tail = tail.next
                tail.next = left if left else right
                merged.append(dummy.next)
            current = merged
        return current[0] if current else None

docs.text:

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Swap each adjacent pair of list nodes and return the new head. Rewire nodes rather than swapping their values; an unmatched final node stays last.

docs.title: Hints

1. Keep a predecessor for the pair being changed.
  2. A dummy predecessor also covers swapping the original head.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Local pair rewiring O(n) O(1) Buffered positional order O(n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Local pair rewiring
docs.text: Walk pairs after a dummy node. Save the first and second nodes, bypass the second, then link second before first. Advance the predecessor to the old first.

docs.title: Buffered positional order
docs.text: Collect node identities, exchange neighboring array entries, and rebuild links from that order. This spends linear storage to make output positions explicit.

docs.title: Local pair rewiring
docs.text: Each step exchanges exactly one adjacent pair and leaves the already processed prefix attached to the untouched suffix.

docs.title: Buffered positional order
docs.text: The array permutation exchanges precisely indices 0/1, 2/3, and so on. Reconnecting those original identities preserves every value and node.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [4,7,2], exchange 4 and 7, leaving the unmatched 2: [7,4,2].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Local pair rewiring: O(n) time; O(1) space. Buffered positional order: O(n) time; O(n) space. Both variants mutate links and reuse original nodes. Terminate the final node to prevent stale links. Empty and one-node lists are unchanged.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Local pair rewiring
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Local pair rewiring
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def swapPairs(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        dummy = ListNode(next=head)
        before = dummy
        while before.next and before.next.next:
            first = before.next
            second = first.next
            first.next = second.next
            second.next = first
            before.next = second
            before = first
        return dummy.next

docs.title: 2. Buffered positional order
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Buffered positional order
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def swapPairs(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        order = []
        while head:
            order.append(head)
            head = head.next
        for index in range(0, len(order) - 1, 2):
            order[index], order[index + 1] = order[index + 1], order[index]
        for index, node in enumerate(order):
            node.next = order[index + 1] if index + 1 < len(order) else None
        return order[0] if order else None

1. Find the end of a complete group before changing any links.
  2. Keep the following group head as the initial reversed tail.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Bounded pointer reversal O(n) O(1) Per-group node stack O(n) O(k)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Bounded pointer reversal
docs.text: Locate the kth node after a group predecessor. Reverse exactly the links before its saved successor, reconnect the group, and continue from the old group head.

docs.title: Per-group node stack
docs.text: Collect up to k original nodes. Pop or traverse a complete group in reverse order; append an incomplete final group unchanged.

docs.title: Bounded pointer reversal
docs.text: Knowing the boundary guarantees that only complete groups change. Reversal points the old first node at the untouched suffix and reconnects the previous prefix to the old last node.

docs.title: Per-group node stack
docs.text: The buffer contains exactly the next k positions or the entire remaining suffix. Reversing only full buffers matches the contract while retaining each original identity once.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [1,2,3,4,5] and k=2, reverse [1,2] and [3,4], then retain [5], giving [2,1,4,3,5].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Bounded pointer reversal: O(n) time; O(1) space. Per-group node stack: O(n) time; O(k) space. Both solutions mutate next pointers. The default meets the constant auxiliary-space follow-up; the stack variant does not. Never partially reverse an undersized final group.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Bounded pointer reversal
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Bounded pointer reversal
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def reverseKGroup(self, head: ListNode, k: int) -> ListNode:
        dummy = ListNode(next=head)
        before = dummy
        while True:
            end = before
            for _ in range(k):
                end = end.next
                if end is None:
                    return dummy.next
            following = end.next
            current = before.next
            previous = following
            while current is not following:
                saved = current.next
                current.next = previous
                previous, current = current, saved
            old_first = before.next
            before.next = end
            before = old_first

docs.title: 2. Per-group node stack
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(k)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Per-group node stack
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(k)
    """

    def reverseKGroup(self, head: ListNode, k: int) -> ListNode:
        dummy = tail = ListNode()
        current = head
        while current:
            group = []
            while current and len(group) < k:
                group.append(current)
                current = current.next
            if len(group) < k:
                tail.next = group[0]
                break
            while group:
                tail.next = group.pop()
                tail = tail.next
            tail.next = current
        return dummy.next

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Repeated largest doubled subtraction O(log squared V) O(1) Binary long division O(log V) O(1)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Repeated largest doubled subtraction
docs.text: For each remainder, repeatedly double the divisor until the next doubling would exceed it, then subtract that block and add its quotient bit.

docs.title: Binary long division
docs.text: Scan candidate quotient bits from highest to lowest and subtract a shifted divisor whenever it fits.

docs.title: Repeated largest doubled subtraction
docs.text: Each subtraction preserves original_dividend = quotient*divisor + remainder. The remainder decreases by at least half when a largest fitting power-of-two block is removed, until it is smaller than the divisor.

docs.title: Binary long division
docs.text: Before each bit, all higher quotient bits are settled and the remaining value is below the next higher divisor multiple. Setting the current bit exactly when its multiple fits reproduces integer long division.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: -7 divided by 3 computes magnitude quotient 2 and then negates it, yielding -2 rather than floor result -3. -2^31 divided by -1 clamps to 2^31-1.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Repeated largest doubled subtraction: O(log squared V) time; O(1) space.

Binary long division: O(log V) time; O(1) space.

Inputs are unchanged; divisor is nonzero. V is the dividend magnitude plus one. All divisions in these implementations use only shifts and subtraction.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Repeated largest doubled subtraction
docs.text:
Time: O(log squared V)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Repeated largest doubled subtraction
    Time: O(log squared V)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def divide(self, dividend: int, divisor: int) -> int:
        negative = (dividend < 0) != (divisor < 0)
        remaining, base = abs(dividend), abs(divisor)
        quotient = 0
        while remaining >= base:
            chunk, count = base, 1
            while chunk << 1 <= remaining:
                chunk <<= 1
                count <<= 1
            remaining -= chunk
            quotient += count
        if negative:
            quotient = -quotient
        return min((1 << 31) - 1, max(-(1 << 31), quotient))

docs.title: 2. Binary long division
docs.text:
Time: O(log V)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary long division
    Time: O(log V)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def divide(self, dividend: int, divisor: int) -> int:
        remaining, base = abs(dividend), abs(divisor)
        quotient = 0
        for bit in range(remaining.bit_length() - 1, -1, -1):
            if base << bit <= remaining:
                remaining -= base << bit
                quotient |= 1 << bit
        if (dividend < 0) != (divisor < 0):
            quotient = -quotient
        return min((1 << 31) - 1, max(-(1 << 31), quotient))

docs.title: Pivot swap and suffix reversal
docs.text: Find the rightmost ascent, swap its left value with the rightmost larger suffix value, and reverse the nonincreasing suffix.

docs.title: Pivot swap and suffix sorting

docs.title: Pivot swap and suffix reversal
docs.text: Changing the latest possible position makes the smallest lexicographic increase. The chosen successor is the smallest larger suffix value; reversing the descending suffix then gives its minimum order.

docs.title: Pivot swap and suffix sorting

docs.title: 1. Pivot swap and suffix reversal
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Pivot swap and suffix reversal
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def nextPermutation(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
        pivot = len(nums) - 2
        while pivot >= 0 and nums[pivot] >= nums[pivot + 1]:
            pivot -= 1
        if pivot >= 0:
            successor = len(nums) - 1
            while nums[successor] <= nums[pivot]:
                successor -= 1
            nums[pivot], nums[successor] = nums[successor], nums[pivot]
        left, right = pivot + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while left < right:
            nums[left], nums[right] = nums[right], nums[left]
            left += 1
            right -= 1

docs.title: 2. Pivot swap and suffix sorting
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Pivot swap and suffix sorting
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def nextPermutation(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
        pivot = len(nums) - 2
        while pivot >= 0 and nums[pivot] >= nums[pivot + 1]:
            pivot -= 1
        if pivot < 0:
            nums.sort()
            return
        successor = min(
            (i for i in range(pivot + 1, len(nums)) if nums[i] > nums[pivot]), key=nums.__getitem__
        )
        nums[pivot], nums[successor] = nums[successor], nums[pivot]
        nums[pivot + 1 :] = sorted(nums[pivot + 1 :])

docs.title: Stack of unmatched indices
docs.text: After a successful match, the stack top is the closest unmatched boundary before the balanced suffix. Its distance is therefore the longest valid suffix ending here.

class Solution:
    """Approach: Stack of unmatched indices
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def longestValidParentheses(self, s: str) -> int:
        stack = [-1]
        best = 0
        for index, character in enumerate(s):
            if character == "(":
                stack.append(index)
            else:
                stack.pop()
                if not stack:
                    stack.append(index)
                else:
                    best = max(best, index - stack[-1])
        return best

docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Forward and backward balance counts
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def longestValidParentheses(self, s: str) -> int:
        best = 0
        for reverse in (False, True):
            opens = closes = 0
            for index in range(len(s) - 1, -1, -1) if reverse else range(len(s)):
                opens += s[index] == "("
                closes += s[index] == ")"
                if opens == closes:
                    best = max(best, opens + closes)
                elif opens > closes if reverse else closes > opens:
                    opens = closes = 0
        return best

docs.title: 1. Sorted-half binary search
docs.text:
Time: O(log n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sorted-half binary search
    Time: O(log n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def search(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
        left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1
        while left <= right:
            middle = (left + right) // 2
            if nums[middle] == target:
                return middle
            if nums[left] <= nums[middle]:
                if nums[left] <= target < nums[middle]:
                    right = middle - 1
                else:
                    left = middle + 1
            elif nums[middle] < target <= nums[right]:
                left = middle + 1
            else:
                right = middle - 1
        return -1

docs.title: 2. Find pivot then binary search
docs.text:
Time: O(log n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Find pivot then binary search
    Time: O(log n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def search(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
        low, high = 0, len(nums) - 1
        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if nums[middle] > nums[high]:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle
        pivot = low
        low, high = 0, len(nums) - 1
        while low <= high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            index = (middle + pivot) % len(nums)
            if nums[index] == target:
                return index
            if nums[index] < target:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle - 1
        return -1

docs.title: 1. Two lower-bound searches
docs.text:
Time: O(log n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Two lower-bound searches
    Time: O(log n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def searchRange(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
        def lower(value):
            left, right = 0, len(nums)
            while left < right:
                middle = (left + right) // 2
                if nums[middle] < value:
                    left = middle + 1
                else:
                    right = middle
            return left

        start = lower(target)
        if start == len(nums) or nums[start] != target:
            return [-1, -1]
        return [start, lower(target + 1) - 1]

docs.title: 2. Directional equality searches
docs.text:
Time: O(log n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Directional equality searches
    Time: O(log n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def searchRange(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
        answer = []
        for first in (True, False):
            low, high, found = 0, len(nums) - 1, -1
            while low <= high:
                middle = (low + high) // 2
                if nums[middle] == target:
                    found = middle
                    if first:
                        high = middle - 1
                    else:
                        low = middle + 1
                elif nums[middle] < target:
                    low = middle + 1
                else:
                    high = middle - 1
            answer.append(found)
        return answer

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sets of occupied digits
    Time: O(81)
    Space: O(81)
    """

    def isValidSudoku(self, board: list[list[str]]) -> bool:
        rows, cols, boxes = (
            [set() for _ in range(9)],
            [set() for _ in range(9)],
            [set() for _ in range(9)],
        )
        for r in range(9):
            for c in range(9):
                value = board[r][c]
                if value == ".":
                    continue
                box = r // 3 * 3 + c // 3
                if value in rows[r] or value in cols[c] or value in boxes[box]:
                    return False
                rows[r].add(value)
                cols[c].add(value)
                boxes[box].add(value)
        return True

Space: O(27)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Bit masks for occupied digits
    Time: O(81)
    Space: O(27)
    """

    def isValidSudoku(self, board: list[list[str]]) -> bool:
        rows, cols, boxes = [0] * 9, [0] * 9, [0] * 9
        for r in range(9):
            for c in range(9):
                if board[r][c] == ".":
                    continue
                bit = 1 << (int(board[r][c]) - 1)
                box = r // 3 * 3 + c // 3
                if rows[r] & bit or cols[c] & bit or boxes[box] & bit:
                    return False
                rows[r] |= bit
                cols[c] |= bit
                boxes[box] |= bit
        return True

docs.text:
Medium · String processing extensions · Extension · Learning step 283 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Start with the string "1". Each next term describes consecutive runs in the previous term as a decimal count followed by the repeated digit. Return term n.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Count consecutive equal digits, not total digit frequencies.
  2. The recurrence can be evaluated iteratively or by first obtaining term n-1.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 282 · #12 · Next: 284 · #443

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Iterative run scanning O(T), summed generated term lengths O(L), largest term length Recursive term construction O(T), summed generated term lengths O(L+n), largest term plus call frames

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Iterative run scanning
docs.text: Keep only the current term. Move two indices across each maximal equal run, append its length and digit to a pieces list, and join to form the next term.

docs.title: Recursive term construction
docs.text: Recursively obtain the preceding term, with term one as the base case. Use groupby to consume its runs, count each run, and join its descriptions. No memoization is needed because each term is requested exactly once.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: The indices and groupby both partition a term into maximal consecutive runs. Each run contributes exactly its length and digit, which defines the next term. Induction from the common base "1" proves that either evaluation order returns term n. There is no branching recursion or repeated subproblem work.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: The first four terms are 1, 11, 21, and 1211. Reading 21 gives one 2 followed by one 1. A frequency map would discard this run order and cannot replace RLE.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Let L be the largest generated term length and T the sum of all generated term lengths through n. Both take O(T) time, including joins and run counting. Iterative scanning uses O(L) space. Recursive construction uses O(L+n) space: the n call frames await smaller terms, but earlier term strings are released as those calls return. Under the stated n<=30, recursion depth is small. Do not concatenate one character at a time into an immutable result string. The input integer is unchanged; the returned string is newly constructed.

docs.title: 1. Iterative run scanning

from itertools import groupby


class Solution:
    """Approach: Iterative run scanning
    Time: O(T), summed generated term lengths
    Space: O(L), largest term length
    """

    def countAndSay(self, n: int) -> str:
        term = "1"
        for _ in range(n - 1):
            parts = []
            start = 0
            while start < len(term):
                end = start + 1
                while end < len(term) and term[end] == term[start]:
                    end += 1
                parts.extend((str(end - start), term[start]))
                start = end
            term = "".join(parts)
        return term

docs.title: 2. Recursive term construction
docs.text:
Time: O(T), summed generated term lengths

Space: O(L+n), largest term plus call frames

from itertools import groupby


class Solution:
    """Approach: Recursive term construction
    Time: O(T), summed generated term lengths
    Space: O(L+n), largest term plus call frames
    """

    def countAndSay(self, n: int) -> str:
        def term(index):
            if index == 1:
                return "1"
            previous = term(index - 1)
            pieces = []
            for digit, group in groupby(previous):
                pieces.extend((str(sum(1 for _ in group)), digit))
            return "".join(pieces)

        return term(n)

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Nondecreasing backtracking O(C log C + C^D*(D+1)) loose bound O(C+D) auxiliary plus output Bottom-up combination lists O(C*T + total intermediate path-copy work) O(T + total intermediate path lengths)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Nondecreasing backtracking
docs.text: Sort a copy of the candidates. Backtrack with a starting index and remaining sum. Stop and save a copy at remaining zero. Stop scanning when a candidate exceeds the remaining sum, since all later candidates are larger.

docs.title: Bottom-up combination lists
docs.text: Keep a list of combinations for each subtotal. Process sorted candidates outside an ascending subtotal loop, extending combinations at subtotal-value. This stores intermediate answers and can use much more space than backtracking.

docs.title: Nondecreasing backtracking
docs.text: Positive values strictly reduce the remainder, so every branch terminates. Every valid multiset has one nondecreasing index sequence, which the search visits. Restricting indices removes alternate orderings without losing a combination.

docs.title: Bottom-up combination lists
docs.text: When processing value v, each new combination appends v to a combination made only from processed values. Ascending subtotals permit reuse of v. A combination is created once when its largest value is processed.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For candidates [2,3,5] and target 7, the successful paths are [2,2,3] and [2,5]. The path [3,2,2] is excluded as a duplicate ordering.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

Let C be candidate count and D=target//min(candidates). A loose time bound is O(C log C + C^D * (D+1)), including path copies. Auxiliary space is O(C+D), plus output. Inputs are unchanged. Recurse at i rather than i+1 to allow reuse. Nonpositive candidates would invalidate the termination argument and are excluded.

Alternative tradeoff: O(C*T + total intermediate path-copy work) time; O(T + total intermediate path lengths) space.

docs.title: 1. Nondecreasing backtracking
docs.text:
Time: O(C log C + C^D*(D+1)) loose bound

Space: O(C+D) auxiliary plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Nondecreasing backtracking
    Time: O(C log C + C^D*(D+1)) loose bound
    Space: O(C+D) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def combinationSum(self, candidates: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        values = sorted(candidates)
        result = []
        path = []

        def visit(start, remaining):
            if remaining == 0:
                result.append(path.copy())
                return
            for i in range(start, len(values)):
                value = values[i]
                if value > remaining:
                    break
                path.append(value)
                visit(i, remaining - value)
                path.pop()

        visit(0, target)
        return result

docs.title: 2. Bottom-up combination lists
docs.text:
Time: O(C*T + total intermediate path-copy work)

Space: O(T + total intermediate path lengths)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Bottom-up combination lists
    Time: O(C*T + total intermediate path-copy work)
    Space: O(T + total intermediate path lengths)
    """

    def combinationSum(self, candidates: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        combinations = [[] for _ in range(target + 1)]
        combinations[0] = [[]]
        for value in sorted(candidates):
            for total in range(value, target + 1):
                combinations[total].extend(path + [value] for path in combinations[total - value])
        return combinations[target]

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Sorted index backtracking
    Time: O(n log n + n*2^n) loose bound
    Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def combinationSum2(self, candidates: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        values = sorted(candidates)
        result, path = [], []

        def visit(start, remaining):
            if remaining == 0:
                result.append(path.copy())
                return
            for index in range(start, len(values)):
                value = values[index]
                if value > remaining:
                    break
                if index > start and value == values[index - 1]:
                    continue
                path.append(value)
                visit(index + 1, remaining - value)
                path.pop()

        visit(0, target)
        return result

docs.title: 2. Bounded multiplicity search
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n + n*product(count+1)) loose bound

Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Bounded multiplicity search
    Time: O(n log n + n*product(count+1)) loose bound
    Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def combinationSum2(self, candidates: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        groups = sorted(Counter(candidates).items())
        result, path = [], []

        def visit(index, remaining):
            if remaining == 0:
                result.append(path.copy())
                return
            if index == len(groups):
                return
            value, count = groups[index]
            limit = min(count, remaining // value)
            for used in range(limit + 1):
                visit(index + 1, remaining - used * value)
                if used < limit:
                    path.append(value)
            if limit:
                del path[-limit:]

        visit(0, target)
        return result
