class Solution:
    """Approach: Two running side maxima
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def trap(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
        left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
        left_max = right_max = water = 0
        while left <= right:
            if left_max <= right_max:
                left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
                water += left_max - height[left]
                left += 1
            else:
                right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
                water += right_max - height[right]
                right -= 1
        return water

docs.title: 2. Monotonic basin stack
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Monotonic basin stack
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def trap(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
        stack = []
        water = 0
        for right, value in enumerate(height):
            while stack and height[stack[-1]] < value:
                bottom = stack.pop()
                if not stack:
                    break
                left = stack[-1]
                water += (min(height[left], value) - height[bottom]) * (right - left - 1)
            stack.append(right)
        return water

docs.title: 3. Prefix and suffix maximum arrays
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Prefix and suffix maximum arrays
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def trap(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
        prefix, suffix = height[:], height[:]
        for i in range(1, len(height)):
            prefix[i] = max(prefix[i - 1], height[i])
        for i in range(len(height) - 2, -1, -1):
            suffix[i] = max(suffix[i + 1], height[i])
        return sum(min(prefix[i], suffix[i]) - value for i, value in enumerate(height))

Space: O(m+n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Digit-array grade-school multiplication
    Time: O(mn)
    Space: O(m+n)
    """

    def multiply(self, num1: str, num2: str) -> str:
        digits = [0] * (len(num1) + len(num2))
        for i in range(len(num1) - 1, -1, -1):
            for j in range(len(num2) - 1, -1, -1):
                total = digits[i + j + 1] + (ord(num1[i]) - 48) * (ord(num2[j]) - 48)
                digits[i + j + 1] = total % 10
                digits[i + j] += total // 10
        return "".join(map(str, digits)).lstrip("0") or "0"

docs.title: 2. Partial-product strings and addition
docs.text:
Time: O(mn+n squared)

Space: O(m+n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Partial-product strings and addition
    Time: O(mn+n squared)
    Space: O(m+n)
    """

    def multiply(self, num1: str, num2: str) -> str:
        def add(left, right):
            i, j, carry = len(left) - 1, len(right) - 1, 0
            digits = []
            while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry:
                total = carry
                if i >= 0:
                    total += ord(left[i]) - 48
                    i -= 1
                if j >= 0:
                    total += ord(right[j]) - 48
                    j -= 1
                carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
                digits.append(str(digit))
            return "".join(reversed(digits))

        answer = "0"
        for shift, char in enumerate(reversed(num2)):
            carry = 0
            digits = []
            for other in reversed(num1):
                carry, digit = divmod((ord(char) - 48) * (ord(other) - 48) + carry, 10)
                digits.append(str(digit))
            if carry:
                digits.append(str(carry))
            partial = "".join(reversed(digits)) + "0" * shift
            answer = add(answer, partial)
        return answer.lstrip("0") or "0"

class Solution:
    """Approach: Greedy retry at the latest star
    Time: O((m+1)*(n+1)) worst case
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def isMatch(self, s: str, p: str) -> bool:
        i = j = 0
        star = -1
        consumed = 0
        while i < len(s):
            if j < len(p) and (p[j] == "?" or p[j] == s[i]):
                i += 1
                j += 1
            elif j < len(p) and p[j] == "*":
                star = j
                consumed = i
                j += 1
            elif star >= 0:
                consumed += 1
                i, j = consumed, star + 1
            else:
                return False
        while j < len(p) and p[j] == "*":
            j += 1
        return j == len(p)

docs.title: 2. Rolling wildcard prefix table
docs.text:
Time: O((m+1)*(n+1))

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Rolling wildcard prefix table
    Time: O((m+1)*(n+1))
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def isMatch(self, s: str, p: str) -> bool:
        previous = [True] + [False] * len(p)
        for j, atom in enumerate(p, 1):
            previous[j] = previous[j - 1] and atom == "*"
        for character in s:
            current = [False] * (len(p) + 1)
            for j, atom in enumerate(p, 1):
                current[j] = (
                    current[j - 1] or previous[j]
                    if atom == "*"
                    else previous[j - 1] and atom in ("?", character)
                )
            previous = current
        return previous[-1]

class Solution:
    """Approach: Greedy jump-layer frontier
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def jump(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        jumps = end = farthest = 0
        for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
            farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
            if i == end:
                jumps += 1
                end = farthest
        return jumps

class Solution:
    """Approach: Dynamic programming over destinations
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def jump(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        distance = [len(nums)] * len(nums)
        distance[0] = 0
        for i, value in enumerate(nums):
            for destination in range(i + 1, min(len(nums), i + value + 1)):
                distance[destination] = min(distance[destination], distance[i] + 1)
        return distance[-1]

class Solution:
    """Approach: Unused-index backtracking
    Time: O(n*n!)
    Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(n*n!) output
    """

    def permute(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        result = []
        path = []
        used = set()

        def visit():
            if len(path) == len(nums):
                result.append(path.copy())
                return
            for i, value in enumerate(nums):
                if i in used:
                    continue
                used.add(i)
                path.append(value)
                visit()
                path.pop()
                used.remove(i)

        visit()
        return result

class Solution:

    Time: O(n*n!)
    Space: O(n*n!)
    """

    def permute(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        result = [[]]
        for value in nums:
            result = [
                path[:index] + [value] + path[index:]
                for path in result
                for index in range(len(path) + 1)
            ]
        return result

    Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(n*P) output
    """

    def permuteUnique(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        values = sorted(nums)
        used = [False] * len(values)
        path, result = [], []

        def visit():
            if len(path) == len(values):
                result.append(path.copy())
                return
            for index, value in enumerate(values):
                if used[index] or (index and value == values[index - 1] and not used[index - 1]):
                    continue
                used[index] = True
                path.append(value)
                visit()
                path.pop()
                used[index] = False

        visit()
        return result

docs.text:
Time: O(n*n!) loose bound

Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(n*P) output

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Remaining-frequency search
    Time: O(n*n!) loose bound
    Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(n*P) output
    """

    def permuteUnique(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        counts = Counter(nums)
        result, path = [], []

        def visit():
            if len(path) == len(nums):
                result.append(path.copy())
                return
            for value in counts:
                if counts[value]:
                    counts[value] -= 1
                    path.append(value)
                    visit()
                    path.pop()
                    counts[value] += 1

        visit()
        return result

docs.title: Transpose then reverse rows
docs.text: Swap entries across the main diagonal, then reverse each row in place.

docs.title: Four-cell layer cycles
docs.text: For every layer, move corresponding left, bottom, right, and top cells around one four-way cycle.

docs.title: Transpose then reverse rows
docs.text: Transposition maps (r,c) to (c,r), and row reversal maps that position to (c,n-1-r), exactly the clockwise rotation coordinate.

docs.title: Four-cell layer cycles
docs.text: The four cells in a cycle are successive clockwise rotations of one coordinate. Every noncentral cell belongs to exactly one such cycle, so all cells rotate once.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: [[1,2],[3,4]] maps its top-left 1 to top-right, producing [[3,1],[4,2]]. The center of an odd- sized matrix stays fixed.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Transpose then reverse rows: O(n squared) time; O(1) space.

Four-cell layer cycles: O(n squared) time; O(1) space.

Both methods mutate existing rows and require square input. Assigning matrix to a new rotated list would not satisfy the in-place contract.

class Solution:
    """Approach: Transpose then reverse rows
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def rotate(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> None:
        size = len(matrix)
        for row in range(size):
            for col in range(row + 1, size):
                matrix[row][col], matrix[col][row] = matrix[col][row], matrix[row][col]
        for row in matrix:
            row.reverse()

docs.title: 2. Four-cell layer cycles
docs.text:
Time: O(n squared)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Four-cell layer cycles
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def rotate(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> None:
        size = len(matrix)
        for first in range(size // 2):
            last = size - 1 - first
            for col in range(first, last):
                offset = col - first
                top = matrix[first][col]
                matrix[first][col] = matrix[last - offset][first]
                matrix[last - offset][first] = matrix[last][last - offset]
                matrix[last][last - offset] = matrix[col][last]
                matrix[col][last] = top

docs.title: Frequency signatures
docs.text: Comparing every pair repeats work. Count the 26 letters in each word and use the count tuple as a dictionary key. Append the original word to that key's group.

docs.title: Sorted signatures
docs.text: Sort each word into its canonical letter order. This is simpler for arbitrary alphabets, at the cost of sorting every word.

docs.title: Frequency signatures
docs.text: Two words are anagrams exactly when all 26 counts agree. Therefore each key collects one complete anagram class, and different classes never mix.

docs.title: Sorted signatures
docs.text: Two words have equal sorted characters exactly when every character has the same multiplicity. Grouping by this key therefore produces exactly the anagram classes.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For ["ab", "ba", "bb"], the first two words have counts a=1, b=1 and share a group. The last has b=2. The result is [["ab", "ba"], ["bb"]].

Let C be the total characters and n the number of words. Time is O(C + 26n); auxiliary key storage is O(26n) in the worst case, plus O(n) output references. Inputs are unchanged. Use a tuple, not a list, as a key. Empty words correctly share the all-zero key. A set of letters would lose multiplicity.

Frequency signatures: O(nL) time; O(nL) space. Sorted signatures: O(nL log L) time; O(nL) space. Sort each word into its canonical letter order. This is simpler for arbitrary alphabets, at the cost of sorting every word.

from collections import defaultdict


class Solution:
    """Approach: Frequency signatures
    Time: O(nL)
    Space: O(nL)
    """

    def groupAnagrams(self, strs: list[str]) -> list[list[str]]:
        groups = defaultdict(list)
        for word in strs:
            counts = [0] * 26
            for char in word:
                counts[ord(char) - ord("a")] += 1
            groups[tuple(counts)].append(word)
        return list(groups.values())

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sorted signatures
    Time: O(nL log L)
    Space: O(nL)
    """

    def groupAnagrams(self, strs: list[str]) -> list[list[str]]:
        groups = {}
        for word in strs:
            key = "".join(sorted(word))
            groups.setdefault(key, []).append(word)
        return list(groups.values())

docs.text: Recursively compute one half-power, square it, and multiply by x for odd exponents.

docs.title: Iterative binary exponentiation
docs.text: The invariant answer*base^remaining equals the desired power. An odd step moves one base into answer; squaring the base and halving the remaining exponent preserves the invariant.

docs.title: Recursive exponent halving
docs.text: For n=2q, x^n=(x^q)^2; for n=2q+1, one additional x is needed. Induction on n proves the recurrence, with x^0=1 as the base.

class Solution:
    """Approach: Iterative binary exponentiation
    Time: O(log(abs(n)+1))
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def myPow(self, x: float, n: int) -> float:
        if n < 0:
            x, n = 1 / x, -n
        answer = 1.0
        while n:
            if n & 1:
                answer *= x
            x *= x
            n >>= 1
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Recursive exponent halving
docs.text:
Time: O(log(abs(n)+1))

Space: O(log(abs(n)+1))

class Solution:
    """Approach: Recursive exponent halving
    Time: O(log(abs(n)+1))
    Space: O(log(abs(n)+1))
    """

    def myPow(self, x: float, n: int) -> float:
        if n < 0:
            x, n = 1 / x, -n

        def power(exponent):
            if exponent == 0:
                return 1.0
            half = power(exponent // 2)
            answer = half * half
            return answer * x if exponent % 2 else answer

        return power(n)

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Column and diagonal sets O(nn! + Sn^2) loose bound O(n) auxiliary; O(S*n^2) output Shifted attack masks O(nn! + Sn^2) loose bound O(n) auxiliary; O(S*n^2) output

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Column and diagonal sets
docs.text: Backtrack row by row with occupied-column and two diagonal sets. For each safe column, record the queen, mark its three constraints, recurse, then undo them. Construct board strings only for complete arrangements.

docs.title: Shifted attack masks
docs.text: Represent columns and diagonal attacks on the next row with bitmasks. Intersect their complements with the n-column mask to obtain legal positions, then take one low bit at a time. Diagonal masks shift when descending a row.

docs.title: Column and diagonal sets
docs.text: One queen per row satisfies the row constraint automatically. The three sets exclude exactly the remaining attacks. Every valid board has one sequence of row-wise column choices, so the recursion visits it once.

docs.title: Shifted attack masks
docs.text: A queen's two diagonal attacks move one column in opposite directions in the next row. Shifting masks therefore maintains exactly the forbidden columns, and choosing only free bits enumerates every safe board once.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For n=4, columns [1,3,0,2] give [".Q..","...Q","Q...","..Q."]. The other solution uses columns [2,0,3,1]. For n=2 there is no solution.

docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

A loose search bound is O(n * n!), plus O(S * n^2) to materialize S boards. Auxiliary search space is O(n); output space is O(S * n^2). All state is local. Undo all three constraints after recursion. Store diagonal identifiers separately: row+column and row-column describe different diagonal families.

Alternative tradeoff: O(nn! + Sn^2) loose bound time; O(n) auxiliary; O(S*n^2) output space.

Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(S*n^2) output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Column and diagonal sets
    Time: O(n*n! + S*n^2) loose bound
    Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(S*n^2) output
    """

    def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> list[list[str]]:
        result = []
        path = []
        columns, ascending, descending = set(), set(), set()

        def visit(row):
            if row == n:
                result.append(["." * col + "Q" + "." * (n - col - 1) for col in path])
                return
            for col in range(n):
                if col in columns or row + col in ascending or row - col in descending:
                    continue
                columns.add(col)
                ascending.add(row + col)
                descending.add(row - col)
                path.append(col)
                visit(row + 1)
                path.pop()
                columns.remove(col)
                ascending.remove(row + col)
                descending.remove(row - col)

        visit(0)
        return result

docs.title: 2. Shifted attack masks
docs.text:
Time: O(nn! + Sn^2) loose bound

Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(S*n^2) output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Shifted attack masks
    Time: O(n*n! + S*n^2) loose bound
    Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(S*n^2) output
    """

    def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> list[list[str]]:
        full = (1 << n) - 1
        result, path = [], []

        def visit(columns, left, right):
            if columns == full:
                result.append(["." * col + "Q" + "." * (n - col - 1) for col in path])
                return
            free = full & ~(columns | left | right)
            while free:
                bit = free & -free
                free -= bit
                path.append(bit.bit_length() - 1)
                visit(columns | bit, ((left | bit) << 1) & full, (right | bit) >> 1)
                path.pop()

        visit(0, 0, 0)
        return result

class Solution:
    """Approach: Kadane ending-here states
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def maxSubArray(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        ending = answer = nums[0]
        for index in range(1, len(nums)):
            ending = max(nums[index], ending + nums[index])
            answer = max(answer, ending)
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Divide and conquer across a midpoint
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(log n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Divide and conquer across a midpoint
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(log n)
    """

    def maxSubArray(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        def solve(left, right):
            if right - left == 1:
                return nums[left]
            middle = (left + right) // 2
            left_sum = right_sum = -float("inf")
            total = 0
            for index in range(middle - 1, left - 1, -1):
                total += nums[index]
                left_sum = max(left_sum, total)
            total = 0
            for index in range(middle, right):
                total += nums[index]
                right_sum = max(right_sum, total)
            return max(solve(left, middle), solve(middle, right), left_sum + right_sum)

        return solve(0, len(nums))

class Solution:
    """Approach: Shrinking rectangular boundaries
    Time: O(mn)
    Space: O(1) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def spiralOrder(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
        top, bottom, left, right = 0, len(matrix) - 1, 0, len(matrix[0]) - 1
        answer = []
        while top <= bottom and left <= right:
            for col in range(left, right + 1):
                answer.append(matrix[top][col])
            top += 1
            for row in range(top, bottom + 1):
                answer.append(matrix[row][right])
            right -= 1
            if top <= bottom:
                for col in range(right, left - 1, -1):
                    answer.append(matrix[bottom][col])
                bottom -= 1
            if left <= right:
                for row in range(bottom, top - 1, -1):
                    answer.append(matrix[row][left])
                left += 1
        return answer

Time: O(mn)

Space: O(mn)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Direction simulation with visited cells
    Time: O(mn)
    Space: O(mn)
    """

    def spiralOrder(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
        rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        visited = [[False] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
        directions = ((0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0))
        row = col = direction = 0
        answer = []
        for _ in range(rows * cols):
            answer.append(matrix[row][col])
            visited[row][col] = True
            dr, dc = directions[direction]
            nr, nc = row + dr, col + dc
            if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols) or visited[nr][nc]:
                direction = (direction + 1) % 4
                dr, dc = directions[direction]
            row, col = row + dr, col + dc
        return answer

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Forward reachable frontier
docs.text: Scan left to right with a farthest-reachable boundary. If the current index lies beyond it, return False. Otherwise extend the boundary using the current index plus its jump length.

docs.title: Backward goal movement
docs.text: Start with the final index as the goal. Move the goal left whenever an earlier position can jump to it.

docs.title: Forward reachable frontier
docs.text: A jump permits any shorter distance, so reaching an endpoint also makes all intermediate positions reachable. Processing a reachable position adds exactly the interval it can reach. The maintained prefix is therefore all reachability known from processed positions.

docs.title: Backward goal movement
docs.text: The goal is always a position known to reach the end. Any earlier index that reaches the goal also reaches the end, and any valid start-to-end path must eventually join this backward reachable set.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [2,0,1,0], index 0 reaches through 2. Index 2 extends reach to 3, so the answer is True. For [1,0,2], index 2 lies beyond reach 1: False.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Forward reachable frontier):

O(n) time and O(1) space; input is unchanged. Never use a jump from an unreachable position to extend reach. A one-element array is already at the destination, even when its value is zero. This asks for existence, not the number of jumps.

Forward reachable frontier: O(n) time; O(1) space. Backward goal movement: O(n) time; O(1) space. Start with the final index as the goal. Move the goal left whenever an earlier position can jump to it.

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Forward reachable frontier
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def canJump(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
        farthest = 0
        for i, distance in enumerate(nums):
            if i > farthest:
                return False
            farthest = max(farthest, i + distance)
        return True

class Solution:
    """Approach: Backward goal movement
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def canJump(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
        goal = len(nums) - 1
        for i in range(len(nums) - 2, -1, -1):
            if i + nums[i] >= goal:
                goal = i
        return goal == 0

docs.title: Sort intervals by start

docs.title: Sort intervals by start

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sort intervals by start
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n) plus output
    """

    def merge(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
        result = []
        for start, end in sorted(intervals):
            if result and start <= result[-1][1]:
                result[-1][1] = max(result[-1][1], end)
            else:
                result.append([start, end])
        return result

docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n) plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sweep endpoint events
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n) plus output
    """

    def merge(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
        events = [
            (point, kind) for start, end in intervals for point, kind in ((start, 1), (end, -1))
        ]
        events.sort(key=lambda event: (event[0], -event[1]))
        active = 0
        result = []
        for point, change in events:
            if active == 0:
                start = point
            active += change
            if active == 0:
                result.append([start, point])
        return result

docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1) auxiliary plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Three-phase interval scan
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def insert(self, intervals: list[list[int]], newInterval: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        result = []
        start, end = newInterval
        i = 0
        while i < len(intervals) and intervals[i][1] < start:
            result.append(intervals[i][:])
            i += 1
        while i < len(intervals) and intervals[i][0] <= end:
            start = min(start, intervals[i][0])
            end = max(end, intervals[i][1])
            i += 1
        result.append([start, end])
        while i < len(intervals):
            result.append(intervals[i][:])
            i += 1
        return result

class Solution:

    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n) plus output

    def insert(self, intervals: list[list[int]], newInterval: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        result = []
        for start, end in sorted([*intervals, newInterval]):
            if result and start <= result[-1][1]:
                result[-1][1] = max(result[-1][1], end)
            else:
                result.append([start, end])
        return result

class Solution:
    """Approach: Layer boundary filling
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(1) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def generateMatrix(self, n: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        matrix = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        top, bottom, left, right, value = 0, n - 1, 0, n - 1, 1
        while top <= bottom and left <= right:
            for col in range(left, right + 1):
                matrix[top][col] = value
                value += 1
            top += 1
            for row in range(top, bottom + 1):
                matrix[row][right] = value
                value += 1
            right -= 1
            if top <= bottom:
                for col in range(right, left - 1, -1):
                    matrix[bottom][col] = value
                    value += 1
                bottom -= 1
            if left <= right:
                for row in range(bottom, top - 1, -1):
                    matrix[row][left] = value
                    value += 1
                left += 1
        return matrix

docs.title: 2. Output-marked direction simulation
docs.text:
Time: O(n squared)

Space: O(1) auxiliary plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Output-marked direction simulation
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(1) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def generateMatrix(self, n: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        matrix = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        directions = ((0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0))
        row = col = direction = 0
        for value in range(1, n * n + 1):
            matrix[row][col] = value
            dr, dc = directions[direction]
            nr, nc = row + dr, col + dc
            if not (0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n) or matrix[nr][nc]:
                direction = (direction + 1) % 4
                dr, dc = directions[direction]
            row, col = row + dr, col + dc
        return matrix

Approach Time Space Factorial block selection O(n^2) O(n) Repeated next permutation O(k*n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Factorial block selection
docs.text: Compute factorial block sizes. At each position, divide the remaining rank by the next block size, remove that indexed available digit, and continue with the remainder.

docs.title: Repeated next permutation
docs.text: Start at ascending digits and apply the standard lexicographic successor k-1 times: find a rising pivot, swap with its smallest larger suffix digit, and reverse the suffix.

docs.title: Factorial block selection
docs.text: Lexicographic permutations form equal blocks by their next digit. Quotient selects the containing block and remainder selects the same relative rank inside it.

docs.title: Repeated next permutation
docs.text: The descending suffix is already maximal. Increasing its preceding pivot minimally and resetting the suffix minimally produces exactly the next lexicographic sequence.

Python list deletion and suffix reversal cost linear time, included above. The successor baseline is much slower at large k; factorial selection skips complete permutation blocks.

docs.title: 1. Factorial block selection
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Factorial block selection
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def getPermutation(self, n: int, k: int) -> str:
        factorials = [1] * (n + 1)
        for index in range(1, n + 1):
            factorials[index] = factorials[index - 1] * index
        available = list(map(str, range(1, n + 1)))
        k -= 1
        result = []
        for remaining in range(n, 0, -1):
            index, k = divmod(k, factorials[remaining - 1])
            result.append(available.pop(index))
        return "".join(result)

docs.title: 2. Repeated next permutation
docs.text:
Time: O(k*n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Repeated next permutation
    Time: O(k*n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def getPermutation(self, n: int, k: int) -> str:
        values = list(range(1, n + 1))
        for _ in range(k - 1):
            pivot = n - 2
            while values[pivot] >= values[pivot + 1]:
                pivot -= 1
            successor = n - 1
            while values[successor] <= values[pivot]:
                successor -= 1
            values[pivot], values[successor] = values[successor], values[pivot]
            values[pivot + 1 :] = reversed(values[pivot + 1 :])
        return "".join(map(str, values))

docs.title: 1. Circularize then cut
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Circularize then cut
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def rotateRight(self, head: ListNode | None, k: int) -> ListNode | None:
        if head is None:
            return None
        tail, length = head, 1
        while tail.next:
            tail = tail.next
            length += 1
        k %= length
        if k == 0:
            return head
        tail.next = head
        before = head
        for _ in range(length - k - 1):
            before = before.next
        result = before.next
        before.next = None
        return result

docs.title: 2. Reorder node references
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Reorder node references
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def rotateRight(self, head: ListNode | None, k: int) -> ListNode | None:
        order = []
        while head:
            order.append(head)
            head = head.next
        if not order:
            return None
        k %= len(order)
        order = order[-k:] + order[:-k] if k else order
        for index, node in enumerate(order):
            node.next = order[index + 1] if index + 1 < len(order) else None
        return order[0]

docs.text:
Approach Time Space Compressed row counts O(m*n) O(min(m,n)) Choose the down-step positions O(min(m,n)) arithmetic operations O(1) integer objects

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Compressed row counts
docs.text: Choose the smaller grid dimension as the row width to minimize memory. Initialize every entry to one: the first row has exactly one path to each cell. For each remaining row, update columns from left to right using dp[column] += dp[column-1]. The old entry counts paths from above; the updated left entry counts paths from the left. The first column stays one.

docs.title: Choose the down-step positions
docs.text: Every route contains m-1 down moves and n-1 right moves. Choose which m-1 positions in the fixed-length move sequence contain down moves using an exact binomial coefficient. Accumulate that coefficient multiplicatively, dividing exactly after each factor.

docs.title: Compressed row counts
docs.text: The last move uniquely partitions paths into two disjoint groups: paths from above and paths from the left. Their sum therefore counts every path exactly once. Boundary cells have only one possible route. Induction over rows and columns proves every updated entry is the correct path count. Transposing the dimensions preserves the right/down path count.

docs.title: Choose the down-step positions
docs.text: There is a bijection between paths and subsets of down-step positions: reading a subset produces one route, and recording a route produces that subset. Counting subsets therefore counts paths exactly.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For a 3 by 3 grid, begin with [1,1,1]. The second row becomes [1,2,3]. The third becomes [1,3,6], so six paths reach the destination.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Compressed row counts approach:

O(m*n) time and O(min(m,n)) auxiliary space; dimensions are unchanged. Update left to right so the left contribution belongs to the current row. A single row or column naturally yields one path. Counting shortest paths does not require BFS because every legal right/down path has the same length.

Compressed row counts: O(m*n) time; O(min(m,n)) space. Choose the down-step positions: O(min(m,n)) arithmetic operations; O(1) integer objects. The combinatorial variant avoids a grid table. Its exact product/division updates use arbitrary-precision arithmetic, so bit cost and integer storage grow with the result.

docs.title: 1. Compressed row counts
docs.text:
Time: O(m*n)

Space: O(min(m,n))

class Solution:
    """Approach: Compressed row counts
    Time: O(m*n)
    Space: O(min(m,n))
    """

    def uniquePaths(self, m: int, n: int) -> int:
        width, height = min(m, n), max(m, n)
        dp = [1] * width
        for _ in range(1, height):
            for column in range(1, width):
                dp[column] += dp[column - 1]
        return dp[-1]

docs.title: 2. Choose the down-step positions
docs.text:
Time: O(min(m,n)) arithmetic operations

Space: O(1) integer objects

class Solution:
    """Approach: Choose the down-step positions
    Time: O(min(m,n)) arithmetic operations
    Space: O(1) integer objects
    """

    def uniquePaths(self, m: int, n: int) -> int:
        steps = m + n - 2
        chosen = min(m - 1, n - 1)
        result = 1
        for count in range(1, chosen + 1):
            result = result * (steps - count + 1) // count
        return result

class Solution:
    """Approach: Rolling obstacle-aware row
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(C)
    """

    def uniquePathsWithObstacles(self, obstacleGrid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        dp = [0] * len(obstacleGrid[0])
        dp[0] = 1
        for row in obstacleGrid:
            for column, blocked in enumerate(row):
                if blocked:
                    dp[column] = 0
                elif column:
                    dp[column] += dp[column - 1]
        return dp[-1]

Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(R*C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Padded full path table
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def uniquePathsWithObstacles(self, obstacleGrid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, columns = len(obstacleGrid), len(obstacleGrid[0])
        table = [[0] * (columns + 1) for _ in range(rows + 1)]
        table[0][1] = 1
        for row in range(1, rows + 1):
            for column in range(1, columns + 1):
                if not obstacleGrid[row - 1][column - 1]:
                    table[row][column] = table[row - 1][column] + table[row][column - 1]
        return table[-1][-1]

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Grid DP.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Find the minimum sum along a path from the top-left to the bottom-right of a nonempty rectangular grid. Moves go right or down, and both endpoint values contribute to the sum.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. The last step into a cell comes from above or from the left.
  2. The best path cost only needs the preceding row and current row's left cell.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 071 · #62 · Next: 073 · #1143

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Compressed minimum-cost row O(R*C) O(C) Shortest path on weighted grid O(RC log(RC)) O(R*C)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Compressed minimum-cost row
docs.text: Use one cost entry per column. Set entries to infinity, then set dp[0] to zero as a virtual predecessor of the starting cell. Process rows from top to bottom and columns from left to right. For each cell, take the smaller of the old entry from above and the updated entry to its left, then add the cell value. At column zero the left cost is infinity.

docs.title: Shortest path on weighted grid
docs.text: View right/down moves as weighted directed edges that charge the destination cell. Seed the heap with the starting cell value, relax improvements, and stop when the target is removed with its best cost.

docs.title: Compressed minimum-cost row
docs.text: Every path reaching a cell uses one of its legal predecessors. An optimal path must use an optimal path to that predecessor: otherwise replacing the prefix reduces its total. The minimum of the two predecessor optima plus the cell value is therefore optimal. Infinity removes nonexistent predecessors; the virtual zero seeds exactly the starting cell.

docs.title: Shortest path on weighted grid
docs.text: All cell values are nonnegative, so Dijkstra finalizes a popped minimum distance. Charging the start once and each destination once gives exactly the required path sum.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[2,5],[1,3]], the first row gives costs [2,7]. On the second row, column zero becomes 3 and column one becomes min(7,3)+3=6. Return 6.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Compressed minimum-cost row approach:

O(rows*columns) time and O(columns) space; input is unchanged. Left-to-right updates are essential to use the current row's left cost. Mutating the grid is unnecessary, and choosing the cheaper immediate neighbor greedily does not account for expensive cells later in the path.

Compressed minimum-cost row: O(RC) time; O(C) space. Shortest path on weighted grid: O(RC log(RC)) time; O(RC) space. Dijkstra demonstrates the graph formulation but is slower and larger than exploiting the grid DAG. Both leave the grid unchanged.

docs.title: 1. Compressed minimum-cost row
docs.text:
Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Compressed minimum-cost row
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(C)
    """

    def minPathSum(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        dp = [float("inf")] * len(grid[0])
        dp[0] = 0
        for row in grid:
            for column, value in enumerate(row):
                left = dp[column - 1] if column else float("inf")
                dp[column] = min(dp[column], left) + value
        return dp[-1]

docs.title: 2. Shortest path on weighted grid
docs.text:
Time: O(RC log(RC))

Space: O(R*C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Shortest path on weighted grid
    Time: O(R*C log(R*C))
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def minPathSum(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        from heapq import heappop, heappush

        rows, columns = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        best = {(0, 0): grid[0][0]}
        heap = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]
        while heap:
            cost, row, column = heappop(heap)
            if best[(row, column)] != cost:
                continue
            if (row, column) == (rows - 1, columns - 1):
                return cost
            for nr, nc in ((row + 1, column), (row, column + 1)):
                if nr < rows and nc < columns:
                    following = cost + grid[nr][nc]
                    if following < best.get((nr, nc), float("inf")):
                        best[(nr, nc)] = following
                        heappush(heap, (following, nr, nc))
        return 0

docs.title: Split components and reduce
docs.text: Split on slashes and reduce components into a directory stack, then join them under root.

docs.title: Streaming character parser
docs.text: Scan characters and flush each component at a slash, avoiding a separate array of all split components.

docs.title: Split components and reduce
docs.text: After every component the stack is the canonical path to that point. Ordinary names descend, dot stays, and double dot removes the latest descent if present.

docs.title: Streaming character parser
docs.text: The parser emits exactly the same component sequence as separator splitting. Reducing each emitted component keeps the stack equal to the canonical prefix path.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: "/a//b/../c/./" becomes "/a/c". A component "..." is an ordinary directory name.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls

Split components and reduce: O(n) time; O(n) space.

Streaming character parser: O(n) time; O(n) space.

Input is unchanged. This is lexical path normalization, with no filesystem or symbolic-link lookup. Both methods retain the root slash.

docs.title: 1. Split components and reduce
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Split components and reduce
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def simplifyPath(self, path: str) -> str:
        directories = []
        for part in path.split("/"):
            if part == "..":
                if directories:
                    directories.pop()
            elif part and part != ".":
                directories.append(part)
        return "/" + "/".join(directories)

docs.title: 2. Streaming character parser
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Streaming character parser
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def simplifyPath(self, path: str) -> str:
        directories, component = [], []
        for char in path + "/":
            if char != "/":
                component.append(char)
                continue
            name = "".join(component)
            component.clear()
            if name == "..":
                if directories:
                    directories.pop()
            elif name and name != ".":
                directories.append(name)
        return "/" + "/".join(directories)

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Find the fewest single-character insertions, deletions, and replacements needed to turn one string into another. Each operation costs one.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Define a state for transforming one prefix into another prefix.
  2. Its last operation depends on the above, left, or diagonal prefix state.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 073 · #1143 · Next: 075 · #97

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Rolling edit-distance row O(m*n+m+n) O(min(m,n)+1) Full prefix edit table O((m+1)*(n+1)) O((m+1)*(n+1))

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Rolling edit-distance row
docs.text: Use the shorter string as columns because edit distance is symmetric. Initialize dp[j]=j: transforming an empty source into j characters requires j insertions. For source row i, set dp[0]=i for deletions. Visit columns left to right while saving the old diagonal. Matching characters reuse that diagonal. Otherwise use one plus the minimum of above, left, and diagonal, which respectively represent deletion, insertion, and replacement.

docs.title: Full prefix edit table
docs.text: Retain all prefix-pair distances. Initialize the top row as insertion counts and first column as deletion counts; fill matching diagonals or the cheapest edit predecessor.

docs.title: Rolling edit-distance row
docs.text: Any optimal transformation either matches the two final characters or ends with one of the three allowed edits. Removing that final action leaves a transformation between one of the predecessor prefix pairs. Choosing its optimal cost cannot worsen the result. Trying all final actions finds the minimum, while each transition constructs a valid transformation. Boundary initialization covers empty prefixes, so induction proves the table correct.

docs.title: Full prefix edit table
docs.text: Each predecessor corresponds to exactly one legal final edit, and a match consumes equal characters for free. The minimum covers every transformation; retaining the full table preserves the same recurrence without overwriting dependencies.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "cat" to "cut", matching c costs zero, replacing a with u costs one, and matching t adds nothing. The final distance is 1. From "cat" to the empty string, initialization records three deletions.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Rolling edit-distance row approach:

O(m*n+m+n) time and O(min(m,n)+1) space; strings are unchanged. Save the old above value before overwriting it so the next diagonal remains available. Matching characters cost zero. Transposition is not one of the allowed operations, so swapping two letters does not automatically cost one.

Rolling edit-distance row: O(mn+m+n) time; O(min(m,n)+1) space. Full prefix edit table: O((m+1)(n+1)) time; O((m+1)*(n+1)) space. The full table makes edit reconstruction possible with an added backward walk; this implementation returns only the cost. Both support empty strings and preserve them.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Rolling edit-distance row
docs.text:
Time: O(m*n+m+n)

Space: O(min(m,n)+1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Rolling edit-distance row
    Time: O(m*n+m+n)
    Space: O(min(m,n)+1)
    """

    def minDistance(self, word1: str, word2: str) -> int:
        if len(word1) < len(word2):
            word1, word2 = word2, word1
        dp = list(range(len(word2) + 1))
        for row, first in enumerate(word1, 1):
            diagonal = dp[0]
            dp[0] = row
            for column, second in enumerate(word2, 1):
                above = dp[column]
                dp[column] = (
                    diagonal if first == second else 1 + min(above, dp[column - 1], diagonal)
                )
                diagonal = above
        return dp[-1]

docs.title: 2. Full prefix edit table
docs.text:
Time: O((m+1)*(n+1))

Space: O((m+1)*(n+1))

class Solution:
    """Approach: Full prefix edit table
    Time: O((m+1)*(n+1))
    Space: O((m+1)*(n+1))
    """

    def minDistance(self, word1: str, word2: str) -> int:
        table = [[0] * (len(word2) + 1) for _ in range(len(word1) + 1)]
        for i in range(len(word1) + 1):
            table[i][0] = i
        for j in range(len(word2) + 1):
            table[0][j] = j
        for i, first in enumerate(word1, 1):
            for j, second in enumerate(word2, 1):
                table[i][j] = (
                    table[i - 1][j - 1]
                    if first == second
                    else 1 + min(table[i - 1][j], table[i][j - 1], table[i - 1][j - 1])
                )
        return table[-1][-1]

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space First-row and first-column markers O(mn) O(1) Explicit zero row and column sets O(mn) O(m+n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: First-row and first-column markers
docs.text: Remember whether the first row or column originally contains zero. Mark interior zeroes on those boundaries, zero the interior, then finish the boundaries.

docs.title: Explicit zero row and column sets
docs.text: Collect all original zero row and column indices before mutating any cell, then zero the indicated cells in a second pass.

docs.title: First-row and first-column markers
docs.text: Markers record exactly the rows and columns containing original zeroes. Delaying writes preserves original observations, and separate boundary flags prevent marker writes from inventing boundary triggers.

docs.title: Explicit zero row and column sets
docs.text: The stored sets contain only original zero coordinates. A cell is overwritten exactly when its row or column belongs to the trigger sets, matching the specification directly.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: [[1,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,1]] becomes [[1,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,1]]. The new zero at (0,1) must not zero row 0 completely.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
First-row and first-column markers: O(mn) time; O(1) space.

Explicit zero row and column sets: O(mn) time; O(m+n) space.

Both methods mutate the original rows and preserve object identity. The set method is a valid simpler alternative but does not meet the optional constant-space follow-up.

docs.title: 1. First-row and first-column markers
docs.text:
Time: O(mn)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: First-row and first-column markers
    Time: O(mn)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def setZeroes(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> None:
        rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        first_row = any(value == 0 for value in matrix[0])
        first_col = any(matrix[row][0] == 0 for row in range(rows))
        for row in range(1, rows):
            for col in range(1, cols):
                if matrix[row][col] == 0:
                    matrix[row][0] = matrix[0][col] = 0
        for row in range(1, rows):
            for col in range(1, cols):
                if matrix[row][0] == 0 or matrix[0][col] == 0:
                    matrix[row][col] = 0
        if first_row:
            for col in range(cols):
                matrix[0][col] = 0
        if first_col:
            for row in range(rows):
                matrix[row][0] = 0

docs.title: 2. Explicit zero row and column sets
docs.text:
Time: O(mn)

Space: O(m+n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Explicit zero row and column sets
    Time: O(mn)
    Space: O(m+n)
    """

    def setZeroes(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> None:
        rows, cols = set(), set()
        for row, values in enumerate(matrix):
            for col, value in enumerate(values):
                if value == 0:
                    rows.add(row)
                    cols.add(col)
        for row, values in enumerate(matrix):
            for col in range(len(values)):
                if row in rows or col in cols:
                    values[col] = 0

docs.title: Hints

  2. You can instead choose a row before searching inside it.

Approach Time Space Virtual flattened binary search O(log(mn)) O(1) Row selection then column search O(log m+log n) O(1)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Virtual flattened binary search
docs.text: Binary-search indices from zero to mn-1 and translate each midpoint with divmod by the column count.

docs.title: Row selection then column search
docs.text: Find the last row whose first value is at most target, then binary-search that row.

docs.title: Virtual flattened binary search
docs.text: The row separation guarantee makes virtual row-major order globally sorted. Ordinary binary- search comparisons therefore discard only impossible indices.

docs.title: Row selection then column search
docs.text: Every earlier row ends below the selected row's first value and every later row starts above target. Only the selected row can contain target; its internal order permits binary search.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: In [[1,3,5],[7,9,11]], target 9 maps to virtual index 4 and row 1, column 1.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Virtual flattened binary search: O(log(mn)) time; O(1) space.

Row selection then column search: O(log m+log n) time; O(1) space.

Input is unchanged. m and n are rows and columns. The stronger row separation guarantee is required; independently sorted rows and columns alone do not suffice.

docs.title: 1. Virtual flattened binary search
docs.text:
Time: O(log(mn))

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Virtual flattened binary search
    Time: O(log(mn))
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def searchMatrix(self, matrix: list[list[int]], target: int) -> bool:
        rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        low, high = 0, rows * cols - 1
        while low <= high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            row, col = divmod(middle, cols)
            if matrix[row][col] == target:
                return True
            if matrix[row][col] < target:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle - 1
        return False

docs.title: 2. Row selection then column search
docs.text:
Time: O(log m+log n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Row selection then column search
    Time: O(log m+log n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def searchMatrix(self, matrix: list[list[int]], target: int) -> bool:
        low, high = 0, len(matrix)
        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if matrix[middle][0] <= target:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle
        if low == 0:
            return False
        row = matrix[low - 1]
        left, right = 0, len(row)
        while left < right:
            middle = (left + right) // 2
            if row[middle] < target:
                left = middle + 1
            else:
                right = middle
        return left < len(row) and row[left] == target

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Dutch national flag partition
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def sortColors(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
        zero = scan = 0
        two = len(nums) - 1
        while scan <= two:
            if nums[scan] == 0:
                nums[zero], nums[scan] = nums[scan], nums[zero]
                zero += 1
                scan += 1
            elif nums[scan] == 2:
                nums[scan], nums[two] = nums[two], nums[scan]
                two -= 1
            else:
                scan += 1

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Count then overwrite
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def sortColors(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
        counts = [0, 0, 0]
        for value in nums:
            counts[value] += 1
        index = 0
        for value, count in enumerate(counts):
            for _ in range(count):
                nums[index] = value
                index += 1

docs.title: 76 Minimum Window Substring
docs.text:
Hard · Sliding windows · Core · Learning step 14 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Sliding windows · Frequency maps.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Find the shortest substring of s containing every required character of t, including repetitions. Return an empty string if none exists.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Count missing occurrences, not only missing distinct characters.
  2. Once a window is valid, shrink it until removing one more character breaks it.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 013 · #567 · Next: 015 · #239

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Deficit-count shrinking window O(n+m) expected O(alphabet) Filtered relevant-position window O(n+m) expected O(n+alphabet)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Deficit-count shrinking window
docs.text: Keep signed remaining counts and a total missing count. Adding a needed occurrence reduces missing; extra occurrences make their counts negative. While nothing is missing, record the window and advance left until validity is lost.

docs.title: Filtered relevant-position window
docs.text: Discard text positions whose character is absent from the pattern, then slide over the remaining (index, character) pairs. This can reduce window bookkeeping when relevant characters are sparse.

docs.title: Deficit-count shrinking window
docs.text: A window is valid exactly when missing is zero. For each right endpoint, shrinking examines its shortest valid ending window. A removed prefix cannot produce a shorter future window than one already recorded with that same left boundary.

docs.title: Filtered relevant-position window
docs.text: A shortest valid window starts and ends at relevant characters, since irrelevant endpoints can be removed. Deficit counts on the filtered sequence therefore examine every potentially optimal boundary pair.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For s="BAAC" and t="AAC", the whole string first becomes valid. Removing B keeps it valid, yielding "AAC". Removing its first A makes one A missing. The answer is "AAC".

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Deficit-count shrinking window):

Expected O(len(s)+len(t)) time and O(alphabet size) auxiliary space, plus the returned substring. Inputs are unchanged. Store indices and slice only once; copying every improving window could add quadratic work. Negative counts encode surplus characters and must not be reset to zero.

Deficit-count shrinking window: O(n+m) expected time; O(alphabet) space. Filtered relevant-position window: O(n+m) expected time; O(n+alphabet) space. Discard text positions whose character is absent from the pattern, then slide over the remaining (index, character) pairs. This can reduce window bookkeeping when relevant characters are sparse.

docs.title: 1. Deficit-count shrinking window
docs.text:
Time: O(n+m) expected

Space: O(alphabet)

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Deficit-count shrinking window
    Time: O(n+m) expected
    Space: O(alphabet)
    """

    def minWindow(self, s: str, t: str) -> str:
        need = Counter(t)
        missing = len(t)
        left = best_start = 0
        best_length = len(s) + 1
        for right, char in enumerate(s):
            if need[char] > 0:
                missing -= 1
            need[char] -= 1
            while missing == 0:
                if right - left + 1 < best_length:
                    best_start, best_length = left, right - left + 1
                outgoing = s[left]
                need[outgoing] += 1
                if need[outgoing] > 0:
                    missing += 1
                left += 1
        return "" if best_length > len(s) else s[best_start : best_start + best_length]

docs.title: 2. Filtered relevant-position window
docs.text:
Time: O(n+m) expected

Space: O(n+alphabet)

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Filtered relevant-position window
    Time: O(n+m) expected
    Space: O(n+alphabet)
    """

    def minWindow(self, s: str, t: str) -> str:
        need = {}
        for char in t:
            need[char] = need.get(char, 0) + 1
        filtered = [(i, char) for i, char in enumerate(s) if char in need]
        have = {}
        missing = len(t)
        left = 0
        best_start, best_size = 0, len(s) + 1
        for index, char in filtered:
            have[char] = have.get(char, 0) + 1
            if have[char] <= need[char]:
                missing -= 1
            while missing == 0:
                start, outgoing = filtered[left]
                if index - start + 1 < best_size:
                    best_start, best_size = start, index - start + 1
                have[outgoing] -= 1
                if have[outgoing] < need[outgoing]:
                    missing += 1
                left += 1
        return "" if best_size > len(s) else s[best_start : best_start + best_size]

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Pruned increasing backtracking O(k*C(n,k)) O(k) auxiliary plus output Lexicographic combination successor O(k*C(n,k)) O(k) auxiliary plus output

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Pruned increasing backtracking
docs.text: Grow increasing paths. Limit each loop's upper bound so enough values remain to fill the remaining positions. Save a copy at length k.

docs.title: Lexicographic combination successor
docs.text: Start at [1,...,k]. Repeatedly increment the rightmost position that can increase, then reset its suffix to consecutive successors.

docs.title: Pruned increasing backtracking
docs.text: Increasing choices give each combination one representation. The upper bound discards only prefixes with insufficient remaining values, so no valid combination is lost.

docs.title: Lexicographic combination successor
docs.text: The rightmost increment changes the smallest possible suffix; filling it minimally produces the next lexicographic combination. Starting at the minimum and stopping at the maximum visits all combinations exactly once.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For n=4 and k=2, the successor sequence is [1,2], [1,3], [1,4], [2,3], [2,4], [3,4].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Pruned increasing backtracking: O(kC(n,k)) time; O(k) auxiliary plus output space. Lexicographic combination successor: O(kC(n,k)) time; O(k) auxiliary plus output space. All state is local. k=n produces one answer. Output copies dominate storage. The successor bound at zero-based index i is n-k+i+1, not n for every slot.

docs.title: 1. Pruned increasing backtracking
docs.text:
Time: O(k*C(n,k))

Space: O(k) auxiliary plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Pruned increasing backtracking
    Time: O(k*C(n,k))
    Space: O(k) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def combine(self, n: int, k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        result, path = [], []

        def visit(start):
            needed = k - len(path)
            if needed == 0:
                result.append(path.copy())
                return
            for value in range(start, n - needed + 2):
                path.append(value)
                visit(value + 1)
                path.pop()

        visit(1)
        return result

docs.title: 2. Lexicographic combination successor
docs.text:
Time: O(k*C(n,k))

Space: O(k) auxiliary plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Lexicographic combination successor
    Time: O(k*C(n,k))
    Space: O(k) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def combine(self, n: int, k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        current = list(range(1, k + 1))
        result = []
        while True:
            result.append(current.copy())
            index = k - 1
            while index >= 0 and current[index] == n - k + index + 1:
                index -= 1
            if index < 0:
                return result
            current[index] += 1
            for following in range(index + 1, k):
                current[following] = current[following - 1] + 1

docs.title: Increasing-index backtracking
docs.text: Backtrack from a starting index. Record the current subset, then choose each remaining value in turn, recurse after its index, and undo the choice. Choosing increasing indices avoids duplicate representations.

docs.title: Subset bitmasks
docs.text: Enumerate masks from zero through 2^n-1. Bit i selects input position i. Build a fresh list from the set bits for each mask; no mutable recursive path is needed.

docs.title: Increasing-index backtracking
docs.text: Every subset has one unique sequence of increasing input indices. The recursion visits exactly those sequences, including the empty sequence, so it enumerates each subset once.

docs.title: Subset bitmasks
docs.text: Every subset corresponds to exactly one n-bit membership vector. Enumerating each vector once therefore enumerates all subsets once, including the empty mask.

Default approach costs and behavior:

O(n * 2^n) time including answer copies, O(n) auxiliary path/recursion space, and O(n * 2^n) output storage. Input is unchanged. Append path.copy(), not the live path object; otherwise later undo operations change saved answers. The index advances after a choice because each value can be used at most once.

Alternative tradeoff: O(n2^n) time; O(n) temporary; O(n2^n) output space.

            result.append(path.copy())

class Solution:
    """Approach: Subset bitmasks
    Time: O(n*2^n)
    Space: O(n) temporary; O(n*2^n) output

    def subsets(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        return [
            [value for index, value in enumerate(nums) if mask & (1 << index)]
            for mask in range(1 << len(nums))
        ]

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Path-set backtracking O(RC4^L) loose bound O(L) Iterative path bitmasks O(RC4^L) loose bound under bounded grid size O(L) under the bounded grid size

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Path-set backtracking
docs.text: Backtrack over row, column, and matched-word index. Reject out-of-bounds, already-used, or mismatching cells. Add a matching cell to the current path, try its four neighbors, then remove it even if a branch succeeds.

docs.title: Iterative path bitmasks
docs.text: Keep candidate paths on an explicit stack with a bitmask of used cells. Each branch receives its own integer mask, so it needs no shared-path undo. The official grid has at most 36 cells, bounding integer-mask size.

docs.title: Path-set backtracking
docs.text: Each recursive step adds exactly one matching, unused neighboring cell. The search therefore generates exactly the legal word paths from each start. Path-local undo lets another branch use cells that an earlier branch abandoned.

docs.title: Iterative path bitmasks
docs.text: The mask records exactly the cells used by a candidate matching prefix. Extending to an unused matching neighbor generates precisely the legal next paths. Exhausting all starts and extensions is complete.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For board [["A","B"],["C","D"]], "ABDC" follows all four cells and succeeds. "ABA" fails because returning to the first A would reuse its cell.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

A loose upper bound is O(rows * cols * 4^L) time for word length L, with O(L) path and recursion space. Board and word are unchanged on success or failure. The official word limit keeps recursion shallow. A global visited set would incorrectly exclude cells from different candidate paths.

Alternative tradeoff: O(RC4^L) loose time bound and O(L) auxiliary stack space. Only a bounded number of sibling states remains pending per path depth; each mask fits the official grid's at-most-36-cell domain.

Time: O(RC4^L) loose bound

Space: O(L)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Path-set backtracking
    Time: O(R*C*4^L) loose bound
    Space: O(L)
    """

    def exist(self, board: list[list[str]], word: str) -> bool:
        rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0])
        path = set()

        def visit(row, col, index):
            if not (0 <= row < rows and 0 <= col < cols):
                return False
            if (row, col) in path or board[row][col] != word[index]:
                return False
            if index == len(word) - 1:
                return True
            path.add((row, col))
            found = any(
                visit(row + dr, col + dc, index + 1)
                for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1))
            )
            path.remove((row, col))
            return found

        return any(visit(row, col, 0) for row in range(rows) for col in range(cols))

docs.title: 2. Iterative path bitmasks
docs.text:
Time: O(RC4^L) loose bound under bounded grid size

Space: O(L) under the bounded grid size

class Solution:
    """Approach: Iterative path bitmasks
    Time: O(R*C*4^L) loose bound under bounded grid size
    Space: O(L) under the bounded grid size
    """

    def exist(self, board: list[list[str]], word: str) -> bool:
        rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0])
        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                if board[row][col] != word[0]:
                    continue
                stack = [(row, col, 0, 1 << (row * cols + col))]
                while stack:
                    r, c, index, mask = stack.pop()
                    if index == len(word) - 1:
                        return True
                    for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                        if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols:
                            bit = 1 << (nr * cols + nc)
                            if not mask & bit and board[nr][nc] == word[index + 1]:
                                stack.append((nr, nc, index + 1, mask | bit))
        return False

class Solution:
    """Approach: Two-slot output comparison
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def removeDuplicates(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        write = 0
        for value in nums:
            if write < 2 or value != nums[write - 2]:
                nums[write] = value
                write += 1
        return write

class Solution:
    """Approach: Explicit input-run counts
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def removeDuplicates(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        previous = None
        count = write = 0
        for read in range(len(nums)):
            value = nums[read]
            count = count + 1 if value == previous else 1
            previous = value
            if count <= 2:
                nums[write] = value
                write += 1
        return write

docs.title: Duplicate-aware sorted-half search
docs.text: Use binary search when one half is distinguishably sorted. When left, middle, and right values match, discard the equal endpoints after checking the midpoint.

docs.title: Run compression then rotated binary search
docs.text: Copy one value per adjacent equal run. If the first and last runs represent the same value, remove the final copy, then search the distinct rotated sequence.

docs.title: Duplicate-aware sorted-half search

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Duplicate-aware sorted-half search
    Time: O(n) worst; O(log n) with informative splits
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def search(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> bool:
        low, high = 0, len(nums) - 1
        while low <= high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if nums[middle] == target:
                return True
            if nums[low] == nums[middle] == nums[high]:
                low += 1
                high -= 1
            elif nums[low] <= nums[middle]:
                if nums[low] <= target < nums[middle]:
                    high = middle - 1
                else:
                    low = middle + 1
            elif nums[middle] < target <= nums[high]:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle - 1
        return False

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Run compression then rotated binary search
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def search(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> bool:
        values = []
        for value in nums:
            if not values or value != values[-1]:
                values.append(value)
        if len(values) > 1 and values[0] == values[-1]:
            values.pop()
        low, high = 0, len(values) - 1
        while low <= high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if values[middle] == target:
                return True
            if values[low] <= values[middle]:
                if values[low] <= target < values[middle]:
                    high = middle - 1
                else:
                    low = middle + 1
            elif values[middle] < target <= values[high]:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle - 1
        return False

docs.title: Skip duplicate runs

docs.title: Count then filter
docs.text: Count values in a first pass. In a second pass, append only original nodes with count one and terminate the result. This avoids relying on run boundaries but uses a map.

docs.title: Skip duplicate runs
docs.text: Sorted order guarantees that a value occurs in exactly one run. A singleton run is therefore exactly a globally unique value, so retaining only those runs is sufficient.

docs.title: 1. Skip duplicate runs
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

from collections import Counter


class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Skip duplicate runs
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def deleteDuplicates(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        dummy = ListNode(next=head)
        before = dummy
        while head:
            end = head.next
            while end and end.val == head.val:
                end = end.next
            if head.next is end:
                before = head
            else:
                before.next = end
            head = end
        return dummy.next

docs.title: 2. Count then filter
docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(n)

from collections import Counter


class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Count then filter
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def deleteDuplicates(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        counts = Counter()
        current = head
        while current:
            counts[current.val] += 1
            current = current.next
        dummy = tail = ListNode()
        while head:
            following = head.next
            if counts[head.val] == 1:
                tail.next = head
                tail = head
            head = following
        tail.next = None
        return dummy.next

docs.title: Increasing-height stack
docs.text: Maintain increasing candidate heights paired with their earliest start indices. When a shorter bar arrives, pop taller candidates and compute their maximal rightward area. Carry the popped start leftward for the new height. A virtual zero-height bar at the end flushes remaining candidates.

docs.title: Nearest smaller boundaries
docs.text: Compute the nearest strictly smaller bar on each side with two stack scans, then use each bar as the limiting height over its widest legal span.

docs.title: Increasing-height stack
docs.text: Each stored height can extend from its saved start through the previous bar. The first shorter bar is its right boundary; it cannot extend farther. Every optimal rectangle has a minimum bar whose full valid span is evaluated.

docs.title: Nearest smaller boundaries
docs.text: Any rectangle has a minimum-height bar. For that bar, the nearest smaller boundaries give the maximal span at its height, which contains the original rectangle and has at least its area.

docs.text: For [2, 4, 4, 1], the final 1 closes height-4 spans of width 1 then 2, giving best area 8. Height 2 covers width 3 for area 6.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Increasing-height stack):

O(n) time and O(n) space; each candidate enters and leaves once. Input is unchanged. Width is current_index-start. Propagate the earliest popped start; forgetting it loses wide rectangles. The sentinel is virtual, so no zero is appended to the input.

Increasing-height stack: O(n) time; O(n) space. Nearest smaller boundaries: O(n) time; O(n) space. Compute the nearest strictly smaller bar on each side with two stack scans, then use each bar as the limiting height over its widest legal span.

class Solution:
    """Approach: Increasing-height stack
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def largestRectangleArea(self, heights: list[int]) -> int:
        stack = []
        best = 0
        for i in range(len(heights) + 1):
            height = heights[i] if i < len(heights) else 0
            start = i
            while stack and stack[-1][1] > height:
                start, previous = stack.pop()
                best = max(best, previous * (i - start))
            stack.append((start, height))
        return best

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Nearest smaller boundaries
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def largestRectangleArea(self, heights: list[int]) -> int:
        size = len(heights)
        left, right = [-1] * size, [size] * size
        stack = []
        for i, value in enumerate(heights):
            while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= value:
                stack.pop()
            if stack:
                left[i] = stack[-1]
            stack.append(i)
        stack.clear()
        for i in range(size - 1, -1, -1):
            while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= heights[i]:
                stack.pop()
            if stack:
                right[i] = stack[-1]
            stack.append(i)
        return max(
            (height * (right[i] - left[i] - 1) for i, height in enumerate(heights)), default=0
        )

class Solution:
    """Approach: Histogram heights and monotone stack
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(C)
    """

    def maximalRectangle(self, matrix: list[list[str]]) -> int:
        heights = [0] * (len(matrix[0]) + 1)
        answer = 0
        for row in matrix:
            for column, value in enumerate(row):
                heights[column] = heights[column] + 1 if value == "1" else 0
            stack = [-1]
            for column, height in enumerate(heights):
                while len(stack) > 1 and heights[stack[-1]] > height:
                    top = stack.pop()
                    answer = max(answer, heights[top] * (column - stack[-1] - 1))
                stack.append(column)
        return answer
