docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Palindrome table and prefix cuts
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def minCut(self, s: str) -> int:
        palindrome = [[False] * len(s) for _ in s]
        cuts = list(range(-1, len(s)))
        for end in range(len(s)):
            for start in range(end + 1):
                if s[start] == s[end] and (end - start < 2 or palindrome[start + 1][end - 1]):
                    palindrome[start][end] = True
                    cuts[end + 1] = min(cuts[end + 1], cuts[start] + 1)
        return cuts[-1]

docs.title: 2. Expand centers while relaxing prefix cuts
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Expand centers while relaxing prefix cuts
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def minCut(self, s: str) -> int:
        cuts = list(range(-1, len(s)))
        for center in range(len(s)):
            for left, right in ((center, center), (center - 1, center)):
                while left >= 0 and right < len(s) and s[left] == s[right]:
                    cuts[right + 1] = min(cuts[right + 1], cuts[left] + 1)
                    left -= 1
                    right += 1
        return cuts[-1]

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Make a deep copy of the connected undirected graph reachable from a supplied node. Every copied node and neighbor list must be separate from the originals.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. A cycle means the same original node can appear through several paths.

Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Breadth-first identity map O(V+E) O(V+E) including output Two-pass stack clone O(V+E) O(V+E) including output

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Breadth-first identity map
docs.text: Use breadth-first search and map original nodes to copies. Create the starting clone immediately. For each original, create and enqueue unseen neighbor clones. Append each neighbor's mapped clone to the current copy's list. Return the starting clone, or None for an empty graph.

docs.title: Two-pass stack clone
docs.text: First discover nodes with an explicit DFS stack and allocate identity-mapped clones. Only after all nodes exist, fill every clone adjacency list in a second pass.

docs.title: Breadth-first identity map
docs.text: The dictionary pairs each original with exactly one new object. Recording a clone before visiting its edges breaks cycles: later paths reuse that clone. Processing every adjacency list copies all edges and their order. Copied edges always point to dictionary clones, never original nodes.

docs.title: Two-pass stack clone
docs.text: The first pass creates exactly one clone per reachable original. The second maps every edge endpoint through that complete dictionary, preserving order and cycles without ever referencing original nodes in copied edges.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: In a triangle 1--2--3--1, create clone 1, then clones 2 and 3 while processing its neighbors. When processing 2, its edges reuse clones 1 and 3. The copied triangle has the same connections with entirely new node identities.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Breadth-first identity map approach:

O(V + E) time, O(V) traversal and mapping space, and O(V + E) output space. The original graph is unchanged. Key the dictionary by node identity. Copying only neighbor lists would still share the original nodes.

Breadth-first identity map: O(V+E) time; O(V+E) including output space. Two-pass stack clone: O(V+E) time; O(V+E) including output space. The stack may hold O(E) pending references; the two-pass structure avoids wiring partially explored nodes. Original nodes and neighbor lists remain unchanged.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Breadth-first identity map
docs.text:
Time: O(V+E)

Space: O(V+E) including output

from collections import deque


class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=0, neighbors=None):
        self.val = val
        self.neighbors = [] if neighbors is None else neighbors


class Solution:
    """Approach: Breadth-first identity map
    Time: O(V+E)
    Space: O(V+E) including output
    """

    def cloneGraph(self, node: Node | None) -> Node | None:
        if node is None:
            return None
        copies = {node: Node(node.val)}
        queue = deque([node])
        while queue:
            original = queue.popleft()
            for neighbor in original.neighbors:
                if neighbor not in copies:
                    copies[neighbor] = Node(neighbor.val)
                    queue.append(neighbor)
                copies[original].neighbors.append(copies[neighbor])
        return copies[node]

docs.title: 2. Two-pass stack clone
docs.text:
Time: O(V+E)

Space: O(V+E) including output

from collections import deque


class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=0, neighbors=None):
        self.val = val
        self.neighbors = [] if neighbors is None else neighbors


class Solution:
    """Approach: Two-pass stack clone
    Time: O(V+E)
    Space: O(V+E) including output
    """

    def cloneGraph(self, node: Node | None) -> Node | None:
        if node is None:
            return None
        copies = {}
        stack = [node]
        while stack:
            original = stack.pop()
            if original in copies:
                continue
            copies[original] = Node(original.val)
            stack.extend(neighbor for neighbor in original.neighbors if neighbor not in copies)
        for original, clone in copies.items():
            clone.neighbors = [copies[neighbor] for neighbor in original.neighbors]
        return copies[node]

docs.title: Task

docs.text:
Approach Time Space Reset after a failed segment O(n) O(1) Start after the minimum prefix balance O(n) O(1)

docs.title: Reset after a failed segment
docs.text: Accumulate total fuel balance and a candidate segment balance. Whenever the candidate balance becomes negative, restart just after that station.

docs.title: Start after the minimum prefix balance
docs.text: Locate the smallest cumulative gas-minus-cost prefix, including the empty prefix. If total balance is nonnegative, start just after that minimum.

docs.title: Reset after a failed segment
docs.text: If a segment from s fails at i, every later start within it has no more available prefix surplus and also fails by i. Thus the reset discards only impossible starts. Nonnegative global total guarantees the final candidate also survives the wraparound.

docs.title: Start after the minimum prefix balance
docs.text: Every suffix prefix after the minimum has nonnegative relative balance. On the wrapped portion, the original prefix minus the minimum is augmented by nonnegative total balance. Both parts therefore keep the tank nonnegative.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: [1,2,3,4,5] gas and [3,4,5,1,2] cost has balance [-2,-2,-2,3,3]. The minimum cumulative balance ends at station 2, so start at 3.

docs.text:
Reset after a failed segment: O(n) time; O(1) space.

Start after the minimum prefix balance: O(n) time; O(1) space.

Inputs are unchanged. The tank has no upper capacity bound. A negative total immediately rules out every start, regardless of local rich stations.

class Solution:
    """Approach: Reset after a failed segment
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def canCompleteCircuit(self, gas: list[int], cost: list[int]) -> int:
        total = tank = start = 0
        for i, (supply, expense) in enumerate(zip(gas, cost, strict=True)):
            difference = supply - expense
            total += difference
            tank += difference
            if tank < 0:
                start = i + 1
                tank = 0
        return start if total >= 0 else -1

docs.text:

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Start after the minimum prefix balance
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def canCompleteCircuit(self, gas: list[int], cost: list[int]) -> int:
        prefix = minimum = 0
        start = 0
        for i in range(len(gas)):
            prefix += gas[i] - cost[i]
            if prefix < minimum:
                minimum = prefix
                start = i + 1
        return -1 if prefix < 0 else start % len(gas)

docs.title: Two directional candy passes
docs.text: The forward count is a necessary lower bound from each increasing prefix run. The backward pass takes the maximum with the necessary decreasing-run bound. These maxima satisfy both neighbors and are componentwise minimal.

docs.title: Slope lengths with peak correction
docs.text: An increasing run needs successive counts 1 through up+1; a decreasing run has the symmetric forced counts. Their shared peak needs the larger requirement, not their sum. The peak>=down correction removes its duplicate contribution until the descending requirement exceeds it.

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Two directional candy passes
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def candy(self, ratings: list[int]) -> int:
        candies = [1] * len(ratings)
        for i in range(1, len(ratings)):
            if ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]:
                candies[i] = candies[i - 1] + 1
        for i in range(len(ratings) - 2, -1, -1):
            if ratings[i] > ratings[i + 1]:
                candies[i] = max(candies[i], candies[i + 1] + 1)
        return sum(candies)

docs.title: 2. Slope lengths with peak correction
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Slope lengths with peak correction
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def candy(self, ratings: list[int]) -> int:
        total = 1
        up = down = peak = 0
        for i in range(1, len(ratings)):
            if ratings[i] > ratings[i - 1]:
                up += 1
                peak = up
                down = 0
                total += up + 1
            elif ratings[i] == ratings[i - 1]:
                up = down = peak = 0
                total += 1
            else:
                up = 0
                down += 1
                total += down + 1
                if peak >= down:
                    total -= 1
        return total

docs.title: Two-mask modulo-three state machine
docs.text: Update masks of bits seen once and twice, clearing bits when their third occurrence arrives.

docs.title: Count each of 32 bits
docs.text: Sum each bit over all values modulo three and reconstruct an unsigned 32-bit result, then convert its sign.

docs.title: Two-mask modulo-three state machine
docs.text: For each bit, the mask transitions cycle through counts 0,1,2,0. Tripled values contribute zero modulo three, leaving exactly the unique value's bits in the once mask.

docs.title: Count each of 32 bits
docs.text: Each repeated value contributes a multiple of three at every bit. The residues are therefore the unique value's two's-complement bits; subtracting 2^32 for a set sign bit recovers the signed value.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: [2,2,3,2] leaves the bits of 3 after modulo-three cancellation. [-2,-2,-2,-7] must reconstruct -7, not its unsigned encoding.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls

Inputs are unchanged. The state-machine update order matters: twice uses the new once mask. The explicit bit-count method must restore the signed interpretation.

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Two-mask modulo-three state machine
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def singleNumber(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        once = twice = 0
        for value in nums:
            once = (once ^ value) & ~twice
            twice = (twice ^ value) & ~once
        return once

docs.title: 2. Count each of 32 bits
docs.text:
Time: O(32n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Count each of 32 bits
    Time: O(32n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def singleNumber(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        answer = 0
        for bit in range(32):
            if sum((value >> bit) & 1 for value in nums) % 3:
                answer |= 1 << bit
        return answer - (1 << 32) if answer & (1 << 31) else answer

Approach Time Space Identity map O(n) expected O(n) auxiliary and output Interleaved copies O(n) O(1) auxiliary; O(n) output

docs.title: Identity map
docs.text: Use a dictionary from original node identity to copied node, including None mapping to None. The first pass allocates nodes; the second connects copied next and random references by dictionary lookup.

docs.title: Interleaved copies
docs.text: Insert each clone directly after its original. A random target's next link now identifies its clone. Wire random links, then separate the alternating chains and restore every original next pointer. This temporarily mutates the input during the call.

docs.title: Identity map
docs.text: The map is a one-to-one correspondence between original and new nodes. Translating each edge through that map preserves the entire pointer structure while ensuring every non-null returned reference belongs to the copy.

docs.title: Interleaved copies
docs.text: Alternation supplies the original-to-copy correspondence without a dictionary. All random edges are translated before separation; restoring alternate next links recovers the original chain and leaves a disjoint copied chain.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Let A(value 4) point next to B(value 4), with A.random=B and B.random=A. Create distinct A' and B', then set A'.next=B', A'.random=B', B'.random=A'. Equal values do not make A and B the same node.

Default approach costs and behavior:

Expected O(n) time and O(n) map space, plus O(n) output nodes. Input pointers are unchanged. Key by object identity, not value. A shallow copy that reuses original random targets violates the deep-copy contract. An empty list returns None.

Alternative tradeoff: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary; O(n) output space.

docs.title: 1. Identity map
docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(n) auxiliary and output

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None, random=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next
        self.random = random


class Solution:
    """Approach: Identity map
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(n) auxiliary and output
    """

    def copyRandomList(self, head: Node | None) -> Node | None:
        copies = {None: None}
        current = head
        while current:
            copies[current] = Node(current.val)
            current = current.next
        current = head
        while current:
            copies[current].next = copies[current.next]
            copies[current].random = copies[current.random]
            current = current.next
        return copies[head]

docs.title: 2. Interleaved copies
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1) auxiliary; O(n) output

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None, random=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next
        self.random = random


class Solution:
    """Approach: Interleaved copies
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1) auxiliary; O(n) output
    """

    def copyRandomList(self, head: Node | None) -> Node | None:
        current = head
        while current:
            current.next = Node(current.val, current.next)
            current = current.next.next
        current = head
        while current:
            current.next.random = current.random.next if current.random else None
            current = current.next.next
        dummy = tail = Node()
        current = head
        while current:
            copy = current.next
            current.next = copy.next
            tail.next = copy
            tail = copy
            current = current.next
        tail.next = None
        return dummy.next

docs.text:
Approach Time Space Reachable prefixes and word lengths O(W + D log D + nDL) O(n+D+K+L) Trie walks from reachable starts O(W+n*L) O(W+n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Reachable prefixes and word lengths
docs.text: Build a word set and sorted distinct word lengths. Let reachable[end] mean the prefix ending just before end can be segmented. Initialize reachable[0] to true. For every end position, try candidate word lengths up to end. If reachable[end-length] and the intervening substring belongs to the word set, mark this prefix reachable and stop. Return the final prefix state.

docs.title: Trie walks from reachable starts
docs.text: Build a character trie with terminal markers. From each reachable prefix, walk forward through matching trie edges and mark every word ending reached. A failed edge stops that start without allocating substrings.

docs.title: Reachable prefixes and word lengths
docs.text: A successful transition appends a dictionary word to an already valid segmentation. Conversely, any segmentation has a final dictionary word; its length is tried, and its preceding prefix is valid. Increasing end positions ensures that earlier prefix is already solved. Thus the table contains exactly the segmentable prefixes.

docs.title: Trie walks from reachable starts
docs.text: Trie terminal nodes correspond exactly to dictionary words. Every marked endpoint appends one such word to a valid prefix, and every valid final word is explored from its reachable start.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "redredblue" and ["red","blue"], positions 3, 6, and 10 become reachable. The second "red" reuses a word, which is allowed. A prefix such as "redr" remains unreachable.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Reachable prefixes and word lengths approach:

Let n be string length, D distinct lengths, L maximum word length, and W total dictionary characters. Expected time is O(W + D log D + nDL): Python slicing and hashing each new substring cost its length. Space is O(n+D+number_of_words+L), including a temporary slice; word strings are referenced. Inputs stay unchanged. Greedy longest-word selection can miss a valid split that starts with a shorter word.

Reachable prefixes and word lengths: O(W + D log D + nDL) time; O(n+D+K+L) space. Trie walks from reachable starts: O(W+n*L) time; O(W+n) space. W is total dictionary characters, D distinct lengths, K word count, and L maximum word length. Trie walks avoid substring copy/hash costs but allocate dictionaries per trie node.

docs.text:
Time: O(W + D log D + nDL)

Space: O(n+D+K+L)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Reachable prefixes and word lengths
    Time: O(W + D log D + n*D*L)
    Space: O(n+D+K+L)
    """

    def wordBreak(self, s: str, wordDict: list[str]) -> bool:
        words = set(wordDict)
        lengths = sorted({len(word) for word in words})
        reachable = [False] * (len(s) + 1)
        reachable[0] = True
        for end in range(1, len(s) + 1):
            for length in lengths:
                if length > end:
                    break
                if reachable[end - length] and s[end - length : end] in words:
                    reachable[end] = True
                    break
        return reachable[-1]

docs.title: 2. Trie walks from reachable starts
docs.text:
Time: O(W+n*L)

Space: O(W+n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Trie walks from reachable starts
    Time: O(W+n*L)
    Space: O(W+n)
    """

    def wordBreak(self, s: str, wordDict: list[str]) -> bool:
        trie = {}
        for word in wordDict:
            node = trie
            for character in word:
                node = node.setdefault(character, {})
            node[None] = True
        reachable = [False] * (len(s) + 1)
        reachable[0] = True
        for start in range(len(s)):
            if not reachable[start]:
                continue
            node = trie
            for end in range(start, len(s)):
                character = s[end]
                if character not in node:
                    break
                node = node[character]
                if None in node:
                    reachable[end + 1] = True
        return reachable[-1]

Space: O(W+n^2+P*n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Feasible word-boundary DAG and iterative paths
    Time: O(W+n^3+P*n^2) expected
    Space: O(W+n^2+P*n^2)
    """

    def wordBreak(self, s: str, wordDict: list[str]) -> list[str]:
        words = set(wordDict)
        lengths = sorted({len(word) for word in words})
        successors = [[] for _ in range(len(s) + 1)]
        feasible = [False] * (len(s) + 1)
        feasible[-1] = True
        for start in range(len(s) - 1, -1, -1):
            for length in lengths:
                end = start + length
                if end > len(s):
                    break
                if feasible[end] and s[start:end] in words:
                    feasible[start] = True
                    successors[start].append(end)
        result = []
        stack = [(0, [])] if feasible[0] else []
        while stack:
            start, path = stack.pop()
            if start == len(s):
                result.append(" ".join(path))
            else:
                stack.extend((end, path + [s[start:end]]) for end in successors[start])
        return result

docs.title: 2. Memoized suffix sentences
docs.text:
Time: O(W+n^3+P*n^2) expected

Space: O(W+n+P*n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Memoized suffix sentences
    Time: O(W+n^3+P*n^2) expected
    Space: O(W+n+P*n^2)
    """

    def wordBreak(self, s: str, wordDict: list[str]) -> list[str]:
        from functools import cache

        words = set(wordDict)

        @cache
        def sentences(start):
            if start == len(s):
                return ("",)
            result = []
            for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1):
                word = s[start:end]
                if word in words:
                    for tail in sentences(end):
                        result.append(word + (" " + tail if tail else ""))
            return tuple(result)

        return list(sentences(0))

docs.text: If the noncyclic prefix has length a and cycle length c, the meeting displacement is congruent to -a modulo c. Advancing both by a steps from head and meeting therefore reaches the entrance simultaneously.

docs.text: For A->B->C->D->B, Floyd eventually meets inside B,C,D. Entry recovery returns the original B, not a new node with its value.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Floyd meeting and entry recovery: O(n) time; O(1) space. First repeated node identity: O(n) expected time; O(n) space. Neither solution mutates links or values. Empty and one-node acyclic lists return None; a self-loop returns that node. Comparing values would misidentify repeated values in an acyclic list.

docs.title: 1. Floyd meeting and entry recovery
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Floyd meeting and entry recovery
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def detectCycle(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        slow = fast = head
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
            if slow is fast:
                entry = head
                while entry is not slow:
                    entry = entry.next
                    slow = slow.next
                return entry
        return None

docs.title: 2. First repeated node identity
docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(n)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: First repeated node identity
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def detectCycle(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        seen = set()
        while head:
            if head in seen:
                return head
            seen.add(head)
            head = head.next
        return None

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Split reverse weave O(n) O(1) Node deque O(n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Split reverse weave
docs.text: Slow and fast pointers find the first half's last node. Detach its successor, reverse that second half iteratively, then alternate one node from each half. The first half is at least as long, simplifying the final merge.

docs.title: Node deque
docs.text: Collect original nodes in a deque. Repeatedly attach its first and last remaining nodes, then terminate the final tail. Buffering makes the requested positional order explicit at the cost of extra storage.

docs.title: Split reverse weave
docs.text: The first half supplies original nodes in forward order and the reversed half supplies the remaining nodes in backward order. Alternating them creates exactly the required sequence. Detaching before reversal prevents links between the two working chains.

docs.title: Node deque
docs.text: Each deque removal chooses the next required first or last unused original position. Removing each node once preserves all identities; terminating the tail removes any stale link that could make a cycle.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [1,2,3,4,5], split into [1,2,3] and [4,5], reverse the latter to [5,4], then weave to obtain [1,5,2,4,3].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Mutates links and reuses every original node; values are unchanged. Save next pointers before rewiring. Forgetting to detach the halves can create a cycle. Odd and even lengths need separate mental traces.

Alternative tradeoff: O(n) time; O(n) space.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Split reverse weave
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

from collections import deque


class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Split reverse weave
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def reorderList(self, head: ListNode) -> None:
        slow = fast = head
        while fast.next and fast.next.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
        current = slow.next
        slow.next = None
        second = None
        while current:
            following = current.next
            current.next = second
            second, current = current, following
        first = head
        while second:
            first_next, second_next = first.next, second.next
            first.next = second
            second.next = first_next
            first, second = first_next, second_next

docs.title: 2. Node deque
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

from collections import deque


class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Node deque
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def reorderList(self, head: ListNode) -> None:
        remaining = deque()
        current = head
        while current:
            remaining.append(current)
            current = current.next
        tail = ListNode()
        while remaining:
            tail.next = remaining.popleft()
            tail = tail.next
            if remaining:
                tail.next = remaining.pop()
                tail = tail.next
        tail.next = None

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Implement a fixed-capacity key-value cache. Get returns a value or -1. Get and put both mark a present key as recently used; overflow evicts the least recent key.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. You need both direct key lookup and movable recency order.
  2. An ordered dictionary provides those operations in the standard library.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 049 · #295 · Next: 051 · #78

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Ordered dictionary recency O(1) expected per operation O(capacity) Hash map and linked recency O(1) expected per operation O(capacity)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Ordered dictionary recency
docs.text: Keep an OrderedDict from least recent at the front to most recent at the back. Successful get moves the key to the back. Put writes the value and moves the key to the back, then removes the front item if capacity is exceeded.

docs.title: Hash map and linked recency
docs.text: Map keys to entries in a circular doubly linked list. The sentinel's next entry is oldest and previous entry newest. Successful access detaches an entry and appends it before the sentinel; overflow removes the oldest.

docs.title: Ordered dictionary recency
docs.text: The dictionary order records the order of last successful use: each use removes the key from its old position and places it newest. The front is consequently the least recently used key, making eviction exact.

docs.title: Hash map and linked recency
docs.text: The map owns exactly the live entries and the list records their last-use order. Moving an accessed entry changes only its recency, while removing the oldest entry updates both representations together.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: At capacity 2, put (1,10), put (2,20), then get(1). Recency becomes [2,1]. Putting (3,30) evicts 2; get(2) now returns -1.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

Expected O(1) per operation and O(capacity) space. The object owns all cache state. Updating an existing key also refreshes recency. A failed get must not insert anything. If library ordering is disallowed in an interview, implement the same invariant with a hash map plus doubly linked list.

Alternative tradeoff: O(1) expected per operation time; O(capacity) space.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Ordered dictionary recency
docs.text:
Time: O(1) expected per operation

Space: O(capacity)

from collections import OrderedDict


class CacheEntry:
    def __init__(self, key=0, value=0):
        self.key = key
        self.value = value
        self.previous = self.next = self


class LRUCache:
    """Approach: Ordered dictionary recency
    Time: O(1) expected per operation
    Space: O(capacity)
    """

    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.values = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        if key not in self.values:
            return -1
        self.values.move_to_end(key)
        return self.values[key]

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        self.values[key] = value
        self.values.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self.values) > self.capacity:
            self.values.popitem(last=False)

docs.title: 2. Hash map and linked recency
docs.text:
Time: O(1) expected per operation

Space: O(capacity)

from collections import OrderedDict


class CacheEntry:
    def __init__(self, key=0, value=0):
        self.key = key
        self.value = value
        self.previous = self.next = self


class LRUCache:
    """Approach: Hash map and linked recency
    Time: O(1) expected per operation
    Space: O(capacity)
    """

    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.entries = {}
        self.root = CacheEntry()

    def _touch(self, entry):
        entry.previous.next = entry.next
        entry.next.previous = entry.previous
        entry.previous = self.root.previous
        entry.next = self.root
        self.root.previous.next = entry
        self.root.previous = entry

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        if key not in self.entries:
            return -1
        entry = self.entries[key]
        self._touch(entry)
        return entry.value

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        if key in self.entries:
            entry = self.entries[key]
            entry.value = value
        else:
            entry = CacheEntry(key, value)
            self.entries[key] = entry
        self._touch(entry)
        if len(self.entries) > self.capacity:
            oldest = self.root.next
            self.root.next = oldest.next
            oldest.next.previous = self.root
            del self.entries[oldest.key]

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Sort a linked list in ascending order using insertion sort. Move original nodes rather than replacing their values or allocating a copied output list.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Insert the next unsorted node into an already sorted prefix.
  2. An array can binary-search insertion positions, although Python insertion still shifts references.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 292 · #142 · Next: 294 · #148

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Linked sorted-prefix insertion O(n^2) worst O(1) Binary insertion of node references O(n^2) worst O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Linked sorted-prefix insertion
docs.text: Detach each next input node, scan a dummy-headed sorted chain to its insertion point, and splice it there. Insert after existing equals for stability.

docs.title: Binary insertion of node references
docs.text: Maintain a sorted node-reference array. Binary-search each value's upper insertion boundary, insert its reference, and finally reconnect the array order.

docs.title: Linked sorted-prefix insertion
docs.text: The prefix starts empty and remains sorted after inserting at the first greater value. Each original node enters once, so the final chain is a stable sorted permutation.

docs.title: Binary insertion of node references
docs.text: The upper boundary places each node after earlier equal nodes and before greater values. Induction maintains sorted stable order; final relinking preserves all node identities.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For values [4,2,3], insert 4 into empty, then 2 before 4, then 3 between them, giving [2,3,4].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Linked sorted-prefix insertion: O(n^2) worst time; O(1) space. Binary insertion of node references: O(n^2) worst time; O(n) space. Both mutate next pointers and preserve values. The array variant reduces comparison search to logarithmic work but not total insertion cost, because list.insert shifts references. Its final tail must point to None.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Linked sorted-prefix insertion
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2) worst

Space: O(1)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Linked sorted-prefix insertion
    Time: O(n^2) worst
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def insertionSortList(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        dummy = ListNode()
        while head:
            following = head.next
            before = dummy
            while before.next and before.next.val <= head.val:
                before = before.next
            head.next = before.next
            before.next = head
            head = following
        return dummy.next

docs.title: 2. Binary insertion of node references
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2) worst

Space: O(n)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary insertion of node references
    Time: O(n^2) worst
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def insertionSortList(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        ordered = []
        while head:
            low, high = 0, len(ordered)
            while low < high:
                middle = (low + high) // 2
                if ordered[middle].val <= head.val:
                    low = middle + 1
                else:
                    high = middle
            ordered.insert(low, head)
            head = head.next
        for index, node in enumerate(ordered):
            node.next = ordered[index + 1] if index + 1 < len(ordered) else None
        return ordered[0] if ordered else None

  2. Bottom-up merge sizes 1,2,4,... avoid recursive stack space.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Bottom-up linked merge sort O(n log(n+1)) O(1) auxiliary Sort buffered node references O(n log(n+1)) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Bottom-up linked merge sort
docs.text: Count nodes, then merge adjacent fixed-width runs in repeated passes. Split runs by cutting links and reconnect each merged run through a tail pointer.

docs.title: Sort buffered node references
docs.text: Collect nodes, use Python's stable comparison sort on their values, then rebuild the next chain in that order.

docs.title: Bottom-up linked merge sort
docs.text: At the start of a width-w pass, every run of at most w nodes is sorted. Stable two-way merging makes sorted runs of at most 2w; doubling eventually covers the whole list.

docs.title: Sort buffered node references
docs.text: The sorted reference array is a stable ascending permutation of the original nodes. Reconnecting it produces a sorted list without changing node values.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [4,1,3,2], width-one merges give [1,4] and [2,3]. The width-two merge gives [1,2,3,4].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Bottom-up linked merge sort: O(n log(n+1)) time; O(1) auxiliary space. Sort buffered node references: O(n log(n+1)) time; O(n) space. Both mutate links and preserve every original node and value. Only the default meets the constant-space follow-up. Python sorting and node buffering require linear auxiliary references. Iteration handles lists beyond recursion limits.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Bottom-up linked merge sort
docs.text:
Time: O(n log(n+1))

Space: O(1) auxiliary

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Bottom-up linked merge sort
    Time: O(n log(n+1))
    Space: O(1) auxiliary
    """

    def sortList(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        def split(first, width):
            if first is None:
                return None
            for _ in range(width - 1):
                if first.next is None:
                    break
                first = first.next
            following = first.next
            first.next = None
            return following

        length, current = 0, head
        while current:
            length += 1
            current = current.next
        dummy = ListNode(next=head)
        width = 1
        while width < length:
            tail, current = dummy, dummy.next
            while current:
                left = current
                right = split(left, width)
                current = split(right, width)
                while left and right:
                    if left.val <= right.val:
                        tail.next, left = left, left.next
                    else:
                        tail.next, right = right, right.next
                    tail = tail.next
                tail.next = left or right
                while tail.next:
                    tail = tail.next
            width *= 2
        return dummy.next

docs.title: 2. Sort buffered node references
docs.text:
Time: O(n log(n+1))

Space: O(n)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Sort buffered node references
    Time: O(n log(n+1))
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def sortList(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        ordered = []
        while head:
            ordered.append(head)
            head = head.next
        ordered.sort(key=lambda node: node.val)
        for index, node in enumerate(ordered):
            node.next = ordered[index + 1] if index + 1 < len(ordered) else None
        return ordered[0] if ordered else None

docs.title: 150 Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
docs.text:
Medium · Stacks · Core · Learning step 16 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Stacks.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Evaluate a valid postfix expression containing integers and the four arithmetic operators. Integer division truncates toward zero, and divisors are nonzero.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. An operator consumes the two most recent unfinished values.
  2. Which popped value is the right operand of subtraction or division?
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 015 · #239 · Next: 017 · #155

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Value stack O(n) O(n) Explicit expression-tree reduction O(n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Value stack
docs.text: Push numbers onto a stack. On an operator, pop right and then left, evaluate left operator right, and push the result. For division, divide absolute values with integer division and restore the sign.

docs.title: Explicit expression-tree reduction
docs.text: First build an expression tree with a node stack, then evaluate it using an iterative postorder traversal. This separates parsing from evaluation and avoids recursion depth limits.

docs.title: Value stack
docs.text: After each token, the stack contains the values of completed subexpressions that have not yet been consumed. Replacing two operands by their result preserves that interpretation. A valid complete expression leaves exactly one result.

docs.title: Explicit expression-tree reduction
docs.text: Each operator joins the two complete operand expressions immediately before it. Iterative postorder computes children before their operator, so every node has the same value as its represented expression.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Tokens ["7", "-3", "/", "2", "*"] first produce 7 / -3 = -2, then -2 * 2 = -4. The final result is -4.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Value stack):

O(n) time and O(n) space for n tokens under the problem's bounded-integer model. Inputs are unchanged. Python // floors negative results, so -7 // 3 is not the required -2. Do not reverse operands. Integer-only division avoids float conversion.

Value stack: O(n) time; O(n) space. Explicit expression-tree reduction: O(n) time; O(n) space. First build an expression tree with a node stack, then evaluate it using an iterative postorder traversal. This separates parsing from evaluation and avoids recursion depth limits.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Value stack
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Value stack
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def evalRPN(self, tokens: list[str]) -> int:
        stack = []
        for token in tokens:
            if token not in {"+", "-", "*", "/"}:
                stack.append(int(token))
                continue
            right, left = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
            if token == "+":
                result = left + right
            elif token == "-":
                result = left - right
            elif token == "*":
                result = left * right
            else:
                result = abs(left) // abs(right)
                if (left < 0) != (right < 0):
                    result = -result
            stack.append(result)
        return stack[0]

docs.title: 2. Explicit expression-tree reduction
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Explicit expression-tree reduction
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def evalRPN(self, tokens: list[str]) -> int:
        expressions = []
        for token in tokens:
            if token not in {"+", "-", "*", "/"}:
                expressions.append((int(token), None, None))
            else:
                right, left = expressions.pop(), expressions.pop()
                expressions.append((token, left, right))
        pending = [(expressions[0], False)]
        values = []
        while pending:
            node, expanded = pending.pop()
            token, left, right = node
            if left is None:
                values.append(token)
            elif not expanded:
                pending.extend(((node, True), (right, False), (left, False)))
            else:
                b, a = values.pop(), values.pop()
                if token == "+":
                    values.append(a + b)
                elif token == "-":
                    values.append(a - b)
                elif token == "*":
                    values.append(a * b)
                else:
                    quotient = abs(a) // abs(b)
                    values.append(-quotient if (a < 0) != (b < 0) else quotient)
        return values[0]

    Time: O(n)

docs.title: 2. Manual backward word scanner
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Manual backward word scanner
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def reverseWords(self, s: str) -> str:
        words = []
        index = len(s) - 1
        while index >= 0:
            while index >= 0 and s[index] == " ":
                index -= 1
            end = index + 1
            while index >= 0 and s[index] != " ":
                index -= 1
            if end > index + 1:
                words.append(s[index + 1 : end])
        return " ".join(words)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Maximum and minimum ending products
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def maxProduct(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        high = low = answer = nums[0]
        for index in range(1, len(nums)):
            value = nums[index]
            high, low = max(value, high * value, low * value), min(value, high * value, low * value)
            answer = max(answer, high)
        return answer

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Prefix and suffix product scans
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def maxProduct(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        answer = nums[0]
        prefix = suffix = 1
        for index in range(len(nums)):
            prefix = (prefix if prefix else 1) * nums[index]
            suffix = (suffix if suffix else 1) * nums[-1 - index]
            answer = max(answer, prefix, suffix)
        return answer

class Solution:

    Time: O(n) worst; O(log n) without ambiguous ties
    Space: O(1)

        low, high = 0, len(nums) - 1

            middle = (low + high) // 2

Time: O(n) worst

Space: O(log n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Divide and combine with sorted-interval pruning
    Time: O(n) worst
    Space: O(log n)
    """

    def findMin(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        def minimum(low, high):
            if low == high or nums[low] < nums[high]:
                return nums[low]
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            return min(minimum(low, middle), minimum(middle + 1, high))

        return minimum(0, len(nums) - 1)

Time: O(1) per operation

Space: O(n)

class MinStack:
    """Approach: Minimum snapshot per entry
    Time: O(1) per operation
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        minimum = min(val, self.stack[-1][1]) if self.stack else val
        self.stack.append((val, minimum))

    def pop(self) -> None:
        self.stack.pop()

    def top(self) -> int:
        return self.stack[-1][0]

    def getMin(self) -> int:
        return self.stack[-1][1]

docs.title: 2. Separate minima stack
docs.text:
Time: O(1) per operation

Space: O(n)

class MinStack:
    """Approach: Separate minima stack
    Time: O(1) per operation
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.values = []
        self.minima = []

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        self.values.append(val)
        if not self.minima or val <= self.minima[-1]:
            self.minima.append(val)

    def pop(self) -> None:
        value = self.values.pop()
        if value == self.minima[-1]:
            self.minima.pop()

    def top(self) -> int:
        return self.values[-1]

    def getMin(self) -> int:
        return self.minima[-1]

class Solution:
    """Approach: Split numeric revisions
    Time: O(n+m)
    Space: O(n+m)
    """

    def compareVersion(self, version1: str, version2: str) -> int:
        from itertools import zip_longest

        first = version1.split(".")
        second = version2.split(".")
        for a, b in zip_longest(first, second, fillvalue="0"):
            left, right = int(a), int(b)
            if left != right:
                return 1 if left > right else -1
        return 0

Time: O(n+m)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Streaming revision accumulators
    Time: O(n+m)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def compareVersion(self, version1: str, version2: str) -> int:
        i = j = 0
        while i < len(version1) or j < len(version2):
            first = second = 0
            while i < len(version1) and version1[i] != ".":
                first = first * 10 + ord(version1[i]) - ord("0")
                i += 1
            while j < len(version2) and version2[j] != ".":
                second = second * 10 + ord(version2[j]) - ord("0")
                j += 1
            if first != second:
                return 1 if first > second else -1
            i += 1
            j += 1
        return 0

class Solution:
    """Approach: Inward two pointers
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def twoSum(self, numbers: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
        left, right = 0, len(numbers) - 1
        while left < right:
            total = numbers[left] + numbers[right]
            if total == target:
                return [left + 1, right + 1]
            if total < target:
                left += 1
            else:
                right -= 1
        raise ValueError("The problem guarantees a solution")

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary search complements
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def twoSum(self, numbers: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
        for i, value in enumerate(numbers):
            left, right = i + 1, len(numbers)
            while left < right:
                middle = (left + right) // 2
                if numbers[middle] < target - value:
                    left = middle + 1
                else:
                    right = middle
            if left < len(numbers) and numbers[left] == target - value:
                return [i + 1, left + 1]
        raise ValueError("The problem guarantees a solution")

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Lazy inorder stack O(h) constructor; O(1) amortized next; O(1) hasNext O(h) Materialized inorder snapshot O(n) constructor; O(1) next and hasNext O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Lazy inorder stack
docs.text: Push the root's left chain initially. Next pops one node, then pushes its right subtree's left chain. HasNext checks whether the stack is nonempty.

docs.title: Materialized inorder snapshot
docs.text: Collect an iterative inorder array at construction and advance an index for subsequent operations. This spends more startup work and storage for constant-time individual queries.

docs.title: Lazy inorder stack
docs.text: The stack top is always the smallest unvisited node. Its left descendants are complete; after visiting it, the right subtree's left chain supplies the next candidates.

docs.title: Materialized inorder snapshot
docs.text: The snapshot stores every node value in exact inorder once. Reading consecutive indices therefore yields precisely the ascending iteration sequence.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: A BST containing [1,3,6] in sorted order returns 1, then 3, then 6. HasNext becomes false after the third next.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Lazy inorder stack: O(h) constructor; O(1) amortized next; O(1) hasNext time; O(h) space. Materialized inorder snapshot: O(n) constructor; O(1) next and hasNext time; O(n) space. The tree is unchanged and is assumed stable during iteration. The snapshot variant misses the O(h)-space follow-up. Lazy next is amortized constant time, not worst-case constant for a single call.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Lazy inorder stack
docs.text:
Time: O(h) constructor; O(1) amortized next; O(1) hasNext

Space: O(h)

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class BSTIterator:
    """Approach: Lazy inorder stack
    Time: O(h) constructor; O(1) amortized next; O(1) hasNext
    Space: O(h)
    """

    def __init__(self, root: TreeNode):
        self.stack = []
        self._push_left(root)

    def _push_left(self, node):
        while node:
            self.stack.append(node)
            node = node.left

    def next(self) -> int:
        node = self.stack.pop()
        self._push_left(node.right)
        return node.val

    def hasNext(self) -> bool:
        return bool(self.stack)

docs.title: 2. Materialized inorder snapshot
docs.text:
Time: O(n) constructor; O(1) next and hasNext

Space: O(n)

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class BSTIterator:
    """Approach: Materialized inorder snapshot
    Time: O(n) constructor; O(1) next and hasNext
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self, root: TreeNode):
        self.values = []
        stack, current = [], root
        while current or stack:
            while current:
                stack.append(current)
                current = current.left
            current = stack.pop()
            self.values.append(current.val)
            current = current.right
        self.index = 0

    def next(self) -> int:
        value = self.values[self.index]
        self.index += 1
        return value

    def hasNext(self) -> bool:
        return self.index < len(self.values)

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Backward required-health row O(R*C) O(C) Binary-search feasible initial health O(RClog B) O(C)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Backward required-health row
docs.text: Work backward, storing the minimum health needed before entering each cell. Choose the cheaper successor requirement, subtract the cell effect, and clamp to one.

docs.title: Binary-search feasible initial health
docs.text: For a trial initial health, propagate the largest positive remaining health through a rolling frontier; dead paths use -1. Binary-search between zero and one plus all negative losses.

docs.title: Backward required-health row
docs.text: A path survives exactly when its health after this cell meets one successor requirement. Choosing the smaller successor and requiring at least one before entry gives the exact optimal requirement.

docs.title: Binary-search feasible initial health
docs.text: More initial health never hurts feasibility. At a fixed cell, greater health dominates smaller health for every future path, so one maximum suffices for the feasibility test. The upper bound survives every possible loss.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[-2,-3],[5,-4]], starting with 3 survives by moving down then right.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Backward required-health row: O(RC) time; O(C) space. Binary-search feasible initial health: O(RC*log B) time; O(C) space.

B is one plus the sum of negative magnitudes. Inputs are unchanged. Minimizing total path sum does not control the lowest intermediate health; the strict positive-health rule matters.

docs.title: 1. Backward required-health row
docs.text:
Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Backward required-health row
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(C)
    """

    def calculateMinimumHP(self, dungeon: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, columns = len(dungeon), len(dungeon[0])
        dp = [float("inf")] * (columns + 1)
        dp[columns - 1] = 1
        for row in range(rows - 1, -1, -1):
            for column in range(columns - 1, -1, -1):
                dp[column] = max(1, min(dp[column], dp[column + 1]) - dungeon[row][column])
        return dp[0]

docs.title: 2. Binary-search feasible initial health
docs.text:
Time: O(RClog B)

Space: O(C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary-search feasible initial health
    Time: O(R*C*log B)
    Space: O(C)
    """

    def calculateMinimumHP(self, dungeon: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        def feasible(initial):
            dp = [-1] * len(dungeon[0])
            for r, row in enumerate(dungeon):
                for c, value in enumerate(row):
                    incoming = initial if r == c == 0 else max(dp[c], dp[c - 1] if c else -1)
                    dp[c] = incoming + value if incoming > 0 and incoming + value > 0 else -1
            return dp[-1] > 0

        low = 0
        high = 1 + sum(-value for row in dungeon for value in row if value < 0)
        while low + 1 < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if feasible(middle):
                high = middle
            else:
                low = middle
        return high

docs.text:
Approach Time Space Concatenation comparator sort O(n log n*d) O(n*d) Explicit insertion by concatenation order O(n^2*d) O(n*d)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Concatenation comparator sort
docs.text: Convert numbers to strings and sort by which pair concatenation is greater, placing the preferable piece first.

docs.title: Explicit insertion by concatenation order
docs.text: Insert each new piece into an already ordered list, shifting preceding pieces while the new pair order improves the result.

docs.title: Concatenation comparator sort
docs.text: Swapping an adjacent inverted pair improves the full concatenation, since its surrounding text is unchanged. The concatenation comparison defines a consistent order, so eliminating inversions gives a global optimum.

docs.title: Explicit insertion by concatenation order
docs.text: The inner shifts remove all inversions involving the new piece while preserving earlier order. Induction yields the same optimal comparator order after every insertion.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [3,30,34,5,9], the greatest concatenation is "9534330"; [0,0] returns "0".

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Concatenation comparator sort: O(n log nd) time; O(nd) space. Explicit insertion by concatenation order: O(n^2d) time; O(nd) space.

d is maximum digit length. Pair concatenations allocate O(d) temporary text per comparison; sorting/insertion use new lists and preserve nums. Insertion is a viable small-n baseline (n at most 100), but scales quadratically. Collapse all-zero output to one zero.

docs.title: 1. Concatenation comparator sort
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n*d)

Space: O(n*d)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Concatenation comparator sort
    Time: O(n log n*d)
    Space: O(n*d)
    """

    def largestNumber(self, nums: list[int]) -> str:
        from functools import cmp_to_key

        def compare(a, b):
            return (b + a > a + b) - (b + a < a + b)

        pieces = sorted(map(str, nums), key=cmp_to_key(compare))
        return "0" if pieces[0] == "0" else "".join(pieces)

docs.title: 2. Explicit insertion by concatenation order
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2*d)

Space: O(n*d)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Explicit insertion by concatenation order
    Time: O(n^2*d)
    Space: O(n*d)
    """

    def largestNumber(self, nums: list[int]) -> str:
        pieces = []
        for number in nums:
            current = str(number)
            position = len(pieces)
            pieces.append(current)
            while position and current + pieces[position - 1] > pieces[position - 1] + current:
                pieces[position] = pieces[position - 1]
                position -= 1
            pieces[position] = current
        return "0" if pieces[0] == "0" else "".join(pieces)

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Substring sets O(nL), L=10 O(nL), L=10 Rolling two-bit encoding O(n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Substring sets
docs.text: Slice each ten-letter window and put it in seen or repeated sets. Fixed L makes slicing a constant bounded cost.

docs.title: Rolling two-bit encoding
docs.text: Maintain a 20-bit rolling code, dropping all but the last ten letters. Slice a sequence only when its code becomes repeated for the first time.

docs.title: Substring sets
docs.text: The first occurrence enters seen, the second enters repeated, and later occurrences cannot add a duplicate set element.

docs.title: Rolling two-bit encoding
docs.text: Two-bit digits give an injective encoding of each fixed-length DNA window. Masking removes exactly the letter leaving the window, so equal codes mean equal ten-letter strings without hash collisions.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For eleven A characters, the same AAAAAAAAAA window occurs twice, so return it once.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Substring sets: O(nL), L=10 time; O(nL), L=10 space.

Rolling two-bit encoding: O(n) time; O(n) space.

Input is unchanged; answer order is arbitrary. Do not start recording rolling codes until ten letters have arrived.

docs.text:
Time: O(nL), L=10

Space: O(nL), L=10

class Solution:
    """Approach: Substring sets
    Time: O(nL), L=10
    Space: O(nL), L=10
    """

    def findRepeatedDnaSequences(self, s: str) -> list[str]:
        seen, repeated = set(), set()
        for i in range(len(s) - 9):
            sequence = s[i : i + 10]
            if sequence in seen:
                repeated.add(sequence)
            seen.add(sequence)
        return sorted(repeated)

docs.title: 2. Rolling two-bit encoding
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Rolling two-bit encoding
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def findRepeatedDnaSequences(self, s: str) -> list[str]:
        codes = {"A": 0, "C": 1, "G": 2, "T": 3}
        seen, repeated = set(), set()
        result = []
        code = 0
        for i, char in enumerate(s):
            code = ((code << 2) | codes[char]) & ((1 << 20) - 1)
            if i < 9:
                continue
            if code in seen and code not in repeated:
                result.append(s[i - 9 : i + 1])
                repeated.add(code)
            seen.add(code)
        return result

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Transaction-indexed cash states O(n*min(k,n)) O(min(k,n)) Transaction rows and best prior purchase O(n*min(k,n)) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Transaction-indexed cash states
docs.text: Use buy/sell arrays indexed by transaction budget and update budgets backward. If the budget permits every profitable adjacent rise, use the unlimited-transactions shortcut.

docs.title: Transaction rows and best prior purchase
docs.text: Add one transaction-budget row at a time. Retain the greatest previous-row profit before a purchase minus its price, then consider selling today.

docs.title: Transaction-indexed cash states
docs.text: A state either waits or takes its next legal buy/sell action. Backward order reads previous-day smaller-budget states. With a nonbinding budget, summing positive adjacent changes equals buying at each valley and selling at its peak.

docs.title: Transaction rows and best prior purchase
docs.text: Any final sale today pairs with some earlier purchase after at most one fewer transaction. The best-buy accumulator maximizes all such candidates; waiting preserves the earlier same-row optimum.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: With k=2 and prices [2,4,1,5], buy/sell twice for profit 2+4=6.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Transaction-indexed cash states: O(nmin(k,n)) time; O(min(k,n)) space. Transaction rows and best prior purchase: O(nmin(k,n)) time; O(n) space.

Inputs are unchanged. The first variant stores transaction states, the second day-prefix states. Zero budget and a single price yield zero; empty prices are handled as well.

docs.title: 1. Transaction-indexed cash states
docs.text:
Time: O(n*min(k,n))

Space: O(min(k,n))

class Solution:
    """Approach: Transaction-indexed cash states
    Time: O(n*min(k,n))
    Space: O(min(k,n))
    """

    def maxProfit(self, k: int, prices: list[int]) -> int:
        if k >= len(prices) // 2:
            return sum(max(0, prices[i] - prices[i - 1]) for i in range(1, len(prices)))
        buy = [-float("inf")] * (k + 1)
        sell = [0] * (k + 1)
        for price in prices:
            for count in range(k, 0, -1):
                sell[count] = max(sell[count], buy[count] + price)
                buy[count] = max(buy[count], sell[count - 1] - price)
        return sell[k]

docs.title: 2. Transaction rows and best prior purchase
docs.text:
Time: O(n*min(k,n))

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Transaction rows and best prior purchase
    Time: O(n*min(k,n))
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def maxProfit(self, k: int, prices: list[int]) -> int:
        if not prices:
            return 0
        previous = [0] * len(prices)
        for _ in range(min(k, len(prices) // 2)):
            current = [0] * len(prices)
            best_buy = -prices[0]
            for day in range(1, len(prices)):
                current[day] = max(current[day - 1], prices[day] + best_buy)
                best_buy = max(best_buy, previous[day - 1] - prices[day])
            previous = current
        return previous[-1]

docs.title: 198 House Robber
docs.text:
Medium · Linear dynamic programming · Core · Learning step 66 of 350

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Choose houses on a street to maximize the money taken. Adjacent houses cannot both be chosen. Values are nonnegative, and choosing no house earns zero.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Separate solutions according to whether the last house is chosen.
  2. Choosing it only requires the optimum from two positions earlier.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 065 · #332 · Next: 067 · #213

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Rolling prefix optimum O(n) O(1) Explicit prefix table O(n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Rolling prefix optimum
docs.text: Let F(k) be the best total using the first k houses. Initialize F(0)=0 and the value before the first house to zero. For each amount, compute max(F(k-1), F(k-2) + amount). Keep just the previous two totals; the entire table is unnecessary. Update both values together so the old states remain available for the transition.

docs.title: Explicit prefix table
docs.text: Store every prefix optimum rather than only two adjacent states. Initialize the empty prefix to zero and compare skipping each house with taking it after the prefix two positions earlier.

docs.title: Rolling prefix optimum
docs.text: Every legal choice either skips the current house or includes it. Skipping leaves the optimum for the previous prefix. Including it forbids the previous house and adds its amount to the optimum two houses back. These cases cover every legal choice, so their maximum is optimal by induction on prefix length.

docs.title: Explicit prefix table
docs.text: The two cases partition valid selections by whether the final house is used. Every table entry therefore equals the optimum of its prefix; retaining entries also makes decisions easier to inspect.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [4,1,7,3], the best prefix totals are 4, 4, 11, and 11. Taking houses with amounts 4 and 7 gives 11; adding the last house would conflict with 7.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Rolling prefix optimum approach:

O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; input is unchanged. Greedily taking the larger amount from each adjacent pair loses information about later conflicts. Do not overwrite the older total before computing the new total.

Rolling prefix optimum: O(n) time; O(1) space. Explicit prefix table: O(n) time; O(n) space. The table trades memory for visible intermediate states. Neither implementation changes the amounts.

docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Rolling prefix optimum
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def rob(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        older = previous = 0
        for amount in nums:
            older, previous = previous, max(previous, older + amount)
        return previous

docs.title: 2. Explicit prefix table
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Explicit prefix table
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def rob(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        best = [0] * (len(nums) + 1)
        for end, value in enumerate(nums, 1):
            best[end] = max(best[end - 1], value + (best[end - 2] if end > 1 else 0))
        return best[-1]

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Breadth-first rightmost values O(n) O(w) auxiliary; O(h) output Right-first DFS O(n) O(h)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Breadth-first rightmost values
docs.text: Run breadth-first search one level at a time. Save the value of the last processed node in each fixed-size level.

docs.title: Right-first DFS
docs.text: Walk a stack of nodes and depths, visiting right children first. Record only the first node seen at each new depth; it is the visible one.

docs.title: Breadth-first rightmost values
docs.text: The queue orders a level from left to right because each parent's left child is enqueued before its right child, and parents themselves have that order. The last node in each level is therefore its rightmost visible node.

docs.title: Right-first DFS
docs.text: All nodes in a right subtree precede equal-depth nodes in its left sibling subtree. The first visit at a depth is therefore its rightmost node even when it lies under a left ancestor.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Root 1 has children 2 and 3; node 2 has right child 5, while 3 has no children. Levels are [1], [2,3], [5], giving the view [1,3,5].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

O(n) time and O(w) auxiliary queue space for maximum width w, plus O(h) output. The tree is unchanged. The view is not just the root's right-child chain: a deeper left-subtree node can be visible when no right-subtree node shares its depth. An empty tree yields an empty list.

Alternative tradeoff: O(n) time; O(h) space.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Breadth-first rightmost values
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(w) auxiliary; O(h) output

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Breadth-first rightmost values
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(w) auxiliary; O(h) output
    """

    def rightSideView(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> list[int]:
        if root is None:
            return []
        queue = deque([root])
        result = []
        while queue:
            width = len(queue)
            for i in range(width):
                node = queue.popleft()
                if i == width - 1:
                    result.append(node.val)
                if node.left:
                    queue.append(node.left)
                if node.right:
                    queue.append(node.right)
        return result

docs.title: 2. Right-first DFS
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(h)

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Right-first DFS
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(h)
    """

    def rightSideView(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> list[int]:
        result = []
        stack = [(root, 0)] if root else []
        while stack:
            node, depth = stack.pop()
            if depth == len(result):
                result.append(node.val)
            if node.left:
                stack.append((node.left, depth + 1))
            if node.right:
                stack.append((node.right, depth + 1))
        return result

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Iterative land-component DFS O(R*C) O(R*C) Union neighboring land cells O(RCalpha(R*C)) O(R*C)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Iterative land-component DFS
docs.text: Scan the grid. Every unvisited land cell starts one new island and an iterative depth-first traversal. A stack holds discovered cells, and a visited set records them. Add only in-bounds, unvisited land neighbors. Keep the grid unchanged so the original map remains available after counting.

docs.title: Union neighboring land cells
docs.text: Start with one component per land cell. Scan only upper and left land edges, merging endpoint roots with size-weighted union and path compression.

docs.title: Iterative land-component DFS
docs.text: The traversal reaches precisely the land component containing its starting cell: each step crosses a legal land edge, and every such neighbor is explored. All cells of that component become visited. The outer scan therefore starts exactly once per component, so its count equals the number of islands.

docs.title: Union neighboring land cells
docs.text: Each merge reduces component count exactly when two previously separate land groups connect. All undirected land edges are considered once, so final sets are exactly the islands.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [["1","0","1"],["1","0","0"]], the upper-left start visits both left-column land cells. The upper-right cell starts another traversal. Return 2.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Iterative land-component DFS approach:

O(rows * cols) time and auxiliary space. Each cell is scanned once and each land cell enters the stack once. The grid is unchanged. Diagonal movement would merge separate islands. Iteration also handles a long connected strip without depending on Python's recursion limit.

Iterative land-component DFS: O(RC) time; O(RC) space. Union neighboring land cells: O(RCalpha(RC)) time; O(RC) space. Neither variant mutates the grid. Union-find stores arrays for water cells too, but only land contributes to the component count; alpha is inverse Ackermann.

docs.title: 1. Iterative land-component DFS
docs.text:
Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(R*C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Iterative land-component DFS
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def numIslands(self, grid: list[list[str]]) -> int:
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        visited = set()
        count = 0
        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                if grid[row][col] != "1" or (row, col) in visited:
                    continue
                count += 1
                visited.add((row, col))
                stack = [(row, col)]
                while stack:
                    r, c = stack.pop()
                    for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                        if (
                            0 <= nr < rows
                            and 0 <= nc < cols
                            and grid[nr][nc] == "1"
                            and (nr, nc) not in visited
                        ):
                            visited.add((nr, nc))
                            stack.append((nr, nc))
        return count

docs.title: 2. Union neighboring land cells
docs.text:
Time: O(RCalpha(R*C))

Space: O(R*C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Union neighboring land cells
    Time: O(R*C*alpha(R*C))
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def numIslands(self, grid: list[list[str]]) -> int:
        rows, columns = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        parent = list(range(rows * columns))
        size = [1] * len(parent)
        count = sum(cell == "1" for row in grid for cell in row)

        def find(node):
            while node != parent[node]:
                parent[node] = parent[parent[node]]
                node = parent[node]
            return node

        for row in range(rows):
            for column in range(columns):
                if grid[row][column] != "1":
                    continue
                for nr, nc in ((row - 1, column), (row, column - 1)):
                    if nr >= 0 and nc >= 0 and grid[nr][nc] == "1":
                        a, b = find(row * columns + column), find(nr * columns + nc)
                        if a != b:
                            if size[a] < size[b]:
                                a, b = b, a
                            parent[b] = a
                            size[a] += size[b]
                            count -= 1
        return count
