docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Breadth-first null markers
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Codec:
    """Approach: Breadth-first null markers
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def serialize(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> str:
        tokens = []
        queue = deque([root])
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            if node is None:
                tokens.append("#")
                continue
            tokens.append(str(node.val))
            queue.append(node.left)
            queue.append(node.right)
        return ",".join(tokens)

    def deserialize(self, data: str) -> TreeNode | None:
        tokens = iter(data.split(","))
        first = next(tokens)
        if first == "#":
            return None
        root = TreeNode(int(first))
        queue = deque([root])
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            left, right = next(tokens), next(tokens)
            if left != "#":
                node.left = TreeNode(int(left))
                queue.append(node.left)
            if right != "#":
                node.right = TreeNode(int(right))
                queue.append(node.right)
        return root

docs.title: 2. Preorder null markers
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Codec:
    """Approach: Preorder null markers
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def serialize(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> str:
        tokens = []
        stack = [root]
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            if node is None:
                tokens.append("#")
            else:
                tokens.append(str(node.val))
                stack.extend((node.right, node.left))
        return ",".join(tokens)

    def deserialize(self, data: str) -> TreeNode | None:
        dummy = TreeNode()
        slots = [(dummy, "left")]
        for token in data.split(","):
            parent, side = slots.pop()
            if token == "#":
                continue
            node = TreeNode(int(token))
            setattr(parent, side, node)
            slots.extend(((node, "right"), (node, "left")))
        return dummy.left

docs.title: 300 Longest Increasing Subsequence
docs.text:
Medium · Linear dynamic programming · Core · Learning step 69 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: LIS.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Selected elements keep their original order but need not occupy adjacent positions.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Among equal-length subsequences, a smaller final value is easier to extend.
  2. Store one smallest tail for each length, then binary-search where a value fits.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 068 · #322 · Next: 070 · #139

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Binary-search smallest tails O(n log n) O(n) Subsequence ending at each index O(n^2) O(n) Fenwick prefix maximum O(n log n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Binary-search smallest tails
docs.text: Maintain tails[k], the smallest possible final value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1 in the processed prefix. For each value, use bisect_left to find the first tail at least as large. Replace that tail, or append if all tails are smaller. The number of tails is the answer. This compresses subsequence-length states without keeping predecessor links.

docs.title: Subsequence ending at each index
docs.text: Let lengths[i] be the longest increasing subsequence ending exactly at i. Start each at one and inspect earlier smaller values as possible predecessors.

docs.title: Fenwick prefix maximum
docs.text: Compress values to sorted ranks. Query the best subsequence length over strictly smaller ranks, add one, and update the current rank in a Fenwick tree storing maxima.

docs.title: Binary-search smallest tails
docs.text: Tails are strictly increasing. A value placed at index k can extend a subsequence of length k because its previous tail is smaller. Replacing the existing length-(k+1) tail improves or preserves future extension possibilities. It cannot create a longer length unless all prior tails are smaller, in which case appending is justified. These updates preserve the smallest-tail invariant for every achievable length.

docs.title: Subsequence ending at each index
docs.text: An increasing subsequence ending at i either contains only that value or extends an earlier smaller final value. Trying all predecessors finds its optimum; the maximum over endpoints gives the answer.

docs.title: Fenwick prefix maximum
docs.text: Each query combines exactly the possible smaller-valued predecessors already processed. Disjoint Fenwick prefix intervals cover every such rank; max updates retain the best endpoint length. Thus it implements the endpoint recurrence in logarithmic time.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [4,1,3,2,5], tails evolves as [4], [1], [1,3], [1,2], [1,2,5]. The answer is 3. Intermediate tails summarize possibilities; they are not necessarily an actual subsequence with consistent stored positions.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Binary-search smallest tails approach:

O(n log n) time and O(n) space; input is unchanged. Assignment replaces an entry in O(1); it does not insert and shift elements. bisect_left ensures duplicate values do not extend a strictly increasing subsequence.

Binary-search smallest tails: O(n log n) time; O(n) space. Subsequence ending at each index: O(n^2) time; O(n) space. The quadratic baseline is useful for the recurrence but may be slow near the largest limits and misses the O(n log n) follow-up. Both preserve input.

Fenwick prefix maximum: O(n log n) time and O(n) space, including coordinate compression. This variant supports value-prefix queries and generalizes to LIS counting; the tails method is shorter when only length is needed. Inputs remain unchanged.

Space: O(n)

from bisect import bisect_left


class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary-search smallest tails
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def lengthOfLIS(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        tails: list[int] = []
        for value in nums:
            position = bisect_left(tails, value)
            if position == len(tails):
                tails.append(value)
            else:
                tails[position] = value
        return len(tails)

docs.title: 2. Subsequence ending at each index
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

from bisect import bisect_left


class Solution:
    """Approach: Subsequence ending at each index
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def lengthOfLIS(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        lengths = [1] * len(nums)
        for end in range(len(nums)):
            for previous in range(end):
                if nums[previous] < nums[end]:
                    lengths[end] = max(lengths[end], lengths[previous] + 1)
        return max(lengths)

docs.title: 3. Fenwick prefix maximum
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

from bisect import bisect_left


class Solution:
    """Approach: Fenwick prefix maximum
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def lengthOfLIS(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        ranks = {value: index + 1 for index, value in enumerate(sorted(set(nums)))}
        tree = [0] * (len(ranks) + 1)
        answer = 0
        for value in nums:
            rank = ranks[value]
            index, length = rank - 1, 0
            while index:
                length = max(length, tree[index])
                index -= index & -index
            length += 1
            answer = max(answer, length)
            index = rank
            while index < len(tree):
                tree[index] = max(tree[index], length)
                index += index & -index
        return answer

docs.title: 301 Remove Invalid Parentheses
docs.text:
Hard · Advanced backtracking · Extension · Learning step 206 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Backtracking · Graph traversal.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Remove the minimum number of parentheses needed to make a string valid and return every distinct result. Non-parenthesis characters must remain in order.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. A scan determines the minimum unmatched opening and closing counts.
  2. Deleting one character per BFS layer also searches by removal count.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 205 · #216 · Next: 207 · #306

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Exact-removal-budget backtracking O(n*2^p) loose bound O(n) auxiliary plus output Deletion-layer BFS O(n^2*2^p) loose bound; may time out O(n*2^p) loose bound

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Exact-removal-budget backtracking
docs.text: Count unmatched openings and closings first. Backtrack keeping or deleting parentheses with exactly those budgets, preserving nonnegative kept balance and all letters. Deduplicate completed strings.

docs.title: Deletion-layer BFS
docs.text: At each layer validate all current strings. Return the first layer with valid results; otherwise remove one parenthesis at every possible position and deduplicate the next layer.

docs.title: Exact-removal-budget backtracking
docs.text: The scan gives unavoidable deletions. Every retained prefix must have nonnegative balance; final zero balance with exhausted minimum budgets yields exactly a valid minimally edited result.

docs.title: Deletion-layer BFS
docs.text: A layer contains strings reachable with the same deletion count. The first successful layer is therefore minimal, and all valid strings in that layer must be returned.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "()())()", minimum one deletion yields "(())()" and "()()()".

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Exact-removal-budget backtracking: O(n2^p) loose bound time; O(n) auxiliary plus output space. Deletion-layer BFS: O(n^22^p) loose bound; may time out time; O(n*2^p) loose bound space. The input is immutable. p is its number of parentheses. Python deletion slices copy strings. The BFS baseline may use much more memory at full limits; the default prunes with exact budgets. Letters are never deleted.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Exact-removal-budget backtracking
docs.text:
Time: O(n*2^p) loose bound

Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Exact-removal-budget backtracking
    Time: O(n*2^p) loose bound
    Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def removeInvalidParentheses(self, s: str) -> list[str]:
        left = right = 0
        for char in s:
            if char == "(":
                left += 1
            elif char == ")":
                if left:
                    left -= 1
                else:
                    right += 1
        result, path = set(), []

        def visit(index, balance, remove_left, remove_right):
            if remove_left + remove_right > len(s) - index:
                return
            if index == len(s):
                if balance == remove_left == remove_right == 0:
                    result.add("".join(path))
                return
            char = s[index]
            if char == "(" and remove_left:
                visit(index + 1, balance, remove_left - 1, remove_right)
            if char == ")" and remove_right:
                visit(index + 1, balance, remove_left, remove_right - 1)
            following = balance + (char == "(") - (char == ")")
            if following >= 0:
                path.append(char)
                visit(index + 1, following, remove_left, remove_right)
                path.pop()

        visit(0, 0, left, right)
        return sorted(result)

docs.title: 2. Deletion-layer BFS
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2*2^p) loose bound; may time out

Space: O(n*2^p) loose bound

class Solution:
    """Approach: Deletion-layer BFS
    Time: O(n^2*2^p) loose bound; may time out
    Space: O(n*2^p) loose bound
    """

    def removeInvalidParentheses(self, s: str) -> list[str]:
        def valid(text):
            balance = 0
            for char in text:
                balance += (char == "(") - (char == ")")
                if balance < 0:
                    return False
            return balance == 0

        level = {s}
        while True:
            accepted = sorted(text for text in level if valid(text))
            if accepted:
                return accepted
            level = {
                text[:index] + text[index + 1 :]
                for text in level
                for index, char in enumerate(text)
                if char in "()" and (index == 0 or char != text[index - 1])
            }

Approach Time Space Two-dimensional prefix sums O(mn) construction; O(1) query O(mn) Independent row prefix sums O(mn) construction; O(m) query O(mn)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Two-dimensional prefix sums
docs.text: Store a padded table of top-left rectangle sums. Answer with four prefix accesses by inclusion- exclusion.

docs.title: Independent row prefix sums
docs.text: Store prefix sums separately in each row and add the requested column-slice sum across the requested rows.

docs.title: Two-dimensional prefix sums
docs.text: Subtracting the top and left strips from the bottom-right prefix removes all outside cells; adding back their intersection corrects double subtraction.

Independent row prefix sums: O(mn) construction; O(m) query time; O(mn) space.

The constructor snapshots sums and does not mutate or retain mutable input rows. m and n are dimensions; all query coordinates are valid and inclusive.

docs.text:
Time: O(mn) construction; O(1) query

Space: O(mn)

class NumMatrix:
    """Approach: Two-dimensional prefix sums
    Time: O(mn) construction; O(1) query
    Space: O(mn)
    """

    def __init__(self, matrix: list[list[int]]):
        rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        self.prefix = [[0] * (cols + 1) for _ in range(rows + 1)]
        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                self.prefix[row + 1][col + 1] = (
                    matrix[row][col]
                    + self.prefix[row][col + 1]
                    + self.prefix[row + 1][col]
                    - self.prefix[row][col]
                )

    def sumRegion(self, row1: int, col1: int, row2: int, col2: int) -> int:
        p = self.prefix
        return p[row2 + 1][col2 + 1] - p[row1][col2 + 1] - p[row2 + 1][col1] + p[row1][col1]

docs.title: 2. Independent row prefix sums
docs.text:
Time: O(mn) construction; O(m) query

Space: O(mn)

class NumMatrix:
    """Approach: Independent row prefix sums
    Time: O(mn) construction; O(m) query
    Space: O(mn)
    """

    def __init__(self, matrix: list[list[int]]):
        self.prefix = []
        for row in matrix:
            sums = [0]
            for value in row:
                sums.append(sums[-1] + value)
            self.prefix.append(sums)

    def sumRegion(self, row1: int, col1: int, row2: int, col2: int) -> int:
        return sum(
            self.prefix[row][col2 + 1] - self.prefix[row][col1] for row in range(row1, row2 + 1)
        )

docs.title: 306 Additive Number
docs.text:
Medium · Advanced backtracking · Extension · Learning step 207 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Decide whether a digit string can be split into at least three numbers where each number after the first two equals their sum. Multi-digit numbers cannot start with zero.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Only the first two numbers are choices; the rest are forced.
  2. Compare each forced sum directly against the next string prefix.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Integer seed-pair enumeration O(n^3) loose bound at bounded numeric length O(n) Decimal-string seed verification O(n^3) loose digit-work bound O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Integer seed-pair enumeration
docs.text: Choose both initial cut positions, rejecting leading zeros. Repeatedly compute the next integer sum and match its decimal string until the whole input is consumed.

docs.title: Decimal-string seed verification
docs.text: Use the same seed choices but add decimal strings right to left with a carry. This avoids parsing whole numbers and makes digit arithmetic explicit.

docs.title: Integer seed-pair enumeration
docs.text: Any additive sequence fixes its first two numbers and every later number. Enumerating all legal seeds and verifying those forced successors is therefore complete.

docs.title: Decimal-string seed verification
docs.text: Column addition produces exactly the required next decimal number. Matching it consecutively consumes the unique sequence determined by each seed pair, while the same leading-zero rule keeps representations canonical.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: "112358" is additive as 1,1,2,3,5,8. "1023" fails: after seeds 1 and 0 the next number must be 1, not 2.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Integer seed-pair enumeration: O(n^3) loose bound at bounded numeric length time; O(n) space. Decimal-string seed verification: O(n^3) loose digit-work bound time; O(n) space. The input is unchanged. String slices, decimal conversions, and addition copies are included in the loose bounds. Do not accept a split containing only two numbers. The official string length is small enough for exhaustive seed pairs.

docs.title: 1. Integer seed-pair enumeration
docs.text:
Time: O(n^3) loose bound at bounded numeric length

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Integer seed-pair enumeration
    Time: O(n^3) loose bound at bounded numeric length
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def isAdditiveNumber(self, num: str) -> bool:
        for first in range(1, len(num) - 1):
            if first > 1 and num[0] == "0":
                break
            for second in range(first + 1, len(num)):
                if second - first > 1 and num[first] == "0":
                    break
                a, b = int(num[:first]), int(num[first:second])
                position, count = second, 2
                while position < len(num):
                    following = str(a + b)
                    if not num.startswith(following, position):
                        break
                    position += len(following)
                    a, b = b, a + b
                    count += 1
                if position == len(num) and count >= 3:
                    return True
        return False

docs.title: 2. Decimal-string seed verification
docs.text:
Time: O(n^3) loose digit-work bound

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Decimal-string seed verification
    Time: O(n^3) loose digit-work bound
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def isAdditiveNumber(self, num: str) -> bool:
        def add(left, right):
            i, j, carry = len(left) - 1, len(right) - 1, 0
            digits = []
            while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry:
                total = carry
                if i >= 0:
                    total += ord(left[i]) - 48
                    i -= 1
                if j >= 0:
                    total += ord(right[j]) - 48
                    j -= 1
                carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
                digits.append(str(digit))
            return "".join(reversed(digits))

        for first in range(1, len(num) - 1):
            if first > 1 and num[0] == "0":
                break
            for second in range(first + 1, len(num)):
                if second - first > 1 and num[first] == "0":
                    break
                left, right = num[:first], num[first:second]
                position, count = second, 2
                while position < len(num):
                    following = add(left, right)
                    if not num.startswith(following, position):
                        break
                    position += len(following)
                    left, right = right, following
                    count += 1
                if position == len(num) and count >= 3:
                    return True
        return False

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Fenwick tree with value snapshots O(n log n) construction; O(log n) operation O(n) Iterative segment tree O(n) construction; O(log n) operation O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Fenwick tree with value snapshots
docs.text: Keep copied values and a one-indexed Fenwick sum tree. Updates add the difference to all containing blocks; queries subtract two prefix sums.

docs.title: Iterative segment tree
docs.text: Place values in the leaves of a flat binary tree. Rebuild ancestors on updates and cover the query range with disjoint tree nodes.

docs.title: Fenwick tree with value snapshots
docs.text: Each Fenwick entry stores the sum over its lowbit-sized suffix block. Update ancestors are exactly the blocks containing the index, and a prefix query partitions its range into disjoint such blocks.

docs.title: Iterative segment tree
docs.text: Every internal node equals the sum of its descendant leaves. Query boundary movement selects disjoint fully enclosed nodes until no interval remains, so their sum equals the requested range.

docs.title: Walkthrough

Iterative segment tree: O(n) construction; O(log n) operation time; O(n) space.

Each object owns its copied state. Query endpoints are inclusive; convert the right boundary to exclusive in the iterative segment tree. Repeated updates replace values rather than append differences blindly.

docs.text:
Time: O(n log n) construction; O(log n) operation

Space: O(n)

class NumArray:
    """Approach: Fenwick tree with value snapshots
    Time: O(n log n) construction; O(log n) operation
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self, nums: list[int]):
        self.values = nums[:]
        self.bit = [0] * (len(nums) + 1)
        for index, value in enumerate(nums, 1):
            while index < len(self.bit):
                self.bit[index] += value
                index += index & -index

    def update(self, index: int, val: int) -> None:
        difference = val - self.values[index]
        self.values[index] = val
        index += 1
        while index < len(self.bit):
            self.bit[index] += difference
            index += index & -index

    def sumRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> int:
        def prefix(end):
            answer = 0
            while end:
                answer += self.bit[end]
                end -= end & -end
            return answer

        return prefix(right + 1) - prefix(left)

docs.title: 2. Iterative segment tree
docs.text:
Time: O(n) construction; O(log n) operation

Space: O(n)

class NumArray:
    """Approach: Iterative segment tree
    Time: O(n) construction; O(log n) operation
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self, nums: list[int]):
        self.size = len(nums)
        self.tree = [0] * self.size + nums[:]
        for index in range(self.size - 1, 0, -1):
            self.tree[index] = self.tree[index * 2] + self.tree[index * 2 + 1]

    def update(self, index: int, val: int) -> None:
        index += self.size
        self.tree[index] = val
        while index > 1:
            index //= 2
            self.tree[index] = self.tree[index * 2] + self.tree[index * 2 + 1]

    def sumRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> int:
        left += self.size
        right += self.size + 1
        answer = 0
        while left < right:
            if left & 1:
                answer += self.tree[left]
                left += 1
            if right & 1:
                right -= 1
                answer += self.tree[right]
            left //= 2
            right //= 2
        return answer

class Solution:
    """Approach: Three cooldown states
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def maxProfit(self, prices: list[int]) -> int:
        hold, sold, rest = -float("inf"), -float("inf"), 0
        for price in prices:
            hold, sold, rest = max(hold, rest - price), hold + price, max(rest, sold)
        return max(sold, rest)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Day-profit table with a two-day buy lag
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def maxProfit(self, prices: list[int]) -> int:
        profits = [0] * len(prices)
        hold = -prices[0]
        for day in range(1, len(prices)):
            profits[day] = max(profits[day - 1], hold + prices[day])
            hold = max(hold, (profits[day - 2] if day >= 2 else 0) - prices[day])
        return profits[-1]

class Solution:
    """Approach: Trim simultaneous leaf layers
    Time: O(V)
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def findMinHeightTrees(self, n: int, edges: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
        from collections import deque

        if n == 1:
            return [0]
        graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for a, b in edges:
            graph[a].append(b)
            graph[b].append(a)
        degree = [len(neighbors) for neighbors in graph]
        queue = deque(i for i in range(n) if degree[i] == 1)
        remaining = n
        while remaining > 2:
            remaining -= len(queue)
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                node = queue.popleft()
                for other in graph[node]:
                    degree[other] -= 1
                    if degree[other] == 1:
                        queue.append(other)
        return list(queue)

docs.title: 2. Find a diameter and choose its midpoint
docs.text:
Time: O(V)

Space: O(V)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Find a diameter and choose its midpoint
    Time: O(V)
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def findMinHeightTrees(self, n: int, edges: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
        from collections import deque

        graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for a, b in edges:
            graph[a].append(b)
            graph[b].append(a)

        def farthest(start):
            parent = [-1] * n
            parent[start] = start
            queue = deque([start])
            node = start
            while queue:
                node = queue.popleft()
                for other in graph[node]:
                    if parent[other] < 0:
                        parent[other] = node
                        queue.append(other)
            return node, parent

        first, _ = farthest(0)
        last, parent = farthest(first)
        path = [last]
        while path[-1] != first:
            path.append(parent[path[-1]])
        middle = len(path) // 2
        return path[middle : middle + 1] if len(path) % 2 else path[middle - 1 : middle + 1]

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Bottom-up last-burst intervals O(n^3) O(n^2) Memoized last-burst intervals O(n^3) O(n^2)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Bottom-up last-burst intervals
docs.text: Copy the values between two virtual boundary balloons of value one. Define dp[left][right] as the optimum for bursting all balloons strictly between those boundaries while leaving them intact. Empty intervals cost zero. Process intervals by increasing boundary distance. Try each interior index as the last balloon: combine the two smaller interval optima with the product of the left boundary, that balloon, and the right boundary.

docs.title: Memoized last-burst intervals
docs.text: Memoize intervals on demand instead of filling them by width. Each call selects the final interior balloon and combines the two independent boundary-preserving subintervals.

docs.title: Bottom-up last-burst intervals
docs.text: If index k is last in an interval, its final neighbors are exactly the fixed boundaries. Earlier bursts on its left and right do not interact because k separates them. Their independent optima plus the final product therefore give the best order ending at k. Every burst order has a last index, so maximizing over all of them covers every possible order.

docs.title: Memoized last-burst intervals
docs.text: Fixing the last balloon keeps its boundary neighbors alive. Left and right burst orders then contribute independently, so testing every last index covers every possible order and memoization reuses equal intervals.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [2,3], bursting 2 first earns 123=6, then 3 earns 3, totaling 9. Bursting 3 first earns 6, then 2 earns 2, totaling 8. The full interval chooses 3 as its last balloon and returns 9.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Bottom-up last-burst intervals approach:

O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space, including an O(n) padded copy; input is unchanged. Boundaries are excluded from their interval. Local greedy choices miss how each removal changes future neighbor products.

Bottom-up last-burst intervals: O(n^3) time; O(n^2) space. Memoized last-burst intervals: O(n^3) time; O(n^2) space. Both allocate a padded O(n) copy and leave nums unchanged. Memo recursion depth is at most n+1 with n at most 300; it does not scale to unbounded input depths.

class Solution:
    """Approach: Bottom-up last-burst intervals
    Time: O(n^3)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def maxCoins(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        values = [1, *nums, 1]
        size = len(values)
        dp = [[0] * size for _ in range(size)]
        for distance in range(2, size):
            for left in range(size - distance):
                right = left + distance
                dp[left][right] = max(
                    dp[left][last] + values[left] * values[last] * values[right] + dp[last][right]
                    for last in range(left + 1, right)
                )
        return dp[0][-1]

docs.title: 2. Memoized last-burst intervals
docs.text:
Time: O(n^3)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Memoized last-burst intervals
    Time: O(n^3)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def maxCoins(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        from functools import cache

        values = [1, *nums, 1]

        @cache
        def solve(left, right):
            if right - left <= 1:
                return 0
            return max(
                solve(left, last) + values[left] * values[last] * values[right] + solve(last, right)
                for last in range(left + 1, right)
            )

        return solve(0, len(values) - 1)

docs.text: Store generated values and one producer index per prime. Append the minimum next product and advance every producer tied at that value.

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Prime-pointer dynamic programming
    Time: O(n*k)
    Space: O(n+k)
    """

    def nthSuperUglyNumber(self, n: int, primes: list[int]) -> int:
        values = [1]
        positions = [0] * len(primes)
        while len(values) < n:
            candidates = [
                prime * values[index] for prime, index in zip(primes, positions, strict=True)
            ]
            following = min(candidates)
            values.append(following)
            for index, candidate in enumerate(candidates):
                if candidate == following:
                    positions[index] += 1
        return values[-1]

docs.title: 2. Heap merge of prime product streams
docs.text:
Time: O(k+A log(k+1)), A<=n*k stream advances

Space: O(n+k)

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Heap merge of prime product streams
    Time: O(k+A log(k+1)), A<=n*k stream advances
    Space: O(n+k)
    """

    def nthSuperUglyNumber(self, n: int, primes: list[int]) -> int:
        values = [1]
        heap = [(prime, prime, 0) for prime in primes]
        heapify(heap)
        while len(values) < n:
            following = heap[0][0]
            values.append(following)
            while heap[0][0] == following:
                _, prime, index = heappop(heap)
                index += 1
                heappush(heap, (prime * values[index], prime, index))
        return values[-1]

Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Compressed Fenwick frequencies
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def countSmaller(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        ordered = sorted(set(nums))
        ranks = {value: i + 1 for i, value in enumerate(ordered)}
        bit = [0] * (len(ordered) + 1)
        result = []
        for value in reversed(nums):
            rank = ranks[value]
            index, count = rank - 1, 0
            while index:
                count += bit[index]
                index -= index & -index
            result.append(count)
            while rank < len(bit):
                bit[rank] += 1
                rank += rank & -rank
        return result[::-1]

docs.title: 2. Merge-sort indexed inversion counts
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Merge-sort indexed inversion counts
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def countSmaller(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        answer = [0] * len(nums)

        def sort(items):
            if len(items) <= 1:
                return items
            middle = len(items) // 2
            left, right = sort(items[:middle]), sort(items[middle:])
            i = j = 0
            merged = []
            while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
                if left[i][0] <= right[j][0]:
                    answer[left[i][1]] += j
                    merged.append(left[i])
                    i += 1
                else:
                    merged.append(right[j])
                    j += 1
            for value, index in left[i:]:
                answer[index] += j
                merged.append((value, index))
            merged.extend(right[j:])
            return merged

        sort([(value, i) for i, value in enumerate(nums)])
        return answer

docs.text: Remove repeated letters so every distinct lowercase letter appears once, producing the lexicographically smallest subsequence.

docs.title: Hints

1. A larger chosen letter may be removed if another copy remains later.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Monotone stack with remaining counts O(n) O(A) Choose the smallest feasible first letter recursively O(A*n) O(A*n) including retained slices

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Monotone stack with remaining counts
docs.text: Skip letters already chosen. Before adding a new letter, pop larger suffix letters only when they can be chosen again later.

docs.title: Choose the smallest feasible first letter recursively
docs.text: The first chosen letter must appear by the earliest last occurrence of any remaining letter. Choose the smallest character in that feasible prefix, then remove its later copies and solve the suffix.

docs.title: Monotone stack with remaining counts
docs.text: Popping creates a smaller first differing letter while preserving feasibility through a later occurrence. A letter with no remaining copy cannot be removed. These exchange steps maintain the smallest feasible chosen prefix.

docs.title: Choose the smallest feasible first letter recursively
docs.text: Choosing after the boundary would lose a required letter. Every position up to it leaves all other letters attainable, so the smallest character is optimal lexicographically; recursion repeats the same argument on remaining letters.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "cbacdcbc", the optimal unique-letter subsequence is "acdb".

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Monotone stack with remaining counts: O(n) time; O(A) space. Choose the smallest feasible first letter recursively: O(An) time; O(An) including retained slices space.

A is alphabet size, at most 26. The recursive variant has bounded alphabet-depth, not input-length depth, but repeatedly copies suffix strings. The stack saves these allocations. Both preserve input and count distinct letters, not distinct positions.

docs.title: 1. Monotone stack with remaining counts
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(A)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Monotone stack with remaining counts
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(A)
    """

    def removeDuplicateLetters(self, s: str) -> str:
        from collections import Counter

        remaining = Counter(s)
        stack, used = [], set()
        for character in s:
            remaining[character] -= 1
            if character in used:
                continue
            while stack and stack[-1] > character and remaining[stack[-1]]:
                used.remove(stack.pop())
            stack.append(character)
            used.add(character)
        return "".join(stack)

docs.title: 2. Choose the smallest feasible first letter recursively
docs.text:
Time: O(A*n)

Space: O(A*n) including retained slices

class Solution:
    """Approach: Choose the smallest feasible first letter recursively
    Time: O(A*n)
    Space: O(A*n) including retained slices
    """

    def removeDuplicateLetters(self, s: str) -> str:
        def choose(text):
            if not text:
                return ""
            last = {character: index for index, character in enumerate(text)}
            boundary = min(last.values())
            position = min(range(boundary + 1), key=lambda index: text[index])
            character = text[position]
            return character + choose(text[position + 1 :].replace(character, ""))

        return choose(s)

docs.title: Approach comparison

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Bottom-up amount table
docs.text: Let dp[x] be the minimum coin count for amount x. Set dp[0]=0. Initialize other entries to amount+1, a sentinel larger than any possible answer because every denomination is at least one. Visit totals in ascending order. For each coin no larger than the total, consider dp[total-coin]+1. Return -1 when the target still has the sentinel value.

docs.title: Breadth-first sums
docs.text: Treat totals 0 through A as vertices and adding one coin as an edge. BFS starts at zero, marks sums when enqueued, and returns the first target distance. C is the number of denominations.

docs.title: Bottom-up amount table
docs.text: Every nonempty combination has a final coin. Removing it leaves a smaller total whose optimum is already known. Trying every possible final coin therefore finds a combination no worse than any valid one. Every finite candidate extends an achievable smaller amount, so it also represents a valid combination. Induction establishes every table entry's optimum.

docs.title: Breadth-first sums
docs.text: Every edge uses exactly one coin, so BFS layers equal coin counts. Every valid combination defines a path. First arrival is therefore the minimum count; exhaustion proves impossibility.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: With coins [2,5] and amount 7, totals 2 and 5 each need one coin. At 7, using 2 after 5 or 5 after 2 needs two coins. Amount 3 stays impossible.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Bottom-up amount table approach:

O(amount * number_of_coins) time and O(amount) space; inputs are unchanged. Ascending totals permit repeated use of the same coin. Greedily selecting the largest denomination fails for sets such as [1,3,4] and target 6.

Bottom-up amount table: O(AC) time; O(A) space. Breadth-first sums: O(AC) time; O(A) space. BFS can stop before solving all sums, but stores a queue and visited set. Positive coin values make the bounded state graph sufficient.

Space: O(A)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Bottom-up amount table
    Time: O(A*C)
    Space: O(A)
    """

    def coinChange(self, coins: list[int], amount: int) -> int:
        impossible = amount + 1
        dp = [impossible] * (amount + 1)
        dp[0] = 0
        for total in range(1, amount + 1):
            for coin in coins:
                if coin <= total:
                    dp[total] = min(dp[total], dp[total - coin] + 1)
        return -1 if dp[amount] == impossible else dp[amount]

docs.title: 2. Breadth-first sums
docs.text:
Time: O(A*C)

Space: O(A)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Breadth-first sums
    Time: O(A*C)
    Space: O(A)
    """

    def coinChange(self, coins: list[int], amount: int) -> int:
        from collections import deque

        queue = deque([(0, 0)])
        seen = {0}
        while queue:
            total, count = queue.popleft()
            if total == amount:
                return count
            for coin in coins:
                following = total + coin
                if following <= amount and following not in seen:
                    seen.add(following)
                    queue.append((following, count + 1))
        return -1

docs.title: Merge-sort prefix difference counting
docs.text: Original prefix order guarantees each left-half prefix precedes every right-half prefix at that merge. Sorted values make both valid-range boundaries monotone; every eligible prefix pair is counted at its unique split.

docs.title: 1. Merge-sort prefix difference counting
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Merge-sort prefix difference counting
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def countRangeSum(self, nums: list[int], lower: int, upper: int) -> int:
        prefix = [0]
        for value in nums:
            prefix.append(prefix[-1] + value)

        def sort(values):
            if len(values) <= 1:
                return values, 0
            middle = len(values) // 2
            left, first = sort(values[:middle])
            right, second = sort(values[middle:])
            answer = first + second
            low = high = 0
            for value in left:
                while low < len(right) and right[low] - value < lower:
                    low += 1
                while high < len(right) and right[high] - value <= upper:
                    high += 1
                answer += high - low
            merged = []
            i = j = 0
            while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
                if left[i] <= right[j]:
                    merged.append(left[i])
                    i += 1
                else:
                    merged.append(right[j])
                    j += 1
            merged.extend(left[i:])
            merged.extend(right[j:])
            return merged, answer

        return sort(prefix)[1]

docs.title: 2. Compressed Fenwick prefix counts
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Compressed Fenwick prefix counts
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def countRangeSum(self, nums: list[int], lower: int, upper: int) -> int:
        prefix = [0]
        for value in nums:
            prefix.append(prefix[-1] + value)
        ordered = sorted(set(prefix))
        bit = [0] * (len(ordered) + 1)

        def count(end):
            result = 0
            while end:
                result += bit[end]
                end -= end & -end
            return result

        answer = 0
        for value in prefix:
            answer += count(bisect_right(ordered, value - lower)) - count(
                bisect_left(ordered, value - upper)
            )
            index = bisect_left(ordered, value) + 1
            while index < len(bit):
                bit[index] += 1
                index += index & -index
        return answer

docs.title: 1. Split interleaved position chains
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Split interleaved position chains
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def oddEvenList(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        if head is None:
            return None
        odd, even = head, head.next
        even_head = even
        while even and even.next:
            odd.next = even.next
            odd = odd.next
            even.next = odd.next
            even = even.next
        odd.next = even_head
        return head

docs.title: 2. Position-indexed reference groups
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Position-indexed reference groups
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def oddEvenList(self, head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
        groups = [[], []]
        index = 0
        while head:
            groups[index % 2].append(head)
            head = head.next
            index += 1
        ordered = groups[0] + groups[1]
        for index, node in enumerate(ordered):
            node.next = ordered[index + 1] if index + 1 < len(ordered) else None
        return ordered[0] if ordered else None

Hard · Advanced dynamic programming · Core · Learning step 79 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Find the longest strictly increasing path through a nonempty matrix. Move to an orthogonal neighbor at each step; diagonal moves are forbidden. The path length counts cells, including its start.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Direct an edge from each cell to every larger neighbor; increasing edges cannot cycle.
  2. Process this directed acyclic graph in layers, starting with cells of indegree zero.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 078 · #123 · Next: 080 · #10

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Topological indegree layers O(R*C) O(R*C) Value-ordered path DP O(RC log(RC)) O(R*C)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Topological indegree layers
docs.text: Count each cell's smaller neighbors as its incoming edges. Queue all cells with zero indegree. Process one queue layer at a time: remove its cells, decrement the indegrees of their larger neighbors, and enqueue neighbors whose indegree becomes zero. Return the number of layers. A neighbor helper keeps boundary handling in one place. The matrix itself remains unchanged.

docs.title: Value-ordered path DP
docs.text: Sort cell records by height. A cell starts with path length one and extends the longest path ending at any strictly smaller neighbor, whose record has already been processed.

docs.title: Topological indegree layers
docs.text: Strictly increasing edges exclude cycles. A source cell has longest incoming path length one. Any other cell is released only after every smaller neighbor has been removed, so its layer is one greater than the latest predecessor layer. This is exactly the longest-path recurrence on a DAG. Consequently the final layer number equals the longest path over all cells.

docs.title: Value-ordered path DP
docs.text: Every increasing path into a cell ends at a smaller neighbor. Value order is a topological order of all increasing edges, so taking the maximum predecessor length computes the exact DAG longest-path recurrence.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[1,2],[4,3]], the only initial source is 1. The layers contain 1, then 2, then 3, then 4. The path follows the square's perimeter and has length 4. Equal neighboring values would create no edge.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Topological indegree layers approach:

O(rows*columns) time and space; each cell has at most four edges. Input is unchanged. Processing the entire current layer before the next is essential. Iteration handles paths of tens of thousands of cells without Python's recursion-depth limit. Ordinary BFS distance finds shortest paths instead.

Topological indegree layers: O(RC) time; O(RC) space. Value-ordered path DP: O(RC log(RC)) time; O(R*C) space. Sorting allocates cell tuples and adds a logarithmic factor. Equal values never extend each other. Both variants avoid recursion and preserve the matrix.

docs.title: 1. Topological indegree layers
docs.text:
Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(R*C)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Topological indegree layers
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def longestIncreasingPath(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, columns = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])

        def neighbors(row: int, column: int):
            for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                other_row, other_column = row + dr, column + dc
                if 0 <= other_row < rows and 0 <= other_column < columns:
                    yield other_row, other_column

        indegree = [[0] * columns for _ in range(rows)]
        queue = deque()
        for row in range(rows):
            for column in range(columns):
                indegree[row][column] = sum(
                    matrix[nr][nc] < matrix[row][column] for nr, nc in neighbors(row, column)
                )
                if indegree[row][column] == 0:
                    queue.append((row, column))
        layers = 0
        while queue:
            layers += 1
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                row, column = queue.popleft()
                for nr, nc in neighbors(row, column):
                    if matrix[nr][nc] > matrix[row][column]:
                        indegree[nr][nc] -= 1
                        if indegree[nr][nc] == 0:
                            queue.append((nr, nc))
        return layers

docs.title: 2. Value-ordered path DP
docs.text:
Time: O(RC log(RC))

Space: O(R*C)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Value-ordered path DP
    Time: O(R*C log(R*C))
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def longestIncreasingPath(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, columns = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        cells = sorted((matrix[r][c], r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(columns))
        best = [[1] * columns for _ in range(rows)]
        answer = 1
        for value, row, column in cells:
            for nr, nc in (
                (row - 1, column),
                (row + 1, column),
                (row, column - 1),
                (row, column + 1),
            ):
                if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < columns and matrix[nr][nc] < value:
                    best[row][column] = max(best[row][column], best[nr][nc] + 1)
            answer = max(answer, best[row][column])
        return answer

Approach Time Space Sorted-list Hierholzer traversal O(E log E) O(E) Heap-adjacency Hierholzer traversal O(E log E) O(E)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Sorted-list Hierholzer traversal
docs.text: Run iterative Hierholzer traversal. Store destinations descending so popping consumes the smallest. Keep the active route on a stack. Follow unused edges; when the top has none, pop that airport into a reversed result. Reverse it.

docs.title: Heap-adjacency Hierholzer traversal
docs.text: Store each airport's outgoing ticket destinations in a min-heap. Consume the smallest edge and append airports only when their outgoing heap is exhausted, then reverse the finish sequence.

docs.title: Sorted-list Hierholzer traversal
docs.text: Each ticket is removed exactly once. Reverse finishing order splices discovered cycles into one complete Eulerian trail. A branch ending the trip is placed after the remaining branches. Sorted consumption makes the first feasible differing destination smallest, giving the lexicographically smallest complete trail under the guaranteed-existence contract.

docs.title: Heap-adjacency Hierholzer traversal
docs.text: Hierholzer postorder splices all ticket edges into an Eulerian trail, including branches that would strand a forward greedy walk. Minimum-edge consumption gives the smallest feasible lexicographic trail under the existence guarantee.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: With JFK->AAA, JFK->BBB, and BBB->JFK, visiting AAA first reaches a dead end. Reverse finishing order places that endpoint last. Return ["JFK","BBB","JFK","AAA"], which uses all three tickets.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Sorted-list Hierholzer traversal approach:

O(E log E) sorting time and O(E) traversal and storage. Tickets are unchanged. Do not deduplicate destinations or use a vertex-visited set. A forward greedy walk alone can stop early even when a complete itinerary exists.

Sorted-list Hierholzer traversal: O(E log E) time; O(E) space. Heap-adjacency Hierholzer traversal: O(E log E) time; O(E) space. Heaps avoid globally sorting tickets but require a logarithmic pop for each edge. Lists sort once and then pop in O(1). Both preserve duplicate tickets and original inputs.

docs.title: 1. Sorted-list Hierholzer traversal
docs.text:
Time: O(E log E)

Space: O(E)

from collections import defaultdict


class Solution:
    """Approach: Sorted-list Hierholzer traversal
    Time: O(E log E)
    Space: O(E)
    """

    def findItinerary(self, tickets: list[list[str]]) -> list[str]:
        outgoing = defaultdict(list)
        for source, target in sorted(tickets, reverse=True):
            outgoing[source].append(target)
        stack = ["JFK"]
        reverse_route = []
        while stack:
            airport = stack[-1]
            if outgoing[airport]:
                stack.append(outgoing[airport].pop())
            else:
                reverse_route.append(stack.pop())
        return reverse_route[::-1]

docs.title: 2. Heap-adjacency Hierholzer traversal
docs.text:
Time: O(E log E)

Space: O(E)

from collections import defaultdict


class Solution:
    """Approach: Heap-adjacency Hierholzer traversal
    Time: O(E log E)
    Space: O(E)
    """

    def findItinerary(self, tickets: list[list[str]]) -> list[str]:
        from heapq import heappop, heappush

        outgoing = {}
        for source, target in tickets:
            heappush(outgoing.setdefault(source, []), target)
        stack, route = ["JFK"], []
        while stack:
            edges = outgoing.get(stack[-1])
            if edges:
                stack.append(heappop(edges))
            else:
                route.append(stack.pop())
        route.reverse()
        return route

docs.text: The only external conflict for a subtree is whether its root is taken. Enumerating those two states captures every legal choice, and independent child optima can be added.

docs.title: Best value with grandchild recurrence
docs.text: Including a root forbids exactly its children, leaving grandchildren independent. Excluding it leaves both child problems unrestricted. Their maximum therefore covers all legal choices.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For root 4 with children 1 and 2 and a value-5 grandchild under 1, choose 4 and 5 for total 9.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Take and skip state pairs: O(n) time; O(n) space. Best value with grandchild recurrence: O(n) time; O(n) space. The tree is unchanged. Greedily choosing an entire even or odd level can miss combinations from different depths. Iterative postorder supports long chains; both state models need completed descendants first.

docs.title: 1. Take and skip state pairs
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Take and skip state pairs
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def rob(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> int:
        values = {None: (0, 0)}
        stack = [(root, False)] if root else []
        while stack:
            node, expanded = stack.pop()
            if expanded:
                left, right = values[node.left], values[node.right]
                values[node] = (node.val + left[1] + right[1], max(left) + max(right))
            else:
                stack.append((node, True))
                for child in (node.left, node.right):
                    if child:
                        stack.append((child, False))
        return max(values[root])

docs.title: 2. Best value with grandchild recurrence
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Best value with grandchild recurrence
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def rob(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> int:
        best = {None: 0}
        stack = [(root, False)] if root else []
        while stack:
            node, expanded = stack.pop()
            if expanded:
                take = node.val
                for child in (node.left, node.right):
                    if child:
                        take += best[child.left] + best[child.right]
                best[node] = max(take, best[node.left] + best[node.right])
            else:
                stack.append((node, True))
                for child in (node.left, node.right):
                    if child:
                        stack.append((child, False))
        return best[root]

docs.text:
Approach Time Space Lazy stack of child iterators O(T) total traversal; O(1) next after hasNext O(depth) Eager flattened snapshot O(T) constructor; O(1) next/hasNext O(T)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Lazy stack of child iterators
docs.text: Maintain iterators for active nested lists. HasNext descends lists until it finds an integer and caches it; exhausted iterators pop. Next consumes only the cached integer.

docs.title: Eager flattened snapshot
docs.text: Flatten with an explicit reverse-push stack at construction, then serve values from an array cursor.

docs.title: Lazy stack of child iterators
docs.text: The iterator stack records exactly the unfinished depth-first traversal. Caching separates discovery from consumption, so repeated availability checks preserve the next value.

docs.title: Eager flattened snapshot
docs.text: Reverse-pushing children makes stack pops follow the original left-to-right order. Each integer is appended once, and cursor iteration preserves that sequence.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [1,[2,[],[3]],4], calls yield 1,2,3,4. Empty lists contribute no integer.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Lazy stack of child iterators: O(T) total traversal; O(1) next after hasNext time; O(depth) space. Eager flattened snapshot: O(T) constructor; O(1) next/hasNext time; O(T) space. The nested input is unchanged. T includes integers and nested containers. Lazy construction is constant time; one hasNext may traverse many empty containers. The local NestedInteger helper mirrors the supplied interview interface for standalone tests.

docs.title: 1. Lazy stack of child iterators
docs.text:
Time: O(T) total traversal; O(1) next after hasNext

Space: O(depth)

class NestedInteger:
    """Standalone value container implementing the supplied nested-list interface."""

    def __init__(self, value=None):
        self._integer = value if isinstance(value, int) else None
        self._list = None if isinstance(value, int) else list(value or [])

    def isInteger(self):
        return self._integer is not None

    def getInteger(self):
        return self._integer

    def getList(self):
        return self._list

    def add(self, value):
        self._list.append(value)


class NestedIterator:
    """Approach: Lazy stack of child iterators
    Time: O(T) total traversal; O(1) next after hasNext
    Space: O(depth)
    """

    def __init__(self, nestedList: list["NestedInteger"]):
        self.stack = [iter(nestedList)]
        self.pending = None

    def hasNext(self) -> bool:
        if self.pending is not None:
            return True
        while self.stack:
            try:
                value = next(self.stack[-1])
            except StopIteration:
                self.stack.pop()
                continue
            if value.isInteger():
                self.pending = value.getInteger()
                return True
            self.stack.append(iter(value.getList()))
        return False

    def next(self) -> int:
        if not self.hasNext():
            raise StopIteration
        value, self.pending = self.pending, None
        return value

docs.title: 2. Eager flattened snapshot
docs.text:
Time: O(T) constructor; O(1) next/hasNext

Space: O(T)

class NestedInteger:
    """Standalone value container implementing the supplied nested-list interface."""

    def __init__(self, value=None):
        self._integer = value if isinstance(value, int) else None
        self._list = None if isinstance(value, int) else list(value or [])

    def isInteger(self):
        return self._integer is not None

    def getInteger(self):
        return self._integer

    def getList(self):
        return self._list

    def add(self, value):
        self._list.append(value)


class NestedIterator:
    """Approach: Eager flattened snapshot
    Time: O(T) constructor; O(1) next/hasNext
    Space: O(T)
    """

    def __init__(self, nestedList: list["NestedInteger"]):
        self.values = []
        self.index = 0
        stack = list(reversed(nestedList))
        while stack:
            value = stack.pop()
            if value.isInteger():
                self.values.append(value.getInteger())
            else:
                stack.extend(reversed(value.getList()))

    def hasNext(self) -> bool:
        return self.index < len(self.values)

    def next(self) -> int:
        value = self.values[self.index]
        self.index += 1
        return value

docs.text:
Approach Time Space Best product by total O(n^2) O(n) Factors of three with a remainder adjustment O(log n) arithmetic operations O(1) integer objects

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Best product by total
docs.text: For each total, choose its first piece and either keep or optimally split the remainder. The outer split always creates at least two pieces.

docs.title: Factors of three with a remainder adjustment
docs.text: Use as many threes as possible, except replace a final 3+1 with 2+2. Handle two and three separately because a split is required.

docs.title: Best product by total
docs.text: Every partition has a first piece; its remainder is either a single piece or another partition. Trying every first value covers every valid partition.

docs.title: Factors of three with a remainder adjustment
docs.text: A piece at least five improves when replaced by 3 and its remainder. Ones reduce product, and three twos improve to two threes. Only threes with at most two twos remain optimal.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For n=8, use 3+3+2 and obtain product 18.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Best product by total: O(n^2) time; O(n) space. Factors of three with a remainder adjustment: O(log n) arithmetic operations time; O(1) integer objects space.

No inputs are mutated. Exponentiation uses growing integers; bit cost is additional to arithmetic-operation counts. Returning n itself for n=2 or n=3 violates the required split.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Best product by total
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Best product by total
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def integerBreak(self, n: int) -> int:
        dp = [0] * (n + 1)
        for total in range(2, n + 1):
            dp[total] = max(
                first * max(total - first, dp[total - first]) for first in range(1, total)
            )
        return dp[n]

docs.title: 2. Factors of three with a remainder adjustment
docs.text:
Time: O(log n) arithmetic operations

Space: O(1) integer objects

class Solution:
    """Approach: Factors of three with a remainder adjustment
    Time: O(log n) arithmetic operations
    Space: O(1) integer objects
    """

    def integerBreak(self, n: int) -> int:
        if n <= 3:
            return n - 1
        threes, remainder = divmod(n, 3)
        if remainder == 1:
            return 3 ** (threes - 1) * 4
        return 3**threes * (2 if remainder else 1)

Approach Time Space Frequency buckets O(n) expected O(n) Size-k frequency heap O(n + u log(k+1)); worst misses linear follow-up O(u+k)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Frequency buckets
docs.text: Count with a frequency map. Place each distinct value in a bucket indexed by its frequency, then scan buckets from high to low until k values are collected. This avoids sorting all distinct values.

docs.title: Size-k frequency heap
docs.text: Count distinct values, then retain a min-heap of the k strongest (frequency,value) pairs. This avoids n frequency buckets but does not guarantee the linear follow-up bound when k grows with n.

docs.title: Frequency buckets
docs.text: Every value appears in exactly its frequency bucket. Descending bucket order visits values in nonincreasing frequency, so the first k are precisely the most frequent set. The uniqueness promise removes ambiguity at the cutoff.

docs.title: Size-k frequency heap
docs.text: After each distinct value, the heap contains the k largest frequency pairs seen. The guaranteed unique cutoff makes tie order irrelevant to the selected set.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [2,2,2,4,4,7] and k=2, buckets 3,2,1 contain [2],[4],[7]. Read buckets 3 and 2 to return [2,4].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

Expected O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space, plus O(k) output. Input is unchanged. This meets the requested better-than-O(n log n) follow-up. Allocate independent bucket lists with a comprehension, not repeated references to one list. A heap is an alternative when avoiding n empty buckets matters.

Alternative tradeoff: O(n + u log(k+1)); worst misses linear follow-up time; O(u+k) space.

docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(n)

from collections import Counter
from heapq import heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Frequency buckets
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def topKFrequent(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
        frequencies = Counter(nums)
        buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
        for number, count in frequencies.items():
            buckets[count].append(number)
        result = []
        for count in range(len(nums), 0, -1):
            for number in buckets[count]:
                result.append(number)
                if len(result) == k:
                    return result
        raise ValueError("k must not exceed the distinct value count")

docs.title: 2. Size-k frequency heap
docs.text:
Time: O(n + u log(k+1)); worst misses linear follow-up

Space: O(u+k)

from collections import Counter
from heapq import heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Size-k frequency heap
    Time: O(n + u log(k+1)); worst misses linear follow-up
    Space: O(u+k)
    """

    def topKFrequent(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
        heap = []
        for value, count in Counter(nums).items():
            heappush(heap, (count, value))
            if len(heap) > k:
                heappop(heap)
        return [value for _, value in heap]

The object owns its intervals and does not expose mutable internal lists. k is interval count and u distinct value count; choosing the set approach favors many writes and few reads.

docs.text:
Time: O(k) add; O(k) get

Space: O(k)

from bisect import bisect_left


class SummaryRanges:
    """Approach: Sorted interval insertion and neighbor merging
    Time: O(k) add; O(k) get
    Space: O(k)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.intervals = []

    def addNum(self, value: int) -> None:
        index = bisect_left(self.intervals, [value])
        start = end = value
        if index and self.intervals[index - 1][1] + 1 >= value:
            index -= 1
            start, end = self.intervals.pop(index)
            end = max(end, value)
        while index < len(self.intervals) and self.intervals[index][0] <= end + 1:
            following = self.intervals.pop(index)
            end = max(end, following[1])
        self.intervals.insert(index, [start, end])

    def getIntervals(self) -> list[list[int]]:
        return [interval[:] for interval in self.intervals]

docs.title: 2. Distinct-value set with read-time compression
docs.text:
Time: O(1) expected add; O(u log u) get

Space: O(u)

from bisect import bisect_left


class SummaryRanges:
    """Approach: Distinct-value set with read-time compression
    Time: O(1) expected add; O(u log u) get
    Space: O(u)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.values = set()

    def addNum(self, value: int) -> None:
        self.values.add(value)

    def getIntervals(self) -> list[list[int]]:
        answer = []
        for value in sorted(self.values):
            if answer and value == answer[-1][1] + 1:
                answer[-1][1] = value
            else:
                answer.append([value, value])
        return answer

docs.text: Sort ascending width and descending height for equal widths. Apply strict increasing-subsequence tails to heights.

docs.text: Sort into a dependency order and explicitly test both dimensions against every earlier envelope.

docs.title: Width sort and height LIS
docs.text: Descending heights prevent an increasing subsequence from selecting two equal-width entries. For different widths, increasing heights exactly characterize valid nesting; the smallest-tail invariant gives the longest chain.

docs.title: All-predecessor nesting DP
docs.text: The final predecessor of any chain ending here must be smaller in both coordinates. All such candidates appear earlier after sorting, so their best lengths provide the exact recurrence.

Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Width sort and height LIS
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def maxEnvelopes(self, envelopes: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        from bisect import bisect_left

        ordered = sorted(envelopes, key=lambda pair: (pair[0], -pair[1]))
        tails = []
        for _, height in ordered:
            position = bisect_left(tails, height)
            if position == len(tails):
                tails.append(height)
            else:
                tails[position] = height
        return len(tails)

docs.title: 2. All-predecessor nesting DP
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: All-predecessor nesting DP
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def maxEnvelopes(self, envelopes: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        ordered = sorted(envelopes)
        dp = [1] * len(ordered)
        for i, (width, height) in enumerate(ordered):
            for j in range(i):
                if ordered[j][0] < width and ordered[j][1] < height:
                    dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1)
        return max(dp)

docs.title: 1. Heap merge of user timelines
docs.text:
Time: O(1) post/follow/unfollow expected; O(f + 10 log(f+1)) feed

Space: O(T+F) stored; O(f) query

from collections import defaultdict
from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Twitter:
    """Approach: Heap merge of user timelines
    Time: O(1) post/follow/unfollow expected; O(f + 10 log(f+1)) feed
    Space: O(T+F) stored; O(f) query
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.clock = 0
        self.posts = defaultdict(list)
        self.following = defaultdict(set)

    def postTweet(self, userId: int, tweetId: int) -> None:
        self.posts[userId].append((self.clock, tweetId))
        self.clock += 1

    def getNewsFeed(self, userId: int) -> list[int]:
        heap = []
        for user in self.following.get(userId, set()) | {userId}:
            posts = self.posts.get(user)
            if posts:
                index = len(posts) - 1
                heap.append((-posts[index][0], user, index))
        heapify(heap)
        result = []
        while heap and len(result) < 10:
            _, user, index = heappop(heap)
            result.append(self.posts[user][index][1])
            if index:
                heappush(heap, (-self.posts[user][index - 1][0], user, index - 1))
        return result

    def follow(self, followerId: int, followeeId: int) -> None:
        self.following[followerId].add(followeeId)

    def unfollow(self, followerId: int, followeeId: int) -> None:
        followees = self.following.get(followerId)
        if followees is not None:
            followees.discard(followeeId)
            if not followees:
                del self.following[followerId]

from collections import defaultdict
from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Twitter:
    """Approach: Scan global timeline
    Time: O(1) post/follow/unfollow expected; O(T) feed
    Space: O(T+F)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.timeline = []
        self.following = defaultdict(set)

    def postTweet(self, userId: int, tweetId: int) -> None:
        self.timeline.append((userId, tweetId))

    def getNewsFeed(self, userId: int) -> list[int]:
        visible = self.following.get(userId, set()) | {userId}
        result = []
        for user, tweet in reversed(self.timeline):
            if user in visible:
                result.append(tweet)
                if len(result) == 10:
                    break
        return result

    def follow(self, followerId: int, followeeId: int) -> None:
        self.following[followerId].add(followeeId)

    def unfollow(self, followerId: int, followeeId: int) -> None:
        followees = self.following.get(followerId)
        if followees is not None:
            followees.discard(followeeId)
            if not followees:
                del self.following[followerId]

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Count integers x with 0 <= x < 10^n whose decimal digits are all distinct.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Count separately by the number of significant digits.
  2. Leading zeroes in a fixed-width representation are padding, not used digits.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Count by significant length O(min(n,10)) O(1) Digit-mask DP with leading padding O(n102^10) O(2^10)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Count by significant length
docs.text: Count zero once. For each positive length, choose a nonzero first digit in nine ways, then choose each following digit from unused digits.

docs.title: Digit-mask DP with leading padding
docs.text: Construct n positions using a digit-used mask and a started flag. Leading zeroes keep the not-started state; after starting, every digit must be unused.

docs.title: Count by significant length
docs.text: A length-k positive number has a unique sequence of digit choices. The first position forbids zero; later positions forbid precisely the digits already used. Summing disjoint lengths counts every valid integer once.

docs.title: Digit-mask DP with leading padding
docs.text: Each integer below 10^n has one padded representation. Padding does not consume zero, and all significant digits consume distinct bits, giving a one-to-one correspondence between accepted DP paths and valid integers.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For n=2, all 10 one-digit values count, and 9*9 two-digit values count, giving 91.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Count by significant length: O(min(n,10)) time; O(1) space. Digit-mask DP with leading padding: O(n102^10) time; O(2^10) space.

Both preserve n and return one when n=0. More than ten significant digits cannot be unique. The combinatorial default avoids the larger mask frontier; Python integers store exact counts.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Count by significant length
docs.text:
Time: O(min(n,10))

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Count by significant length
    Time: O(min(n,10))
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def countNumbersWithUniqueDigits(self, n: int) -> int:
        answer = 1
        ways = 9
        for length in range(1, min(n, 10) + 1):
            if length > 1:
                ways *= 11 - length
            answer += ways
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Digit-mask DP with leading padding
docs.text:
Time: O(n102^10)

Space: O(2^10)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Digit-mask DP with leading padding
    Time: O(n*10*2^10)
    Space: O(2^10)
    """

    def countNumbersWithUniqueDigits(self, n: int) -> int:
        counts = {(0, False): 1}
        for _ in range(n):
            following = {}
            for (mask, started), count in counts.items():
                for digit in range(10):
                    if not started and digit == 0:
                        state = (0, False)
                    elif mask & (1 << digit):
                        continue
                    else:
                        state = (mask | (1 << digit), True)
                    following[state] = following.get(state, 0) + count
            counts = following
        return sum(counts.values())

docs.title: Lengths and predecessor links
docs.text: Divisibility is transitive. Extending a divisible predecessor chain preserves pairwise divisibility, and every valid sorted subset has such a predecessor chain.
