Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Lengths and predecessor links
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def largestDivisibleSubset(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        ordered = sorted(nums)
        lengths, previous = [1] * len(nums), [-1] * len(nums)
        best = 0
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            for j in range(i):
                if ordered[i] % ordered[j] == 0 and lengths[j] + 1 > lengths[i]:
                    lengths[i], previous[i] = lengths[j] + 1, j
            if lengths[i] > lengths[best]:
                best = i
        result = []
        while best >= 0:
            result.append(ordered[best])
            best = previous[best]
        return result[::-1]

docs.title: 2. Explicit best chains by endpoint
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Explicit best chains by endpoint
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def largestDivisibleSubset(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        ordered = sorted(nums)
        chains = []
        for i, value in enumerate(ordered):
            best = []
            for j in range(i):
                if value % ordered[j] == 0 and len(chains[j]) > len(best):
                    best = chains[j]
            chains.append(best + [value])
        return max(chains, key=len)

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Parallel carry propagation O(W) worst case O(1) Bit-by-bit full adder O(W) O(1)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Parallel carry propagation
docs.text: Repeatedly compute XOR partial sums and shifted AND carries under a 32-bit mask. Decode the final sign bit.

docs.title: Bit-by-bit full adder
docs.text: Process 32 positions with a one-bit carry. A full-adder truth table gives the sum bit and outgoing carry.

docs.title: Parallel carry propagation
docs.text: For every bit, XOR plus the shifted carry represents the same total value modulo 2^32. Carry bits move left each iteration and eventually vanish; the promised sum fits the decoded signed range.

docs.title: Bit-by-bit full adder
docs.text: The sum bit is x XOR y XOR carry, and a carry exists when at least two input bits are set. Induction over bit positions reproduces binary addition without arithmetic plus or minus.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: 1 and 3 first produce XOR 2 and carry 2; the next rounds move the carry and settle at binary 100, or 4.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Parallel carry propagation: O(W) worst case time; O(1) space.

Bit-by-bit full adder: O(W) time; O(1) space.

Inputs are unchanged. W=32. Python negative integers have unbounded sign extension; omitting the mask from parallel carry propagation can prevent termination.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Parallel carry propagation
docs.text:
Time: O(W) worst case

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Parallel carry propagation
    Time: O(W) worst case
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def getSum(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
        mask = 0xFFFFFFFF
        a &= mask
        b &= mask
        while b:
            a, b = (a ^ b) & mask, ((a & b) << 1) & mask
        return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF else ~(a ^ mask)

docs.title: 2. Bit-by-bit full adder
docs.text:
Time: O(W)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Bit-by-bit full adder
    Time: O(W)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def getSum(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
        answer = carry = 0
        for bit in range(32):
            x, y = (a >> bit) & 1, (b >> bit) & 1
            answer |= (x ^ y ^ carry) << bit
            carry = (x & y) | (x & carry) | (y & carry)
        return answer if answer <= 0x7FFFFFFF else ~(answer ^ 0xFFFFFFFF)

docs.text: Seed row heads (i,0) for at most k first-array positions. Pop the smallest pair and advance only its row to (i,j+1).

docs.title: Two-dimensional best-first frontier
docs.text: Start at pair (0,0). After extracting a pair, enqueue unseen right and downward neighbors using an index-pair set.

docs.title: Heap merge of sum rows
docs.text: Each row is sorted, and the heap holds its smallest unreported pair. Rows beyond the first k cannot be needed before k earlier row heads, so seeding only k rows is sufficient.

Two-dimensional best-first frontier: O(k log(k+1)) time; O(k) auxiliary plus output space. Both inputs are unchanged. Duplicate values at different indices are distinct pair choices. The heap bounds use the number of returned pairs, capped by m*n. A seen set is essential in the two-direction frontier.

docs.title: 1. Heap merge of sum rows
docs.text:
Time: O(min(k,m) + k log(min(k,m)+1))

Space: O(min(k,m)) auxiliary plus output

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Heap merge of sum rows
    Time: O(min(k,m) + k log(min(k,m)+1))
    Space: O(min(k,m)) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def kSmallestPairs(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int], k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        if not nums1 or not nums2:
            return []
        heap = [(nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0) for i in range(min(k, len(nums1)))]
        heapify(heap)
        result = []
        while heap and len(result) < k:
            _, i, j = heappop(heap)
            result.append([nums1[i], nums2[j]])
            if j + 1 < len(nums2):
                heappush(heap, (nums1[i] + nums2[j + 1], i, j + 1))
        return result

docs.title: 2. Two-dimensional best-first frontier
docs.text:
Time: O(k log(k+1))

Space: O(k) auxiliary plus output

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Two-dimensional best-first frontier
    Time: O(k log(k+1))
    Space: O(k) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def kSmallestPairs(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int], k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        if not nums1 or not nums2:
            return []
        heap = [(nums1[0] + nums2[0], 0, 0)]
        seen = {(0, 0)}
        result = []
        while heap and len(result) < k:
            _, i, j = heappop(heap)
            result.append([nums1[i], nums2[j]])
            for row, col in ((i + 1, j), (i, j + 1)):
                if row < len(nums1) and col < len(nums2) and (row, col) not in seen:
                    seen.add((row, col))
                    heappush(heap, (nums1[row] + nums2[col], row, col))
        return result

docs.text: Compare adjacent values. A rise extends the best down-ending length by one; a fall extends the best up-ending length.

docs.title: Per-index alternating-subsequence DP
docs.text: For each endpoint, inspect every earlier endpoint and extend only a subsequence ending with the opposite direction. This slower baseline may time out if input limits are enlarged.

docs.title: Compressed up/down greedy states
docs.text: Within a run moving in one direction, retaining its more extreme endpoint leaves at least as much room for a future reversal. Only direction changes need extend the chosen subsequence, which the two states count.

docs.title: Per-index alternating-subsequence DP

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Compressed up/down greedy states
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def wiggleMaxLength(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        up = down = 1
        for i in range(1, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] > nums[i - 1]:
                up = down + 1
            elif nums[i] < nums[i - 1]:
                down = up + 1
        return max(up, down)

docs.title: 2. Per-index alternating-subsequence DP
docs.text:
Time: O(n squared)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Per-index alternating-subsequence DP
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def wiggleMaxLength(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        up = [1] * len(nums)
        down = [1] * len(nums)
        for i, value in enumerate(nums):
            for j in range(i):
                if nums[j] < value:
                    up[i] = max(up[i], down[j] + 1)
                elif nums[j] > value:
                    down[i] = max(down[i], up[j] + 1)
        return max(max(up), max(down))

docs.text: Keep a sparse dictionary of reachable sums and propagate each solved count along all one-number append edges.

docs.title: Final-element amount DP
docs.text: Every nonempty sequence has one unique final value. Removing it leaves a sequence at a smaller total, so summing predecessor counts counts each ordered sequence once.

docs.text: Positive values give a topological increasing-sum order. Every path to a total represents exactly one ordered sequence, and distributing its count along each outgoing edge counts all extensions.

Time: O(n*T)

Space: O(T)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Final-element amount DP
    Time: O(n*T)
    Space: O(T)
    """

    def combinationSum4(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
        dp = [0] * (target + 1)
        dp[0] = 1
        for total in range(1, target + 1):
            dp[total] = sum(dp[total - value] for value in nums if value <= total)
        return dp[target]

docs.title: 2. Forward path propagation
docs.text:
Time: O(n*T)

Space: O(T)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Forward path propagation
    Time: O(n*T)
    Space: O(T)
    """

    def combinationSum4(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
        ways = {0: 1}
        for total in range(target + 1):
            count = ways.get(total, 0)
            if not count:
                continue
            for value in nums:
                following = total + value
                if following <= target:
                    ways[following] = ways.get(following, 0) + count
        return ways.get(target, 0)

docs.title: 1. Binary search the value range
docs.text:
Time: O(n log(W+1))

Space: O(1)

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary search the value range
    Time: O(n log(W+1))
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def kthSmallest(self, matrix: list[list[int]], k: int) -> int:
        n = len(matrix)
        low, high = matrix[0][0], matrix[-1][-1]
        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            row, col, count = n - 1, 0, 0
            while row >= 0 and col < n:
                if matrix[row][col] <= middle:
                    count += row + 1
                    col += 1
                else:
                    row -= 1
            if count < k:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle
        return low

Space: O(n)

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Heap merge sorted rows
    Time: O(n + k log(n+1))
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def kthSmallest(self, matrix: list[list[int]], k: int) -> int:
        heap = [(row[0], index, 0) for index, row in enumerate(matrix)]
        heapify(heap)
        for _ in range(k):
            value, row, col = heappop(heap)
            if col + 1 < len(matrix):
                heappush(heap, (matrix[row][col + 1], row, col + 1))
        return value

from random import choice


class RandomizedSet:
    """Approach: Dense array and index map
    Time: O(1) expected per operation
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.values = []
        self.indices = {}

    def insert(self, val: int) -> bool:
        if val in self.indices:
            return False
        self.indices[val] = len(self.values)
        self.values.append(val)
        return True

    def remove(self, val: int) -> bool:
        if val not in self.indices:
            return False
        index = self.indices[val]
        last = self.values[-1]
        self.values[index] = last
        self.indices[last] = index
        self.values.pop()
        del self.indices[val]
        return True

    def getRandom(self) -> int:
        return choice(self.values)

from collections import defaultdict
from random import choice, randrange


class RandomizedCollection:
    """Approach: Dense occurrences and index sets
    Time: O(1) expected per operation
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.values = []
        self.positions = defaultdict(set)

    def insert(self, val: int) -> bool:
        absent = not self.positions[val]
        self.positions[val].add(len(self.values))
        self.values.append(val)
        return absent

    def remove(self, val: int) -> bool:
        if val not in self.positions:
            return False
        index = self.positions[val].pop()
        last_index = len(self.values) - 1
        last = self.values[-1]
        if index != last_index:
            self.values[index] = last
            self.positions[last].remove(last_index)
            self.positions[last].add(index)
        self.values.pop()
        if not self.positions[val]:
            del self.positions[val]
        return True

    def getRandom(self) -> int:
        return choice(self.values)

from collections import defaultdict
from random import choice, randrange


class RandomizedCollection:
    """Approach: Frequency map and weighted scan
    Time: O(1) expected insert/remove; O(u) getRandom; misses required O(1)
    Space: O(u)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.counts = {}
        self.total = 0

    def insert(self, val: int) -> bool:
        absent = val not in self.counts
        self.counts[val] = self.counts.get(val, 0) + 1
        self.total += 1
        return absent

    def remove(self, val: int) -> bool:
        if val not in self.counts:
            return False
        self.counts[val] -= 1
        self.total -= 1
        if self.counts[val] == 0:
            del self.counts[val]
        return True

    def getRandom(self) -> int:
        index = randrange(self.total)
        for value, count in self.counts.items():
            if index < count:
                return value
            index -= count
        raise AssertionError("Unreachable for a nonempty collection")

from random import choice, randrange


class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next


class Solution:
    """Approach: Reservoir sampling
    Time: O(1) constructor; O(n) getRandom
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def __init__(self, head: ListNode):
        self.head = head

    def getRandom(self) -> int:
        current = self.head
        count = 0
        selected = current.val
        while current:
            count += 1
            if randrange(count) == 0:
                selected = current.val
            current = current.next
        return selected

docs.title: Forward Fisher-Yates swaps
docs.text: Copy the original values. Shuffle a fresh copy by choosing a random position from i through n-1 and swapping into position i.

docs.title: Inside-out permutation construction

docs.title: Forward Fisher-Yates swaps

docs.title: Inside-out permutation construction
docs.text: Inductively the previous prefix is uniform. Inserting the new item into any of i+1 equally likely positions yields each larger permutation with equal probability.

The constructor copies the input and every returned array is fresh, so caller mutations cannot alter the stored original. Both use linear output memory and exact uniform integer draws, rather than sorting approximate random keys.

from random import randrange


class Solution:
    """Approach: Forward Fisher-Yates swaps
    Time: O(n) constructor/reset/shuffle
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self, nums: list[int]):
        self.original = tuple(nums)

    def reset(self) -> list[int]:
        return list(self.original)

    def shuffle(self) -> list[int]:
        result = list(self.original)
        for index in range(len(result)):
            chosen = randrange(index, len(result))
            result[index], result[chosen] = result[chosen], result[index]
        return result

from random import randrange


class Solution:
    """Approach: Inside-out permutation construction
    Time: O(n) constructor/reset/shuffle
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self, nums: list[int]):
        self.original = tuple(nums)

    def reset(self) -> list[int]:
        return list(self.original)

    def shuffle(self) -> list[int]:
        result = []
        for index, value in enumerate(self.original):
            chosen = randrange(index + 1)
            result.append(value)
            result[index] = result[chosen]
            result[chosen] = value
        return result

class Solution:
    """Approach: Stack of suspended output chunks
    Time: O(n+L*d) worst case
    Space: O(n+L*d) worst case
    """

    def decodeString(self, s: str) -> str:
        stack = []
        chunks = []
        count = 0
        for char in s:
            if char.isdigit():
                count = count * 10 + int(char)
            elif char == "[":
                stack.append((chunks, count))
                chunks, count = [], 0
            elif char == "]":
                text = "".join(chunks)
                chunks, repetitions = stack.pop()
                chunks.append(text * repetitions)
            else:
                chunks.append(char)
        return "".join(chunks)

docs.title: 2. Recursive descent by bracket scope
docs.text:
Time: O(n+L*d) worst case

Space: O(n+L*d) worst case

class Solution:
    """Approach: Recursive descent by bracket scope
    Time: O(n+L*d) worst case
    Space: O(n+L*d) worst case
    """

    def decodeString(self, s: str) -> str:
        index = 0

        def parse():
            nonlocal index
            pieces = []
            while index < len(s) and s[index] != "]":
                if s[index].isdigit():
                    count = 0
                    while s[index].isdigit():
                        count = count * 10 + int(s[index])
                        index += 1
                    index += 1
                    inner = parse()
                    index += 1
                    pieces.append(inner * count)
                else:
                    pieces.append(s[index])
                    index += 1
            return "".join(pieces)

        return parse()

docs.text:
Time: O(E+Q*(V+E))

Space: O(V+E)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Ratio-product graph search
    Time: O(E+Q*(V+E))
    Space: O(V+E)
    """

    def calcEquation(self, equations, values, queries):
        graph = {}
        for (a, b), value in zip(equations, values, strict=True):
            graph.setdefault(a, []).append((b, value))
            graph.setdefault(b, []).append((a, 1 / value))
        answers = []
        for start, end in queries:
            if start not in graph or end not in graph:
                answers.append(-1.0)
                continue
            stack, seen = [(start, 1.0)], {start}
            answer = -1.0
            while stack:
                node, ratio = stack.pop()
                if node == end:
                    answer = ratio
                    break
                for other, factor in graph[node]:
                    if other not in seen:
                        seen.add(other)
                        stack.append((other, ratio * factor))
            answers.append(answer)
        return answers

docs.title: 2. Weighted union-find ratios
docs.text:
Time: O((E+Q)*alpha(V)) expected

Space: O(V)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Weighted union-find ratios
    Time: O((E+Q)*alpha(V)) expected
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def calcEquation(self, equations, values, queries):
        parent, weight, size = {}, {}, {}

        def find(node):
            trail = []
            root = node
            while parent[root] != root:
                trail.append(root)
                root = parent[root]
            ratio = 1.0
            for item in reversed(trail):
                ratio *= weight[item]
                parent[item], weight[item] = root, ratio
            return root, weight[node]

        for (a, b), value in zip(equations, values, strict=True):
            for node in (a, b):
                if node not in parent:
                    parent[node], weight[node], size[node] = node, 1.0, 1
            ra, wa = find(a)
            rb, wb = find(b)
            if ra == rb:
                continue
            if size[ra] < size[rb]:
                parent[ra], weight[ra] = rb, value * wb / wa
                size[rb] += size[ra]
            else:
                parent[rb], weight[rb] = ra, wa / (value * wb)
                size[ra] += size[rb]
        answers = []
        for a, b in queries:
            if a not in parent or b not in parent:
                answers.append(-1.0)
                continue
            ra, wa = find(a)
            rb, wb = find(b)
            answers.append(wa / wb if ra == rb else -1.0)
        return answers

docs.title: Approach comparison

docs.title: Subtract complete digit-width blocks
docs.text: Remove all digits belonging to shorter numbers, then index the containing number in the remaining width block.

docs.title: Binary search containing integer
docs.text: Binary-search the smallest integer x whose cumulative written digit count reaches n, then locate n inside x.

docs.title: Subtract complete digit-width blocks
docs.text: Each removed block has exactly width*count digits. Once n lies in the current block, zero-based offset n-1 splits uniquely into a number offset and an in-number digit index.

docs.title: Binary search containing integer
docs.text: The cumulative digit count is strictly increasing. Its lower bound is exactly the integer containing the nth digit, and subtracting the preceding cumulative count yields the digit's one- based offset.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: n=11 skips the nine one-digit numbers, leaving offset 2 in the two-digit block. Number 10 contains that position, and its second digit is 0.

Binary search containing integer: O(log squared n) time; O(log n) space.

docs.title: 1. Subtract complete digit-width blocks
docs.text:
Time: O(log n)

Space: O(log n) for decimal conversion

class Solution:
    """Approach: Subtract complete digit-width blocks
    Time: O(log n)
    Space: O(log n) for decimal conversion
    """

    def findNthDigit(self, n: int) -> int:
        width, start, count = 1, 1, 9
        while n > width * count:
            n -= width * count
            width += 1
            start *= 10
            count *= 10
        number = start + (n - 1) // width
        return int(str(number)[(n - 1) % width])

docs.title: 2. Binary search containing integer
docs.text:
Time: O(log squared n)

Space: O(log n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary search containing integer
    Time: O(log squared n)
    Space: O(log n)
    """

    def findNthDigit(self, n: int) -> int:
        def digits_through(value):
            total, start, width = 0, 1, 1
            while start <= value:
                end = min(value, start * 10 - 1)
                total += (end - start + 1) * width
                start *= 10
                width += 1
            return total

        low, high = 1, n
        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if digits_through(middle) >= n:
                high = middle
            else:
                low = middle + 1
        offset = n - digits_through(low - 1) - 1
        return int(str(low)[offset])

docs.title: Monotonic digit stack

docs.title: Greedy next-digit selection
docs.text: Choose the smallest feasible next retained digit from the positions reachable with the remaining deletion budget. This educational baseline may time out on long decreasing inputs.

docs.title: Monotonic digit stack
docs.text: At the first larger-before-smaller pair, deleting the larger earlier digit yields a smaller number than any deletion later in that prefix. Repeating this exchange gives the lexicographically minimal retained digit sequence.

docs.title: 1. Monotonic digit stack
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Monotonic digit stack
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def removeKdigits(self, num: str, k: int) -> str:
        stack = []
        for char in num:
            while k and stack and stack[-1] > char:
                stack.pop()
                k -= 1
            stack.append(char)
        if k:
            del stack[-k:]
        return "".join(stack).lstrip("0") or "0"

docs.title: 2. Greedy next-digit selection
docs.text:
Time: O(n squared)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Greedy next-digit selection
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def removeKdigits(self, num: str, k: int) -> str:
        keep = len(num) - k
        start = 0
        answer = []
        while keep:
            end = len(num) - keep
            index = min(range(start, end + 1), key=num.__getitem__)
            answer.append(num[index])
            start = index + 1
            keep -= 1
        return "".join(answer).lstrip("0") or "0"

docs.text: Decide whether a frog can reach the last sorted stone, starting with a jump of one and then using previous jump length minus one, equal, or plus one, always positive.

docs.title: Hints

  2. A dense index-pair recurrence can derive the needed last jump from stone positions.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Sparse jump-length sets by stone position O(n^2) expected O(n^2) Dense arrival-index and last-jump table O(n^2) O(n^2)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Sparse jump-length sets by stone position
docs.text: Associate every stone position with reachable last-jump lengths. Starting at position zero with length zero forces the first positive choice to one; propagate only to existing stones.

docs.title: Dense arrival-index and last-jump table
docs.text: For every earlier stone pair, compute their distance as the required arriving jump. It is reachable if the earlier stone supports a last jump one smaller, equal, or one larger.

docs.title: Sparse jump-length sets by stone position
docs.text: Each propagated state appends one allowed jump to an existing valid route. Conversely, every route arrives from an earlier stone with one of those three predecessor-length transitions, so scanning positions ascending discovers it.

docs.title: Dense arrival-index and last-jump table
docs.text: After visiting at most n stones, jump length cannot exceed n because it starts at one and grows by at most one. Thus a bounded jump dimension covers every route; the predecessor recurrence checks exactly the legal final transitions.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Stones [0,1,3,5,6,8,12,17] permit jumps 1,2,2,3,4,5 and reach the end.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Sparse jump-length sets by stone position: O(n^2) expected time; O(n^2) space. Dense arrival-index and last-jump table: O(n^2) time; O(n^2) space.

Both preserve stones. Sparse sets can avoid many impossible jump states, while the dense table guarantees quadratic scanning and allocates n*(n+1) references. Neither uses recursion, important at n=2000. Positions are strictly increasing, so no state updates its own set.

docs.title: 1. Sparse jump-length sets by stone position
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2) expected

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sparse jump-length sets by stone position
    Time: O(n^2) expected
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def canCross(self, stones: list[int]) -> bool:
        jumps = {position: set() for position in stones}
        jumps[0].add(0)
        for position in stones:
            for previous in jumps[position]:
                for following in (previous - 1, previous, previous + 1):
                    target = position + following
                    if following > 0 and target in jumps:
                        jumps[target].add(following)
        return bool(jumps[stones[-1]])

docs.title: 2. Dense arrival-index and last-jump table
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Dense arrival-index and last-jump table
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def canCross(self, stones: list[int]) -> bool:
        n = len(stones)
        dp = [[False] * (n + 1) for _ in stones]
        dp[0][0] = True
        for end in range(1, n):
            for previous in range(end):
                jump = stones[end] - stones[previous]
                if jump > n:
                    continue
                dp[end][jump] = (
                    dp[end][jump]
                    or dp[previous][jump - 1]
                    or dp[previous][jump]
                    or (jump < n and dp[previous][jump + 1])
                )
        return any(dp[-1])

class Solution:
    """Approach: Descending heights and list insertion
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def reconstructQueue(self, people: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
        queue = []
        for height, count in sorted(people, key=lambda person: (-person[0], person[1])):
            queue.insert(count, [height, count])
        return queue

docs.title: 2. Ascending heights and Fenwick free-slot selection
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Ascending heights and Fenwick free-slot selection
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def reconstructQueue(self, people: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
        size = len(people)
        bit = [0] + [i & -i for i in range(1, size + 1)]
        queue = [None] * size
        for height, count in sorted(people, key=lambda person: (person[0], -person[1])):
            rank = count + 1
            index = 0
            step = 1 << (size.bit_length() - 1)
            while step:
                following = index + step
                if following <= size and bit[following] < rank:
                    rank -= bit[following]
                    index = following
                step >>= 1
            queue[index] = [height, count]
            update = index + 1
            while update <= size:
                bit[update] -= 1
                update += update & -update
        return queue

Approach Time Space Binary search a feasible maximum sum O(n log(S+1)) O(1) Exact-piece dynamic programming O(k*n squared) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Binary search a feasible maximum sum
docs.text: Search between the maximum element and total sum. Greedily extend each piece until adding the next value would exceed the candidate limit.

docs.title: Exact-piece dynamic programming
docs.text: For each piece count, compute the optimal maximum sum for each prefix by trying every valid final-piece start. This educational baseline may time out at full constraints.

docs.title: Binary search a feasible maximum sum
docs.text: For a fixed limit, ending a piece as late as possible cannot use more pieces than any earlier cut. Feasibility is monotone in the limit. A partition with at most k pieces can be refined into exactly k because all values are nonnegative and k<=n.

docs.title: Exact-piece dynamic programming
docs.text: Every partition of a prefix into c pieces consists of an optimal c-1-piece prefix and one nonempty final interval. Minimizing the maximum of their costs over every split enumerates exactly all legal partitions.

Exact-piece dynamic programming: O(k*n squared) time; O(n) space.

Inputs are unchanged. S is total sum. Zero values are permitted; splitting an existing piece never raises its sum. Exactly-k DP states must leave enough elements for nonempty pieces.

docs.title: 1. Binary search a feasible maximum sum
docs.text:
Time: O(n log(S+1))

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary search a feasible maximum sum
    Time: O(n log(S+1))
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def splitArray(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        low, high = max(nums), sum(nums)
        while low < high:
            limit = (low + high) // 2
            pieces, total = 1, 0
            for value in nums:
                if total + value > limit:
                    pieces += 1
                    total = 0
                total += value
            if pieces <= k:
                high = limit
            else:
                low = limit + 1
        return low

docs.title: 2. Exact-piece dynamic programming
docs.text:
Time: O(k*n squared)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Exact-piece dynamic programming
    Time: O(k*n squared)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def splitArray(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        prefix = [0]
        for value in nums:
            prefix.append(prefix[-1] + value)
        previous = [0] + [float("inf")] * len(nums)
        for pieces in range(1, k + 1):
            current = [float("inf")] * (len(nums) + 1)
            for end in range(pieces, len(nums) + 1):
                current[end] = min(
                    max(previous[start], prefix[end] - prefix[start])
                    for start in range(pieces - 1, end)
                )
            previous = current
        return int(previous[-1])

class Solution:
    """Approach: Count arithmetic suffixes ending here
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def numberOfArithmeticSlices(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        ending = answer = 0
        for index in range(2, len(nums)):
            ending = (
                ending + 1
                if nums[index] - nums[index - 1] == nums[index - 1] - nums[index - 2]
                else 0
            )
            answer += ending
        return answer

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sum maximal equal-difference runs
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def numberOfArithmeticSlices(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        answer = run = 0
        previous = None
        for index in range(1, len(nums)):
            difference = nums[index] - nums[index - 1]
            if difference != previous:
                answer += run * (run - 1) // 2
                run = 0
            run += 1
            previous = difference
        return answer + run * (run - 1) // 2

docs.text:

Space: O(T/w) machine words

class Solution:
    """Approach: Bitset subset reachability
    Time: O(n*T/w) machine-word work
    Space: O(T/w) machine words
    """

    def canPartition(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
        total = sum(nums)
        if total % 2:
            return False
        target = total // 2
        bits = 1
        mask = (1 << (target + 1)) - 1
        for value in nums:
            bits = (bits | (bits << value)) & mask
        return bool(bits & (1 << target))

Space: O(T)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Explicit set of achievable sums
    Time: O(n*T) expected
    Space: O(T)
    """

    def canPartition(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
        total = sum(nums)
        if total % 2:
            return False
        target = total // 2
        reachable = {0}
        for value in nums:
            following = {previous + value for previous in reachable if previous + value <= target}
            reachable.update(following)
        return target in reachable

docs.title: 417 Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
docs.text:
Medium · Graph traversal · Core · Learning step 59 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Graph traversal.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Return cells whose water can reach both oceans. The Pacific touches the top and left edges; the Atlantic touches the bottom and right edges. Water moves orthogonally to cells of equal or lower height.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Searching downhill from every cell repeats much of the same work.
  2. Reverse the direction: start at each ocean and move uphill or across equal heights.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Two reversed-flow DFS traversals O(R*C) O(R*C) Fused ocean-label propagation O(R*C) O(R*C)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Two reversed-flow DFS traversals
docs.text: Seed two iterative traversals with the respective ocean boundaries. In reversed flow, a neighbor is reachable when its height is at least the current height. Each traversal records its reachable set. Return their intersection in row order.

docs.title: Fused ocean-label propagation
docs.text: Use one queue carrying newly learned Pacific or Atlantic bits. Seed border cells, then propagate each ocean bit to equal-or-higher neighbors; return cells with both bits.

docs.title: Two reversed-flow DFS traversals
docs.text: Reversing edges turns a downhill path to an ocean into an uphill path from that ocean. Each traversal thus finds exactly the cells that can drain to its ocean. Membership in both sets means the cell has a path to each ocean; these paths need not be the same.

docs.title: Fused ocean-label propagation
docs.text: Reversed paths exactly represent downhill routes to an ocean. Each bit is propagated once per cell, so the fixed point contains exactly reachable ocean labels; mask three means both routes exist.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[1,2],[4,3]], reversed Pacific flow reaches all four cells through 1->2->3 and 1->4. Reversed Atlantic flow cannot move down to height 1. The cells reaching both oceans are [0,1], [1,0], and [1,1].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Two reversed-flow DFS traversals approach:

O(rows * cols) time and auxiliary space, including the result. Heights are unchanged. Reversed traversal must allow equal heights. Using the original downhill comparison from the ocean would compute the wrong reachability set.

Two reversed-flow DFS traversals: O(RC) time; O(RC) space. Fused ocean-label propagation: O(RC) time; O(RC) space. The fused version stores one small mask grid rather than two coordinate sets. Both are iterative and preserve heights. Equal-height edges must remain traversable.

docs.title: 1. Two reversed-flow DFS traversals
docs.text:
Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(R*C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Two reversed-flow DFS traversals
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def pacificAtlantic(self, heights: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
        rows, cols = len(heights), len(heights[0])

        def reach(starts):
            visited = set(starts)
            stack = list(visited)
            while stack:
                row, col = stack.pop()
                for nr, nc in ((row + 1, col), (row - 1, col), (row, col + 1), (row, col - 1)):
                    if (
                        0 <= nr < rows
                        and 0 <= nc < cols
                        and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[row][col]
                        and (nr, nc) not in visited
                    ):
                        visited.add((nr, nc))
                        stack.append((nr, nc))
            return visited

        pacific = reach([(0, col) for col in range(cols)] + [(row, 0) for row in range(rows)])
        atlantic = reach(
            [(rows - 1, col) for col in range(cols)] + [(row, cols - 1) for row in range(rows)]
        )
        return [
            [row, col]
            for row in range(rows)
            for col in range(cols)
            if (row, col) in pacific and (row, col) in atlantic
        ]

docs.title: 2. Fused ocean-label propagation
docs.text:
Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(R*C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Fused ocean-label propagation
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def pacificAtlantic(self, heights: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
        from collections import deque

        rows, columns = len(heights), len(heights[0])
        masks = [[0] * columns for _ in range(rows)]
        queue = deque()

        def add(row, column, bit):
            if not masks[row][column] & bit:
                masks[row][column] |= bit
                queue.append((row, column, bit))

        for row in range(rows):
            add(row, 0, 1)
            add(row, columns - 1, 2)
        for column in range(columns):
            add(0, column, 1)
            add(rows - 1, column, 2)
        while queue:
            row, column, bit = queue.popleft()
            for nr, nc in (
                (row - 1, column),
                (row + 1, column),
                (row, column - 1),
                (row, column + 1),
            ):
                if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < columns and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[row][column]:
                    add(nr, nc, bit)
        return [[r, c] for r in range(rows) for c in range(columns) if masks[r][c] == 3]

docs.title: 424 Longest Repeating Character Replacement
docs.text:

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Find the longest substring that can become one repeated uppercase letter after changing at most k characters.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Which existing character should you keep within a chosen window?
  2. Express the required replacements using window length and a frequency.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Exact-frequency window O(26n) O(26) Binary search a feasible length O(26n log n) O(26)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Exact-frequency window
docs.text: Maintain 26 character counts. A window needs length minus its largest count replacements. Expand right and shrink left until this cost is at most k. Recompute the true maximum over 26 counts to keep the window invariant direct.

docs.title: Binary search a feasible length
docs.text: Binary-search the answer length. For each tested width, slide a fixed window and check whether its size minus its highest frequency fits the budget.

docs.title: Exact-frequency window
docs.text: Keeping the most frequent letter minimizes replacements. Extending a window cannot decrease the required replacements; removing a left character cannot increase them. Therefore a discarded left boundary cannot become useful for a longer window later, and each right endpoint yields its longest valid window.

docs.title: Binary search a feasible length
docs.text: A valid length-L window contains a valid length-(L-1) subwindow after deleting one endpoint: the minimum replacement count cannot increase. Feasible lengths therefore form a prefix for binary search.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "ABBA" with k=1, "ABB" needs one replacement and has length 3. "ABBA" needs two, so discard its first A; "BBA" again has length 3.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Exact-frequency window):

O(26n)=O(n) time and O(26)=O(1) space; input is unchanged. Count letters in the current window, including decrements on removal. This implementation uses the actual maximum, avoiding the extra proof needed for a stale historical maximum.

Exact-frequency window: O(26n) time; O(26) space. Binary search a feasible length: O(26n log n) time; O(26) space. Binary-search the answer length. For each tested width, slide a fixed window and check whether its size minus its highest frequency fits the budget.

docs.title: 1. Exact-frequency window
docs.text:
Time: O(26n)

Space: O(26)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Exact-frequency window
    Time: O(26n)
    Space: O(26)
    """

    def characterReplacement(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        counts = [0] * 26
        left = best = 0
        for right, char in enumerate(s):
            counts[ord(char) - ord("A")] += 1
            while right - left + 1 - max(counts) > k:
                counts[ord(s[left]) - ord("A")] -= 1
                left += 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best

docs.title: 2. Binary search a feasible length
docs.text:
Time: O(26n log n)

Space: O(26)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary search a feasible length
    Time: O(26n log n)
    Space: O(26)
    """

    def characterReplacement(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        def feasible(width):
            counts = [0] * 26
            for right, char in enumerate(s):
                counts[ord(char) - ord("A")] += 1
                if right >= width:
                    counts[ord(s[right - width]) - ord("A")] -= 1
                if right >= width - 1 and width - max(counts) <= k:
                    return True
            return False

        low, high = 0, len(s)
        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high + 1) // 2
            if feasible(middle):
                low = middle
            else:
                high = middle - 1
        return low

docs.text:
Medium · Linked structures and tree queries · Extension · Learning step 296 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Doubly linked lists · Tree traversal.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Flatten a multilevel doubly linked list in place. Visit a node's entire child list before its original next node, clear every child link, and maintain reciprocal prev/next links.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. The required order is depth-first preorder.
  2. Save the original next chain before descending into a child.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 295 · #328 · Next: 297 · #513

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Explicit deferred-next stack O(n) O(n) worst Splice child lists in place O(n) amortized O(1)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Explicit deferred-next stack
docs.text: Use a preorder stack, pushing next before child. Append each popped original node to a new traversal chain by rewriting next and prev, and clear child.

docs.title: Splice child lists in place
docs.text: When a child exists, find the last node of that still-unflattened child-level chain. Attach the saved next chain after it, move the child after its parent, clear child, and continue through next.

docs.title: Explicit deferred-next stack
docs.text: The stack visits children before saved siblings. Linking consecutive visits gives exactly the required flattened order while preserving every original identity and reciprocal adjacency.

docs.title: Splice child lists in place
docs.text: Splicing places the whole child chain before the original suffix. Later child splices refine its interior in the same preorder. Each original same-level edge is scanned in at most one child-tail search, giving linear total work.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For 1<->2<->3 with 2.child pointing to 4<->5, flatten to 1<->2<->4<->5<->3, with all child pointers None.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Explicit deferred-next stack: O(n) time; O(n) worst space. Splice child lists in place: O(n) amortized time; O(1) space. Both mutate and reuse all nodes, including prev links. The returned head has prev=None and the final tail has next=None. Iteration supports deep child nesting without recursion.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Explicit deferred-next stack
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n) worst

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=0, prev=None, next=None, child=None):
        self.val, self.prev, self.next, self.child = val, prev, next, child


class Solution:
    """Approach: Explicit deferred-next stack
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n) worst
    """

    def flatten(self, head: "Node | None") -> "Node | None":
        stack = [head] if head else []
        previous = None
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            if node.next:
                stack.append(node.next)
            if node.child:
                stack.append(node.child)
            node.prev = previous
            if previous:
                previous.next = node
            node.child = None
            previous = node
        if previous:
            previous.next = None
        return head

docs.title: 2. Splice child lists in place
docs.text:
Time: O(n) amortized

Space: O(1)

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=0, prev=None, next=None, child=None):
        self.val, self.prev, self.next, self.child = val, prev, next, child


class Solution:
    """Approach: Splice child lists in place
    Time: O(n) amortized
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def flatten(self, head: "Node | None") -> "Node | None":
        if head:
            head.prev = None
        current = head
        while current:
            if current.child:
                first = current.child
                last = first
                while last.next:
                    last = last.next
                last.next = current.next
                if current.next:
                    current.next.prev = last
                current.next = first
                first.prev = current
                current.child = None
            current = current.next
        return head

docs.title: Task

docs.text:
Approach Time Space Keep earliest finishing intervals O(n log n) O(n) Start-order overlap replacement O(n log n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Keep earliest finishing intervals
docs.text: Sort by ending position. Greedily keep an interval if its start is at least the last kept end. Subtract the number kept from the input count.

docs.title: Start-order overlap replacement
docs.text: Sort by start. When intervals overlap, remove one and retain the smaller end; otherwise advance the kept end.

docs.title: Keep earliest finishing intervals
docs.text: Among available compatible intervals, the earliest-finishing one leaves at least as much room as any other choice. Replacing an optimal solution's first choice with this one cannot reduce how many later intervals fit. Apply that exchange argument repeatedly.

docs.title: Start-order overlap replacement
docs.text: Among overlapping intervals, keeping the earlier end leaves at least as much room for every future interval. Replacing a later-ending candidate therefore preserves an optimal kept count.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[1,4],[2,3],[3,5]], keep [2,3] first, then [3,5]. Two intervals remain, so remove one.

docs.text:
Default approach (Keep earliest finishing intervals):

O(n log n) time and O(n) sorting space in this Python implementation. Inputs are unchanged. Compare start>=end so touching intervals are allowed. Sorting by start and always keeping the first interval can retain a long interval that blocks several short ones.

Keep earliest finishing intervals: O(n log n) time; O(n) space. Start-order overlap replacement: O(n log n) time; O(n) space. Sort by start. When intervals overlap, remove one and retain the smaller end; otherwise advance the kept end.

docs.title: 1. Keep earliest finishing intervals
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Keep earliest finishing intervals
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def eraseOverlapIntervals(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        end = float("-inf")
        kept = 0
        for start, finish in sorted(intervals, key=lambda interval: interval[1]):
            if start >= end:
                kept += 1
                end = finish
        return len(intervals) - kept

docs.title: 2. Start-order overlap replacement
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Start-order overlap replacement
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def eraseOverlapIntervals(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        end = float("-inf")
        removed = 0
        for start, finish in sorted(intervals):
            if start < end:
                removed += 1
                end = min(end, finish)
            else:
                end = finish
        return removed

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Count downward paths with sum targetSum. A path may begin and end at any nodes, but must always follow parent-to-child edges.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. A path sum is the difference of two root-prefix sums.
  2. Only prefixes on the current ancestor path may contribute.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Active prefix frequencies O(n) expected O(h) Enumerate downward starts O(n*h), O(n^2) worst O(h)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Active prefix frequencies
docs.text: Maintain frequencies of root-prefix sums using iterative enter/exit frames. Count prefix-target matches before adding the current prefix; remove it when leaving the subtree.

docs.title: Enumerate downward starts
docs.text: Start a sum traversal at each node, counting matching descendant endpoints. This educational baseline avoids prefix maps but repeats descendant work.

docs.title: Active prefix frequencies
docs.text: Each active prefix identifies one permissible start just below an ancestor. Its difference from the current sum equals the downward path sum. Undo prevents counting paths across sibling subtrees.

docs.title: Enumerate downward starts
docs.text: Every downward path has a unique start and endpoint. The outer traversal chooses its start once, and that start's inner traversal reaches its endpoint once.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For a chain [1,1,1] and target 2, the top-middle and middle-bottom paths match, giving 2.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Active prefix frequencies: O(n) expected time; O(h) space. Enumerate downward starts: O(n*h), O(n^2) worst time; O(h) space. The tree is unchanged. Seed prefix zero with frequency one so paths starting at the root count. Frequencies, rather than a set, are needed when zero-sum prefixes repeat. The baseline is slower on deep chains.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Active prefix frequencies
docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(h)

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Active prefix frequencies
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(h)
    """

    def pathSum(self, root: TreeNode | None, targetSum: int) -> int:
        counts = {0: 1}
        result = 0
        stack = [(root, 0, False)] if root else []
        while stack:
            node, prefix, exiting = stack.pop()
            if exiting:
                counts[prefix] -= 1
                if counts[prefix] == 0:
                    del counts[prefix]
                continue
            prefix += node.val
            result += counts.get(prefix - targetSum, 0)
            counts[prefix] = counts.get(prefix, 0) + 1
            stack.append((node, prefix, True))
            if node.right:
                stack.append((node.right, prefix, False))
            if node.left:
                stack.append((node.left, prefix, False))
        return result

docs.title: 2. Enumerate downward starts
docs.text:
Time: O(n*h), O(n^2) worst

Space: O(h)

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Enumerate downward starts
    Time: O(n*h), O(n^2) worst
    Space: O(h)
    """

    def pathSum(self, root: TreeNode | None, targetSum: int) -> int:
        result = 0
        starts = [root] if root else []
        while starts:
            start = starts.pop()
            if start.left:
                starts.append(start.left)
            if start.right:
                starts.append(start.right)
            pending = [(start, 0)]
            while pending:
                node, total = pending.pop()
                total += node.val
                result += total == targetSum
                for child in (node.left, node.right):
                    if child:
                        pending.append((child, total))
        return result

docs.title: 1. Fixed count vectors
docs.text:
Time: O(26n+m)

Space: O(26) plus output

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Fixed count vectors
    Time: O(26n+m)
    Space: O(26) plus output
    """

    def findAnagrams(self, s: str, p: str) -> list[int]:
        need, have = [0] * 26, [0] * 26
        for char in p:
            need[ord(char) - 97] += 1
        answer = []
        for i, char in enumerate(s):
            have[ord(char) - 97] += 1
            if i >= len(p):
                have[ord(s[i - len(p)]) - 97] -= 1
            if i >= len(p) - 1 and have == need:
                answer.append(i - len(p) + 1)
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Deficit-based window
docs.text:
Time: O(n+m) expected

Space: O(alphabet) plus output

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Deficit-based window
    Time: O(n+m) expected
    Space: O(alphabet) plus output
    """

    def findAnagrams(self, s: str, p: str) -> list[int]:
        need = Counter(p)
        missing = len(p)
        answer = []
        for i, char in enumerate(s):
            if need[char] > 0:
                missing -= 1
            need[char] -= 1
            if i >= len(p):
                outgoing = s[i - len(p)]
                need[outgoing] += 1
                if need[outgoing] > 0:
                    missing += 1
            if i >= len(p) - 1 and missing == 0:
                answer.append(i - len(p) + 1)
        return answer

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Compress consecutive runs in a character list. Write each run's character and, if its length exceeds one, the decimal count into the same list. Return the length of the meaningful prefix; anything after that prefix is irrelevant.

docs.title: Hints

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space In-place read and write pointers O(n) O(1) auxiliary Buffered run encoding O(n) O(n); educational baseline exceeding the O(1) auxiliary-space goal

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: In-place read and write pointers
docs.text: Scan to the end of a run before writing its encoding. Emit its character, then divide the count by descending decimal place values to emit digits. The write cursor never passes the next unread run, so no source is lost.

docs.title: Buffered run encoding
docs.text: Collect run encodings into a separate list, then replace the original list's contents with that buffer. This is a straightforward reference implementation but uses O(n) extra memory and does not meet the problem's constant-space goal.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Each maximal run is found exactly once. Its encoding is the required character plus optional count. A run of length one occupies one slot; for length c>1, 1+digits(c)<=c. Thus the in-place writer stays within already-read positions. The buffered version constructs the same concatenation before copying it back.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [a,a,a,b,c,c], emit a3, then b, then c2. Return 5; the first five slots are [a,3,b,c,2]. A run of twelve a characters must emit [a,1,2], not [a,12].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: In-place pointers take O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. The integer digit loop writes at most as many slots as the runs consumed. Buffered encoding takes O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space, including Python's list replacement and temporary strings. Both mutate chars and preserve the identity of the list. The default leaves its unused suffix intact; the reference shrinks the list, which is allowed because only the returned prefix matters.

docs.title: 1. In-place read and write pointers
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1) auxiliary

from itertools import groupby


class Solution:
    """Approach: In-place read and write pointers
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1) auxiliary
    """

    def compress(self, chars: list[str]) -> int:
        read = write = 0
        while read < len(chars):
            end = read + 1
            while end < len(chars) and chars[end] == chars[read]:
                end += 1
            chars[write] = chars[read]
            write += 1
            count = end - read
            if count > 1:
                place = 1
                while place * 10 <= count:
                    place *= 10
                while place:
                    digit, count = divmod(count, place)
                    chars[write] = chr(ord("0") + digit)
                    write += 1
                    place //= 10
            read = end
        return write

docs.title: 2. Buffered run encoding
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n); educational baseline exceeding the O(1) auxiliary-space goal

from itertools import groupby


class Solution:
    """Approach: Buffered run encoding
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n); educational baseline exceeding the O(1) auxiliary-space goal
    """

    def compress(self, chars: list[str]) -> int:
        output = []
        for char, group in groupby(chars):
            count = sum(1 for _ in group)
            output.append(char)
            if count > 1:
                output.extend(str(count))
        chars[:] = output
        return len(output)

docs.title: 446 Arithmetic Slices II - Subsequence
docs.text:

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Count index-distinct arithmetic subsequences of length at least three; selected positions need not be contiguous.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. A pair has a difference but is not yet a counted answer.
  2. Every longer subsequence has a unique final pair of positions.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 322 · #413 · Next: 324 · #467

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Endpoint maps keyed by common difference O(n^2) expected O(n^2) Explicit final-pair recurrence O(n^3) worst case O(n^2)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Endpoint maps keyed by common difference
docs.text: Store counts of length-at-least-two subsequences by endpoint and difference. A new pair seeds one state; only extensions of existing states contribute to the requested answer.

docs.title: Explicit final-pair recurrence
docs.text: Let pairs[j][i] count length-at-least-three subsequences with final positions j,i. Enumerate earlier positions k with value 2*nums[j]-nums[i], adding the new triple and every prior subsequence ending k,j.

docs.title: Endpoint maps keyed by common difference
docs.text: Every arithmetic subsequence of length at least three arises once by removing its final position. The remaining state has the same difference, and counting only extensions excludes bare pairs.

docs.title: Explicit final-pair recurrence
docs.text: Each counted sequence has one unique penultimate pair. Its third-last position must have the derived value, and it is either the triple itself or an extension of a longer sequence counted at that earlier pair.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Endpoint maps keyed by common difference: O(n^2) expected time; O(n^2) space. Explicit final-pair recurrence: O(n^3) worst case time; O(n^2) space.

Both preserve nums and support negative differences and repeated values. The explicit-pair baseline can time out near n=1000, especially on equal values; use the quadratic default. Dictionaries use expected constant-time lookups.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Endpoint maps keyed by common difference
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2) expected

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Endpoint maps keyed by common difference
    Time: O(n^2) expected
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def numberOfArithmeticSlices(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        ending = [{} for _ in nums]
        answer = 0
        for end, value in enumerate(nums):
            for previous in range(end):
                difference = value - nums[previous]
                extensions = ending[previous].get(difference, 0)
                answer += extensions
                ending[end][difference] = ending[end].get(difference, 0) + extensions + 1
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Explicit final-pair recurrence
docs.text:
Time: O(n^3) worst case

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Explicit final-pair recurrence
    Time: O(n^3) worst case
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def numberOfArithmeticSlices(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        positions = {}
        for index, value in enumerate(nums):
            positions.setdefault(value, []).append(index)
        pairs = [[0] * len(nums) for _ in nums]
        answer = 0
        for end in range(len(nums)):
            for previous in range(end):
                required = 2 * nums[previous] - nums[end]
                for earlier in positions.get(required, ()):
                    if earlier >= previous:
                        break
                    pairs[previous][end] += 1 + pairs[earlier][previous]
                answer += pairs[previous][end]
        return answer

docs.title: 449 Serialize and Deserialize BST
docs.text:
