docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Prefix trie
docs.text:
Time: O(D+L)

Space: O(D+L), including split words and output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Prefix trie
    Time: O(D+L)
    Space: O(D+L), including split words and output
    """

    def replaceWords(self, dictionary: list[str], sentence: str) -> str:
        trie = {}
        for root in dictionary:
            node = trie
            for char in root:
                node = node.setdefault(char, {})
            node[""] = True
        result = []
        for word in sentence.split():
            node = trie
            replacement = word
            for end, char in enumerate(word, 1):
                if char not in node:
                    break
                node = node[char]
                if "" in node:
                    replacement = word[:end]
                    break
            result.append(replacement)
        return " ".join(result)

docs.title: 2. Length-ordered root scan
docs.text:
Time: O(R log R+W*D+L); slower dictionary-scan baseline

Space: O(R+L), including output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Length-ordered root scan
    Time: O(R log R+W*D+L); slower dictionary-scan baseline
    Space: O(R+L), including output
    """

    def replaceWords(self, dictionary: list[str], sentence: str) -> str:
        roots = sorted(dictionary, key=len)
        words = sentence.split()
        for index, word in enumerate(words):
            for root in roots:
                if len(root) > len(word):
                    break
                if word.startswith(root):
                    words[index] = root
                    break
        return " ".join(words)

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Simulate a round-based senate of Radiant (R) and Dire (D) senators. Each active senator bans an opponent who loses all future turns. Return the winning party under optimal play.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Banning the earliest upcoming opponent is always at least as good as banning a later one.
  2. Keep the future turn order either as two index queues or as one queue with pending bans.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 274 · #406 · Next: 276 · #678

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Competing queues of future turn indices O(n) O(n) One turn queue with deferred ban counts O(n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Competing queues of future turn indices
docs.text: Queue positions of each party. Pop their next senators; the earlier one bans the later one and reenters its queue with index increased by n.

docs.title: One turn queue with deferred ban counts
docs.text: Track living senators and pending bans by party. A banned queued senator disappears; an unbanned one creates an opposite-party ban and queues its next turn.

docs.title: Competing queues of future turn indices
docs.text: The earlier senator can remove the opponent with the soonest potential action, preventing at least as much opposition as any later ban. Requeueing at index+n preserves round order; every comparison removes one senator permanently.

docs.title: One turn queue with deferred ban counts
docs.text: A pending ban always applies to the next opponent in turn order, realizing the same earliest- opponent greedy choice. Every surviving action creates a ban; consumed bans remove senators, so total queue work is linear in the initial population.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: "RDD": the first R bans the next D, but the final D bans R on its own turn, so Dire wins.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Competing queues of future turn indices: O(n) time; O(n) space.

One turn queue with deferred ban counts: O(n) time; O(n) space.

Input is unchanged. Requeued indices may exceed n and must keep increasing rather than wrapping modulo n. Pending bans do not themselves consume an opponent turn until that senator is reached.

docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Competing queues of future turn indices
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def predictPartyVictory(self, senate: str) -> str:
        radiant = deque(i for i, party in enumerate(senate) if party == "R")
        dire = deque(i for i, party in enumerate(senate) if party == "D")
        while radiant and dire:
            r, d = radiant.popleft(), dire.popleft()
            if r < d:
                radiant.append(r + len(senate))
            else:
                dire.append(d + len(senate))
        return "Radiant" if radiant else "Dire"

docs.title: 2. One turn queue with deferred ban counts
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: One turn queue with deferred ban counts
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def predictPartyVictory(self, senate: str) -> str:
        queue = deque(senate)
        alive = {"R": senate.count("R"), "D": senate.count("D")}
        bans = {"R": 0, "D": 0}
        while alive["R"] and alive["D"]:
            party = queue.popleft()
            if bans[party]:
                bans[party] -= 1
                alive[party] -= 1
            else:
                opponent = "D" if party == "R" else "R"
                bans[opponent] += 1
                queue.append(party)
        return "Radiant" if alive["R"] else "Dire"

docs.text:

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Return one original root for every subtree shape and value pattern that occurs at least twice in a binary tree.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Equal subtrees have equal root values and equal left/right subtree descriptions.
  2. Intern descriptions as small IDs instead of repeatedly copying long strings.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 198 · #449 · Next: 200 · #212

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Interned structural IDs O(n) expected O(n) Full subtree signatures O(n^2) worst due to copied signatures O(n^2) worst

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Interned structural IDs
docs.text: Process iterative postorder. Assign a unique integer ID to each (value,left-ID,right-ID) tuple. Count IDs and return a root exactly when its count reaches two.

docs.title: Full subtree signatures
docs.text: Build a fully delimited string signature for each subtree in postorder and count those strings. This educational baseline copies growing descendant encodings.

docs.title: Interned structural IDs
docs.text: Induction makes IDs equal exactly for structurally identical valued subtrees. Counting a repeated ID detects duplicates; emitting only at count two produces one representative per duplicate class.

docs.title: Full subtree signatures
docs.text: Explicit null markers and ordered child delimiters make the string encoding unambiguous. Equal signatures therefore identify exactly equal subtrees, though large repeated copies are unnecessary.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: If two different parents each have a value-7 leaf, the value-7 leaf signature occurs twice, so return one of those original leaves.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Interned structural IDs: O(n) expected time; O(n) space. Full subtree signatures: O(n^2) worst due to copied signatures time; O(n^2) worst space. The tree is unchanged and returned nodes are original identities. The string baseline may time out or use excessive memory on long trees; IDs preserve linear storage. Equal root values alone do not establish duplicate subtrees.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Interned structural IDs
docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(n)

from collections import Counter


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Interned structural IDs
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def findDuplicateSubtrees(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> list[TreeNode]:
        identifiers = {None: 0}
        interned, counts, result = {}, Counter(), []
        stack = [(root, False)] if root else []
        while stack:
            node, expanded = stack.pop()
            if expanded:
                key = (node.val, identifiers[node.left], identifiers[node.right])
                if key not in interned:
                    interned[key] = len(interned) + 1
                identifier = identifiers[node] = interned[key]
                counts[identifier] += 1
                if counts[identifier] == 2:
                    result.append(node)
            else:
                stack.append((node, True))
                for child in (node.left, node.right):
                    if child:
                        stack.append((child, False))
        return result

docs.title: 2. Full subtree signatures
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2) worst due to copied signatures

Space: O(n^2) worst

from collections import Counter


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Full subtree signatures
    Time: O(n^2) worst due to copied signatures
    Space: O(n^2) worst
    """

    def findDuplicateSubtrees(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> list[TreeNode]:
        signatures = {None: "#"}
        counts, result = Counter(), []
        stack = [(root, False)] if root else []
        while stack:
            node, expanded = stack.pop()
            if expanded:
                signature = f"{node.val}({signatures[node.left]})({signatures[node.right]})"
                signatures[node] = signature
                counts[signature] += 1
                if counts[signature] == 2:
                    result.append(node)
            else:
                stack.append((node, True))
                for child in (node.left, node.right):
                    if child:
                        stack.append((child, False))
        return result

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Construct a tree from distinct array values: its root is the maximum, and its left and right subtrees come from the values before and after that maximum.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. A newly encountered larger value becomes an ancestor of smaller recent values.
  2. Maintain a decreasing stack of the unfinished right spine.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 124 · #450 · Next: 126 · #264

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Decreasing Cartesian-tree stack O(n) O(n) auxiliary and output Repeated interval maxima O(n^2) worst O(h) auxiliary; O(n) output

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Decreasing Cartesian-tree stack
docs.text: For each value create one node. Pop smaller stack nodes, assigning the last popped subtree as its left child. If a larger stack ancestor remains, link its right child to the new node.

docs.title: Repeated interval maxima
docs.text: Use explicit interval tasks. Scan each interval for its maximum, create its root, and schedule the left and right intervals. This simple baseline repeats scans on ordered arrays.

docs.title: Decreasing Cartesian-tree stack
docs.text: The stack is the processed tree's decreasing right spine. Popped suffix values lie before the new maximum and become its left subtree; the remaining larger ancestor still bounds the new right descendant.

docs.title: Repeated interval maxima
docs.text: Selecting the interval maximum is exactly the recursive definition. The two remaining intervals partition all other values and preserve their relative positions, so induction constructs the required tree.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [3,1,4,2], root 4 has left subtree rooted at 3 with right child 1, and right leaf 2.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Decreasing Cartesian-tree stack: O(n) time; O(n) auxiliary and output space. Repeated interval maxima: O(n^2) worst time; O(h) auxiliary; O(n) output space. The input array is unchanged. The scanning baseline may be slow on large ordered inputs; the default is linear because each node is pushed and popped once. Both avoid deep recursion.

docs.title: 1. Decreasing Cartesian-tree stack
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n) auxiliary and output

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Decreasing Cartesian-tree stack
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n) auxiliary and output
    """

    def constructMaximumBinaryTree(self, nums: list[int]) -> TreeNode:
        stack = []
        for value in nums:
            node = TreeNode(value)
            while stack and stack[-1].val < value:
                node.left = stack.pop()
            if stack:
                stack[-1].right = node
            stack.append(node)
        return stack[0]

docs.title: 2. Repeated interval maxima
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2) worst

Space: O(h) auxiliary; O(n) output

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Repeated interval maxima
    Time: O(n^2) worst
    Space: O(h) auxiliary; O(n) output
    """

    def constructMaximumBinaryTree(self, nums: list[int]) -> TreeNode:
        dummy = TreeNode()
        stack = [(0, len(nums), dummy, "left")]
        while stack:
            low, high, parent, side = stack.pop()
            if low == high:
                continue
            middle = max(range(low, high), key=nums.__getitem__)
            node = TreeNode(nums[middle])
            setattr(parent, side, node)
            stack.extend(((middle + 1, high, node, "right"), (low, middle, node, "left")))
        return dummy.left

docs.title: 658 Find K Closest Elements
docs.text:
Medium · Search and partition extensions · Extension · Learning step 267 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Return the k closest elements to x from a sorted array, in ascending order. Prefer the smaller value when distances tie.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. The chosen values form a consecutive length-k window.
  2. Compare the two values that compete when moving a candidate window one position right.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 266 · #540 · Next: 268 · #719

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Binary search the chosen window start O(log(n-k+1)+k) O(k) output; O(1) auxiliary Discard the farther endpoint O(n) O(k) output; O(1) auxiliary

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Binary search the chosen window start
docs.text: Search possible starts from 0 to n-k. Compare x-arr[mid] with arr[mid+k]-x to decide whether the left edge should be replaced by the competing right value.

docs.title: Discard the farther endpoint
docs.text: Keep a surviving interval and discard its farther endpoint until exactly k values remain. On ties discard the larger right endpoint.

docs.title: Binary search the chosen window start
docs.text: The edge-distance comparison changes monotonically with the start. If the left edge is strictly farther, moving right improves the window; otherwise keeping the earlier window preserves the smaller-value tie rule.

docs.title: Discard the farther endpoint
docs.text: In sorted order, a farthest remaining value always lies at an endpoint. Removing the worse endpoint cannot remove a preferred top-k value; repeated removal leaves exactly the required multiset in sorted order.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: [1,2,3,4,5], k=4, x=3 discards 5 on the distance tie with 1, leaving [1,2,3,4].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Binary search the chosen window start: O(log(n-k+1)+k) time; O(k) output; O(1) auxiliary space.

Discard the farther endpoint: O(n) time; O(k) output; O(1) auxiliary space.

Inputs are unchanged; the returned slice is a fresh list. Include O(k) copying time in the binary-search variant, and keep the output sorted rather than sorting by distance.

docs.text:
Time: O(log(n-k+1)+k)

Space: O(k) output; O(1) auxiliary

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary search the chosen window start
    Time: O(log(n-k+1)+k)
    Space: O(k) output; O(1) auxiliary
    """

    def findClosestElements(self, arr: list[int], k: int, x: int) -> list[int]:
        low, high = 0, len(arr) - k
        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if x - arr[middle] > arr[middle + k] - x:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle
        return arr[low : low + k]

docs.title: 2. Discard the farther endpoint
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(k) output; O(1) auxiliary

class Solution:
    """Approach: Discard the farther endpoint
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(k) output; O(1) auxiliary
    """

    def findClosestElements(self, arr: list[int], k: int, x: int) -> list[int]:
        left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
        while right - left + 1 > k:
            if abs(arr[left] - x) > abs(arr[right] - x):
                left += 1
            else:
                right -= 1
        return arr[left : right + 1]

docs.title: Task

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Give children of position i positions 2i and 2i+1.
  2. Subtract each level's first index before computing children to bound integer growth.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Normalized breadth-first positions O(n) O(w) Leftmost index per depth O(n) O(h)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Normalized breadth-first positions
docs.text: Queue nodes with complete-tree positions. At each layer, subtract its first position and compute width from the first and last occupied positions.

docs.title: Leftmost index per depth
docs.text: Use left-first DFS, recording the first index at each depth. Normalize every visited index by that depth's first, update the width, and derive child indices from the normalized offset.

docs.title: Normalized breadth-first positions
docs.text: Affine translation preserves position differences, hence widths. The binary child-index formula preserves every internal gap, including positions occupied by missing nodes.

docs.title: Leftmost index per depth
docs.text: Left-first DFS encounters the leftmost occupied position first at every depth. All indices at a depth share the same translation, so each normalized offset measures distance from that left edge.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For root 1 with children 2 and 3, where 2 has only a left child and 3 only a right child, the last level occupies positions 0 and 3: width 4.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Normalized breadth-first positions: O(n) time; O(w) space. Leftmost index per depth: O(n) time; O(h) space. The tree is unchanged. Queue length is not width when gaps exist. Normalization avoids integers growing with depth on narrow chains; the official maximum answer fits a 32-bit signed integer.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Normalized breadth-first positions
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(w)

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Normalized breadth-first positions
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(w)
    """

    def widthOfBinaryTree(self, root: TreeNode) -> int:
        queue = deque([(root, 0)])
        best = 0
        while queue:
            first = queue[0][1]
            width = queue[-1][1] - first + 1
            best = max(best, width)
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                node, index = queue.popleft()
                index -= first
                if node.left:
                    queue.append((node.left, 2 * index))
                if node.right:
                    queue.append((node.right, 2 * index + 1))
        return best

docs.title: 2. Leftmost index per depth
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(h)

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Leftmost index per depth
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(h)
    """

    def widthOfBinaryTree(self, root: TreeNode) -> int:
        first = {}
        stack = [(root, 0, 0)]
        best = 0
        while stack:
            node, depth, index = stack.pop()
            first.setdefault(depth, index)
            offset = index - first[depth]
            best = max(best, offset + 1)
            if node.right:
                stack.append((node.right, depth + 1, 2 * offset + 1))
            if node.left:
                stack.append((node.left, depth + 1, 2 * offset))
        return best

docs.title: 664 Strange Printer
docs.text:
Hard · Advanced optimization dynamic programming · Extension · Learning step 347 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Interval DP.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: A printer can print one repeated character over any contiguous interval, overwriting existing characters. Find the minimum turns to print s.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Equal characters can share a turn even when other characters must be fixed between them later.
  2. Consecutive equal characters never require separate turns.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 346 · #552 · Next: 348 · #879

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Compressed bottom-up left-end intervals O(n^3) O(n^2) Memoized right-end turn merging O(n^3) O(n^2)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Compressed bottom-up left-end intervals
docs.text: Collapse equal adjacent letters, then fill intervals. Either print the left letter separately or merge its turn with a matching later letter while printing the intervening interval afterward.

docs.title: Memoized right-end turn merging
docs.text: Work from the right endpoint without preprocessing. Print it separately or extend a turn printing an equal earlier character through that endpoint, solving the middle separately.

docs.title: Compressed bottom-up left-end intervals
docs.text: A shared-character turn can span both equal positions, with intervening cells repaired independently. Conversely, in an optimal schedule the leftmost letter is either isolated from all later equal positions or shares such a turn, yielding one tested split.

docs.title: Memoized right-end turn merging
docs.text: Extending the equal-character turn need not add a turn; any unwanted middle characters can be restored by the independent middle schedule. The final turn covering the right endpoint identifies a matching earlier position or a standalone case, making the alternatives exhaustive.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "aba", print aaa in one turn and overwrite the middle with b, totaling 2.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Compressed bottom-up left-end intervals: O(n^3) time; O(n^2) space. Memoized right-end turn merging: O(n^3) time; O(n^2) space.

n is original string length; compression can reduce actual DP size. Both preserve s. The default builds an O(n) copied compressed string; memo uses index ranges and depth at most 100, within the stated limit. Ordinary run counting misses useful overwrite merges.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Compressed bottom-up left-end intervals
docs.text:
Time: O(n^3)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Compressed bottom-up left-end intervals
    Time: O(n^3)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def strangePrinter(self, s: str) -> int:
        text = "".join(
            character
            for index, character in enumerate(s)
            if index == 0 or character != s[index - 1]
        )
        n = len(text)
        dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        for left in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
            dp[left][left] = 1
            for right in range(left + 1, n):
                dp[left][right] = 1 + dp[left + 1][right]
                for same in range(left + 1, right + 1):
                    if text[same] == text[left]:
                        middle = dp[left + 1][same - 1] if same > left + 1 else 0
                        dp[left][right] = min(dp[left][right], middle + dp[same][right])
        return dp[0][-1]

docs.title: 2. Memoized right-end turn merging
docs.text:
Time: O(n^3)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Memoized right-end turn merging
    Time: O(n^3)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def strangePrinter(self, s: str) -> int:
        from functools import cache

        @cache
        def turns(left, right):
            if left > right:
                return 0
            answer = turns(left, right - 1) + 1
            for same in range(left, right):
                if s[same] == s[right]:
                    answer = min(answer, turns(left, same) + turns(same + 1, right - 1))
            return answer

        return turns(0, len(s) - 1)

  2. A Fenwick tree can merge these pairs over all smaller values.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Endpoint lengths and multiplicities O(n^2) O(n) Coordinate-compressed Fenwick maxima and counts O(n log n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Endpoint lengths and multiplicities
docs.text: For each earlier smaller value, replace the endpoint count when a longer predecessor is found or add its count when lengths tie.

docs.title: Coordinate-compressed Fenwick maxima and counts
docs.text: Compress values into ranks. A prefix query below the current rank merges the longest predecessor lengths and their counts; update the current rank with its new endpoint pair.

docs.title: Endpoint lengths and multiplicities
docs.text: Each longer subsequence has a unique penultimate index. Counts from equally good predecessors are therefore disjoint and additive, while shorter predecessor lengths cannot contribute to an optimum.

docs.title: Coordinate-compressed Fenwick maxima and counts
docs.text: The merge operation retains longer lengths and sums equal-length counts, matching the endpoint recurrence. Strictly lower-rank queries exclude equal values. Fenwick disjoint intervals avoid double-counting during a query.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [1,3,5,4,7], [1,3,5,7] and [1,3,4,7] give 2 longest subsequences.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Endpoint lengths and multiplicities: O(n^2) time; O(n) space. Coordinate-compressed Fenwick maxima and counts: O(n log n) time; O(n) space.

Inputs are unchanged. Repeated equal values contribute separate length-one subsequences but never extend each other. Fenwick storage is faster asymptotically but requires careful count merging.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Endpoint lengths and multiplicities
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Endpoint lengths and multiplicities
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def findNumberOfLIS(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        lengths, counts = [1] * len(nums), [1] * len(nums)
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            for j in range(i):
                if nums[j] >= nums[i]:
                    continue
                candidate = lengths[j] + 1
                if candidate > lengths[i]:
                    lengths[i], counts[i] = candidate, counts[j]
                elif candidate == lengths[i]:
                    counts[i] += counts[j]
        longest = max(lengths)
        return sum(
            count for length, count in zip(lengths, counts, strict=True) if length == longest
        )

docs.title: 2. Coordinate-compressed Fenwick maxima and counts
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Coordinate-compressed Fenwick maxima and counts
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def findNumberOfLIS(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        ranks = {value: index + 1 for index, value in enumerate(sorted(set(nums)))}
        tree = [(0, 0)] * (len(ranks) + 1)

        def merge(first, second):
            if first[0] != second[0]:
                return max(first, second, key=lambda pair: pair[0])
            return first[0], first[1] + second[1]

        answer = (0, 0)
        for value in nums:
            rank = ranks[value]
            index, best = rank - 1, (0, 0)
            while index:
                best = merge(best, tree[index])
                index -= index & -index
            candidate = (best[0] + 1, best[1] if best[0] else 1)
            answer = merge(answer, candidate)
            index = rank
            while index < len(tree):
                tree[index] = merge(tree[index], candidate)
                index += index & -index
        return answer[1]

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Interval of possible opening counts
docs.text: Maintain low and high unmatched-opening counts. A star widens the range by one each way; clamp low to zero and reject if high becomes negative.

docs.title: Opening and star position stacks
docs.text: Match each closing parenthesis with a real opening if possible, otherwise a prior star. After scanning, match remaining openings with later stars.

docs.title: Interval of possible opening counts
docs.text: Every possible unmatched count between the bounds remains achievable after each character. A negative high means even the most opening-friendly choices fail; final low zero means at least one assignment ends balanced.

docs.title: Opening and star position stacks
docs.text: Using a real opening first preserves flexible stars for later needs. Any unmatched opening can only be closed by a later star; matching the latest positions detects exactly whether all remaining openings have such substitutes.

docs.title: Walkthrough

Interval of possible opening counts: O(n) time; O(1) space.

Opening and star position stacks: O(n) time; O(n) space.

docs.title: 1. Interval of possible opening counts
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Interval of possible opening counts
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def checkValidString(self, s: str) -> bool:
        low = high = 0
        for char in s:
            if char == "(":
                low += 1
                high += 1
            elif char == ")":
                low -= 1
                high -= 1
            else:
                low -= 1
                high += 1
            if high < 0:
                return False
            low = max(0, low)
        return low == 0

docs.title: 2. Opening and star position stacks
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Opening and star position stacks
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def checkValidString(self, s: str) -> bool:
        openings = []
        stars = []
        for i, char in enumerate(s):
            if char == "(":
                openings.append(i)
            elif char == "*":
                stars.append(i)
            elif openings:
                openings.pop()
            elif stars:
                stars.pop()
            else:
                return False
        while openings and stars:
            if openings.pop() > stars.pop():
                return False
        return not openings

docs.title: 684 Redundant Connection
docs.text:
Medium · Graph ordering and connectivity · Core · Learning step 63 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Union find.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: An undirected graph was formed by adding one edge to a tree. Return an edge whose removal restores a tree. When several edges qualify, choose the one that occurs latest in the input.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Adding an edge creates a cycle exactly when its endpoints are already connected.
  2. Process edges in order while maintaining connected components with union-find.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 062 · #210 · Next: 064 · #743

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Size-weighted union-find O(E*alpha(V)) O(V) Check reachability before each insertion O(E*(V+E)) O(V+E)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Size-weighted union-find
docs.text: Start with every vertex in its own disjoint set. Find each edge's endpoint roots. Equal roots identify the redundant edge. Otherwise join the smaller component under the larger root. Compress paths during searches to speed future root lookups. The linked Union find template also shows union by rank: compare root ranks, attach the lower rank, and increment only after merging equal-rank roots. Rank bounds historical tree height; size counts vertices. Either heuristic with path compression gives the same amortized bound for this problem.

docs.title: Check reachability before each insertion
docs.text: Maintain the accepted forest explicitly. Before adding an edge, traverse from its first endpoint; an already-reachable second endpoint means the edge closes a cycle.

docs.title: Size-weighted union-find
docs.text: Accepted edges form a forest. The sets describe its connected components because every accepted edge merges its endpoint components. An edge within one component closes a cycle. The promised graph has only one cycle, so its last encountered edge is the first rejected edge and the latest eligible removal.

docs.title: Check reachability before each insertion
docs.text: A forest gains a cycle exactly when an inserted edge connects vertices already connected by a path. Input order makes the rejected edge the last edge of the unique cycle, satisfying the requested tie rule.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[1,2],[2,3],[1,3]], the first two edges combine all three vertices. The final edge joins vertices already connected by 1--2--3. Return [1,3].

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Size-weighted union-find approach:

O(E * alpha(V)) amortized time and O(V) space, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function. Inputs are unchanged. The vertex labels fit 1 through E under the tree-plus-one-edge contract. Joining endpoints directly without first finding their roots would break the component representation.

Size-weighted union-find: O(Ealpha(V)) time; O(V) space. Check reachability before each insertion: O(E(V+E)) time; O(V+E) space. Repeated traversal is a slower educational baseline, though the problem has at most 1000 edges. Both preserve edge order and contents.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Size-weighted union-find
docs.text:
Time: O(E*alpha(V))

Space: O(V)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Size-weighted union-find
    Time: O(E*alpha(V))
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def findRedundantConnection(self, edges: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
        parent = list(range(len(edges) + 1))
        size = [1] * len(parent)

        def find(node):
            while node != parent[node]:
                parent[node] = parent[parent[node]]
                node = parent[node]
            return node

        for left, right in edges:
            left_root, right_root = find(left), find(right)
            if left_root == right_root:
                return [left, right]
            if size[left_root] < size[right_root]:
                left_root, right_root = right_root, left_root
            parent[right_root] = left_root
            size[left_root] += size[right_root]
        return []

docs.title: 2. Check reachability before each insertion
docs.text:
Time: O(E*(V+E))

Space: O(V+E)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Check reachability before each insertion
    Time: O(E*(V+E))
    Space: O(V+E)
    """

    def findRedundantConnection(self, edges: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
        graph = [[] for _ in range(len(edges) + 1)]
        for left, right in edges:
            seen = {left}
            stack = [left]
            while stack:
                node = stack.pop()
                for other in graph[node]:
                    if other not in seen:
                        seen.add(other)
                        stack.append(other)
            if right in seen:
                return [left, right]
            graph[left].append(right)
            graph[right].append(left)
        return []

docs.title: 686 Repeated String Match
docs.text:
Medium · String processing extensions · Extension · Learning step 288 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Prefix function · Z function.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Return the fewest repetitions of nonempty string a whose concatenation contains nonempty string b as a substring. Return -1 when no repetition works.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. A match can always be shifted to start within the first copy of a.
  2. Prefix-function or Z-function matching avoids repeated candidate comparisons.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 287 · #648 · Next: 289 · #791

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space KMP over virtual repetitions O(A+B) O(B) Z-function over a bounded text O(A+B) O(A+B)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: KMP over virtual repetitions
docs.text: Build b's prefix-function table. Scan a virtual periodic string by reading a[index % len(a)], keeping the length of the matched prefix of b. A mismatch falls back along the prefix table. Scan only len(a)+len(b)-1 characters. When a full match ends, ceil((end+1)/len(a)) is the required repetition count.

docs.title: Z-function over a bounded text
docs.text: Build a repeated text of the same bounded length. Compute Z values for b + '#' + text, where '#' cannot occur in the lowercase inputs. The first text position with a Z value at least len(b) starts a complete match. Convert its ending position to a repetition count.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Any match in an infinite periodic string can be shifted left by whole copies of a until its start is below len(a). Its end then lies within the bounded scan. KMP and Z matching both identify exact matches, without hash collisions. All matches have the same length, so the first ending match minimizes the number of whole copies needed. Exhausting the bound proves impossibility.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For a="abc" and b="cabca", the earliest match starts at position 2 and ends at position 6 in "abcabcabc". Seven required characters need three copies. For a="ab" and b="ac", no match exists regardless of the repetition count.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: With A=len(a), B=len(b), both algorithms take O(A+B) time. KMP uses O(B) space for its prefix table and never builds repeated text. Z matching uses O(A+B) space for the materialized text and Z table. Fallbacks and reused Z intervals give amortized linear comparisons, even on repetitive strings. Inputs are unchanged. A match may cross a copy boundary; testing only one copy or exactly ceil(B/A) copies misses valid answers.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. KMP over virtual repetitions
docs.text:
Time: O(A+B)

Space: O(B)

class Solution:
    """Approach: KMP over virtual repetitions
    Time: O(A+B)
    Space: O(B)
    """

    def repeatedStringMatch(self, a: str, b: str) -> int:
        prefix = [0] * len(b)
        matched = 0
        for index in range(1, len(b)):
            while matched and b[index] != b[matched]:
                matched = prefix[matched - 1]
            if b[index] == b[matched]:
                matched += 1
            prefix[index] = matched
        matched = 0
        for index in range(len(a) + len(b) - 1):
            char = a[index % len(a)]
            while matched and char != b[matched]:
                matched = prefix[matched - 1]
            if char == b[matched]:
                matched += 1
            if matched == len(b):
                return (index + len(a)) // len(a)
        return -1

docs.title: 2. Z-function over a bounded text
docs.text:
Time: O(A+B)

Space: O(A+B)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Z-function over a bounded text
    Time: O(A+B)
    Space: O(A+B)
    """

    def repeatedStringMatch(self, a: str, b: str) -> int:
        length = len(a) + len(b) - 1
        text = (a * ((length + len(a) - 1) // len(a)))[:length]
        combined = b + "#" + text
        offset = len(b) + 1
        z = [0] * len(combined)
        left = right = 0
        for index in range(1, len(combined)):
            if index < right:
                z[index] = min(right - index, z[index - left])
            while (
                index + z[index] < len(combined)
                and combined[z[index]] == combined[index + z[index]]
            ):
                z[index] += 1
            if index + z[index] > right:
                left, right = index, index + z[index]
            if index >= offset and z[index] >= len(b):
                end_exclusive = index - offset + len(b)
                return (end_exclusive + len(a) - 1) // len(a)
        return -1

docs.text:

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Return the probability a knight remains on an n by n board after exactly k uniformly random choices among its eight moves.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Off-board probability mass is lost, not renormalized.
  2. Survival from a cell can also be computed backward by remaining moves.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Forward knight probability layers O((k+1)*n^2) O(n^2) Backward survival probabilities O((k+1)*n^2) O((k+1)*n^2)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Forward knight probability layers
docs.text: Track probability mass at each surviving location and send one eighth to each valid move destination at every step.

docs.title: Backward survival probabilities
docs.text: Cache the survival probability for position and remaining moves. Outside states are zero and inside zero-move states are one.

docs.title: Forward knight probability layers
docs.text: Independence and equal move probabilities multiply each incoming path weight by one eighth. Summing disjoint arriving paths gives each state probability, and the final board sum is survival probability.

docs.title: Backward survival probabilities
docs.text: Conditioning on the first of eight equally likely moves yields the average of successor survival probabilities. These cases exhaust the next move, proving the recurrence by remaining-step induction.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: On a 3x3 board from a corner with one move, two of eight destinations are valid, giving 0.25.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls

Forward knight probability layers: O((k+1)*n^2) time; O(n^2) space. Backward survival probabilities: O((k+1)*n^2) time; O((k+1)*n^2) space.

Inputs are unchanged. k=0 returns one at every valid starting cell. Memo depth is at most 100, while its cache may retain every step layer; forward propagation saves that factor. Do not divide by the number of valid moves.

docs.title: 1. Forward knight probability layers
docs.text:
Time: O((k+1)*n^2)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Forward knight probability layers
    Time: O((k+1)*n^2)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def knightProbability(self, n: int, k: int, row: int, column: int) -> float:
        moves = ((1, 2), (2, 1), (-1, 2), (-2, 1), (1, -2), (2, -1), (-1, -2), (-2, -1))
        current = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        current[row][column] = 1.0
        for _ in range(k):
            following = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
            for r in range(n):
                for c in range(n):
                    for dr, dc in moves:
                        nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                        if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n:
                            following[nr][nc] += current[r][c] / 8
            current = following
        return sum(map(sum, current))

docs.title: 2. Backward survival probabilities
docs.text:
Time: O((k+1)*n^2)

Space: O((k+1)*n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Backward survival probabilities
    Time: O((k+1)*n^2)
    Space: O((k+1)*n^2)
    """

    def knightProbability(self, n: int, k: int, row: int, column: int) -> float:
        from functools import cache

        moves = ((1, 2), (2, 1), (-1, 2), (-2, 1), (1, -2), (2, -1), (-1, -2), (-2, -1))

        @cache
        def survive(r, c, remaining):
            if not (0 <= r < n and 0 <= c < n):
                return 0.0
            if remaining == 0:
                return 1.0
            return sum(survive(r + dr, c + dc, remaining - 1) for dr, dc in moves) / 8

        return survive(row, column, k)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Iterative area flood-fill
docs.text: Start a stack traversal at each unseen one, mark on discovery, and count popped cells. Keep the largest finished component area.

docs.title: Size-weighted land unions
docs.text: Assign each position a union-find slot and merge upper/left land neighbors. Maintain size only at roots and update the maximum after each land cell.

docs.title: Iterative area flood-fill
docs.text: Each traversal reaches exactly its starting component and counts each member once. Distinct starts are disjoint components, so their maximum area is the answer.

docs.title: Size-weighted land unions
docs.text: Root size starts at one per land singleton and sums exactly on merging disjoint components. Considering every land adjacency produces precisely the islands and their cell counts.

docs.title: Walkthrough

Both preserve the input grid and avoid recursion depth limits. All-water input returns zero; diagonal adjacency never joins land.

docs.title: 1. Iterative area flood-fill
docs.text:
Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(R*C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Iterative area flood-fill
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def maxAreaOfIsland(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, columns = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        seen = set()
        answer = 0
        for r in range(rows):
            for c in range(columns):
                if not grid[r][c] or (r, c) in seen:
                    continue
                stack, area = [(r, c)], 0
                seen.add((r, c))
                while stack:
                    row, column = stack.pop()
                    area += 1
                    for nr, nc in (
                        (row - 1, column),
                        (row + 1, column),
                        (row, column - 1),
                        (row, column + 1),
                    ):
                        if (
                            0 <= nr < rows
                            and 0 <= nc < columns
                            and grid[nr][nc]
                            and (nr, nc) not in seen
                        ):
                            seen.add((nr, nc))
                            stack.append((nr, nc))
                answer = max(answer, area)
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Size-weighted land unions
docs.text:
Time: O(RCalpha(R*C))

Space: O(R*C)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Size-weighted land unions
    Time: O(R*C*alpha(R*C))
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def maxAreaOfIsland(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, columns = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        parent = list(range(rows * columns))
        size = [1] * len(parent)

        def find(node):
            while node != parent[node]:
                parent[node] = parent[parent[node]]
                node = parent[node]
            return node

        answer = 0
        for r in range(rows):
            for c in range(columns):
                if not grid[r][c]:
                    continue
                root = find(r * columns + c)
                for nr, nc in ((r - 1, c), (r, c - 1)):
                    if nr >= 0 and nc >= 0 and grid[nr][nc]:
                        other = find(nr * columns + nc)
                        root = find(root)
                        if root != other:
                            if size[root] < size[other]:
                                root, other = other, root
                            parent[other] = root
                            size[root] += size[other]
                answer = max(answer, size[find(root)])
        return answer

docs.title: Hints

1. The total must divide evenly by the group count.
  2. Either place large values into symmetric buckets or remember the remainder for each used-index mask.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Descending bucket assignment O(n log n + k^n) loose bound O(n*k) Used-mask remainder DP O(n*2^n) O(2^n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Descending bucket assignment
docs.text: Sort a copy descending and place each next value into a bucket that stays within the target. Skip buckets with a load already tried at this depth; stop after a failed empty bucket.

docs.title: Used-mask remainder DP
docs.text: For each reachable index mask store the current unfinished bucket sum. Add an unused value if it fits; a completed bucket resets the remainder to zero.

docs.title: Descending bucket assignment
docs.text: Each placement assigns one value without exceeding the required total. Equal-load buckets are interchangeable, so symmetry pruning removes duplicate states rather than distinct feasible partitions.

docs.title: Used-mask remainder DP
docs.text: A mask fixes the total selected sum and thus its remainder modulo target. Remembering one remainder is sufficient, and every legal ordered group filling corresponds to a path through these masks.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [2,2,2,2] and k=2, the target is 4 and two groups [2,2] succeed.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Descending bucket assignment: O(n log n + k^n) loose bound time; O(nk) space. Used-mask remainder DP: O(n2^n) time; O(2^n) space. Inputs are unchanged. Exponential search is appropriate for the small maximum n (15 or 16). Sorting largest first exposes impossible assignments earlier. The bitmask table trades predictable work for exponential storage. Bucket search can retain up to k tried loads at each of n active recursive frames.

docs.title: 1. Descending bucket assignment
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n + k^n) loose bound

Space: O(n*k)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Descending bucket assignment
    Time: O(n log n + k^n) loose bound
    Space: O(n*k)
    """

    def canPartitionKSubsets(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> bool:
        values = sorted(nums, reverse=True)
        total = sum(values)
        if total % k:
            return False
        target = total // k
        if values[0] > target:
            return False
        loads = [0] * k

        def place(index):
            if index == len(values):
                return True
            tried = set()
            for bucket, load in enumerate(loads):
                if load in tried or load + values[index] > target:
                    continue
                tried.add(load)
                loads[bucket] += values[index]
                if place(index + 1):
                    return True
                loads[bucket] -= values[index]
                if load == 0:
                    break
            return False

        return place(0)

docs.title: 2. Used-mask remainder DP
docs.text:
Time: O(n*2^n)

Space: O(2^n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Used-mask remainder DP
    Time: O(n*2^n)
    Space: O(2^n)
    """

    def canPartitionKSubsets(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> bool:
        values = nums
        total = sum(values)
        if total % k:
            return False
        target = total // k
        if target == 0:
            return True
        remainders = [-1] * (1 << len(values))
        remainders[0] = 0
        for mask, remainder in enumerate(remainders):
            if remainder < 0:
                continue
            for index, value in enumerate(values):
                bit = 1 << index
                if not mask & bit and remainder + value <= target:
                    remainders[mask | bit] = (remainder + value) % target
        return remainders[-1] == 0

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Doubly linked sentinels
docs.text: Maintain head/tail sentinels and size. Locate indexed nodes from the closer boundary, then splice or unlink with reciprocal pointer updates.

docs.title: Dummy-headed singly linked list
docs.text: Keep one dummy head and size. Walk to the indexed predecessor before insertions and deletions; get walks directly to its target.

docs.title: Doubly linked sentinels
docs.text: The sentinel chain contains exactly size live nodes in list order. Searching counts the requested number of links; local splice/unlink changes exactly that indexed position while preserving all others.

docs.title: Dummy-headed singly linked list
docs.text: The predecessor is the unique incoming link for the target position. Replacing that link implements insertion or deletion without needing backward pointers.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls

Dummy-headed singly linked list: O(n) indexed/tail operations; O(1) head insertion time; O(n) space. Objects own all nodes. Index equal to size is valid insertion but invalid get/deletion. Nonpositive insertion indices act as head insertion. Return no replacement nodes to callers; index bounds use the current size.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Doubly linked sentinels
docs.text:
Time: O(1) end insertion; O(min(i,n-i)+1) indexed operations

Space: O(n)

class ListEntry:
    def __init__(self, value=0):
        self.value = value
        self.previous = self.next = None


class MyLinkedList:
    """Approach: Doubly linked sentinels
    Time: O(1) end insertion; O(min(i,n-i)+1) indexed operations
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.head, self.tail = ListEntry(), ListEntry()
        self.head.next = self.tail
        self.tail.previous = self.head
        self.size = 0

    def _node(self, index):
        if index < self.size // 2:
            node = self.head.next
            for _ in range(index):
                node = node.next
        else:
            node = self.tail.previous
            for _ in range(self.size - index - 1):
                node = node.previous
        return node

    def get(self, index: int) -> int:
        return self._node(index).value if 0 <= index < self.size else -1

    def addAtHead(self, val: int) -> None:
        self.addAtIndex(0, val)

    def addAtTail(self, val: int) -> None:
        self.addAtIndex(self.size, val)

    def addAtIndex(self, index: int, val: int) -> None:
        index = max(index, 0)
        if index > self.size:
            return
        after = self.tail if index == self.size else self._node(index)
        before = after.previous
        node = ListEntry(val)
        node.previous, node.next = before, after
        before.next = after.previous = node
        self.size += 1

    def deleteAtIndex(self, index: int) -> None:
        if not 0 <= index < self.size:
            return
        node = self._node(index)
        node.previous.next = node.next
        node.next.previous = node.previous
        self.size -= 1

docs.title: 2. Dummy-headed singly linked list
docs.text:
Time: O(n) indexed/tail operations; O(1) head insertion

Space: O(n)

class ListEntry:
    def __init__(self, value=0):
        self.value = value
        self.previous = self.next = None


class MyLinkedList:
    """Approach: Dummy-headed singly linked list
    Time: O(n) indexed/tail operations; O(1) head insertion
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.head = ListEntry()
        self.size = 0

    def get(self, index: int) -> int:
        if not 0 <= index < self.size:
            return -1
        node = self.head.next
        for _ in range(index):
            node = node.next
        return node.value

    def addAtHead(self, val: int) -> None:
        self.addAtIndex(0, val)

    def addAtTail(self, val: int) -> None:
        self.addAtIndex(self.size, val)

    def addAtIndex(self, index: int, val: int) -> None:
        index = max(index, 0)
        if index > self.size:
            return
        before = self.head
        for _ in range(index):
            before = before.next
        node = ListEntry(val)
        node.next = before.next
        before.next = node
        self.size += 1

    def deleteAtIndex(self, index: int) -> None:
        if not 0 <= index < self.size:
            return
        before = self.head
        for _ in range(index):
            before = before.next
        before.next = before.next.next
        self.size -= 1

docs.title: 712 Minimum ASCII Delete Sum for Two Strings
docs.text:
Medium · Grid and counting dynamic programming extensions · Extension · Learning step 333 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: String DP.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Delete characters from two strings until they become equal, minimizing the sum of deleted ASCII values.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. A mismatch must delete at least one of its two endpoint characters.
  2. Equivalently maximize the total character weight of a common subsequence that is kept.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 332 · #688 · Next: 334 · #718

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Rolling minimum-deletion prefix costs O(m*n+m+n) O(min(m,n)+1) Maximum-weight common subsequence O(m*n+m+n) O(n+1)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Rolling minimum-deletion prefix costs
docs.text: Initialize empty-prefix deletion costs. Matching letters reuse the diagonal; otherwise delete either current character and pay its ASCII value. Save the diagonal during row compression.

docs.title: Maximum-weight common subsequence
docs.text: Compute a common subsequence maximizing the sum of retained ASCII values. Subtract twice that weight from the combined original string weights.

docs.title: Rolling minimum-deletion prefix costs
docs.text: A common final character can be retained for free. If final characters differ, at least one must be deleted; considering both possibilities covers every transformation and chooses its minimum cost.

docs.title: Maximum-weight common subsequence
docs.text: The retained common text survives once in each string, saving twice its weight. Maximizing those savings is exactly minimizing deletions, and weighted LCS considers every legal retention order.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For "sea" and "eat", retain "ea" and delete s and t, costing 115+116=231.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Rolling minimum-deletion prefix costs: O(mn+m+n) time; O(min(m,n)+1) space. Maximum-weight common subsequence: O(mn+m+n) time; O(n+1) space.

m and n are string lengths. Both preserve inputs and avoid slices. A longest common subsequence by character count need not maximize ASCII weight; use weighted states. All weights are positive.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Rolling minimum-deletion prefix costs
docs.text:
Time: O(m*n+m+n)

Space: O(min(m,n)+1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Rolling minimum-deletion prefix costs
    Time: O(m*n+m+n)
    Space: O(min(m,n)+1)
    """

    def minimumDeleteSum(self, s1: str, s2: str) -> int:
        if len(s1) < len(s2):
            s1, s2 = s2, s1
        dp = [0]
        for character in s2:
            dp.append(dp[-1] + ord(character))
        for first in s1:
            diagonal = dp[0]
            dp[0] += ord(first)
            for j, second in enumerate(s2, 1):
                above = dp[j]
                dp[j] = (
                    diagonal
                    if first == second
                    else min(above + ord(first), dp[j - 1] + ord(second))
                )
                diagonal = above
        return dp[-1]

docs.title: 2. Maximum-weight common subsequence
docs.text:
Time: O(m*n+m+n)

Space: O(n+1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Maximum-weight common subsequence
    Time: O(m*n+m+n)
    Space: O(n+1)
    """

    def minimumDeleteSum(self, s1: str, s2: str) -> int:
        dp = [0] * (len(s2) + 1)
        for first in s1:
            diagonal = 0
            for j, second in enumerate(s2, 1):
                above = dp[j]
                dp[j] = diagonal + ord(first) if first == second else max(above, dp[j - 1])
                diagonal = above
        return sum(map(ord, s1)) + sum(map(ord, s2)) - 2 * dp[-1]

docs.title: Hints

1. For one right endpoint, every suffix of a valid window is valid.
  2. If k is at most one, no positive product qualifies.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Multiplicative sliding window O(n) arithmetic operations O(1) integer variables Exact prefix products with binary search O(n log n) big-integer operations O(n squared log M) bits worst case

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Multiplicative sliding window
docs.text: Multiply in each value and divide outgoing factors while the product is too large. Add the number of possible starts in the surviving window.

docs.title: Exact prefix products with binary search
docs.text: Build arbitrary-precision prefix products. For each end, binary-search earlier prefix products greater than prefix[end] // k. This avoids logarithm rounding, but huge integers make it an educational baseline that may time out.

docs.title: Multiplicative sliding window
docs.text: Positive integer factors make shortening a window nonincreasing in product. The surviving left endpoint is the earliest valid start, so exactly right-left+1 subarrays ending here qualify.

docs.title: Exact prefix products with binary search
docs.text: For positive prefix products P, P[end]/P[start] < k is equivalent to P[start] > P[end]//k. Prefix products are nondecreasing even with ones, so upper bound counts all eligible starts exactly.

docs.title: Walkthrough

docs.text:
Multiplicative sliding window: O(n) arithmetic operations time; O(1) integer variables space.

Exact prefix products with binary search: O(n log n) big-integer operations time; O(n squared log M) bits worst case space.

Inputs are unchanged. Strict inequality needs an upper bound in the prefix method. M is the maximum value; the default maintains products bounded by k times one incoming value.

docs.title: 1. Multiplicative sliding window
docs.text:
Time: O(n) arithmetic operations

Space: O(1) integer variables

from bisect import bisect_right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Multiplicative sliding window
    Time: O(n) arithmetic operations
    Space: O(1) integer variables
    """

    def numSubarrayProductLessThanK(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        if k <= 1:
            return 0
        product = 1
        left = answer = 0
        for right, value in enumerate(nums):
            product *= value
            while product >= k:
                product //= nums[left]
                left += 1
            answer += right - left + 1
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Exact prefix products with binary search
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n) big-integer operations

Space: O(n squared log M) bits worst case

from bisect import bisect_right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Exact prefix products with binary search
    Time: O(n log n) big-integer operations
    Space: O(n squared log M) bits worst case
    """

    def numSubarrayProductLessThanK(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        if k <= 1:
            return 0
        prefix = [1]
        for value in nums:
            prefix.append(prefix[-1] * value)
        answer = 0
        for end in range(1, len(prefix)):
            first = bisect_right(prefix, prefix[end] // k, 0, end)
            answer += end - first
        return answer

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Backward-updated matching suffix lengths O(m*n) O(n) Binary-search exact tuple windows O((m+n)Llog(L+1)) expected O(m*L)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Backward-updated matching suffix lengths
docs.text: Store lengths of equal suffixes ending at the current pair of endpoints. Update the second-array positions backward so the old diagonal remains available.

docs.title: Binary-search exact tuple windows
docs.text: For a candidate length, store all exact tuple windows from the first array and test windows from the second. Binary-search the greatest feasible length.

docs.title: Backward-updated matching suffix lengths
docs.text: Equal final elements extend the equal suffix one step; unequal elements force length zero. Every common contiguous block ends at some endpoint pair, so the maximum state gives the optimum.

docs.title: Binary-search exact tuple windows
docs.text: A common window of length L contains common windows of every smaller length, so feasibility is monotone. Tuple equality confirms exact contents even when hashes collide, making this deterministic in correctness.

docs.title: Walkthrough

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Backward-updated matching suffix lengths: O(mn) time; O(n) space. Binary-search exact tuple windows: O((m+n)Llog(L+1)) expected time; O(mL) space.

L=min(m,n). Both preserve arrays. Tuple construction, input slicing, and tuple hashing each cost O(window length); the window baseline is not a linear-time rolling hash and may be slower near full limits. The suffix DP finds contiguous blocks, not subsequences.

docs.title: 1. Backward-updated matching suffix lengths
docs.text:
Time: O(m*n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Backward-updated matching suffix lengths
    Time: O(m*n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def findLength(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> int:
        dp = [0] * (len(nums2) + 1)
        answer = 0
        for first in nums1:
            for j in range(len(nums2), 0, -1):
                dp[j] = dp[j - 1] + 1 if first == nums2[j - 1] else 0
                answer = max(answer, dp[j])
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Binary-search exact tuple windows
docs.text:
Time: O((m+n)Llog(L+1)) expected

Space: O(m*L)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary-search exact tuple windows
    Time: O((m+n)*L*log(L+1)) expected
    Space: O(m*L)
    """

    def findLength(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> int:
        def possible(length):
            windows = {
                tuple(nums1[start : start + length]) for start in range(len(nums1) - length + 1)
            }
            return any(
                tuple(nums2[start : start + length]) in windows
                for start in range(len(nums2) - length + 1)
            )

        low, high = 0, min(len(nums1), len(nums2)) + 1
        while low + 1 < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if possible(middle):
                low = middle
            else:
                high = middle
        return low

docs.title: Binary search a pair-count threshold
docs.text: Sort a copy. Binary-search the distance whose count of pairs at most that distance first reaches k; compute each count with a moving left boundary.

docs.title: Heap merge of fixed-left distance streams
docs.text: For each left index, seed the pair with its immediate successor. Pop the smallest distance and advance only that stream until k pairs have been removed. This baseline may time out when k is quadratic in n.

docs.title: Binary search a pair-count threshold
docs.text: For every right index, the valid left indices form one suffix of earlier indices and contribute right-left pairs. The count is monotone in the bound, so its first count reaching k is the kth order statistic.

docs.title: Heap merge of fixed-left distance streams
docs.text: Each stream lists all distances sharing one left index in nondecreasing order. A min-heap of stream heads emits the union in global order, counting every index pair once, so its kth pop is correct.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: [1,3,1] has sorted pair distances [0,2,2], so k=1 returns 0. The two equal 1 values belong to different indices.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:

Heap merge of fixed-left distance streams: O(n log n+k log n) time; O(n) space.

Inputs are unchanged. W is max(nums)-min(nums). Do not deduplicate the array, because multiplicity determines the pair rank.

docs.text:

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary search a pair-count threshold
    Time: O(n log n+n log(W+1))
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def smallestDistancePair(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        values = sorted(nums)
        low, high = 0, values[-1] - values[0]
        while low < high:
            distance = (low + high) // 2
            left = count = 0
            for right, value in enumerate(values):
                while value - values[left] > distance:
                    left += 1
                count += right - left
            if count >= k:
                high = distance
            else:
                low = distance + 1
        return low

docs.title: 2. Heap merge of fixed-left distance streams
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n+k log n)

Space: O(n)

from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Heap merge of fixed-left distance streams
    Time: O(n log n+k log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def smallestDistancePair(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        values = sorted(nums)
        heap = [(values[i + 1] - values[i], i, i + 1) for i in range(len(values) - 1)]
        heapify(heap)
        for _ in range(k):
            distance, left, right = heappop(heap)
            if right + 1 < len(values):
                heappush(heap, (values[right + 1] - values[left], left, right + 1))
        return distance

from bisect import bisect_left


class MyCalendar:
    """Approach: Sorted bookings with neighbor checks
    Time: O(n) per book
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.bookings = []

    def book(self, startTime: int, endTime: int) -> bool:
        index = bisect_left(self.bookings, (startTime, endTime))
        if index and self.bookings[index - 1][1] > startTime:
            return False
        if index < len(self.bookings) and self.bookings[index][0] < endTime:
            return False
        self.bookings.insert(index, (startTime, endTime))
        return True

class MyCalendarTwo:
    """Approach: Store bookings and double intersections
    Time: O(n squared) worst case per book
    Space: O(n squared)

    def __init__(self):
        self.bookings = []
        self.doubles = []

    def book(self, startTime: int, endTime: int) -> bool:
        if any(max(start, startTime) < min(end, endTime) for start, end in self.doubles):
            return False
        for start, end in self.bookings:
            left, right = max(start, startTime), min(end, endTime)
            if left < right:
                self.doubles.append((left, right))
        self.bookings.append((startTime, endTime))

docs.title: 2. Sweep event counts with rollback
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n) per book

Space: O(n)

class MyCalendarTwo:
    """Approach: Sweep event counts with rollback
    Time: O(n log n) per book
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.events = {}

    def book(self, startTime: int, endTime: int) -> bool:
        self.events[startTime] = self.events.get(startTime, 0) + 1
        self.events[endTime] = self.events.get(endTime, 0) - 1
        active = 0
        for point in sorted(self.events):
            active += self.events[point]
            if active > 2:
                self.events[startTime] -= 1
                self.events[endTime] += 1
                if self.events[startTime] == 0:
                    del self.events[startTime]
                if self.events.get(endTime) == 0:
                    del self.events[endTime]
                return False
        return True

docs.title: 2. Sparse lazy segment tree
docs.text:
Time: O(log U) per book

Space: O(n log U)

class MyCalendarThree:
    """Approach: Sparse lazy segment tree
    Time: O(log U) per book
    Space: O(n log U)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.maximum = {}
        self.lazy = {}

    def book(self, startTime: int, endTime: int) -> int:
        def add(node, left, right):
            if endTime <= left or right < startTime:
                return
            if startTime <= left and right < endTime:
                self.maximum[node] = self.maximum.get(node, 0) + 1
                self.lazy[node] = self.lazy.get(node, 0) + 1
                return
            middle = (left + right) // 2
            add(node * 2, left, middle)
            add(node * 2 + 1, middle + 1, right)
            self.maximum[node] = self.lazy.get(node, 0) + max(
                self.maximum.get(node * 2, 0), self.maximum.get(node * 2 + 1, 0)
            )

        add(1, 0, 10**9 - 1)
        return self.maximum[1]

docs.title: Right-to-left decrement and nine suffix
docs.text: Scan digits right to left. On a descent, decrement the preceding digit and mark the later suffix for replacement by nines.

docs.title: Memoized upper-bound digit construction
docs.text: Use states (position,previous_digit,tight). Try next digits from largest to smallest while respecting nondecreasing order and the bound; retain the first feasible suffix.

docs.title: Right-to-left decrement and nine suffix
docs.text: At a descent, keeping the earlier prefix unchanged cannot produce a legal suffix. Reducing the latest possible offending digit gives the smallest necessary decrease; filling everything after it with nines maximizes the result. Right-to-left scanning propagates any new descent.

docs.title: Memoized upper-bound digit construction
docs.text: The state captures every constraint on a suffix. Descending candidate order chooses the largest feasible first differing digit, and recursively optimal suffixes complete the greatest valid number. Leading zeroes represent shorter numbers without a separate case.

from functools import cache


class Solution:
    """Approach: Right-to-left decrement and nine suffix
    Time: O(L)
    Space: O(L)
    """

    def monotoneIncreasingDigits(self, n: int) -> int:
        digits = list(str(n))
        boundary = len(digits)
        for i in range(len(digits) - 1, 0, -1):
            if digits[i] < digits[i - 1]:
                digits[i - 1] = str(int(digits[i - 1]) - 1)
                boundary = i
        for i in range(boundary, len(digits)):
            digits[i] = "9"
        return int("".join(digits))

docs.text:
Time: O(100L)

Space: O(10L)

from functools import cache


class Solution:
    """Approach: Memoized upper-bound digit construction
    Time: O(100L)
    Space: O(10L)
    """

    def monotoneIncreasingDigits(self, n: int) -> int:
        digits = tuple(map(int, str(n)))

        @cache
        def build(position, previous, tight):
            if position == len(digits):
                return 0
            limit = digits[position] if tight else 9
            for digit in range(limit, previous - 1, -1):
                suffix = build(position + 1, digit, tight and digit == limit)
                if suffix is not None:
                    return digit * 10 ** (len(digits) - position - 1) + suffix
            return None

        return build(0, 0, True)

docs.text: Maintain a stack of unresolved indices with nonincreasing temperatures. When a warmer day arrives, pop every cooler top index and fill its waiting distance. Push the current day after resolving those earlier days.

docs.text: Scan backward and jump through already-computed next-warmer links until a warmer day appears. This avoids a separate stack, but its conservative quadratic worst-case bound may time out at full constraints.

docs.title: Unresolved-day stack
docs.text: An index stays unresolved until the first later day warmer than it arrives. If such a day had appeared earlier, that index would already have been popped. Thus every assigned distance is to the earliest valid warmer day.
