docs.text: When a future day is not warmer, any days it skips before its own next warmer day are no warmer than it and cannot answer the current query. Following its link preserves the first possible answer.

Default approach (Unresolved-day stack):

O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space, plus O(n) output. Every index is pushed and popped at most once. Inputs are unchanged. Equal temperatures are not warmer, so pop only on a strict increase. Store indices, since values alone do not give waiting distances.

Unresolved-day stack: O(n) time; O(n) space. Reverse jump pointers: O(n squared) worst case time; O(1) auxiliary, O(n) output space. class Solution:
    """Approach: Unresolved-day stack
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def dailyTemperatures(self, temperatures: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        result = [0] * len(temperatures)
        waiting = []
        for day, temperature in enumerate(temperatures):
            while waiting and temperatures[waiting[-1]] < temperature:
                previous = waiting.pop()
                result[previous] = day - previous
            waiting.append(day)
        return result

Time: O(n squared) worst case

Space: O(1) auxiliary, O(n) output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Reverse jump pointers
    Time: O(n squared) worst case
    Space: O(1) auxiliary, O(n) output
    """

    def dailyTemperatures(self, temperatures: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        result = [0] * len(temperatures)
        for i in range(len(temperatures) - 2, -1, -1):
            j = i + 1
            while j < len(temperatures) and temperatures[j] <= temperatures[i]:
                if result[j] == 0:
                    j = len(temperatures)
                else:
                    j += result[j]
            if j < len(temperatures):
                result[i] = j - i
        return result

docs.title: Sparse sorted-value take and skip
docs.text: Once x is chosen, taking all its identical copies adds earnings without creating new conflicts. Only neighboring integer values conflict, so the take/skip path recurrence is exhaustive.

docs.title: Dense value-axis robber DP

Space: O(u)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sparse sorted-value take and skip
    Time: O(n+u log u) expected
    Space: O(u)
    """

    def deleteAndEarn(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        points = {}
        for value in nums:
            points[value] = points.get(value, 0) + value
        take = skip = 0
        previous = None
        for value in sorted(points):
            best = max(take, skip)
            take, skip = (
                (skip if previous is not None and value == previous + 1 else best) + points[value],
                best,
            )
            previous = value
        return max(take, skip)

docs.title: 2. Dense value-axis robber DP
docs.text:
Time: O(n+U)

Space: O(U)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Dense value-axis robber DP
    Time: O(n+U)
    Space: O(U)
    """

    def deleteAndEarn(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        points = [0] * (max(nums) + 1)
        for value in nums:
            points[value] += value
        older = previous = 0
        for gain in points:
            older, previous = previous, max(previous, older + gain)
        return previous

Approach Time Space Heap Dijkstra arrival times O((V+E) log V) O(V+E) Repeated directed-edge relaxation O(V*E) O(V)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Heap Dijkstra arrival times
docs.text: Run Dijkstra's algorithm on outgoing adjacency lists. Initialize the source distance to zero and others to infinity. Expand heap entries matching current best distances, relax outgoing edges, and push improvements. Ignore stale entries. Return the maximum distance, unless a node remains unreachable.

docs.title: Repeated directed-edge relaxation
docs.text: Relax all directed edges for up to V-1 rounds, stopping when a round changes nothing. Distances start infinite except the source.

docs.title: Heap Dijkstra arrival times
docs.text: The smallest unsettled distance cannot improve through another unsettled node: reaching that node already costs at least as much, and edges never decrease path cost. Its expansion uses the final earliest arrival. Relaxation propagates improvements along outgoing edges. The maximum earliest arrival is when the whole network has received the signal.

docs.title: Repeated directed-edge relaxation
docs.text: After r full scans, shortest paths of at most r edges are represented, possibly sooner with in-place propagation. A nonnegative shortest simple path uses at most V-1 edges, so all shortest distances are found.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[1,2,6],[1,3,2],[3,2,1]] from 1, node 3 arrives at time 2 and improves node 2 from 6 to 3. Return 3 and ignore the stale 6.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Heap Dijkstra arrival times approach:

O((V + E) log V) time and O(V + E) space for this graph's distinct directed edges. Inputs are unchanged. A FIFO BFS cannot handle unequal weights. Take the maximum shortest distance, not the sum of edge weights or arrivals.

Heap Dijkstra arrival times: O((V+E) log V) time; O(V+E) space. Repeated directed-edge relaxation: O(V*E) time; O(V) space. Bellman-Ford avoids a heap and uses only a distance array, but repeats edge scans. The final distance slice allocates O(V) temporary space. Inputs remain unchanged.

from heapq import heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Heap Dijkstra arrival times
    Time: O((V+E) log V)
    Space: O(V+E)
    """

    def networkDelayTime(self, times: list[list[int]], n: int, k: int) -> int:
        outgoing = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
        for source, target, weight in times:
            outgoing[source].append((target, weight))
        distances = [float("inf")] * (n + 1)
        distances[k] = 0
        queue = [(0, k)]
        while queue:
            distance, node = heappop(queue)
            if distance != distances[node]:
                continue
            for target, weight in outgoing[node]:
                candidate = distance + weight
                if candidate < distances[target]:
                    distances[target] = candidate
                    heappush(queue, (candidate, target))
        delay = max(distances[1:])
        return -1 if delay == float("inf") else int(delay)

docs.title: 2. Repeated directed-edge relaxation
docs.text:
Time: O(V*E)

Space: O(V)

from heapq import heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Repeated directed-edge relaxation
    Time: O(V*E)
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def networkDelayTime(self, times: list[list[int]], n: int, k: int) -> int:
        distance = [float("inf")] * (n + 1)
        distance[k] = 0
        for _ in range(n - 1):
            changed = False
            for source, target, weight in times:
                if distance[source] + weight < distance[target]:
                    distance[target] = distance[source] + weight
                    changed = True
            if not changed:
                break
        answer = max(distance[1:])
        return -1 if answer == float("inf") else answer

Space: O(10^4)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Single-source lock BFS
    Time: O(10^4) states with fixed four-digit work
    Space: O(10^4)
    """

    def openLock(self, deadends: list[str], target: str) -> int:
        from collections import deque

        seen = set(deadends)
        if "0000" in seen:
            return -1
        seen.add("0000")
        queue = deque([("0000", 0)])
        while queue:
            state, steps = queue.popleft()
            if state == target:
                return steps
            for index in range(4):
                for change in (-1, 1):
                    following = (
                        state[:index] + str((int(state[index]) + change) % 10) + state[index + 1 :]
                    )
                    if following not in seen:
                        seen.add(following)
                        queue.append((following, steps + 1))
        return -1

docs.title: 2. Two frontier distance maps
docs.text:
Time: O(10^4) states with fixed four-digit work

Space: O(10^4)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Two frontier distance maps
    Time: O(10^4) states with fixed four-digit work
    Space: O(10^4)
    """

    def openLock(self, deadends: list[str], target: str) -> int:
        blocked = set(deadends)
        if "0000" in blocked or target in blocked:
            return -1
        if target == "0000":
            return 0
        front, back = {"0000"}, {target}
        first, second = {"0000": 0}, {target: 0}
        while front and back:
            if len(front) > len(back):
                front, back, first, second = back, front, second, first
            following = set()
            for state in front:
                for index in range(4):
                    for change in (-1, 1):
                        other = (
                            state[:index]
                            + str((int(state[index]) + change) % 10)
                            + state[index + 1 :]
                        )
                        if other in blocked or other in first:
                            continue
                        if other in second:
                            return first[state] + 1 + second[other]
                        first[other] = first[state] + 1
                        following.add(other)
            front = following
        return -1

docs.title: Greedy last-occurrence boundary
docs.text: Record each letter's last index. Extend the current piece end to include every letter encountered and close when the scan reaches that end.

docs.title: Merge character-span intervals
docs.text: Build one first-to-last interval per character and merge intersecting intervals. The merged lengths are the maximal partition lengths.

docs.title: Greedy last-occurrence boundary
docs.text: Every piece must include the last occurrence of each of its letters. The maintained end is therefore a necessary lower bound; reaching it makes the earliest possible valid cut, maximizing the number of pieces.

docs.title: Merge character-span intervals
docs.text: A character's entire span must be in one piece. Intersecting spans force the same piece transitively; separate span components have no shared letter, so each component can be cut apart.

docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(A)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Greedy last-occurrence boundary
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(A)
    """

    def partitionLabels(self, s: str) -> list[int]:
        last = {char: i for i, char in enumerate(s)}
        start = end = 0
        answer = []
        for i, char in enumerate(s):
            end = max(end, last[char])
            if i == end:
                answer.append(i - start + 1)
                start = i + 1
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Merge character-span intervals
docs.text:
Time: O(n+A log A)

Space: O(A)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Merge character-span intervals
    Time: O(n+A log A)
    Space: O(A)
    """

    def partitionLabels(self, s: str) -> list[int]:
        spans = {}
        for i, char in enumerate(s):
            if char not in spans:
                spans[char] = [i, i]
            spans[char][1] = i
        answer = []
        start = end = -1
        for left, right in sorted(spans.values()):
            if left > end:
                if end >= 0:
                    answer.append(end - start + 1)
                start, end = left, right
            else:
                end = max(end, right)
        if end >= 0:
            answer.append(end - start + 1)
        return answer

Approach Time Space Heap with one delayed character O(n log(u+1)) O(n+u) Fill even then odd positions O(n + u log u) O(n+u)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Heap with one delayed character
docs.text: Pop the most frequent available character. Keep its remaining count outside the heap for one turn, reinserting the previously delayed character after choosing the next one.

docs.title: Fill even then odd positions
docs.text: Sort characters by decreasing count, fill indices 0,2,4,..., then 1,3,5,... . Reject a count larger than ceil(n/2).

docs.title: Heap with one delayed character
docs.text: The held character cannot be chosen immediately again. Choosing the most frequent eligible character consumes the most constrained supply; the frequency feasibility condition ensures the schedule can finish.

docs.title: Fill even then odd positions
docs.text: The largest block fits entirely in the even positions. Remaining frequency blocks fill separated slots, and descending block sizes prevent a repeated block from creating adjacent equal characters across the even/odd boundary.

docs.text: Heap with one delayed character: O(n log(u+1)) time; O(n+u) space. Fill even then odd positions: O(n + u log u) time; O(n+u) space. The input string is immutable. u is the distinct-character count, at most 26 here. Validate output multiplicities and adjacency rather than requiring one incidental valid arrangement.

docs.title: 1. Heap with one delayed character
docs.text:
Time: O(n log(u+1))

Space: O(n+u)

from collections import Counter
from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Heap with one delayed character
    Time: O(n log(u+1))
    Space: O(n+u)
    """

    def reorganizeString(self, s: str) -> str:
        counts = Counter(s)
        if max(counts.values(), default=0) > (len(s) + 1) // 2:
            return ""
        heap = [(-count, char) for char, count in counts.items()]
        heapify(heap)
        previous_count, previous_char = 0, ""
        result = []
        while heap:
            count, char = heappop(heap)
            result.append(char)
            if previous_count < 0:
                heappush(heap, (previous_count, previous_char))
            previous_count, previous_char = count + 1, char
        return "".join(result)

docs.title: 2. Fill even then odd positions
docs.text:
Time: O(n + u log u)

Space: O(n+u)

from collections import Counter
from heapq import heapify, heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Fill even then odd positions
    Time: O(n + u log u)
    Space: O(n+u)
    """

    def reorganizeString(self, s: str) -> str:
        counts = Counter(s)
        if max(counts.values(), default=0) > (len(s) + 1) // 2:
            return ""
        result = [""] * len(s)
        index = 0
        for char, count in sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda item: -item[1]):
            for _ in range(count):
                if index >= len(s):
                    index = 1
                result[index] = char
                index += 2
        return "".join(result)

  2. Reachability is monotone as the water level rises.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Minimax elevation Dijkstra O(n^2 log n) O(n^2) Binary-search water level and flood-fill O(n^2 log n) O(n^2)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Minimax elevation Dijkstra
docs.text: Heap-expand the smallest achievable maximum elevation and relax neighbors by taking the maximum with their elevation.

docs.title: Binary-search water level and flood-fill
docs.text: Binary-search levels between the endpoint minimum requirement and n²-1, testing each with an iterative flood-fill restricted to submerged cells.

docs.title: Minimax elevation Dijkstra
docs.text: Path costs never decrease on extension, so the smallest pending bottleneck finalizes just as in Dijkstra. The popped goal has the least possible water requirement.

docs.title: Binary-search water level and flood-fill
docs.text: Increasing level only adds traversable cells, so feasibility is monotone. Flood-fill exactly decides a level, and binary search isolates its first feasible value.

docs.title: Walkthrough

docs.text:
Minimax elevation Dijkstra: O(n^2 log n) time; O(n^2) space. Binary-search water level and flood-fill: O(n^2 log n) time; O(n^2) space.

Both preserve the grid and avoid recursion. n is side length; elevations are a permutation of 0 through n²-1. Water cost is maximum cell height, unlike maximum adjacent difference in problem 1631.

docs.title: 1. Minimax elevation Dijkstra
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2 log n)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Minimax elevation Dijkstra
    Time: O(n^2 log n)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def swimInWater(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        from heapq import heappop, heappush

        n = len(grid)
        best = {(0, 0): grid[0][0]}
        heap = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]
        while heap:
            level, r, c = heappop(heap)
            if level != best[(r, c)]:
                continue
            if (r, c) == (n - 1, n - 1):
                return level
            for nr, nc in ((r - 1, c), (r + 1, c), (r, c - 1), (r, c + 1)):
                if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n:
                    candidate = max(level, grid[nr][nc])
                    if candidate < best.get((nr, nc), float("inf")):
                        best[(nr, nc)] = candidate
                        heappush(heap, (candidate, nr, nc))
        return -1

docs.title: 2. Binary-search water level and flood-fill
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2 log n)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary-search water level and flood-fill
    Time: O(n^2 log n)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def swimInWater(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)

        def reachable(level):
            seen, stack = {(0, 0)}, [(0, 0)]
            while stack:
                r, c = stack.pop()
                if (r, c) == (n - 1, n - 1):
                    return True
                for nr, nc in ((r - 1, c), (r + 1, c), (r, c - 1), (r, c + 1)):
                    if (
                        0 <= nr < n
                        and 0 <= nc < n
                        and grid[nr][nc] <= level
                        and (nr, nc) not in seen
                    ):
                        seen.add((nr, nc))
                        stack.append((nr, nc))
            return False

        low = max(grid[0][0], grid[-1][-1]) - 1
        high = n * n - 1
        while low + 1 < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if reachable(middle):
                high = middle
            else:
                low = middle
        return high

1. Assign a vertex the opposite color of every neighbor.
  2. A disjoint-set model can represent each vertex and its required opposite.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Component-wise two-color BFS O(V+E) O(V) Union-find with opposite copies O((V+E)*alpha(V)) O(V)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Component-wise two-color BFS
docs.text: Start an uncolored component at color zero and BFS its edges. Assign unseen neighbors the opposite color; reject any edge joining equal colors.

docs.title: Union-find with opposite copies
docs.text: Represent vertex u and its opposite as u and u+V. Each edge joins u with opposite(v) and opposite(u) with v. Reject when any vertex becomes equivalent to its own opposite.

docs.title: Component-wise two-color BFS
docs.text: Every traversed edge enforces exactly the bipartition constraint. A conflict proves an inconsistent parity cycle; without conflicts the resulting colors explicitly provide a valid partition.

docs.title: Union-find with opposite copies
docs.text: The unions encode every edge's inequality as equivalence to an opposite. A vertex equaling its opposite is precisely a contradiction; otherwise each equivalence component can be assigned consistently opposite its paired component.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: A triangle 0-1-2-0 forces the third edge to join equal colors and fails. A four-cycle alternates colors and succeeds.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Component-wise two-color BFS: O(V+E) time; O(V) space. Union-find with opposite copies: O((V+E)*alpha(V)) time; O(V) space. The graph is unchanged. Start every disconnected component, not only vertex zero. Union-find uses two copies per vertex; alpha denotes inverse Ackermann. Iteration avoids deep recursive traversal.

docs.title: 1. Component-wise two-color BFS
docs.text:
Time: O(V+E)

Space: O(V)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Component-wise two-color BFS
    Time: O(V+E)
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def isBipartite(self, graph: list[list[int]]) -> bool:
        colors = [-1] * len(graph)
        for start in range(len(graph)):
            if colors[start] != -1:
                continue
            colors[start] = 0
            queue = deque([start])
            while queue:
                node = queue.popleft()
                for neighbor in graph[node]:
                    if colors[neighbor] == -1:
                        colors[neighbor] = 1 - colors[node]
                        queue.append(neighbor)
                    elif colors[neighbor] == colors[node]:
                        return False
        return True

docs.title: 2. Union-find with opposite copies
docs.text:
Time: O((V+E)*alpha(V))

Space: O(V)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Union-find with opposite copies
    Time: O((V+E)*alpha(V))
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def isBipartite(self, graph: list[list[int]]) -> bool:
        n = len(graph)
        parent = list(range(2 * n))
        size = [1] * (2 * n)

        def find(node):
            while parent[node] != node:
                parent[node] = parent[parent[node]]
                node = parent[node]
            return node

        def union(left, right):
            left, right = find(left), find(right)
            if left == right:
                return
            if size[left] < size[right]:
                left, right = right, left
            parent[right] = left
            size[left] += size[right]

        for node, neighbors in enumerate(graph):
            for neighbor in neighbors:
                union(node, neighbor + n)
                union(node + n, neighbor)
        return all(find(node) != find(node + n) for node in range(n))

docs.title: Bounded-edge Bellman-Ford rows
docs.text: Copy the preceding distance row before each full edge relaxation. A row permits one additional flight, and copying retains routes with fewer flights.

docs.title: Dijkstra on node and flights-used states
docs.text: Use a heap of cost, city, and flights-used states, relaxing an edge only while budget remains. Keep separate best costs for each budget state.

docs.title: Bounded-edge Bellman-Ford rows
docs.text: Transitions read only the old row, so no round can chain multiple new edges. Induction makes row r exactly the best route cost with at most r edges.

docs.title: Dijkstra on node and flights-used states
docs.text: Positive prices permit Dijkstra finalization on this expanded state graph. A cheap arrival with no remaining budget must not erase a costlier arrival that can still continue.

docs.text: For 0->1 costing 4, 1->2 costing 4, and 0->2 costing 12, k=0 gives 12 and k=1 gives 8.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Bounded-edge Bellman-Ford rows: O((k+1)(V+E)) time; O(V) space. Dijkstra on node and flights-used states: O((k+1)(V+E)*log((k+1)V+1)) time; O((k+1)(V+E)) space.

Inputs remain unchanged. Bellman-Ford copies cost O(V) per round, included above. A single cost per city is insufficient when routes use different numbers of flights.

docs.text:
Time: O((k+1)*(V+E))

Space: O(V)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Bounded-edge Bellman-Ford rows
    Time: O((k+1)*(V+E))
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def findCheapestPrice(
        self, n: int, flights: list[list[int]], src: int, dst: int, k: int
    ) -> int:
        costs = [float("inf")] * n
        costs[src] = 0
        for _ in range(k + 1):
            following = costs.copy()
            for a, b, price in flights:
                following[b] = min(following[b], costs[a] + price)
            costs = following
        return -1 if costs[dst] == float("inf") else costs[dst]

docs.title: 2. Dijkstra on node and flights-used states
docs.text:
Time: O((k+1)*(V+E)*log((k+1)*V+1))

Space: O((k+1)*(V+E))

class Solution:
    """Approach: Dijkstra on node and flights-used states
    Time: O((k+1)*(V+E)*log((k+1)*V+1))
    Space: O((k+1)*(V+E))
    """

    def findCheapestPrice(
        self, n: int, flights: list[list[int]], src: int, dst: int, k: int
    ) -> int:
        from heapq import heappop, heappush

        graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for a, b, price in flights:
            graph[a].append((b, price))
        best = {(src, 0): 0}
        heap = [(0, src, 0)]
        while heap:
            cost, node, used = heappop(heap)
            if best[(node, used)] != cost:
                continue
            if node == dst:
                return cost
            if used == k + 1:
                continue
            for other, price in graph[node]:
                candidate = cost + price
                if candidate < best.get((other, used + 1), float("inf")):
                    best[(other, used + 1)] = candidate
                    heappush(heap, (candidate, other, used + 1))
        return -1

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Reorder s so characters present in the distinct-character order string respect that order. Characters absent from order may occur anywhere.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Emit the requested characters in order using their multiplicities.
  2. Alternatively, turn the custom order into numeric sort keys.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Frequency emission O(n+r) expected O(n+u), including output Rank-key sorting O(r+n log n) O(r+n), including output

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Frequency emission
docs.text: Count s. For each character in order, remove its count from the map and emit that many copies. Then emit all leftover characters. Removing used keys keeps the final pass from duplicating them.

docs.title: Rank-key sorting
docs.text: Map each ordered character to its index, assigning absent characters a common rank after all listed characters. Sort s by that key and join. Stability preserves the original relative order of unlisted characters, though the problem does not require this property.

docs.title: Why it works
docs.text: Frequency emission preserves every count and emits constrained characters in the required order. The remaining characters have no constraints. Rank sorting preserves the input multiset and ensures every earlier rank precedes every later rank, which is precisely the custom ordering condition.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: With order="cba" and s="abcdab", emit c once, b twice, a twice, then d. One answer is "cbbaad". Moving d elsewhere would also be valid.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Let n=len(s), r=len(order), and u be the number of distinct characters in s. Frequency emission takes O(n+r) expected time and O(n+u) space including output. Rank sorting takes O(r+n log n) time and O(r+n) space including keys and output. The lowercase alphabet bounds r and u, but n remains variable. Both leave their inputs unchanged. Do not drop characters absent from order or invent an unnecessary lexicographic tie requirement.

docs.title: 1. Frequency emission
docs.text:
Time: O(n+r) expected

Space: O(n+u), including output

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Frequency emission
    Time: O(n+r) expected
    Space: O(n+u), including output
    """

    def customSortString(self, order: str, s: str) -> str:
        counts = Counter(s)
        pieces = []
        for char in order:
            count = counts.pop(char, 0)
            if count:
                pieces.append(char * count)
        pieces.extend(char * count for char, count in counts.items())
        return "".join(pieces)

docs.title: 2. Rank-key sorting
docs.text:
Time: O(r+n log n)

Space: O(r+n), including output

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Rank-key sorting
    Time: O(r+n log n)
    Space: O(r+n), including output
    """

    def customSortString(self, order: str, s: str) -> str:
        rank = {char: index for index, char in enumerate(order)}
        return "".join(sorted(s, key=lambda char: rank.get(char, len(order))))

1. Acyclicity guarantees every exploration terminates.
  2. You can enumerate paths forward or combine already known suffix paths backward.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Path-local DAG backtracking O(V*2^V) loose bound O(V) auxiliary plus output Topological suffix-path DP O(V+E+total copied suffix lengths) O(V+E+total stored suffix lengths)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Path-local DAG backtracking
docs.text: Append each next neighbor to a shared path, recurse, and undo. Copy the path when the target is reached, then stop that branch.

docs.title: Topological suffix-path DP
docs.text: Compute a topological order, then process it backward. Seed the target with its one-node suffix and prepend each vertex to every suffix of its outgoing neighbors.

docs.title: Path-local DAG backtracking
docs.text: Every directed source-to-target path has one neighbor-choice sequence. The search explores each such sequence once; no visited set may suppress a vertex reached through another prefix.

docs.title: Topological suffix-path DP
docs.text: All child suffix catalogs are complete before a parent is processed. A path from that parent uniquely chooses its first edge and one target-reaching suffix, so the combination is exact.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[1,2],[3],[3],[]], output [0,1,3] and [0,2,3]. Both paths legitimately share vertex 3.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Path-local DAG backtracking: O(V*2^V) loose bound time; O(V) auxiliary plus output space. Topological suffix-path DP: O(V+E+total copied suffix lengths) time; O(V+E+total stored suffix lengths) space. The graph is unchanged. Recursive depth is safe under the official small vertex limit; output may be exponential. Suffix DP can store paths from vertices unreachable from zero, whereas backtracking stores only one live prefix plus answers.

docs.text:
Time: O(V*2^V) loose bound

Space: O(V) auxiliary plus output

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Path-local DAG backtracking
    Time: O(V*2^V) loose bound
    Space: O(V) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def allPathsSourceTarget(self, graph: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
        path, result = [0], []

        def visit(node):
            if node == len(graph) - 1:
                result.append(path.copy())
                return
            for neighbor in graph[node]:
                path.append(neighbor)
                visit(neighbor)
                path.pop()

        visit(0)
        return result

docs.title: 2. Topological suffix-path DP
docs.text:
Time: O(V+E+total copied suffix lengths)

Space: O(V+E+total stored suffix lengths)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Topological suffix-path DP
    Time: O(V+E+total copied suffix lengths)
    Space: O(V+E+total stored suffix lengths)
    """

    def allPathsSourceTarget(self, graph: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
        indegree = [0] * len(graph)
        for neighbors in graph:
            for neighbor in neighbors:
                indegree[neighbor] += 1
        queue = deque(node for node, count in enumerate(indegree) if count == 0)
        order = []
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            order.append(node)
            for neighbor in graph[node]:
                indegree[neighbor] -= 1
                if indegree[neighbor] == 0:
                    queue.append(neighbor)
        paths = [[] for _ in graph]
        paths[-1] = [[len(graph) - 1]]
        for node in reversed(order):
            if node != len(graph) - 1:
                paths[node] = [
                    [node] + suffix for neighbor in graph[node] for suffix in paths[neighbor]
                ]
        return paths[0]

  2. Alternatively detect whether a DFS path can reach a cycle.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Reverse edges and remove terminal layers O(V+E) O(V+E) Iterative DFS with safe and unsafe outcomes O(V+E) O(V)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Reverse edges and remove terminal layers
docs.text: Start from terminal nodes and decrement their predecessors' remaining outgoing-edge counts. A predecessor becomes safe when all outgoing edges lead to removed safe nodes.

docs.title: Iterative DFS with safe and unsafe outcomes
docs.text: Use statuses unseen, active, safe, and unsafe with explicit child iterators. If an active frame reaches an active ancestor or known unsafe vertex, mark the entire current path unsafe; otherwise finish it safe.

docs.title: Reverse edges and remove terminal layers
docs.text: Every released node terminates through already-safe successors. Unreleased nodes retain an outgoing edge within the unreleased graph, so following such edges eventually enters a cycle.

docs.title: Iterative DFS with safe and unsafe outcomes
docs.text: Finishing after all safe children proves safety. A back edge reaches a cycle, and every frame in the active path can reach it; reaching an unsafe child has the same implication. These outcomes classify every visited vertex correctly.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: In [[1],[2],[1],[]], only vertex 3 is safe because 1 and 2 form a cycle.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Reverse edges and remove terminal layers: O(V+E) time; O(V+E) space. Iterative DFS with safe and unsafe outcomes: O(V+E) time; O(V) space.

Inputs are unchanged. DFS uses the original adjacency lists instead of storing a reverse graph and avoids recursion depth failure. A vertex merely having some terminating path is insufficient; all paths must terminate.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Reverse edges and remove terminal layers
docs.text:
Time: O(V+E)

Space: O(V+E)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Reverse edges and remove terminal layers
    Time: O(V+E)
    Space: O(V+E)
    """

    def eventualSafeNodes(self, graph: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
        from collections import deque

        reverse = [[] for _ in graph]
        remaining = [len(edges) for edges in graph]
        for node, edges in enumerate(graph):
            for other in edges:
                reverse[other].append(node)
        queue = deque(node for node, count in enumerate(remaining) if count == 0)
        safe = [False] * len(graph)
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            safe[node] = True
            for parent in reverse[node]:
                remaining[parent] -= 1
                if remaining[parent] == 0:
                    queue.append(parent)
        return [node for node, good in enumerate(safe) if good]

docs.title: 2. Iterative DFS with safe and unsafe outcomes
docs.text:
Time: O(V+E)

Space: O(V)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Iterative DFS with safe and unsafe outcomes
    Time: O(V+E)
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def eventualSafeNodes(self, graph: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
        state = [0] * len(graph)
        for start in range(len(graph)):
            if state[start]:
                continue
            state[start] = 1
            stack = [(start, iter(graph[start]))]
            while stack:
                node, children = stack[-1]
                other = next(children, None)
                if other is None:
                    state[node] = 2
                    stack.pop()
                elif state[other] in (1, 3):
                    for active, _ in stack:
                        state[active] = 3
                    stack.clear()
                elif state[other] == 0:
                    state[other] = 1
                    stack.append((other, iter(graph[other])))
        return [node for node, status in enumerate(state) if status == 2]

docs.text:
Medium · Grid and counting dynamic programming extensions · Extension · Learning step 335 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Compute P(A empties first)+0.5*P(both empty together) for the four equally likely simultaneous soup-serving choices.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Round volume upward into units of 25mL.
  2. For large equal initial amounts, returning one needs an error proof rather than an empirical threshold.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 334 · #718 · Next: 336 · #931

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Backward remaining-soup probability table O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above Forward unfinished-state probability frontiers O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above O(m) below cutoff; O(1) above

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Backward remaining-soup probability table
docs.text: Normalize to m=ceil(n/25). Empty A with nonempty B has value one, empty B alone zero, and both empty one half. Fill increasing A because every move decreases A. Return one when m>=480.

docs.title: Forward unfinished-state probability frontiers
docs.text: Propagate probability only among states where both soups remain positive. Collect A-first mass and half the simultaneous-empty mass; discard B-first mass. Use the same justified large-volume cutoff.

docs.title: Backward remaining-soup probability table
docs.text: Conditioning on the first serving gives the average of four smaller-A states, so increasing-A order solves the exact recurrence. Rounding is exact because every requested removal is a multiple of 25 and only whether remaining volume is positive matters.

docs.title: Forward unfinished-state probability frontiers
docs.text: Each frontier represents one serving round, so terminal outcomes partition all probability paths exactly once. Before termination, A+B=2m-4t, leaving only O(m) possible states per round and O(m) rounds.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For n=50, the four first moves contribute 1,1,0.5,0, so the result is 0.625. For n=0, both are already empty and the result is 0.5.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Backward remaining-soup probability table: O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above time; O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above space. Forward unfinished-state probability frontiers: O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above time; O(m) below cutoff; O(1) above space.

Both preserve n. Cutoff proof: pre-sample independent B removals Y in {0,1,2,3}, mean 1.5. The process stops by T=ceil(m/2), since each unfinished round removes four total units. If B empties no later than A, sum(Y_1..Y_T)>=m. Hoeffding therefore bounds the error of returning one by exp(-2*(m-1.5T)^2/(9T)), at most exp(-(m-3)^2/(36*(m+1)))<1.97e-6 for m>=480. This is below the official 1e-5 tolerance, with room for floating-point rounding. Sources: official rules and tolerance and Hoeffding inequality, Theorem 2. The inequality is a derived bound here, not a claim that the official page specifies this cutoff.

Space: O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above

class Solution:
    """Approach: Backward remaining-soup probability table
    Time: O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above
    Space: O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above
    """

    def soupServings(self, n: int) -> float:
        size = (n + 24) // 25
        if size >= 480:
            return 1.0
        dp = [[0.0] * (size + 1) for _ in range(size + 1)]
        dp[0] = [1.0] * (size + 1)
        dp[0][0] = 0.5
        for a in range(1, size + 1):
            for b in range(1, size + 1):
                dp[a][b] = (
                    sum(
                        dp[max(0, a - da)][max(0, b - db)]
                        for da, db in ((4, 0), (3, 1), (2, 2), (1, 3))
                    )
                    / 4
                )
        return dp[size][size]

docs.title: 2. Forward unfinished-state probability frontiers
docs.text:
Time: O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above

Space: O(m) below cutoff; O(1) above

class Solution:
    """Approach: Forward unfinished-state probability frontiers
    Time: O(m^2) below cutoff; O(1) above
    Space: O(m) below cutoff; O(1) above
    """

    def soupServings(self, n: int) -> float:
        size = (n + 24) // 25
        if size >= 480:
            return 1.0
        if size == 0:
            return 0.5
        frontier = {(size, size): 1.0}
        answer = 0.0
        while frontier:
            following = {}
            for (a, b), probability in frontier.items():
                for da, db in ((4, 0), (3, 1), (2, 2), (1, 3)):
                    na, nb = a - da, b - db
                    mass = probability / 4
                    if na <= 0:
                        answer += mass * (0.5 if nb <= 0 else 1.0)
                    elif nb > 0:
                        state = (na, nb)
                        following[state] = following.get(state, 0.0) + mass
            frontier = following
        return answer

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Translate one binary n by n image horizontally and vertically, without rotation, to maximize the number of positions where both images contain one.

docs.title: Hints

  2. Row bit masks can count overlaps by AND and bit_count.

docs.text:
Approach Time Space Translation votes from one-cell pairs O(n squared+a*b) O(n squared) Shifted row bit masks O(n cubed) word operations for n<=30 O(n) words

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Translation votes from one-cell pairs
docs.text: List the one coordinates in both images. Count the displacement between each pair; its frequency is the overlap for that translation.

docs.title: Shifted row bit masks
docs.text: Encode every row as one integer. For each vertical and horizontal translation, shift row masks and count their bit intersections.

docs.title: Translation votes from one-cell pairs
docs.text: For a fixed translation, each overlapping cell corresponds uniquely to a pair whose displacement equals that translation. The vote count is therefore exactly its overlap, and the maximum vote is optimal.

docs.title: Shifted row bit masks
docs.text: A mask bit represents exactly one image column. Horizontal shifts implement translation and bitwise AND retains exactly overlapping ones; summing matched rows gives the overlap for the chosen displacement.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Two single one-cells anywhere in their images can always be aligned, producing overlap 1. Empty images produce zero translation votes and answer zero.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Translation votes from one-cell pairs: O(n squared+a*b) time; O(n squared) space.

Shifted row bit masks: O(n cubed) word operations for n<=30 time; O(n) words space.

Inputs are unchanged. a and b are the numbers of one-cells. The bit-row bound uses the stated n<=30; wider arbitrary-size integers would add a word-length factor.

Space: O(n squared)

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Translation votes from one-cell pairs
    Time: O(n squared+a*b)
    Space: O(n squared)
    """

    def largestOverlap(self, img1: list[list[int]], img2: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        first = [(r, c) for r, row in enumerate(img1) for c, value in enumerate(row) if value]
        second = [(r, c) for r, row in enumerate(img2) for c, value in enumerate(row) if value]
        votes = Counter((r2 - r1, c2 - c1) for r1, c1 in first for r2, c2 in second)
        return max(votes.values(), default=0)

docs.title: 2. Shifted row bit masks
docs.text:
Time: O(n cubed) word operations for n<=30

Space: O(n) words

from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    """Approach: Shifted row bit masks
    Time: O(n cubed) word operations for n<=30
    Space: O(n) words
    """

    def largestOverlap(self, img1: list[list[int]], img2: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        size = len(img1)
        first = [sum(value << col for col, value in enumerate(row)) for row in img1]
        second = [sum(value << col for col, value in enumerate(row)) for row in img2]
        best = 0
        for dr in range(1 - size, size):
            for dc in range(1 - size, size):
                overlap = 0
                for row in range(size):
                    other = row + dr
                    if 0 <= other < size:
                        shifted = first[row] << dc if dc >= 0 else first[row] >> -dc
                        overlap += (shifted & second[other]).bit_count()
                best = max(best, overlap)
        return best

docs.title: 841 Keys and Rooms
docs.text:

docs.title: Task

docs.title: Hints

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Iterative key-reachability DFS O(V+E) O(V) Layered key-reachability BFS O(V+E) O(V)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Iterative key-reachability DFS
docs.text: Keep a stack of discovered rooms and a visited set seeded with zero. Add each unseen keyed room immediately when pushing it.

docs.title: Layered key-reachability BFS
docs.text: Use a FIFO queue and a boolean array of unlocked rooms. Queue each room once when its key first becomes available.

docs.title: Iterative key-reachability DFS
docs.text: Every visited room has a legal key chain from zero. Conversely, following all outgoing keys inductively discovers every room with such a chain, so full reachability exactly decides the task.

docs.title: Layered key-reachability BFS
docs.text: The queue processes reachable rooms by increasing key-chain length. Marking upon discovery preserves exactly the reachable set while preventing duplicate processing from repeated keys.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For rooms [[1],[2],[]], keys from zero open 1 and then 2, so return true. For [[1],[],[0]], room 2 remains unreachable.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Iterative key-reachability DFS: O(V+E) time; O(V) space. Layered key-reachability BFS: O(V+E) time; O(V) space. The input room/key lists are unchanged. E counts key entries, including repeated keys. Neither algorithm treats edges as undirected: possessing a key inside an unreachable room does not help.

docs.title: 1. Iterative key-reachability DFS
docs.text:
Time: O(V+E)

Space: O(V)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Iterative key-reachability DFS
    Time: O(V+E)
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def canVisitAllRooms(self, rooms: list[list[int]]) -> bool:
        seen = {0}
        stack = [0]
        while stack:
            room = stack.pop()
            for key in rooms[room]:
                if key not in seen:
                    seen.add(key)
                    stack.append(key)
        return len(seen) == len(rooms)

Time: O(V+E)

Space: O(V)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Layered key-reachability BFS
    Time: O(V+E)
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def canVisitAllRooms(self, rooms: list[list[int]]) -> bool:
        unlocked = [False] * len(rooms)
        unlocked[0] = True
        queue = deque([0])
        while queue:
            room = queue.popleft()
            for key in rooms[room]:
                if not unlocked[key]:
                    unlocked[key] = True
                    queue.append(key)
        return all(unlocked)

docs.title: Sorted frequency consumption

from collections import Counter, deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Sorted frequency consumption
    Time: O(n log n+n*g) worst case
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def isNStraightHand(self, hand: list[int], groupSize: int) -> bool:
        if len(hand) % groupSize:
            return False
        counts = Counter(hand)
        for start in sorted(counts):
            count = counts[start]
            if not count:
                continue
            for value in range(start, start + groupSize):
                if counts[value] < count:
                    return False
                counts[value] -= count
        return True

docs.title: 2. Sweep active consecutive groups
docs.text:
Time: O(n+u log u)

Space: O(u)

from collections import Counter, deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Sweep active consecutive groups
    Time: O(n+u log u)
    Space: O(u)
    """

    def isNStraightHand(self, hand: list[int], groupSize: int) -> bool:
        if len(hand) % groupSize:
            return False
        counts = Counter(hand)
        opened = deque()
        active = 0
        previous = None
        for value in sorted(counts):
            if active and previous is not None and value != previous + 1:
                return False
            if counts[value] < active:
                return False
            opened.append(counts[value] - active)
            active = counts[value]
            if len(opened) == groupSize:
                active -= opened.popleft()
            previous = value
        return active == 0

docs.text:

Space: O(V*2^V)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Multi-source visited-mask BFS
    Time: O((V+E)*2^V)
    Space: O(V*2^V)
    """

    def shortestPathLength(self, graph: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        from collections import deque

        full = (1 << len(graph)) - 1
        queue = deque((node, 1 << node, 0) for node in range(len(graph)))
        seen = {(node, 1 << node) for node in range(len(graph))}
        while queue:
            node, mask, steps = queue.popleft()
            if mask == full:
                return steps
            for other in graph[node]:
                following = mask | (1 << other)
                if (other, following) not in seen:
                    seen.add((other, following))
                    queue.append((other, following, steps + 1))
        return -1

docs.title: 2. Metric closure and subset endpoint DP
docs.text:
Time: O(V*(V+E)+V^2*2^V)

Space: O(V*2^V+V^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Metric closure and subset endpoint DP
    Time: O(V*(V+E)+V^2*2^V)
    Space: O(V*2^V+V^2)
    """

    def shortestPathLength(self, graph: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        from collections import deque

        n = len(graph)
        distance = [[n] * n for _ in graph]
        for start in range(n):
            distance[start][start] = 0
            queue = deque([start])
            while queue:
                node = queue.popleft()
                for other in graph[node]:
                    if distance[start][other] == n:
                        distance[start][other] = distance[start][node] + 1
                        queue.append(other)
        dp = [[float("inf")] * n for _ in range(1 << n)]
        for node in range(n):
            dp[1 << node][node] = 0
        for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
            for last in range(n):
                if not mask & (1 << last):
                    continue
                for other in range(n):
                    if not mask & (1 << other):
                        following = mask | (1 << other)
                        dp[following][other] = min(
                            dp[following][other], dp[mask][last] + distance[last][other]
                        )
        return min(dp[-1])

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary slope search
    Time: O(log n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def peakIndexInMountainArray(self, arr: list[int]) -> int:
        low, high = 0, len(arr) - 1
        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if arr[middle] < arr[middle + 1]:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle
        return low

docs.title: 2. Ternary mountain search
docs.text:
Time: O(log n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Ternary mountain search
    Time: O(log n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def peakIndexInMountainArray(self, arr: list[int]) -> int:
        low, high = 0, len(arr) - 1
        while high - low > 2:
            left = low + (high - low) // 3
            right = high - (high - low) // 3
            if arr[left] < arr[right]:
                low = left + 1
            elif arr[left] > arr[right]:
                high = right - 1
            else:
                low, high = left + 1, right - 1
        return max(range(low, high + 1), key=arr.__getitem__)

docs.title: Descending-position fleet times
docs.text: Sort position-speed pairs by decreasing position. Track the arrival time of the last fleet. A car with an arrival time no greater than that fleet catches it; a car with a larger time creates a new fleet. Only the last fleet matters.

docs.title: Ascending-position fleet stack
docs.text: Scan cars from farthest to nearest. Keep a stack of candidate fleet arrival fractions; a nearer slower car absorbs all faster trailing fleets whose arrival time is no later.

docs.title: Descending-position fleet times
docs.text: A car cannot bypass the nearest fleet ahead of it. If it reaches the target no later than that fleet would, their paths must meet by the target. Otherwise it stays behind and starts a separate fleet.

docs.title: Ascending-position fleet stack
docs.text: A trailing fleet catches the next fleet exactly when its free arrival time is no greater. Popping all such fleets and retaining the nearer fleet time produces exactly the surviving fleets in road order.

O(n log n) time and O(n) sorting space. Input lists are unchanged. Keep each speed paired with its position. Equality merges fleets. This implementation uses integer cross-products to compare arrival fractions without floating-point rounding.

Descending-position fleet times: O(n log n) time; O(n) space. Ascending-position fleet stack: O(n log n) time; O(n) space. Scan cars from farthest to nearest. Keep a stack of candidate fleet arrival fractions; a nearer slower car absorbs all faster trailing fleets whose arrival time is no later.

class Solution:
    """Approach: Descending-position fleet times
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def carFleet(self, target: int, position: list[int], speed: list[int]) -> int:
        fleets = 0
        fleet_distance, fleet_speed = -1, 1
        for start, velocity in sorted(zip(position, speed, strict=True), reverse=True):
            distance = target - start
            if distance * fleet_speed > fleet_distance * velocity:
                fleets += 1
                fleet_distance, fleet_speed = distance, velocity
        return fleets

docs.title: 2. Ascending-position fleet stack
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Ascending-position fleet stack
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def carFleet(self, target: int, position: list[int], speed: list[int]) -> int:
        fleets = []
        for start, velocity in sorted(zip(position, speed, strict=True)):
            distance = target - start
            while fleets and fleets[-1][0] * velocity <= distance * fleets[-1][1]:
                fleets.pop()
            fleets.append((distance, velocity))
        return len(fleets)

docs.text:
Time: O(n log n+n log k)

Space: O(n+k)

from heapq import heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Ratio sweep with a largest-quality heap
    Time: O(n log n+n log k)
    Space: O(n+k)
    """

    def mincostToHireWorkers(self, quality: list[int], wage: list[int], k: int) -> float:
        workers = sorted(
            (required / amount, amount) for amount, required in zip(quality, wage, strict=True)
        )
        heap = []
        total = 0
        answer = float("inf")
        for ratio, amount in workers:
            heappush(heap, -amount)
            total += amount
            if len(heap) > k:
                total += heappop(heap)
            if len(heap) == k:
                answer = min(answer, ratio * total)
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Enumerate exact rate thresholds
docs.text:
Time: O(n squared log n)

Space: O(n)

from heapq import heappop, heappush


class Solution:
    """Approach: Enumerate exact rate thresholds
    Time: O(n squared log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def mincostToHireWorkers(self, quality: list[int], wage: list[int], k: int) -> float:
        answer = float("inf")
        for denominator, numerator in zip(quality, wage, strict=True):
            eligible = sorted(
                amount
                for amount, required in zip(quality, wage, strict=True)
                if required * denominator <= numerator * amount
            )
            if len(eligible) >= k:
                cost = sum(eligible[:k]) * numerator / denominator
                answer = min(answer, cost)
        return answer

docs.title: 1. Parent map and distance BFS
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Parent map and distance BFS
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def distanceK(self, root: TreeNode, target: TreeNode, k: int) -> list[int]:
        parents = {root: None}
        stack = [root]
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            for child in (node.left, node.right):
                if child:
                    parents[child] = node
                    stack.append(child)
        queue = deque([target])
        seen = {target}
        for _ in range(k):
            if not queue:
                return []
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                node = queue.popleft()
                for neighbor in (node.left, node.right, parents[node]):
                    if neighbor and neighbor not in seen:
                        seen.add(neighbor)
                        queue.append(neighbor)
        return [node.val for node in queue]

docs.title: 2. Ancestor path and excluded-branch searches
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(h) auxiliary plus output

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Ancestor path and excluded-branch searches
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(h) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def distanceK(self, root: TreeNode, target: TreeNode, k: int) -> list[int]:
        path = []
        stack = [(root, False)]
        while stack:
            node, exiting = stack.pop()
            if exiting:
                path.pop()
                continue
            path.append(node)
            if node is target:
                break
            stack.append((node, True))
            if node.right:
                stack.append((node.right, False))
            if node.left:
                stack.append((node.left, False))
        result = []
        excluded = None
        for upward, ancestor in enumerate(reversed(path)):
            remaining = k - upward
            if remaining < 0:
                break
            pending = [(ancestor, remaining)]
            while pending:
                node, depth = pending.pop()
                if depth == 0:
                    result.append(node.val)
                    continue
                for child in (node.left, node.right):
                    if child and child is not excluded:
                        pending.append((child, depth - 1))
            excluded = ancestor
        return result

docs.text: The mask records every history fact needed for future legal moves. Each edge is one step, so first reaching the complete-key mask is the shortest collecting walk.

docs.title: Dijkstra between newly collected keys
docs.text: Every collecting walk splits at newly obtained keys. The inner BFS finds shortest legal segments before the next new key, and stopping there preserves its required mask update. Dijkstra therefore minimizes total segment length over all key orders.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For ["@.a","##A","..b"], collect a before crossing A to reach b.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Cell and key-mask BFS: O(RC2^K) time; O(RC2^K) space. Dijkstra between newly collected keys: O(K2^KRC + K^22^Klog(K2^K+1)) time; O(RC+K^22^K) space.

K is key count, at most six. Inputs stay unchanged. Keys already held remain traversable; an uncollected key must update state before continuing. The compressed variant uses fewer endpoint states but repeats grid searches.

docs.title: 1. Cell and key-mask BFS
docs.text:
Time: O(RC2^K)

Space: O(RC2^K)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Cell and key-mask BFS
    Time: O(R*C*2^K)
    Space: O(R*C*2^K)
    """

    def shortestPathAllKeys(self, grid: list[str]) -> int:
        from collections import deque

        rows, columns = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        goal = 0
        start = None
        for r, row in enumerate(grid):
            for c, char in enumerate(row):
                if char == "@":
                    start = (r, c)
                elif "a" <= char <= "z":
                    goal |= 1 << (ord(char) - ord("a"))
        queue = deque([(*start, 0, 0)])
        seen = {(*start, 0)}
        while queue:
            r, c, mask, steps = queue.popleft()
            if mask == goal:
                return steps
            for nr, nc in ((r - 1, c), (r + 1, c), (r, c - 1), (r, c + 1)):
                if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < columns) or grid[nr][nc] == "#":
                    continue
                char = grid[nr][nc]
                if "A" <= char <= "Z" and not mask & (1 << (ord(char) - ord("A"))):
                    continue
                following = mask | (1 << (ord(char) - ord("a"))) if "a" <= char <= "z" else mask
                if (nr, nc, following) not in seen:
                    seen.add((nr, nc, following))
                    queue.append((nr, nc, following, steps + 1))
        return -1

docs.title: 2. Dijkstra between newly collected keys
docs.text:
Time: O(K2^KRC + K^22^Klog(K2^K+1))

Space: O(RC+K^22^K)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Dijkstra between newly collected keys
    Time: O(K*2^K*R*C + K^2*2^K*log(K*2^K+1))
    Space: O(R*C+K^2*2^K)
    """

    def shortestPathAllKeys(self, grid: list[str]) -> int:
        from collections import deque
        from heapq import heappop, heappush

        rows, columns = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        start = next((r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(columns) if grid[r][c] == "@")
        goal = 0
        for row in grid:
            for char in row:
                if "a" <= char <= "z":
                    goal |= 1 << (ord(char) - ord("a"))
        best = {(*start, 0): 0}
        heap = [(0, *start, 0)]
        while heap:
            cost, r, c, mask = heappop(heap)
            if cost != best[(r, c, mask)]:
                continue
            if mask == goal:
                return cost
            queue, seen = deque([(r, c, 0)]), {(r, c)}
            while queue:
                row, column, steps = queue.popleft()
                for nr, nc in (
                    (row - 1, column),
                    (row + 1, column),
                    (row, column - 1),
                    (row, column + 1),
                ):
                    if (
                        not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < columns)
                        or (nr, nc) in seen
                        or grid[nr][nc] == "#"
                    ):
                        continue
                    char = grid[nr][nc]
                    if "A" <= char <= "Z" and not mask & (1 << (ord(char) - ord("A"))):
                        continue
                    seen.add((nr, nc))
                    bit = 1 << (ord(char) - ord("a")) if "a" <= char <= "z" else 0
                    if bit and not mask & bit:
                        state, candidate = (nr, nc, mask | bit), cost + steps + 1
                        if candidate < best.get(state, float("inf")):
                            best[state] = candidate
                            heappush(heap, (candidate, *state))
                    else:
                        queue.append((nr, nc, steps + 1))
        return -1

docs.text:
Approach Time Space Binary search feasible speed O(n log M) O(1) Enumerate candidate speeds O(nM) O(1)

docs.title: Binary search feasible speed
docs.text: Binary search the answer from 1 through the largest pile. A speed is feasible when the sum of its per-pile ceiling hours is at most h. Keep the lower half when feasible and the upper half otherwise.

docs.title: Enumerate candidate speeds
docs.text: Try speeds in increasing order and return the first meeting the hour budget. This educational baseline may time out for large pile values; it exposes the monotone predicate used by binary search.

docs.title: Binary search feasible speed
docs.text: Increasing speed never increases required hours, so feasibility changes from False to True at most once. The interval always contains the first feasible speed; max(piles) is feasible because it finishes each pile within one hour.

docs.title: Enumerate candidate speeds
docs.text: Each tested speed consumes the sum of ceiling-divided pile sizes. Testing every smaller speed before returning proves that the first feasible one is minimal.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For piles [4, 8] and h=4, speed 2 needs 2+4=6 hours, while speed 3 needs 2+3=5. Speed 4 needs 1+2=3, so the minimum is 4.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Binary search feasible speed):

O(n log M) time and O(1) auxiliary space for maximum pile M; input is unchanged. Use (pile+speed-1)//speed for exact integer ceilings. Averaging total bananas across hours ignores the restriction against sharing an hour between piles.

Binary search feasible speed: O(n log M) time; O(1) space. Enumerate candidate speeds: O(nM) time; O(1) space. Try speeds in increasing order and return the first meeting the hour budget. This educational baseline may time out for large pile values; it exposes the monotone predicate used by binary search.

docs.title: 1. Binary search feasible speed
docs.text:
Time: O(n log M)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary search feasible speed
    Time: O(n log M)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def minEatingSpeed(self, piles: list[int], h: int) -> int:
        left, right = 1, max(piles)
        while left < right:
            speed = (left + right) // 2
            hours = sum((pile + speed - 1) // speed for pile in piles)
            if hours <= h:
                right = speed
            else:
                left = speed + 1
        return left

docs.title: 2. Enumerate candidate speeds
docs.text:
Time: O(nM)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Enumerate candidate speeds
    Time: O(nM)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def minEatingSpeed(self, piles: list[int], h: int) -> int:
        for speed in range(1, max(piles) + 1):
            if sum((pile + speed - 1) // speed for pile in piles) <= h:
                return speed
        raise ValueError("The problem guarantees enough hours")

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Dense capped-profit knapsack O(CnP) O(n*P) Sparse copied state frontier O(CnP) expected O(n*P)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Dense capped-profit knapsack
docs.text: Track exact people used and profit capped at the goal. Visit used people backward for each crime, adding take choices while existing counts represent skip choices.

docs.title: Sparse copied state frontier
docs.text: Store only reachable (people used, capped profit) states in a dictionary. Copy the skip frontier, then add every feasible take transition from the old frontier.

docs.title: Dense capped-profit knapsack
docs.text: All profits at or above the goal have identical future relevance and may merge. Backward people iteration reads only pre-crime source states because every crime uses at least one person, so each crime is counted at most once.

docs.title: Sparse copied state frontier
docs.text: Take and skip subsets are disjoint, so their counts add. Reading the old dictionary prevents repeated use of the current crime; merging equal states preserves all multiplicities while discarding irrelevant history.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For n=5, minProfit=3, group=[2,2], profit=[2,3], choose the second crime alone or both, giving 2.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Dense capped-profit knapsack: O(CnP) time; O(nP) space. Sparse copied state frontier: O(CnP) expected time; O(nP) space.

C is crime count and P=minProfit+1, so the zero-target case is included in the bounds. Inputs remain unchanged. Dense storage has lower per-state overhead; sparse storage can skip unreachable combinations but copies its frontier each round. The empty subset is valid when minProfit=0.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Dense capped-profit knapsack
docs.text:
Time: O(CnP)

Space: O(n*P)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Dense capped-profit knapsack
    Time: O(C*n*P)
    Space: O(n*P)
    """

    def profitableSchemes(self, n: int, minProfit: int, group: list[int], profit: list[int]) -> int:
        modulus = 1_000_000_007
        dp = [[0] * (minProfit + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
        dp[0][0] = 1
        for people, gain in zip(group, profit, strict=True):
            for used in range(n - people, -1, -1):
                for earned in range(minProfit, -1, -1):
                    following = min(minProfit, earned + gain)
                    dp[used + people][following] = (
                        dp[used + people][following] + dp[used][earned]
                    ) % modulus
        return sum(row[minProfit] for row in dp) % modulus

docs.title: 2. Sparse copied state frontier
docs.text:
Time: O(CnP) expected

Space: O(n*P)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sparse copied state frontier
    Time: O(C*n*P) expected
    Space: O(n*P)
    """

    def profitableSchemes(self, n: int, minProfit: int, group: list[int], profit: list[int]) -> int:
        modulus = 1_000_000_007
        counts = {(0, 0): 1}
        for people, gain in zip(group, profit, strict=True):
            following = counts.copy()
            for (used, earned), count in counts.items():
                if used + people <= n:
                    state = (used + people, min(minProfit, earned + gain))
                    following[state] = (following.get(state, 0) + count) % modulus
            counts = following
        return sum(count for (_, earned), count in counts.items() if earned == minProfit) % modulus

docs.title: Sort and pair extremes

docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sort and pair extremes
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def numRescueBoats(self, people: list[int], limit: int) -> int:
        weights = sorted(people)
        left, right, boats = 0, len(weights) - 1, 0
        while left <= right:
            if left < right and weights[left] + weights[right] <= limit:
                left += 1
            right -= 1
            boats += 1
        return boats

docs.title: 2. Weight-frequency pairing
docs.text:
Time: O(n+limit)

Space: O(limit)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Weight-frequency pairing
    Time: O(n+limit)
    Space: O(limit)
    """

    def numRescueBoats(self, people: list[int], limit: int) -> int:
        counts = [0] * (limit + 1)
        for weight in people:
            counts[weight] += 1
        light, heavy, remaining, boats = 1, limit, len(people), 0
        while remaining:
            while counts[heavy] == 0:
                heavy -= 1
            counts[heavy] -= 1
            remaining -= 1
            boats += 1
            if not remaining:
                break
            while counts[light] == 0:
                light += 1
            if light + heavy <= limit:
                counts[light] -= 1
                remaining -= 1
        return boats

Approach Time Space Expanding step simulation O(R squared), R=max(rows,cols) O(1) auxiliary plus output Sort by square-ring spiral rank O(rowscols log(rowscols)) O(rows*cols)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Expanding step simulation
docs.text: Walk two directions at each step length and record only coordinates inside the grid.

docs.title: Sort by square-ring spiral rank
docs.text: Compute each cell's Chebyshev ring and offset along that ring, then sort all in-grid cells by that rank. This avoids walking outside a very thin grid.

docs.title: Expanding step simulation
docs.text: Pairs of equal-length perpendicular legs complete successively larger square boundaries around the start. Every grid coordinate eventually lies on a visited boundary and is recorded exactly once.

docs.title: Sort by square-ring spiral rank
docs.text: Ring k starts after (2k-1)^2 visited positions. The four edge formulas assign offsets 0 through 8k-1 in clockwise order, so rank sorting exactly reproduces the infinite spiral subsequence.

docs.title: Walkthrough

Expanding step simulation: O(R squared), R=max(rows,cols) time; O(1) auxiliary plus output space.

Sort by square-ring spiral rank: O(rowscols log(rowscols)) time; O(rows*cols) space.

The output contains exactly rows*cols distinct coordinates. The simulation may continue a short leg after the last in-grid visit, but cannot record a coordinate twice.

docs.text:

Space: O(1) auxiliary plus output

class Solution:
    """Approach: Expanding step simulation
    Time: O(R squared), R=max(rows,cols)
    Space: O(1) auxiliary plus output
    """

    def spiralMatrixIII(self, rows: int, cols: int, rStart: int, cStart: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        answer = [[rStart, cStart]]
        row, col, length, direction = rStart, cStart, 1, 0
        directions = ((0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0))
        while len(answer) < rows * cols:
            for _ in range(2):
                dr, dc = directions[direction % 4]
                for _ in range(length):
                    row, col = row + dr, col + dc
                    if 0 <= row < rows and 0 <= col < cols:
                        answer.append([row, col])
                direction += 1
            length += 1
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Sort by square-ring spiral rank
docs.text:
Time: O(rowscols log(rowscols))

Space: O(rows*cols)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sort by square-ring spiral rank
    Time: O(rows*cols log(rows*cols))
    Space: O(rows*cols)
    """

    def spiralMatrixIII(self, rows: int, cols: int, rStart: int, cStart: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        def rank(cell):
            dr, dc = cell[0] - rStart, cell[1] - cStart
            ring = max(abs(dr), abs(dc))
            if ring == 0:
                return 0
            if dc == ring and dr > -ring:
                offset = dr + ring - 1
            elif dr == ring:
                offset = 2 * ring + ring - 1 - dc
            elif dc == -ring:
                offset = 4 * ring + ring - 1 - dr
            else:
                offset = 6 * ring + dc + ring - 1
            return (2 * ring - 1) ** 2 + offset

        cells = [[row, col] for row in range(rows) for col in range(cols)]
        cells.sort(key=rank)
        return cells

docs.title: BFS two-coloring
docs.text: Start each unseen connected component with one color and propagate opposite colors along edges, rejecting equal-colored endpoints.

docs.text: All neighbors of a person must share the opposite group, so union them. Reject if a dislike ever connects two members of the same forced group.

docs.title: BFS two-coloring
docs.text: Any valid grouping fixes alternating colors along every path from a start. A conflicting edge disproves all colorings of that component; if none occurs, the constructed coloring satisfies every dislike.

docs.title: Union opposite-neighbor groups

docs.title: 1. BFS two-coloring
docs.text:
Time: O(V+E)

Space: O(V+E)

class Solution:
    """Approach: BFS two-coloring
    Time: O(V+E)
    Space: O(V+E)
    """

    def possibleBipartition(self, n: int, dislikes: list[list[int]]) -> bool:
        from collections import deque

        graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for a, b in dislikes:
            graph[a - 1].append(b - 1)
            graph[b - 1].append(a - 1)
        color = [-1] * n
        for start in range(n):
            if color[start] >= 0:
                continue
            color[start] = 0
            queue = deque([start])
            while queue:
                node = queue.popleft()
                for other in graph[node]:
                    if color[other] == color[node]:
                        return False
                    if color[other] < 0:
                        color[other] = color[node] ^ 1
                        queue.append(other)
        return True

docs.title: 2. Union opposite-neighbor groups
docs.text:
Time: O((V+E)*alpha(V))

Space: O(V+E)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Union opposite-neighbor groups
    Time: O((V+E)*alpha(V))
    Space: O(V+E)
    """

    def possibleBipartition(self, n: int, dislikes: list[list[int]]) -> bool:
        graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for a, b in dislikes:
            graph[a - 1].append(b - 1)
            graph[b - 1].append(a - 1)
        parent, size = list(range(n)), [1] * n

        def find(node):
            while node != parent[node]:
                parent[node] = parent[parent[node]]
                node = parent[node]
            return node

        for node, others in enumerate(graph):
            if not others:
                continue
            for other in others:
                if find(node) == find(other):
                    return False
                a, b = find(others[0]), find(other)
                if a != b:
                    if size[a] < size[b]:
                        a, b = b, a
                    parent[b] = a
                    size[a] += size[b]
        return True
