docs.title: Task
docs.text: Support push and pop on a frequency stack. Pop removes a value with greatest current frequency, breaking ties by most recent remaining push.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Every push has both a frequency level and a timestamp.
  2. Store most-recent pushes within each frequency level.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Frequency-level stacks O(1) expected per operation O(n) Occurrence-priority heap O(log(n+1)) per operation O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Frequency-level stacks
docs.text: Count each value, append it to a stack for its new frequency, and track the maximum frequency. Pop the latest value from that level, then reduce its count.

docs.title: Occurrence-priority heap
docs.text: Push (-frequency,-timestamp,value) for every occurrence. Pop the minimum heap entry and decrement that value's current count.

docs.title: Frequency-level stacks
docs.text: Each remaining value has one historical push entry at every frequency through its current count. The maximum level contains exactly highest-frequency candidates, ordered by the tie-breaking push recency.

docs.title: Occurrence-priority heap
docs.text: For each value the highest remaining occurrence level equals its current frequency. Ranking all live occurrence entries by level then recency therefore selects the same required maximum and tie winner.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Push 5,7,5,7,4,5. Pops yield 5,7,5,4: first highest count, then latest push among equal counts.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Frequency-level stacks: O(1) expected per operation time; O(n) space. Occurrence-priority heap: O(log(n+1)) per operation time; O(n) space. Objects own state. Pop is called only when nonempty. n is the peak number of live pushes. Zero-count values and empty frequency buckets can be removed. The heap alternative retains per-occurrence metadata and does not achieve constant-time operations.

docs.title: 1. Frequency-level stacks
docs.text:
Time: O(1) expected per operation

Space: O(n)

from heapq import heappop, heappush


class FreqStack:
    """Approach: Frequency-level stacks
    Time: O(1) expected per operation
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.counts = {}
        self.levels = {}
        self.maximum = 0

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        frequency = self.counts.get(val, 0) + 1
        self.counts[val] = frequency
        self.levels.setdefault(frequency, []).append(val)
        self.maximum = max(self.maximum, frequency)

    def pop(self) -> int:
        value = self.levels[self.maximum].pop()
        self.counts[value] -= 1
        if self.counts[value] == 0:
            del self.counts[value]
        if not self.levels[self.maximum]:
            del self.levels[self.maximum]
            self.maximum -= 1
        return value

docs.title: 2. Occurrence-priority heap
docs.text:
Time: O(log(n+1)) per operation

Space: O(n)

from heapq import heappop, heappush


class FreqStack:
    """Approach: Occurrence-priority heap
    Time: O(log(n+1)) per operation
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.counts = {}
        self.heap = []
        self.clock = 0

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        frequency = self.counts.get(val, 0) + 1
        self.counts[val] = frequency
        heappush(self.heap, (-frequency, -self.clock, val))
        self.clock += 1

    def pop(self) -> int:
        _, _, value = heappop(self.heap)
        self.counts[value] -= 1
        if self.counts[value] == 0:
            del self.counts[value]
        return value

1. A previous larger price is the boundary of the span.
  2. Merge consecutive dominated days into one summarized block.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Monotonic price-span stack O(1) amortized per next O(n) Fenwick maximum over reversed prices O(log P) per next O(P)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Monotonic price-span stack
docs.text: Store decreasing prices with the spans they summarize. Pop and absorb all blocks whose price is at most the incoming price.

docs.title: Fenwick maximum over reversed prices
docs.text: Reverse the bounded price coordinate. A Fenwick tree stores the latest day for prices strictly greater than the current price; subtract that day from today.

docs.title: Monotonic price-span stack
docs.text: Every popped block consists entirely of prices bounded by its maximum, which the incoming price dominates. The first surviving larger price stops the span, so the absorbed lengths plus today are exact.

docs.title: Fenwick maximum over reversed prices
docs.text: The prefix query covers exactly greater prices and returns their greatest day index, the nearest larger-price blocker. All later days are at most today's price, so their count is the span.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Prices [100,80,60,70,60,75,85] return [1,1,1,2,1,4,6]. Equal prices are absorbed into the span.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Monotonic price-span stack: O(1) amortized per next time; O(n) space.

Fenwick maximum over reversed prices: O(log P) per next time; O(P) space.

The object owns its price history; next mutates only that object. P=100000 is the promised price bound. The tree pays fixed storage even for a short history.

docs.title: 1. Monotonic price-span stack
docs.text:
Time: O(1) amortized per next

Space: O(n)

class StockSpanner:
    """Approach: Monotonic price-span stack
    Time: O(1) amortized per next
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []

    def next(self, price: int) -> int:
        span = 1
        while self.stack and self.stack[-1][0] <= price:
            span += self.stack.pop()[1]
        self.stack.append((price, span))
        return span

docs.title: 2. Fenwick maximum over reversed prices
docs.text:
Time: O(log P) per next

Space: O(P)

class StockSpanner:
    """Approach: Fenwick maximum over reversed prices
    Time: O(log P) per next
    Space: O(P)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.latest = [0] * 100001
        self.day = 0

    def next(self, price: int) -> int:
        self.day += 1
        coordinate = 100001 - price
        index, blocker = coordinate - 1, 0
        while index:
            blocker = max(blocker, self.latest[index])
            index -= index & -index
        index = coordinate
        while index < len(self.latest):
            self.latest[index] = max(self.latest[index], self.day)
            index += index & -index
        return self.day - blocker

  2. Alternatively track the last run of one value and the preceding two-type suffix.

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Frequency-map window
docs.text: Count the current window and shrink until it contains at most two types.

docs.title: Last-run state compression
docs.text: Track the latest type, the other type, the length of the latest equal run, and the best two-type suffix ending here.

docs.title: Frequency-map window
docs.text: After shrinking, every suffix of the current window is valid and every earlier start would include a third type. Recording the largest window therefore captures the optimum.

docs.title: Last-run state compression
docs.text: A third type can extend only the immediately preceding equal run. A known type extends the whole suffix. Updating the latest run preserves exactly the information needed for the next element.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [1,2,3,2,2], introducing 3 discards the initial 1. The suffix [2,3,2,2] uses two types and has length 4.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Frequency-map window: O(n) expected time; O(1) space.

Last-run state compression: O(n) time; O(1) space.

Inputs are unchanged. Zero-count keys must leave the frequency map. The compressed method tracks a contiguous run, not the total count of the latest type.

docs.title: 1. Frequency-map window
docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Frequency-map window
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def totalFruit(self, fruits: list[int]) -> int:
        counts = {}
        left = best = 0
        for right, value in enumerate(fruits):
            counts[value] = counts.get(value, 0) + 1
            while len(counts) > 2:
                outgoing = fruits[left]
                counts[outgoing] -= 1
                if counts[outgoing] == 0:
                    del counts[outgoing]
                left += 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best

docs.title: 2. Last-run state compression
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Last-run state compression
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def totalFruit(self, fruits: list[int]) -> int:
        latest = other = None
        run = current = best = 0
        for value in fruits:
            current = current + 1 if value in (latest, other) else run + 1
            if value == latest:
                run += 1
            else:
                other, latest = latest, value
                run = 1
            best = max(best, current)
        return best

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Reach the final square in the fewest dice rolls on a boustrophedon board, applying at most one snake or ladder per move.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Map a square number to its alternating row direction.
  2. After applying a jump, do not chain another jump during the same roll.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 225 · #886 · Next: 227 · #1192

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space BFS over post-jump squares O(n^2) O(n^2) Repeated relaxation of fixed move edges O(n^4) O(n^2)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: BFS over post-jump squares
docs.text: Construct each outgoing dice edge on demand, applying its landing-cell jump exactly once. BFS counts rolls and visits each resulting square once.

docs.title: Repeated relaxation of fixed move edges
docs.text: Materialize up to six directed move edges per square and apply Bellman-Ford relaxation, stopping at a fixed point.

docs.title: BFS over post-jump squares
docs.text: Each edge represents precisely one legal roll, regardless of jump distance. BFS therefore finds a shortest roll sequence and exhaustion proves the goal unreachable.

docs.title: Repeated relaxation of fixed move edges
docs.text: A shortest walk can be chosen simple in the post-jump state graph and thus uses at most n²-1 edges. That many relaxation rounds cover it, including backward snakes and cycles.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: On an empty 2x2 board, square 1 reaches square 4 in one roll.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
BFS over post-jump squares: O(n^2) time; O(n^2) space. Repeated relaxation of fixed move edges: O(n^4) time; O(n^2) space.

Both preserve the board. Relaxation is a slower educational baseline with a conservative quartic side-length bound; BFS is preferred. Count rolls, not squares skipped by a ladder.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. BFS over post-jump squares
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: BFS over post-jump squares
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def snakesAndLadders(self, board: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        from collections import deque

        n = len(board)

        def destination(square):
            row, column = divmod(square - 1, n)
            value = board[n - row - 1][column if row % 2 == 0 else n - column - 1]
            return square if value == -1 else value

        queue, seen = deque([(1, 0)]), {1}
        while queue:
            square, rolls = queue.popleft()
            if square == n * n:
                return rolls
            for landing in range(square + 1, min(square + 6, n * n) + 1):
                following = destination(landing)
                if following not in seen:
                    seen.add(following)
                    queue.append((following, rolls + 1))
        return -1

docs.title: 2. Repeated relaxation of fixed move edges
docs.text:
Time: O(n^4)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Repeated relaxation of fixed move edges
    Time: O(n^4)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def snakesAndLadders(self, board: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(board)
        edges = []
        for start in range(1, n * n):
            for square in range(start + 1, min(start + 6, n * n) + 1):
                row, column = divmod(square - 1, n)
                value = board[n - row - 1][column if row % 2 == 0 else n - column - 1]
                edges.append((start, square if value == -1 else value))
        distance = [float("inf")] * (n * n + 1)
        distance[1] = 0
        for _ in range(n * n - 1):
            changed = False
            for a, b in edges:
                if distance[a] + 1 < distance[b]:
                    distance[b] = distance[a] + 1
                    changed = True
            if not changed:
                break
        return -1 if distance[-1] == float("inf") else distance[-1]

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Record a chronological sequence of votes and answer who leads at time t. Votes at t count, and equal vote counts favor the candidate with the most recent vote.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Only the candidate receiving a new vote can become a new leader.
  2. Store the leader after each vote, then binary-search query time.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Precomputed leader timeline O(V) constructor; O(log(V+1)) query O(V) Per-candidate vote histories O(V) constructor; O(U log(V+1)) query; may time out O(V)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Precomputed leader timeline
docs.text: Scan votes, updating counts and replacing the leader whenever the current candidate ties or exceeds its count. Store the leader at every timestamp.

docs.title: Per-candidate vote histories
docs.text: Group timestamps by candidate. For each query binary-search every candidate's vote count and last included vote, then maximize (count,last_vote_time).

docs.title: Precomputed leader timeline
docs.text: The previous leader still beats every unchanged candidate. If the updated candidate ties it, that candidate has the most recent vote, so the greater-or-equal update exactly preserves the leader rule.

docs.title: Per-candidate vote histories
docs.text: Each binary search computes the exact prefix count at t. The pair directly expresses the count and recency rule, so maximizing it over candidates returns the correct leader.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Votes for [1,2,2,1] at times [0,3,5,8] produce leaders [1,2,2,1]. Queries at 4 and 8 return 2 and 1.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Precomputed leader timeline: O(V) constructor; O(log(V+1)) query time; O(V) space. Per-candidate vote histories: O(V) constructor; O(U log(V+1)) query; may time out time; O(V) space. Constructor inputs are copied or read into owned histories. Query times are at least the first vote time. U is candidate count; the scan baseline may time out on large query batches. Use bisect_right so a vote exactly at t is included.

docs.title: 1. Precomputed leader timeline
docs.text:
Time: O(V) constructor; O(log(V+1)) query

Space: O(V)

from bisect import bisect_right


class TopVotedCandidate:
    """Approach: Precomputed leader timeline
    Time: O(V) constructor; O(log(V+1)) query
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def __init__(self, persons: list[int], times: list[int]):
        self.times = times.copy()
        self.leaders = []
        counts = {}
        leader = persons[0]
        for person in persons:
            counts[person] = counts.get(person, 0) + 1
            if counts[person] >= counts.get(leader, 0):
                leader = person
            self.leaders.append(leader)

    def q(self, t: int) -> int:
        return self.leaders[bisect_right(self.times, t) - 1]

docs.title: 2. Per-candidate vote histories
docs.text:
Time: O(V) constructor; O(U log(V+1)) query; may time out

Space: O(V)

from bisect import bisect_right


class TopVotedCandidate:
    """Approach: Per-candidate vote histories
    Time: O(V) constructor; O(U log(V+1)) query; may time out
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def __init__(self, persons: list[int], times: list[int]):
        self.histories = {}
        for person, time in zip(persons, times, strict=True):
            self.histories.setdefault(person, []).append(time)

    def q(self, t: int) -> int:
        winner = None
        best = (-1, -1)
        for person, history in self.histories.items():
            count = bisect_right(history, t)
            if count and (count, history[count - 1]) > best:
                best = (count, history[count - 1])
                winner = person
        return winner

Approach Time Space Prefix-sum frequency map O(n) expected O(n) Difference of bounded-sum windows O(n) O(1)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Prefix-sum frequency map
docs.text: Count earlier prefix sums. Before inserting the current prefix, add how many earlier prefixes equal current-goal.

docs.title: Difference of bounded-sum windows
docs.text: Run a shrinking nonnegative-sum window for each of the two bounds and subtract their counts. Each endpoint contributes its number of valid starting positions.

docs.title: Prefix-sum frequency map
docs.text: Each earlier matching prefix defines exactly one nonempty subarray ending here. Recording after querying excludes an empty subarray when goal is zero.

docs.title: Difference of bounded-sum windows
docs.text: Nonnegative values make all suffixes of a valid window valid. Thus each helper counts exactly the subarrays at most its bound, and subtraction leaves only sum goal.

docs.title: Walkthrough

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls

Prefix-sum frequency map: O(n) expected time; O(n) space.

Difference of bounded-sum windows: O(n) time; O(1) space.

Inputs are unchanged. The window method relies on nonnegative entries. The negative-bound helper must return zero so goal=0 works.

docs.title: 1. Prefix-sum frequency map
docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Prefix-sum frequency map
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def numSubarraysWithSum(self, nums: list[int], goal: int) -> int:
        counts = {0: 1}
        prefix = answer = 0
        for value in nums:
            prefix += value
            answer += counts.get(prefix - goal, 0)
            counts[prefix] = counts.get(prefix, 0) + 1
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Difference of bounded-sum windows
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Difference of bounded-sum windows
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def numSubarraysWithSum(self, nums: list[int], goal: int) -> int:
        def at_most(bound):
            if bound < 0:
                return 0
            left = total = answer = 0
            for right, value in enumerate(nums):
                total += value
                while total > bound:
                    total -= nums[left]
                    left += 1
                answer += right - left + 1
            return answer

        return at_most(goal) - at_most(goal - 1)

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Find the minimum sum of a falling path through a square matrix, moving to the same or adjacent column in the next row.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. A path ending in a cell comes from at most three preceding columns.
  2. A suffix recurrence can instead choose among its three children.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 335 · #808 · Next: 337 · #1049

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Forward rolling row minima O(n^2) O(n) Memoized suffix path costs O(n^2) O(n^2)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Forward rolling row minima
docs.text: Copy the first row as initial endpoint costs. For every later row, build a fresh row from the minimum legal predecessor cost and add the cell value.

docs.title: Memoized suffix path costs
docs.text: Memoize the cheapest path starting at each cell; invalid columns cost infinity and final-row cells cost their own value. Choose the best top-row starting column.

docs.title: Forward rolling row minima
docs.text: Every falling path has one predecessor among the three tested columns. Optimal prefixes can replace nonoptimal ones without altering the final step, so the minimum recurrence is exact.

docs.title: Memoized suffix path costs
docs.text: Each suffix must choose one valid child, so minimizing child optima gives the exact current suffix cost. All start columns are allowed, making the outer minimum necessary.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[2,1,3],[6,5,4],[7,8,9]], a minimum path is 1,4,8 with total 13.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Forward rolling row minima: O(n^2) time; O(n) space. Memoized suffix path costs: O(n^2) time; O(n^2) space.

Both preserve matrix and support negative entries. The default first-row copy and matrix[1:] reference slice each cost O(n) space; no nested input rows are modified. Memo depth is bounded by side length<=100.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Forward rolling row minima
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Forward rolling row minima
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def minFallingPathSum(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        previous = matrix[0].copy()
        for row in matrix[1:]:
            current = []
            for column, value in enumerate(row):
                best = previous[column]
                if column:
                    best = min(best, previous[column - 1])
                if column + 1 < len(row):
                    best = min(best, previous[column + 1])
                current.append(value + best)
            previous = current
        return min(previous)

docs.title: 2. Memoized suffix path costs
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2)

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Memoized suffix path costs
    Time: O(n^2)
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def minFallingPathSum(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        from functools import cache

        @cache
        def suffix(row, column):
            if column < 0 or column >= len(matrix):
                return float("inf")
            if row == len(matrix) - 1:
                return matrix[row][column]
            return matrix[row][column] + min(
                suffix(row + 1, column + change) for change in (-1, 0, 1)
            )

        return min(suffix(0, column) for column in range(len(matrix)))

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Island discovery and multi-source BFS
docs.text: Iteratively mark one whole island, then expand a BFS through water from all its cells. Touching unmarked land reaches the second island; the current distance is the flip count.

docs.title: All-pairs island Manhattan distance
docs.text: Discover both island cell lists and minimize Manhattan distance minus one over their Cartesian product. This educational baseline avoids BFS but compares many pairs.

docs.title: Island discovery and multi-source BFS
docs.text: The source frontier permits any departure point on the first island. BFS explores water by minimum number of flips, so its first contact with the second island is optimal.

docs.title: All-pairs island Manhattan distance
docs.text: Any bridge path between endpoint cells needs at least their Manhattan distance minus one water positions. A shortest coordinate path for a closest pair attains that minimum; encountering island land earlier would only provide a closer endpoint pair.

docs.text: For [[1,0,0],[0,0,1],[0,0,1]], a closest pair of island cells has Manhattan distance 3, so two water flips suffice.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls

A and B are island sizes; the pairwise baseline may time out for large islands. Mark the entire first island before expansion, and do not count its existing land as flipped water.

docs.title: 1. Island discovery and multi-source BFS
docs.text:
Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(R*C)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Island discovery and multi-source BFS
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def shortestBridge(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        start = next((r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols) if grid[r][c])
        seen = {start}
        stack = [start]
        while stack:
            row, col = stack.pop()
            for r, c in ((row + 1, col), (row - 1, col), (row, col + 1), (row, col - 1)):
                if 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols and grid[r][c] and (r, c) not in seen:
                    seen.add((r, c))
                    stack.append((r, c))
        queue = deque((r, c, 0) for r, c in seen)
        while queue:
            row, col, distance = queue.popleft()
            for r, c in ((row + 1, col), (row - 1, col), (row, col + 1), (row, col - 1)):
                if 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols and (r, c) not in seen:
                    if grid[r][c]:
                        return distance
                    seen.add((r, c))
                    queue.append((r, c, distance + 1))
        raise AssertionError("The input contains exactly two islands")

docs.title: 2. All-pairs island Manhattan distance
docs.text:
Time: O(RC+AB); may time out

Space: O(R*C)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: All-pairs island Manhattan distance
    Time: O(R*C+A*B); may time out
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def shortestBridge(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        seen, islands = set(), []
        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                if not grid[row][col] or (row, col) in seen:
                    continue
                island = []
                stack = [(row, col)]
                seen.add((row, col))
                while stack:
                    r, c = stack.pop()
                    island.append((r, c))
                    for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                        if (
                            0 <= nr < rows
                            and 0 <= nc < cols
                            and grid[nr][nc]
                            and (nr, nc) not in seen
                        ):
                            seen.add((nr, nc))
                            stack.append((nr, nc))
                islands.append(island)
        return min(abs(a - c) + abs(b - d) - 1 for a, b in islands[0] for c, d in islands[1])

docs.title: Hints

1. Buy the cheapest remaining token and sell the most expensive when extra power is needed.
  2. An offline formulation can enumerate how many largest tokens are sold.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Sorted buy-low sell-high pointers O(n log n) O(n) Sale-count enumeration with prefix budgets O(n log n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Sorted buy-low sell-high pointers
docs.text: Sort a copy. Buy the lightest affordable token; otherwise, if a sale can still help, sell the largest token. Record the greatest score before any later sale.

docs.title: Sale-count enumeration with prefix budgets
docs.text: Sort tokens and build prefix sums. For each number d of sold largest tokens, binary-search how many disjoint smallest tokens their total power can buy, maximizing bought-d.

docs.title: Sorted buy-low sell-high pointers
docs.text: Buying a cheaper token produces the same score with at least as much remaining power; selling a larger token produces at least as much power for the same lost score. These exchanges preserve an optimal sequence while the pointers make those choices.

docs.title: Sale-count enumeration with prefix budgets
docs.text: Any plan with b buys and d sales is improved by choosing the b smallest and d largest disjoint tokens. For positive final score, b>d. If the first smallest token is affordable, execute one buy before each sale; each largest sale funds the next smallest buy, and the aggregate budget then funds all remaining buys. Thus the prefix-budget inequality is both necessary and sufficient for every candidate improving the answer.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: [100,200,300,400], power=200 buys 100, sells 400, then buys 200 and 300 for a best score of 2. The offline plan sells one token and buys three.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Sorted buy-low sell-high pointers: O(n log n) time; O(n) space.

Sale-count enumeration with prefix budgets: O(n log n) time; O(n) space.

Inputs are unchanged. Empty token lists return zero. Buying zero-valued tokens is permitted. A final sale cannot improve the maximum score, which is why only plans with more buys than sales need examination.

docs.title: 1. Sorted buy-low sell-high pointers
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

from bisect import bisect_right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Sorted buy-low sell-high pointers
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def bagOfTokensScore(self, tokens: list[int], power: int) -> int:
        values = sorted(tokens)
        left, right = 0, len(values) - 1
        score = best = 0
        while left <= right:
            if power >= values[left]:
                power -= values[left]
                left += 1
                score += 1
                best = max(best, score)
            elif score and left < right:
                power += values[right]
                right -= 1
                score -= 1
            else:
                break
        return best

docs.title: 2. Sale-count enumeration with prefix budgets
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n)

from bisect import bisect_right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Sale-count enumeration with prefix budgets
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def bagOfTokensScore(self, tokens: list[int], power: int) -> int:
        values = sorted(tokens)
        if not values or power < values[0]:
            return 0
        prefix = [0]
        for value in values:
            prefix.append(prefix[-1] + value)
        best = sold_power = 0
        for sold in range((len(values) - 1) // 2 + 1):
            if sold:
                sold_power += values[-sold]
            bought = bisect_right(prefix, power + sold_power, 0, len(values) - sold + 1) - 1
            best = max(best, bought - sold)
        return best

  2. Alternatively summarize whether each subtree is perfect, complete, and how tall it is.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Breadth-first first-gap rule O(n) O(w) Bottom-up structural states O(n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Breadth-first first-gap rule
docs.text: Queue both real and missing child slots. After encountering None, reject any later real node.

docs.title: Bottom-up structural states
docs.text: Compute height, perfectness, and completeness in iterative postorder. A complete root has either equal child heights with a perfect left side, or a left side one taller and a perfect right side.

docs.title: Breadth-first first-gap rule
docs.text: Complete-tree occupied slots form one prefix of breadth-first positions. A real node after a missing slot is exactly a hole before an occupied position.

docs.title: Bottom-up structural states
docs.text: These are exactly the two ways the last incomplete level can sit: in the right subtree after a full left, or in the left subtree above a shorter full right. Requiring the remaining subtree complete closes the induction.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: A root with only a left child is complete. A root with only a right child has a missing slot before an occupied one and is not complete.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Breadth-first first-gap rule: O(n) time; O(w) space. Bottom-up structural states: O(n) time; O(n) space. The tree is unchanged. The empty tree is complete. Counting nodes at a level alone misses misplaced gaps. Explicit structural traversal avoids large positional integers and recursion-depth limits.

docs.title: 1. Breadth-first first-gap rule
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(w)

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Breadth-first first-gap rule
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(w)
    """

    def isCompleteTree(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> bool:
        queue = deque([root])
        gap = False
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            if node is None:
                gap = True
            else:
                if gap:
                    return False
                queue.extend((node.left, node.right))
        return True

docs.title: 2. Bottom-up structural states
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

from collections import deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Bottom-up structural states
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def isCompleteTree(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> bool:
        states = {None: (0, True, True)}
        stack = [(root, False)] if root else []
        while stack:
            node, expanded = stack.pop()
            if not expanded:
                stack.append((node, True))
                for child in (node.left, node.right):
                    if child:
                        stack.append((child, False))
                continue
            lh, lp, lc = states[node.left]
            rh, rp, rc = states[node.right]
            perfect = lp and rp and lh == rh
            complete = (lp and rc and lh == rh) or (lc and rp and lh == rh + 1)
            states[node] = (1 + max(lh, rh), perfect, complete)
        return states[root][2]

  2. Among the retained points, expose the farthest one so it can be replaced.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Size-k distance heap O(n log(k+1)) O(k) Sort by squared distance O(n log n) O(n) auxiliary; O(k) output

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Size-k distance heap
docs.text: Use a size-k max-heap represented by negative squared distances in Python's min-heap. Store each point's index to identify it and resolve heap ties. Replace the farthest retained point when a closer one appears.

docs.title: Sort by squared distance
docs.text: Sort a new list of point references by squared distance, select its first k entries, and copy their coordinates. This trades a simpler implementation for sorting all n points.

docs.title: Size-k distance heap
docs.text: After each point, the heap contains k closest candidates from the processed prefix, or all points if fewer than k were seen. A farther candidate cannot improve that set; a closer one replaces its worst member.

docs.title: Sort by squared distance
docs.text: Squared distance has the same order as Euclidean distance. The first k sorted entries therefore have no greater distance than any omitted point; ties permit either choice.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[1,2],[4,0],[-1,0]] and k=2, squared distances are 5,16,1. The last point replaces distance 16, so return the points at distances 1 and 5.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach costs and behavior:

O(n log(k+1)) time and O(k) auxiliary space, plus O(k) output. Input points are unchanged and output coordinates are copied. Negative heap priorities reverse the comparison: a better point has a larger stored priority. Comparing actual square roots adds work without changing the selection.

Alternative tradeoff: O(n log n) time; O(n) auxiliary; O(k) output space.

docs.title: 1. Size-k distance heap
docs.text:
Time: O(n log(k+1))

Space: O(k)

from heapq import heappush, heapreplace


class Solution:
    """Approach: Size-k distance heap
    Time: O(n log(k+1))
    Space: O(k)
    """

    def kClosest(self, points: list[list[int]], k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        heap = []
        for i, (x, y) in enumerate(points):
            entry = (-(x * x + y * y), i)
            if len(heap) < k:
                heappush(heap, entry)
            elif entry > heap[0]:
                heapreplace(heap, entry)
        return [points[i][:] for _, i in heap]

docs.title: 2. Sort by squared distance
docs.text:
Time: O(n log n)

Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(k) output

from heapq import heappush, heapreplace


class Solution:
    """Approach: Sort by squared distance
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n) auxiliary; O(k) output
    """

    def kClosest(self, points: list[list[int]], k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        ordered = sorted(points, key=lambda point: point[0] ** 2 + point[1] ** 2)
        return [point.copy() for point in ordered[:k]]

class Solution:
    """Approach: Online remainder frequencies
    Time: O(n+k)
    Space: O(k)
    """

    def subarraysDivByK(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        counts = [0] * k
        counts[0] = 1
        remainder = answer = 0
        for value in nums:
            remainder = (remainder + value) % k
            answer += counts[remainder]
            counts[remainder] += 1
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Batch grouping of prefix remainders
docs.text:
Time: O(n) expected

Space: O(min(n,k))

class Solution:
    """Approach: Batch grouping of prefix remainders
    Time: O(n) expected
    Space: O(min(n,k))
    """

    def subarraysDivByK(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        counts = {0: 1}
        remainder = 0
        for value in nums:
            remainder = (remainder + value) % k
            counts[remainder] = counts.get(remainder, 0) + 1
        return sum(count * (count - 1) // 2 for count in counts.values())

docs.title: Upward and downward suffix lengths
docs.text: A greater current value extends the preceding downward run; a smaller value extends the upward run. Equality resets both to one.

docs.title: Alternating-sign window boundary
docs.text: Keep the start of the longest alternating comparison window. Equal values reset after the pair; a repeated nonzero comparison restarts at the preceding element.

docs.title: Upward and downward suffix lengths
docs.text: Every turbulent suffix ends with one direction and can extend only the opposite-direction suffix. Tracking both longest possibilities therefore gives every optimal ending suffix.

docs.title: Alternating-sign window boundary
docs.text: A repeated comparison invalidates every window containing both of its last two steps, while their shared endpoint can start a new valid pair. The maintained left boundary is thus the earliest valid start for each right endpoint.

Both preserve arr, count elements rather than comparison signs, and return one for all-equal input. No copied differences or slices are required.

Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Upward and downward suffix lengths
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def maxTurbulenceSize(self, arr: list[int]) -> int:
        up = down = answer = 1
        for index in range(1, len(arr)):
            if arr[index] > arr[index - 1]:
                up, down = down + 1, 1
            elif arr[index] < arr[index - 1]:
                up, down = 1, up + 1
            else:
                up = down = 1
            answer = max(answer, up, down)
        return answer

docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Alternating-sign window boundary
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def maxTurbulenceSize(self, arr: list[int]) -> int:
        left = 0
        previous = 0
        answer = 1
        for right in range(1, len(arr)):
            sign = (arr[right] > arr[right - 1]) - (arr[right] < arr[right - 1])
            if sign == 0:
                left = right
            elif sign == previous:
                left = right - 1
            answer = max(answer, right - left + 1)
            previous = sign
        return answer

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Memoized position and visited mask
docs.text: Index traversable cells and cache the count for (position,visited-mask). Reaching the end succeeds only when every traversable bit is set.

docs.title: Path-local backtracking
docs.text: Keep a path-local used-cell set, recursively try unused neighbors, and undo on return. Count reaching the endpoint only after all traversable cells are used.

docs.title: Memoized position and visited mask
docs.text: Future legal moves depend only on current position and used cells, so cached states are equivalent. The terminal condition admits precisely Hamiltonian start-to-end grid walks.

docs.title: Path-local backtracking
docs.text: Each recursive branch adds one distinct legal neighboring cell. Every accepted branch is a complete walk, and every legal complete walk follows one explored branch sequence.

Memoization can consume exponential memory but avoids repeated suffix computations. Do not walk through the endpoint and leave it again.

docs.title: 1. Memoized position and visited mask
docs.text:
Time: O(V*2^V)

Space: O(V*2^V)

from functools import cache


class Solution:
    """Approach: Memoized position and visited mask
    Time: O(V*2^V)
    Space: O(V*2^V)
    """

    def uniquePathsIII(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        cells = [(r, c) for r, row in enumerate(grid) for c, value in enumerate(row) if value != -1]
        indices = {cell: index for index, cell in enumerate(cells)}
        adjacency = [[] for _ in cells]
        start = end = 0
        for index, (row, col) in enumerate(cells):
            if grid[row][col] == 1:
                start = index
            elif grid[row][col] == 2:
                end = index
            for neighbor in ((row + 1, col), (row - 1, col), (row, col + 1), (row, col - 1)):
                if neighbor in indices:
                    adjacency[index].append(indices[neighbor])
        full = (1 << len(cells)) - 1

        @cache
        def visit(position, mask):
            if position == end:
                return int(mask == full)
            return sum(
                visit(neighbor, mask | (1 << neighbor))
                for neighbor in adjacency[position]
                if not mask & (1 << neighbor)
            )

        return visit(start, 1 << start)

docs.title: 2. Path-local backtracking
docs.text:
Time: O(4^V) loose bound

Space: O(V)

from functools import cache


class Solution:
    """Approach: Path-local backtracking
    Time: O(4^V) loose bound
    Space: O(V)
    """

    def uniquePathsIII(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        count = sum(value != -1 for row in grid for value in row)
        start = next((r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols) if grid[r][c] == 1)
        used = set()

        def visit(row, col):
            if grid[row][col] == 2:
                return int(len(used) + 1 == count)
            used.add((row, col))
            total = sum(
                visit(r, c)
                for r, c in ((row + 1, col), (row - 1, col), (row, col + 1), (row, col - 1))
                if 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols and grid[r][c] != -1 and (r, c) not in used
            )
            used.remove((row, col))
            return total

        return visit(*start)

docs.title: 981 Time Based Key-Value Store
docs.text:
Medium · Binary search · Core · Learning step 24 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

Quick review: Binary search.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Store timestamped values for each key. A lookup returns the value at the greatest stored timestamp no later than its query, or an empty string if none exists. Set timestamps arrive in strictly increasing order.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. The timestamp guarantee means each key's history is already sorted.
  2. Find the first stored timestamp strictly greater than the query, then step back.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 023 · #875 · Next: 025 · #4

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Bisect timestamp histories O(1) set; O(log m) get O(N) Manual binary search with parallel arrays O(1) set; O(log m) get O(N)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Bisect timestamp histories
docs.text: Each key owns a list of (timestamp, value) records. Set appends one record. Get uses bisect_right with a timestamp key, then reads the preceding record. A single record list keeps timestamps and values paired.

docs.title: Manual binary search with parallel arrays
docs.text: Store timestamps and values in parallel arrays per key and implement upper-bound binary search directly. This avoids tuple keys and makes the predecessor boundary explicit.

docs.title: Bisect timestamp histories
docs.text: Append order preserves sorted history. Binary search partitions it into timestamps at most the query and timestamps greater than it. The last entry in the first part is exactly the requested version.

docs.title: Manual binary search with parallel arrays
docs.text: The globally increasing set timestamps make every per-key timestamp array sorted. Upper bound separates timestamps at most the query from larger timestamps, so the preceding value is the latest eligible write.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Set ("color","red",2) and ("color","blue",5). Get at 1 returns "", at 4 returns "red", and at 5 returns "blue".

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Default approach (Bisect timestamp histories):

Set is amortized O(1); get is O(log v) for v versions of the key. Storage is O(total versions), excluding string content already supplied. Get does not create missing keys. bisect's key parameter requires Python 3.10+, as used here.

Bisect timestamp histories: O(1) set; O(log m) get time; O(N) space. Manual binary search with parallel arrays: O(1) set; O(log m) get time; O(N) space. Store timestamps and values in parallel arrays per key and implement upper-bound binary search directly. This avoids tuple keys and makes the predecessor boundary explicit.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Bisect timestamp histories
docs.text:
Time: O(1) set; O(log m) get

Space: O(N)

from bisect import bisect_right
from collections import defaultdict


class TimeMap:
    """Approach: Bisect timestamp histories
    Time: O(1) set; O(log m) get
    Space: O(N)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.history = defaultdict(list)

    def set(self, key: str, value: str, timestamp: int) -> None:
        self.history[key].append((timestamp, value))

    def get(self, key: str, timestamp: int) -> str:
        history = self.history.get(key, [])
        index = bisect_right(history, timestamp, key=lambda item: item[0])
        return history[index - 1][1] if index else ""

docs.title: 2. Manual binary search with parallel arrays
docs.text:
Time: O(1) set; O(log m) get

Space: O(N)

from bisect import bisect_right
from collections import defaultdict


class TimeMap:
    """Approach: Manual binary search with parallel arrays
    Time: O(1) set; O(log m) get
    Space: O(N)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.history = {}

    def set(self, key: str, value: str, timestamp: int) -> None:
        times, values = self.history.setdefault(key, ([], []))
        times.append(timestamp)
        values.append(value)

    def get(self, key: str, timestamp: int) -> str:
        times, values = self.history.get(key, ([], []))
        low, high = 0, len(times)
        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2
            if times[middle] <= timestamp:
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                high = middle
        return values[low - 1] if low else ""

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Group a binary tree into vertical columns. Within each column, order nodes by row, breaking equal-row ties by node value. Columns run left to right.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Record each node's row and column coordinates.
  2. A BFS already supplies row order, leaving only same-row column ties to sort.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 299 · #863 · Next: 301 · #785

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Sort coordinate triples O(n log(n+1)) O(n) BFS row buckets by column O(n log(n+1)) worst O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Sort coordinate triples
docs.text: Iteratively gather (column,row,value) triples, globally sort them, then group consecutive equal columns.

docs.title: BFS row buckets by column
docs.text: At each BFS level collect values into column buckets, sort values within each bucket, and append them to accumulated columns. Return columns in sorted order.

docs.title: Sort coordinate triples
docs.text: Lexicographic triple order is exactly the specified column, row, and value priority. Grouping by the first coordinate therefore produces the requested traversal.

docs.title: BFS row buckets by column
docs.text: BFS fixes row order before appending. Sorting a level's column bucket resolves exactly its equal-row ties; later levels append after all shallower rows.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Root 5 has children 2 and 8; 2.right=7 and 8.left=3. Column zero is [5,3,7], since the two grandchildren share row and column and sort by value.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text: Sort coordinate triples: O(n log(n+1)) time; O(n) space. BFS row buckets by column: O(n log(n+1)) worst time; O(n) space. The tree is unchanged. Ordinary left-to-right BFS alone does not satisfy equal-position value ties. Duplicate values are separate nodes and must remain in the output. Both traversals avoid recursion.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Sort coordinate triples
docs.text:
Time: O(n log(n+1))

Space: O(n)

from collections import defaultdict, deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: Sort coordinate triples
    Time: O(n log(n+1))
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def verticalTraversal(self, root: TreeNode) -> list[list[int]]:
        coordinates = []
        stack = [(root, 0, 0)]
        while stack:
            node, row, col = stack.pop()
            coordinates.append((col, row, node.val))
            if node.left:
                stack.append((node.left, row + 1, col - 1))
            if node.right:
                stack.append((node.right, row + 1, col + 1))
        coordinates.sort()
        result = []
        previous = None
        for col, _, value in coordinates:
            if col != previous:
                result.append([])
                previous = col
            result[-1].append(value)
        return result

docs.title: 2. BFS row buckets by column
docs.text:
Time: O(n log(n+1)) worst

Space: O(n)

from collections import defaultdict, deque


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


class Solution:
    """Approach: BFS row buckets by column
    Time: O(n log(n+1)) worst
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def verticalTraversal(self, root: TreeNode) -> list[list[int]]:
        columns = defaultdict(list)
        queue = deque([(root, 0)])
        while queue:
            level = defaultdict(list)
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                node, col = queue.popleft()
                level[col].append(node.val)
                if node.left:
                    queue.append((node.left, col - 1))
                if node.right:
                    queue.append((node.right, col + 1))
            for col, values in level.items():
                columns[col].extend(sorted(values))
        return [columns[col] for col in sorted(columns)]

docs.title: 994 Rotting Oranges
docs.text:
Medium · Graph traversal · Core · Learning step 58 of 350

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Each minute, rotten oranges infect fresh oranges in their four neighboring cells. Return the time until no fresh oranges remain, or -1 if some cannot rot. An input with no fresh oranges needs zero minutes.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Infection spreads from every initially rotten orange at the same time.
  2. A breadth-first search layer represents one minute of simultaneous spread.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 057 · #133 · Next: 059 · #417

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Multi-source infection BFS O(R*C) O(R*C) Synchronous copied-grid rounds O((R*C)^2) O(R*C)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Multi-source infection BFS
docs.text: Count fresh oranges and queue all rotten cells. A set records cells already rotten or scheduled to rot. Process a fixed layer, enqueue newly infected neighbors, and decrease the fresh count. Advance time after the layer. Stop when no fresh oranges or queued cells remain.

docs.title: Synchronous copied-grid rounds
docs.text: Copy the grid and repeatedly scan for fresh cells adjacent to current rotten cells. Record all changes, then apply them together after the scan.

docs.title: Multi-source infection BFS
docs.text: The initial queue contains the minute-zero sources. A layer of cells infected at minute t discovers the newly reachable cells at minute t+1. Immediate marking prevents duplicate counts. Breadth-first layers give each orange its earliest infection time; fresh cells remaining after exhaustion have no path from a source.

docs.title: Synchronous copied-grid rounds
docs.text: A scan reads only the preceding minute, so newly rotten cells cannot infect another cell too early. If fresh cells remain without changes, the process has reached a fixed point and they are unreachable.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [[2,1,1],[0,0,1]], the two top-row fresh oranges rot at minutes 1 and 2. The lower-right orange then rots at minute 3, which is the answer.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
For the default Multi-source infection BFS approach:

O(rows * cols) time and auxiliary space. The grid is unchanged; infection state lives in the set. Counting each source separately would lose simultaneous spread. Do not increment time while processing individual oranges within a layer.

Multi-source infection BFS: O(RC) time; O(RC) space. Synchronous copied-grid rounds: O((RC)^2) time; O(RC) space. The simulation is a simple baseline; repeated full scans are quadratic in cell count and may be slow on generalized large grids. Changes are staged to preserve simultaneous spread, and input stays unchanged.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Multi-source infection BFS
docs.text:
Time: O(R*C)

Space: O(R*C)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Multi-source infection BFS
    Time: O(R*C)
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def orangesRotting(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        rotten = set()
        fresh = 0
        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                if grid[row][col] == 2:
                    rotten.add((row, col))
                elif grid[row][col] == 1:
                    fresh += 1
        queue = deque(rotten)
        minutes = 0
        while queue and fresh:
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                row, col = queue.popleft()
                for nr, nc in ((row + 1, col), (row - 1, col), (row, col + 1), (row, col - 1)):
                    if (
                        0 <= nr < rows
                        and 0 <= nc < cols
                        and grid[nr][nc] == 1
                        and (nr, nc) not in rotten
                    ):
                        rotten.add((nr, nc))
                        queue.append((nr, nc))
                        fresh -= 1
            minutes += 1
        return -1 if fresh else minutes

docs.title: 2. Synchronous copied-grid rounds
docs.text:
Time: O((R*C)^2)

Space: O(R*C)

from collections import deque


class Solution:
    """Approach: Synchronous copied-grid rounds
    Time: O((R*C)^2)
    Space: O(R*C)
    """

    def orangesRotting(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        state = [row.copy() for row in grid]
        rows, columns = len(state), len(state[0])
        minutes = 0
        while True:
            changes = []
            fresh = 0
            for r in range(rows):
                for c in range(columns):
                    if state[r][c] != 1:
                        continue
                    fresh += 1
                    if any(
                        0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < columns and state[nr][nc] == 2
                        for nr, nc in ((r - 1, c), (r + 1, c), (r, c - 1), (r, c + 1))
                    ):
                        changes.append((r, c))
            if not fresh:
                return minutes
            if not changes:
                return -1
            for r, c in changes:
                state[r][c] = 2
            minutes += 1

docs.text:

Official LeetCode statement · All Python implementations · Roadmap

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Return the longest binary subarray that can become all ones by changing at most k zeroes.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
1. Count zeroes rather than changed positions.
  2. Zero positions can delimit every candidate window.
Show approaches, complexity comparison, proofs, and Python solutions

Previous: 093 · #904 · Next: 095 · #438

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Zero-budget window O(n) O(1) Sentinel zero-position intervals O(n) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Zero-budget window
docs.text: Extend right and shrink from left until the number of zeroes is at most k.

docs.title: Sentinel zero-position intervals
docs.text: Record zero positions with sentinels -1 and n. A block containing k consecutive zeroes extends between the zero just before and just after that block.

docs.title: Zero-budget window
docs.text: For each right endpoint, the smallest left endpoint satisfying the zero budget gives the longest valid suffix. Earlier starts are invalid, so taking the largest suffix is optimal.

docs.title: Sentinel zero-position intervals
docs.text: Every maximal valid window lies between two excluded zeroes and contains at most k zeroes. Enumerating blocks of exactly k zeroes covers the optimum unless all zeroes can be flipped, when the full array is valid.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: [1,1,0,0,1,1,1,0], k=1 has best length 4, from either zero next to the final run of three ones.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Zero-budget window: O(n) time; O(1) space.

Sentinel zero-position intervals: O(n) time; O(n) space.

Inputs are unchanged. k=0 still works: consecutive excluded zeroes delimit ordinary runs of ones.

docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Zero-budget window
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Zero-budget window
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def longestOnes(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        left = zeroes = best = 0
        for right, value in enumerate(nums):
            zeroes += value == 0
            while zeroes > k:
                zeroes -= nums[left] == 0
                left += 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best

docs.title: 2. Sentinel zero-position intervals
docs.text:
Time: O(n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sentinel zero-position intervals
    Time: O(n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def longestOnes(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        zeroes = [-1] + [i for i, value in enumerate(nums) if value == 0] + [len(nums)]
        count = len(zeroes) - 2
        if count <= k:
            return len(nums)
        return max(zeroes[i + k + 1] - zeroes[i] - 1 for i in range(count - k + 1))

docs.title: Task
docs.text: Ship packages in their original order within days days. Return the smallest ship capacity; each day carries a consecutive block.

docs.title: Hints

1. A capacity is feasible if a greedy scan uses at most days trips.
  2. Larger capacities never require more trips.

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Binary search with greedy loading O(n log S) O(1) Partition dynamic programming O(days*n squared) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Binary search with greedy loading
docs.text: Search capacities between the largest package and total weight. Greedily fill each day as far as possible to test feasibility.

docs.title: Partition dynamic programming
docs.text: Let dp[i] be the least maximum load for the first i packages using at most the current number of days. Try every possible final-day start. This educational baseline may time out at full constraints.

docs.title: Binary search with greedy loading
docs.text: For a fixed capacity, any valid first day ends no later than the greedy first day. Induction shows greedy uses the fewest days. Feasibility is monotone, so lower-bound search returns the minimum capacity.

docs.title: Partition dynamic programming
docs.text: Every ordered partition has a final block. Its capacity is the maximum of that block sum and the optimal preceding partition capacity. Minimizing over all splits implements this exhaustive optimal substructure.

docs.title: Walkthrough

Binary search with greedy loading: O(n log S) time; O(1) space.

Partition dynamic programming: O(days*n squared) time; O(n) space.

Inputs are unchanged. S is total weight. The requirement is at most days trips, so unused days are allowed; package order cannot be changed.

docs.title: Python implementations
docs.text: Each code block is independent and uses the canonical LeetCode class name. Choose one block to paste into the Python3 editor. Shared node definitions are included where needed.

docs.title: 1. Binary search with greedy loading
docs.text:
Time: O(n log S)

Space: O(1)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Binary search with greedy loading
    Time: O(n log S)
    Space: O(1)
    """

    def shipWithinDays(self, weights: list[int], days: int) -> int:
        low, high = max(weights), sum(weights)
        while low < high:
            capacity = (low + high) // 2
            used, load = 1, 0
            for weight in weights:
                if load + weight > capacity:
                    used += 1
                    load = 0
                load += weight
            if used <= days:
                high = capacity
            else:
                low = capacity + 1
        return low

docs.title: 2. Partition dynamic programming
docs.text:
Time: O(days*n squared)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Partition dynamic programming
    Time: O(days*n squared)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def shipWithinDays(self, weights: list[int], days: int) -> int:
        size = len(weights)
        prefix = [0]
        for weight in weights:
            prefix.append(prefix[-1] + weight)
        previous = [0] + [float("inf")] * size
        for _ in range(days):
            current = [0] + [float("inf")] * size
            for end in range(1, size + 1):
                current[end] = min(
                    max(previous[start], prefix[end] - prefix[start]) for start in range(end)
                )
            previous = current
        return int(previous[-1])

docs.title: Endpoint and difference dictionaries
docs.text: For every earlier endpoint, extend its state for the required difference, or seed a length-two pair when that state is absent.

docs.title: Scan each feasible difference by ending value
docs.text: For one fixed difference, scan input order and retain the longest chain ending at each value. Repeat over the bounded difference interval.

docs.title: Endpoint and difference dictionaries
docs.text: Every arithmetic subsequence has a final predecessor and a fixed difference. Trying all predecessors covers its possible final extension, and the maximum retains the best state for future extensions.

docs.title: Scan each feasible difference by ending value
docs.text: For a fixed difference, a value can follow only value-difference, so its best previous chain suffices. Every valid common difference lies between negative and positive value span and is tested.

D is twice the value span plus one, U the number of distinct input values. Official values lie in 0..500, so scanning differences is viable. Both preserve nums; the zero-difference update must read the preceding value state before writing it.

docs.title: 1. Endpoint and difference dictionaries
docs.text:
Time: O(n^2) expected

Space: O(n^2)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Endpoint and difference dictionaries
    Time: O(n^2) expected
    Space: O(n^2)
    """

    def longestArithSeqLength(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        ending = [{} for _ in nums]
        answer = 2
        for i, value in enumerate(nums):
            for j in range(i):
                difference = value - nums[j]
                length = ending[j].get(difference, 1) + 1
                ending[i][difference] = max(ending[i].get(difference, 0), length)
                answer = max(answer, length)
        return answer

docs.title: 2. Scan each feasible difference by ending value
docs.text:
Time: O(n*D) expected

Space: O(U)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Scan each feasible difference by ending value
    Time: O(n*D) expected
    Space: O(U)
    """

    def longestArithSeqLength(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        span = max(nums) - min(nums)
        answer = 1
        for difference in range(-span, span + 1):
            best = {}
            for value in nums:
                length = best.get(value - difference, 0) + 1
                best[value] = max(best.get(value, 0), length)
                answer = max(answer, length)
        return answer

docs.title: 1. Sort by A-minus-B cost difference
docs.text:

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Sort by A-minus-B cost difference
    Time: O(n log n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def twoCitySchedCost(self, costs: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        ordered = sorted(costs, key=lambda pair: pair[0] - pair[1])
        half = len(costs) // 2
        return sum(pair[0] if i < half else pair[1] for i, pair in enumerate(ordered))

docs.title: 2. City-capacity prefix dynamic programming
docs.text:
Time: O(n squared)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: City-capacity prefix dynamic programming
    Time: O(n squared)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def twoCitySchedCost(self, costs: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        half = len(costs) // 2
        previous = [0] + [float("inf")] * half
        for processed, (first, second) in enumerate(costs, 1):
            current = [float("inf")] * (half + 1)
            for count in range(min(half, processed) + 1):
                if count and processed - count <= half:
                    current[count] = min(current[count], previous[count - 1] + first)
                if processed - count <= half:
                    current[count] = min(current[count], previous[count] + second)
            previous = current
        return int(previous[half])

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Rolling longest-common-subsequence DP O(m*n) O(n) LIS over streamed matching positions O(m+n+r*log(n+1)) O(n)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Rolling longest-common-subsequence DP
docs.text: Treat the problem as LCS: matching values may extend the diagonal, and differing values require skipping an endpoint. Retain one row plus the old diagonal.

docs.title: LIS over streamed matching positions
docs.text: Index every occurrence in the second array. For each first-array value, process matching second-array positions descending and feed them into strict LIS tails.

docs.title: Rolling longest-common-subsequence DP
docs.text: Two lines cross exactly when their endpoint orders disagree. Thus a legal set of lines is an equal-valued common subsequence, and maximizing its length maximizes uncrossed lines.

docs.title: LIS over streamed matching positions
docs.text: Increasing positions select noncrossing equal-valued connections. Descending matches from one source element cannot both enter an increasing subsequence, so endpoint reuse is excluded. Every legal line set appears among the streamed match choices.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [1,4,2] and [1,2,4], either 1 then 4 or 1 then 2 gives two uncrossed lines.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Rolling longest-common-subsequence DP: O(mn) time; O(n) space. LIS over streamed matching positions: O(m+n+rlog(n+1)) time; O(n) space.

m,n are input lengths and r the number of equal-valued position pairs. Both preserve arrays. Match events are streamed, not stored as an O(r) list; repeated values can make r=m*n and favor the simple DP instead.

Time: O(m*n)

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Rolling longest-common-subsequence DP
    Time: O(m*n)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def maxUncrossedLines(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> int:
        dp = [0] * (len(nums2) + 1)
        for first in nums1:
            diagonal = 0
            for j, second in enumerate(nums2, 1):
                above = dp[j]
                dp[j] = diagonal + 1 if first == second else max(above, dp[j - 1])
                diagonal = above
        return dp[-1]

docs.title: 2. LIS over streamed matching positions
docs.text:
Time: O(m+n+r*log(n+1))

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: LIS over streamed matching positions
    Time: O(m+n+r*log(n+1))
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def maxUncrossedLines(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> int:
        from bisect import bisect_left

        positions = {}
        for index, value in enumerate(nums2):
            positions.setdefault(value, []).append(index)
        tails = []
        for value in nums1:
            for position in reversed(positions.get(value, ())):
                index = bisect_left(tails, position)
                if index == len(tails):
                    tails.append(position)
                else:
                    tails[index] = position
        return len(tails)

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Prefix DP with backward block extension O(n*k) O(n) Suffix DP with a rolling ring buffer O(n*k) O(k)

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Prefix DP with backward block extension
docs.text: For every ending prefix, extend its final block backward up to k entries and maintain the maximum as one more entry joins.

docs.title: Suffix DP with a rolling ring buffer
docs.text: Solve suffixes backward and try the first block of each suffix. Store only the next k suffix answers in a circular buffer of k+1 positions.

docs.title: Prefix DP with backward block extension
docs.text: Every partition has one final block of a tested length. Its preceding prefix is already optimal, so maximizing these exhaustive final-block choices produces the best total.

docs.title: Suffix DP with a rolling ring buffer
docs.text: All referenced suffixes start within k positions, so none has been overwritten in the ring. Trying each possible first block is exhaustive and combines it with an optimal remaining suffix.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [1,5,2] and k=2, blocks [1,5] and [2] yield 5+5+2=12.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Prefix DP with backward block extension: O(nk) time; O(n) space. Suffix DP with a rolling ring buffer: O(nk) time; O(k) space.

Both preserve the array. The ring variant saves memory and performs no slices, but modulo indexing is less transparent. Nonnegative entries justify the zero initial maximum.

Space: O(n)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Prefix DP with backward block extension
    Time: O(n*k)
    Space: O(n)
    """

    def maxSumAfterPartitioning(self, arr: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        dp = [0] * (len(arr) + 1)
        for end in range(1, len(arr) + 1):
            maximum = 0
            for length in range(1, min(k, end) + 1):
                maximum = max(maximum, arr[end - length])
                dp[end] = max(dp[end], dp[end - length] + maximum * length)
        return dp[-1]

docs.title: 2. Suffix DP with a rolling ring buffer
docs.text:
Time: O(n*k)

Space: O(k)

class Solution:
    """Approach: Suffix DP with a rolling ring buffer
    Time: O(n*k)
    Space: O(k)
    """

    def maxSumAfterPartitioning(self, arr: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        size = min(k, len(arr)) + 1
        dp = [0] * size
        for start in range(len(arr) - 1, -1, -1):
            maximum = answer = 0
            for end in range(start, min(len(arr), start + k)):
                maximum = max(maximum, arr[end])
                answer = max(answer, maximum * (end - start + 1) + dp[(end + 1) % size])
            dp[start % size] = answer
        return dp[0]

docs.title: Approach comparison
docs.text:
Approach Time Space Subset-sum bitset near half total O(n*S/w) machine-word work O(S/w) machine words Meet-in-the-middle subset sums O(n*2^(n/2)) O(2^(n/2))

Read each approach's limits and mutation notes below. Educational baselines may exceed a required complexity bound; the default is the first implementation.

docs.title: Subset-sum bitset near half total
docs.text: Mark all subset sums up to half total in a Python integer bitset. Its highest set bit is the best achievable smaller-side weight.

docs.title: Meet-in-the-middle subset sums
docs.text: Enumerate subset sums independently in each index half. Sort one half and binary-search the largest partner fitting the half-total target for every sum in the other.

docs.title: Subset-sum bitset near half total
docs.text: Every smash subtracts the signed contributions of two groups, and an optimal minimum-difference partition can be realized by repeatedly smashing stones from opposite groups; a smaller final difference would contradict optimality. Thus maximizing a subset no larger than half solves the game.

docs.title: Meet-in-the-middle subset sums
docs.text: Every full subset splits uniquely across the two halves. The binary-search partner is the greatest feasible sum for its fixed first-half choice, so maximizing over those choices finds the optimal partition.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: For [2,7,4,1,8,1], two groups can differ by 1, which is the minimum final weight.

docs.title: Cost and pitfalls
docs.text:
Subset-sum bitset near half total: O(nS/w) machine-word work time; O(S/w) machine words space. Meet-in-the-middle subset sums: O(n2^(n/2)) time; O(2^(n/2)) space.

S is total weight+1, w the integer word width, and n<=30. Both preserve stones. Bit shifts process multiple machine words rather than costing O(1); meet-in-the-middle avoids dependence on weight magnitude but allocates exponential lists and temporary comprehensions.

docs.text:
